title: app.frontend() with fallback="index.html" returns 404 for client side routes that have a dot in the last path segment (like /users/john.doe or /v/1.2.3)
text:
app.frontend() with fallback="index.html" returns 404 for client side routes that have a dot in the last path segment (like /users/john.doe or /v/1.2.3). ### Discussed in
Originally posted by **UditDewan** July 12, 2026 ### First Check - [x] I added a very descriptive title here. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [x] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [x] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic. - [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI. - [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc. ### Commit to Help - [x] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description Hi 👋 I have been trying out the new helper to serve a single page app, using so that client side routes fall back to the shell and the frontend router can take over. This is the behavior described in the "Client side routing" part of the docs, and it works fine for a path like or . The problem shows up when a client side route has a dot in its last path segment. Plenty of real apps have these, for example a profile at , a version deep link at , or a slug like . When I open one of those directly, or just hit refresh while I am already on that page, I get a 404 instead of the shell, so the app never loads and the client router never gets a chance to handle the route. The part that surprised me is that setting explicitly does not change this. As far as I can tell there is currently no way to get these routes to fall back to the shell. I spent some time reading the code and I think it comes from in . It takes the last path segment and if finds an extension it returns early and treats the request as an asset request, before it ever looks at the header. Because returns , any segment with a dot in it is treated as a file and never gets the fallback, even when the browser clearly asked for . What makes me think this is fixable without regressions is that the two situations are easy to tell apart. A real browser navigation sends , while a missing asset requested from a script tag, an image tag, or a fetch call sends or a specific type like . If I request a genuinely missing asset such as with it still returns 404 as expected, so checking the header first would fix the navigation case and keep the asset case working. I did notice there is already a test that pins the current behavior. has a case that expects a 404, so before proposing a change I wanted to ask whether the current behavior is intentional. If the idea is that dotted client routes should be servable, would a change that treats an explicit request as navigation regardless of the path be acceptable? Or would you rather keep the extension heuristic as the default for and add an opt in for apps that use dotted client side routes? I am happy to open a PR with a failing test and the change for whichever direction you prefer. Thanks a lot for the work on this feature. ### Operating System Windows ### Operating System Details Also reproduced on current master. The logic involved is pure routing code, so it is not tied to any particular operating system. ### FastAPI Version 0.139.0 ### Pydantic Version 2.13.4 ### Python Version 3.11 ### Additional Context _No response_

title: Document 415 on the receiving json section
text: Document 415 on the receiving json section. Documentation on "json" request throwing a 415 as well as 400. The problem text is on > Receiving JSON in Views > > Use the [json]( property of the [request]( object to decode the request’s body as JSON. If the body is not valid JSON, or the Content-Type header is not set to application/json, a 400 Bad Request error will be raised I believe you want to indicate that it's a 415 instead of 400 when the Content-Type header doesn't match as it's done on 400 is still valid for when the body isn't json (even though the content-type is json). So maybe something like this ? > Receiving JSON in Views > > Use the [json]( property of the [request]( object to decode the request’s body as JSON. If the body is not valid JSON, a 400 Bad Request error will be raised. If the Content-Type header is not set to application/json, a 415 Unsupported Media Type error will be raised Environment: - Python version: N/A - Flask version: latest doc This is in no way a bug, but it's for being aligned everywhere in your doc :). title: asyncio is not compatible with gevent
text: asyncio is not compatible with gevent. See #5256 async-await: < > Using async with greenlet > When using gevent or eventlet to serve an application or patch the runtime, greenlet>=1.0 is required. When using PyPy, PyPy>=7.3.7 is required. Flask uses asgiref, which is not compatible with gevent: < BTW: ASGI: < > The asgiref [WsgiToAsgi]( adapter is recommended as it integrates with the event loop used for Flask’s [Using async and await]( support. This makes it seem like the event loop integration means a single worker could process multiple requests concurently, which it can't, the worker will block on . --- I'm not the only one that found this the hard way: [Flask, Gunicorn, Gevent and Asyncio Don't Mix](

title: document that leaves query string percent encoded
text: document that leaves query string percent encoded. WHAT IS THE BUG? is documented as *“Requested path as unicode, including the query string.”* However, Werkzeug URL-unquotes only the **path** (before “?”); the **query string** is returned **raw**. Code that searches or whitelists on can therefore be bypassed by percent-encoding a slash inside a parameter. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- HOW TO REPLICATE python from flask import Flask, request app = Flask(__name__) .route("/show_picture") def show_picture(): # naïve traversal filter if "../" in request.full_path: return "Blocked", 400 return f"full_path = {request.full_path}", 200 # run: flask --app poc run # bypass: "../" hidden as "%2F" curl " Result → 200 OK; the filter misses the traversal because ../ appears as ..%2F. ` ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- EXPECTED BEHAVIOR Documentation (and the full_path docstring) should warn clearly: "Only the portion before “?” is URL-unquoted. The query string is returned raw; unquote it manually (e.g. urllib.parse.unquote_plus) before using it for validation or filtering." Without that notice, filters like if "../" in request.full_path: ... if request.full_path.startswith("/admin"): ... can be bypassed with %2F inside the query string. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Python version: 3.12.3 Flask version: 2.3.3 Werkzeug version: 3.1.3 OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Acknowledgements Discovery: Jefferson Gozanels GHomez Proof-of-concept & report: Sebastián Alba Vives

title: Recommend Warning and Safer Defaults for url_for(..., _external=True)
text: Recommend Warning and Safer Defaults for url_for(..., _external=True). Hi Flask team, We recently analyzed several Flask-based applications and noticed a recurring security concern related to url_for(..., _external=True) when used in untrusted request contexts. Specifically, since it uses request.host by default to construct the external URL, applications that do not explicitly configure SERVER_NAME or sanitize headers can be vulnerable to host header injection. To improve developer awareness and reduce misuse, we suggest: Add a warning to the url_for documentation about the risk of relying on request.host, and recommend the use of SERVER_NAME or trusted_hosts when generating external URLs. We’d be happy to help draft the relevant documentation or contribute a pull request if this direction aligns with the maintainers' goals. Best regards, Rui Yang and Zhengyu Liu Johns Hopkins University

title: BUG: metrics.auc returns incorrect areas for decreasing unsigned coordinates and fails monotonicity validation
text: BUG: metrics.auc returns incorrect areas for decreasing unsigned coordinates and fails monotonicity validation. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Introduce yourself Hi, I’m Saurav Singla, a Head of Data Science working on machine learning and model evaluation. While investigating metric correctness with AI assistance, I found that can silently return an incorrect area when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers. The investigation reproduced this behavior in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. Equivalent floating-point inputs produce the expected result. I’m reporting this because decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by the documentation, and unsigned inputs also appear to bypass the monotonicity check. I could not find an existing scikit-learn issue describing this specific behavior. I’ve included a minimal reproducer and environment details below. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact silently computes incorrect areas when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers, although decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by its documentation. For example, with and , the expected area is , but returns without a warning. Converting the same coordinates to , or reversing both arrays, returns . Unsigned inputs also bypass monotonicity validation: returns a numeric result, whereas the equivalent floating-point input raises . I encountered this during a targeted investigation of metric correctness with AI assistance, rather than through a production incident. I care about evaluation results being consistent across equivalent numeric representations. For users passing unsigned coordinate arrays directly to , the behavior can silently corrupt reported areas and allow invalid curves through validation. The behavior was reproduced in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. This report concerns direct calls to ; it does not demonstrate a problem with ordinary usage. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce import numpy as np import sklearn from sklearn.metrics import auc print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__) y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Valid decreasing coordinates: all three results should be 1.0. x = np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.uint8) print("Unsigned:", auc(x, y)) # 255.0 print("Float:", auc(x.astype(np.float64), y)) # 1.0 print("Reversed:", auc(x[::-1], y[::-1])) # 1.0 # Non-monotonic coordinates: both calls should raise ValueError. for dtype in (np.uint8, np.float64): x = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=dtype) try: print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic:", auc(x, y)) except ValueError: print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic: ValueError") ### Expected Results For the valid decreasing coordinates, all three representations should return . Converting the coordinates from unsigned integers to floats, or reversing both arrays, should not change the area. For the non-monotonic coordinates , both unsigned integer and floating-point inputs should raise . Expected output, excluding the version line: ### Actual Results Observed output on scikit-learn 1.9.1: The decreasing unsigned coordinates produce instead of . The non-monotonic unsigned coordinates return instead of raising . Both incorrect unsigned-input results are returned silently, without a warning or exception, so there is no traceback for the reported failures. The for the floating-point control is expected and caught by the reproducer. The same results were also reproduced on scikit-learn 1.7.2 and 1.8.0, using NumPy 2.3.5 and SciPy 1.17.0. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR after maintainers confirm and triage the issue, with AI assistance disclosed. The apparent root cause is that uses to determine direction and validate monotonicity. For unsigned inputs, decreasing differences wrap to positive values, so these checks fail. The subsequent trapezoidal integration also performs subtraction on the unsigned coordinates. A possible fix would: * Determine monotonicity and direction using direct comparisons between adjacent coordinates, avoiding subtraction. * Ensure coordinate differences used for integration are computed safely. * Add regression tests for decreasing and non-monotonic inputs across unsigned integer types, with signed integer and floating-point controls. The dtype strategy needs care: blindly converting to can overflow, while converting to can lose precision for large integers. I would discuss the preferred handling with maintainers before implementing it. I will wait for triage before opening a PR.

title: BUG: MinMaxScaler and MaxAbsScaler partial_fit produce NaN statistics after an all-NaN batch
text: BUG: MinMaxScaler and MaxAbsScaler partial_fit produce NaN statistics after an all-NaN batch. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Introduce yourself Hi, I’m Rugved, an AI Engineer Intern and machine-learning practitioner. I use scikit-learn for preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and practical machine-learning projects. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact While investigating incremental preprocessing with missing values, I found that and can discard valid statistics learned from earlier batches. If a feature contains valid values in one batch but only NaN values in a later batch, the later batch replaces the feature's accumulated statistics with NaN. This affects users processing large or streaming datasets in batches. A batch with no valid observations for a feature should not invalidate statistics already learned for that feature. Currently, subsequent transformations of finite values in that feature also produce NaN. ### Steps to Reproduce ### Expected Results The all-NaN values in the first feature of the second batch should be treated as missing and ignored during the incremental update. Previously learned valid statistics should be preserved. The incremental results should match fitting on the combined dataset. For the example above: Finite input values should not be transformed to NaN merely because a later batch contains no valid observations for that feature. ### Actual Results The second call completes without raising an exception, but it corrupts the statistics for the first feature. Observed output with scikit-learn 1.6.1: The update also emits: No exception is raised, but finite values in the affected feature are transformed to NaN. ### Versions - Python: 3.12.13 - scikit-learn: 1.6.1 - NumPy: 2.0.2 - SciPy: 1.16.3 - Runtime: Linux x86_64 ### Additional Context The documentation for both scalers states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting. A related issue involving the same pattern in is [#35070]( ### Interest in Fixing the Bug Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR if the issue is confirmed and triaged by the maintainers. The apparent root cause is in the incremental aggregation logic. For an all-NaN feature, the per-batch statistic is NaN: - computes and , which return NaN for an all-NaN feature. - computes the maximum absolute value, which also returns NaN for an all-NaN feature. During subsequent calls, these NaN batch statistics are merged with the previously stored statistics using ordinary minimum/maximum operations. Those operations propagate NaN and overwrite valid statistics. A possible fix would be to merge statistics while treating a NaN batch statistic as “no new observation”: - If the previous statistic is valid and the new batch statistic is NaN, preserve the previous value. - If the previous statistic is NaN and the new batch statistic is valid, use the new value. - If both values are NaN, preserve NaN because no valid observation has been seen. I would add regression tests covering both scalers, including comparisons between incremental fitting and fitting on the combined dataset. I would wait for maintainer feedback on the intended behavior and edge cases before opening a PR.

I'm a machine learning developer. I use scikit-learn regularly for building predictive models and data analysis. While researching how tree-based models handle highly separable datasets, I noticed an unexpected drop in accuracy in a specific edge case. I dug into the source code to understand why the model was failing to learn the separation and managed to trace it down to this specific floating-point rounding tie in the binning logic. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact There is a floating-point precision flaw in the HistGradientBoosting binning logic. When the algorithm computes the arithmetic midpoint between two very close, distinct floating-point values, the finite midpoint can round upward to equal the upper data value. Because the threshold comparison is upper-inclusive (<= threshold), both distinct values are incorrectly lumped into the exact same bin. This prevents perfectly separable targets from being learned by the model. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Here is a minimal reproducer where 20 zeros and 20 ones are perfectly separable, but the model completely fails to distinguish them and predicts 0.5 for everything due to the midpoint rounding tie: ### Expected Results The distinct values should be separated into different bins, allowing the tree to split them and predict [0, 1] accurately. ### Actual Results The midpoint rounds to the upper value, placing both sets of data into bin 0. The model predicts 0.5 for all samples. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I am interested in fixing this. Root cause and strategy: The root cause is that the arithmetic midpoint of two adjacent distinct floats can round upward to precisely equal the upper float. Because the threshold split uses <=, both values are assigned to the same bin. The strategy for the fix is to detect when the computed finite midpoint equals the upper bound and in that specific case, replace the threshold with the lower bound. This mathematically guarantees the values are separated. I already have a C-level patch and a suite of 84 regression tests prepared locally that successfully implements this strategy. I will wait for this issue to be triaged, but I am ready to open a PR for this as soon as the team approves. Disclosure: An AI assistant helped me isolate the binary64 rounding mechanism that causes this failure. I have manually verified the math and the failure.

title: META: lock contention can make thread-parallel code collapse on many-core machines (free-threading)
text: META: lock contention can make thread-parallel code collapse on many-core machines (free-threading). On free-threaded Python, a lock that many threads take at the same time can make thread-parallel code collapse on a machine with hundreds of cores, while the same code looks fine on a laptop. I hit this with random forests. I'm opening this issue to share what I found, discuss how to avoid it in scikit-learn, and track the related work. #### How I got here As you might know, I'm benchmarking scikit-learn on several machines, one of them is a 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P (344 hardware threads). On this machine, random forests fitted with 344 threads (what you get with ) were often slower on free-threaded 3.14 than with the GIL (median 0.45x over 31 representative benchmark cases). For instance, the reproducer below takes ~3s with the GIL and ~12s free-threaded. With gdb, I first found most threads parked on CPython's specialization lock (python/cpython#152075, fixed on CPython ). Then I saw the same collapse on other locks, taken once per tree: - the lookups of function-level imports and the behind , both from narwhals' dataframe checks in ; - the module lock, taken by the per-task warning filters handling of . The slowdown always appeared suddenly past a few tens of threads. This comes from CPython's locks (python/cpython#158901): once a thread has waited more than 1 ms, each lock acquisition costs a thread wake-up, so the waits get longer and the lock never gets back to the fast path. On a 14 or 16-core laptop this threshold is barely reached, so nothing shows. #### Reproducer Fit time on the 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P, 3 runs, one fresh process per run: | | GIL (3.14.7) | free-threaded (3.14.7t) | | --- | --- | --- | | (6ad9bb9ed6) | 2.2 to 3.3 s | 12.3 to 13.0 s | | cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 | 1.7 to 1.9 s | 0.70 to 0.74 s | #### What fixed it for forests cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 makes the reproducer 17x faster free-threaded: - Trees are fitted with a thread pool that starts its threads lazily, one per task ( , through the of #34914). The threads start a bit apart, so they rarely take the same lock at the same time. joblib's threading backend starts all its workers before dispatching, so they run the same code in lockstep. With the GIL it's the opposite: starting the workers first is faster, so the thread pool does that only when the GIL is enabled. - Trees don't validate again the inputs already validated by the forest ( no longer calls per tree). - no longer resets the warning filters in each task (now in its own issue and PR: #35089, #35090). This also fixes a race on GIL Python with threads: the user's warning filters could be silently lost, and spurious " should be used with " warnings raised. #### What to watch for Code that runs in many threads at the same time should avoid process-wide locks in each task. The ones I found: - and changes of the warning filters; - 'd functions (cache hits included), including stdlib ones like ; - statements inside functions; - checks against an ABC, true or false, including ( ): the ABC's caches are sets shared by all threads, and each lookup takes the set's lock. So every call from every thread goes through one ; - input validation ( and its narwhals checks): validate once, before the parallel loop. Benchmarks on 16 cores can hide a 10x to 100x collapse. Close to the threshold, timings are also bimodal (4.8 to 9.6 s for the same fit at 344 threads), so repeats are needed. Note for benchmarks: measure warm fits too (several fits in one process), not only fresh processes. On free-threaded Python, the specialization contention is paid by the first fit only: on , the reproducer's first fit takes 10 to 12 s, the next ones ~4 s. Thread-based parallelism in scikit-learn today: forests ( , , , ), , queries, , SGD one-vs-all, coordinate descent paths, HGB binning, and free-threaded. #### Tracking Upstream: - [ ] specialization contention: python/cpython#152075 (fixed on CPython , backported to 3.14 in python/cpython#158904, 3.15 backport in python/cpython#158905) - [ ] fair handoff makes contention collapse: python/cpython#158901 - [ ] joblib's threading backend overhead: joblib/joblib#1830 - [ ] narwhals' dataframe checks contend (mostly ): not reported yet, depends on python/cpython#158901 - [ ] contends on the ABC cache of : not reported yet. Seen with gdb on with (all but one thread waiting in from ), once the lock contention was removed. A fast path in for exact types (scipy) or lock-free ABC cache lookups (CPython) would avoid it - [x] doesn't join its threads: already reported in python/cpython#107616, no performance impact seen scikit-learn: - Forests (cakedev0/scikit-learn#19): - [ ] lazy thread pool: should be less needed once python/cpython#152075 is in. With as a stand-in for that fix, joblib was still 1.5x to 4x slower on 344 threads with fast-to-build trees (0.1 to 1 s each). The gap shrinks for slow-to-build trees (~1.1x for year_prediction_msd). - [ ] no per-tree validation (works around the narwhals contention, and saves a per tree) - [ ] Warning filters race/lock in (bug on ): #35089, fixed by #35090 - [ ] Audit the other thread-parallel code paths on a many-core machine (list above) - [ ] Write down what to watch for, for contributors (see #34596) #### Related issues - #30007 - #20666

title: BUG: thread-based can corrupt the process-wide warning filters
text: BUG: thread-based can corrupt the process-wide warning filters. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact On Python without context-aware warnings (every GIL build, and free-threaded 3.13), with a thread-based backend can corrupt the process-wide warning filters. The user's own filters can be silently lost, and spurious " should be used with " warnings are raised. To propagate the caller's warning filters to joblib workers (#30380), every task runs: Without context-aware warnings, is one list shared by the whole process, and isn't thread-safe (the Python docs say so). With threads, tasks enter and exit these blocks out of order: 1. Thread 1 enters: it saves the user's list (L0), the global becomes a copy (L1), and it starts emptying and refilling L1. 2. Thread 2 enters while L1 is half-refilled: it saves L1, the global becomes L2. 3. Thread 1 exits and restores L0. 4. Thread 2 exits and restores L1: the half-reset copy. A task's can also run while the global list is the very list captured by (after another thread restored it), and empty it: the next tasks then see no filters and raise the warning above. It needs a thread switch at the wrong moment, so it's rare with the default switch interval (5 ms) and a few threads. It's more frequent with many threads, with calls inside the tasks ( and do that), and when tests run in several threads at once: I think this is the intermittent failure of #32631 on free-threaded 3.13, xfailed in #33320. On free-threaded 3.14 (context-aware warnings) there is no race, but the same code takes the module lock in every task, which makes many threads queue on it. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ### Expected Results and no warning. ### Actual Results On every run (3 runs, GIL 3.14.7, 344-thread machine): and 88 to 172 spurious warnings per run: On a 14-core laptop (GIL 3.14.6) it happens as well, for instance with hundreds of warnings. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug I have a fix, I'll open a PR.

title: BUG: StandardScaler.partial_fit replaces an existing variance with NaN when a new dense batch has an all-NaN feature
text: BUG: StandardScaler.partial_fit replaces an existing variance with NaN when a new dense batch has an all-NaN feature. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Introduce yourself I'm exploring numerical reliability in scientific Python through AI-assisted investigation and testing. This issue came from checking how StandardScaler.partial_fit handles batches with missing observations and comparing incremental results with batch fitting. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact After StandardScaler learns valid statistics for a feature, a subsequent dense batch containing only NaNs in that feature changes its var_ and scale_ to NaN, while its mean_ and sample count remain correct. In the recorded checks, this also causes finite values in that feature to be transformed to NaN. The StandardScaler documentation states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting. The example below supplies no new valid observations for the first feature. Documentation: Related work: PR #16466 included preserving sparse incremental statistics when a new batch contributes zero valid observations, including all-NaN second-batch tests. This report concerns the dense-array counterpart. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ### Expected Results The final assertion should pass. After processing B, the first feature should retain its mean of 2, variance of 1, scale of 1, and sample count of 2, because B contains no new non-missing observations for that feature. The second feature should have a mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4. ### Actual Results The final assertion fails because the variance of the first feature becomes NaN. After processing B, the first feature has a mean of 2, variance of NaN, scale of NaN, and sample count of 2. The mean and sample count remain correct, but the previously valid variance and scale are lost. The second feature has the expected mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4. The update also emits RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in divide. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I would be interested in working on a fix after maintainer triage, with AI assistance. My investigation points to the dense incremental variance update when a feature receives zero new non-missing observations. A possible strategy is to preserve the existing statistics for that feature when it already has valid observations, while updating the other features normally. I have tested a limited local prototype for this case. It is not yet a general fix and does not address features that have no valid observations in the initial batch. I would start with a regression test for the example above and discuss the intended scope with the maintainers before opening a PR.

title: ENH Ridge: support for array API inputs
text: ENH Ridge: support for array API inputs. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. Credit to for the idea. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable With array API dispatch, only supports , and resolves to with a warning (#27800 started with SVD only). The SVD is much more expensive than the Cholesky path used for NumPy inputs, so on GPU is often slower than on CPU with NumPy, and sometimes much slower. I'd like (and so ) to work with array API inputs, and be fast on GPU. ### Describe your proposed solution Split the Cholesky solver in two: compute the Gram matrix on the device ( , or in the dual case when ), move it to the host, and solve it with the existing NumPy/SciPy code. Then move the coefficients back to the device: Let's call this policy A. The system to solve is only (or ), so the host solve and the transfers are cheap compared to the Gram matrix. And the solve behaves exactly like for NumPy inputs, whatever the namespace: same SPD solver, same handling for singular systems. could then resolve to for array API inputs, like for NumPy inputs, and the warning would go away. I prototyped it by swapping during ( , , one target, standard normal data, best of 3 after a warmup, torch 2.13). Coefficients match the NumPy Cholesky solver to ~1e-6 in float32 and ~1e-14 in float64. Fit times in seconds, policy B is the fully on-device alternative described below: NVIDIA L4, NumPy on 8 vCPUs (AMD EPYC 7R13): | shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.13 | 0.091 | 0.011 | 0.011 | | 500,000 x 100 | float64 | 0.20 | 0.45 | 0.059 | 0.059 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.27 | 0.21 | 0.024 | 0.018 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.44 | 2.3 | 0.29 | 0.28 | | 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.9 | not run | 0.15 | 0.15 | | 463,810 x 990 | float64 | 3.6 | not run | 2.5 | 2.5 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.52 | 1.5 | 0.12 | 0.044 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.93 | 13 | 0.80 | 0.69 | | 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 3.1 | not run | 0.66 | 0.27 | Intel Arc B390 iGPU (Panther Lake), NumPy on the 16 cores of the Core Ultra X7 358H: | shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.12 | 0.49 | 0.021 | 0.021 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.14 | 1.1 | 0.037 | 0.036 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.35 | 2.0 | 0.27 | 0.27 | | 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.1 | not run | 0.30 | 0.30 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.27 | 10 | 0.11 | 0.075 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.66 | 17 | 0.79 | 0.71 | | 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 2.5 | not run | 0.85 | 0.74 | Policy A is 7x to 90x faster than the current SVD, and in float32 2.5x to 13x faster than NumPy on CPU. In float64, with ~1000 features or more, it is only 0.8x to 1.5x the speed of NumPy: both GPUs have a low float64 throughput (~450 GFLOP/s measured on the Arc B390), and the Gram matrix is a float64 matmul. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant Policy B: solve on the device with , which is in the array API extension. It is faster than policy A only when the system to solve is large, in practice in the dual case: up to 2.7x in float32 on the L4. Elsewhere both are within noise, because the Gram matrix dominates. But each namespace handles the solve its own way, and checking them all is hard. For instance, on a singular system raises a , while returns NaNs by default. Some namespaces may also not implement the extension. Policy A avoids all of this by reusing the code path we already test with NumPy. ### Additional context #34793 (centering trick for the Cholesky solver) would help here too: it avoids the centered copy of , which halves the device memory needed by . I'd go with policy A. We could switch the solve to the device later for large systems if it turns out to matter.

title: ARDRegression.scores_ combines updated precisions with the previous posterior
text: ARDRegression.scores_ combines updated precisions with the previous posterior. ### Introduce yourself Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact With , computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates and , then calculates using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation. If is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state. There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately and . No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference. ### Expected Results The final entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted and . For this reproducer, that value is approximately . Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration. ### Actual Results With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints: The first value is ; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately . ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. I would be interested in working on a PR after the issue is triaged. The likely cause of the no-pruning discrepancy is that the score uses updated precisions with a posterior covariance and residual sum of squares computed before the update. I would make the score use a consistent parameter state and add a regression test for the reproducer. That's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via ). Within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public is ( ), which is safe only because it rejects NaNs upfront. So this mostly affects third-party code using (which the docstring discourages: "Don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing"). More broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). Possible ways forward: 1. **Compute the mask even when ** on the public (when none is provided). It's one pass over , cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct. 2. **Document** that missing values aren't supported with . Cheap, but leaves a silent trap. 3. **Deprecate in the public ** of trees, and switch gradient boosting to (like forests). With 1. applied during the deprecation cycle. text: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis. ### Introduce yourself _No response_ ### Describe the issue linked to the documentation The [ API reference]( documents both and as arrays with shape . Both arrays actually have shape , where is the number of original input features, . Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape . ### User-facing impact The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation. This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested. ### Minimal reproducer ### Observed shapes The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features. ### Verification scope Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7. The affected documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report. title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
text:
BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - , , , go through , which centers and (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed , shifting by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - , , , (the + /lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw . There is no -equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - builds its Hessian from the raw design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong / for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
### Expected Results Fitting on should not change (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio ( , unit-variance ) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of against the ratio=0 reference, for both and , with marking points where a warning was raised:

title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1
text: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1. ### Introduce yourself I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and permutation importance to understand which features matter. That is background context: this bug was found through an agent-led source-code investigation using Claude Code, rather than encountered during that analysis. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact **What:** When is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used. **My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With , both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions ( ) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution. **Cause** (I read ): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias. **Impact on users (corrected 2026-10-26):** exists to save time on large datasets. The full-data baseline and shared-subsample permuted scores differ by a constant offset, , applied to every feature. This can change the sign of near-zero importances, making unused features appear useful or harmful, but this offset does not change feature ranking. The reported standard deviation is conditional on the single subsample and does not account for subsampling variability. **AI usage disclosure (clarified 2026-10-26):** This report came from a broader agent-led bug search across repositories using Claude Code. The agent inspected source code, generated and ran the reproducer, and helped prepare the report. Before posting, I personally reran the reproducer on my computer and checked the results against the relevant code. I nevertheless missed the incorrect ranking claim, which is corrected above. My use of permutation importance is genuine background context, not how this bug was found. Codex helped prepare these corrections from my factual clarifications. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ### Expected Results For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with . ### Actual Results ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I'd be willing to fix this. Idea: draw a fresh subsample for every repetition, and compute both the baseline and the shuffled scores on the same subsampled rows before subtracting. Add a regression test asserting that features the model does not use have exactly 0 importance when .

title: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)
text: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported). > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable Hello, I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those. Currently: This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in ( ): A second guard in (same file) does the same at predict time. Both guards live on , shared by all four tree classes; / call the same method rather than duplicating it. / don't set and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites. ### Describe your proposed solution The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too). check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.

title: Add support for NumPy
text: Add support for NumPy. ### Goal Support NumPy inputs where scikit-learn already accepts string labels or categories, while keeping numeric-only validation strict. A minimal example is: On NumPy 2.2.4, this fails because rejects . This particular example passes on NumPy 2.5.3, so the failures depend on the NumPy version. ### Compatibility gaps found during investigation - **Type detection:** older NumPy versions can raise before downstream operations are reached. - **Numeric validation:** should reject StringDType strings, including numeric-looking strings. Explicitly requested numeric conversion is a separate case. - **Unique-value caching:** attaching dtype metadata is unsupported for StringDType. Correctness should not depend on that optimization. - **Encoding and missing values:** mixed StringDType/Unicode inputs and missing sentinels need focused coverage for lookup, unique values and counts. These are separate problems; fixing type detection alone does not resolve them all. ### Proposed next steps Following the developer-meeting feedback below, start by extending existing tests, using for reproduced failures and skipping StringDType cases on NumPy < 2.0. Then address the failures in small, separate PRs. The first tests-only PR is #35094. It extends two existing tests: classification-target detection and numeric-only string rejection. It is a first step, not complete compatibility coverage. Some downstream failures are masked by type detection on older NumPy, but other tests can already exercise them independently or on newer NumPy. The broader implementation in closed PR #35082 remains a reference. Performance/caching redesign would need a separate discussion. Related: #34383, which proposes using StringDType internally in encoders.

title: Add Population Stability Index (PSI) as a model/data drift metric
text: Add Population Stability Index (PSI) as a model/data drift metric. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable I want to detect when a feature's or a model score's distribution has shifted between two datasets (e.g. training vs. a more recent production sample). Using Population Stability Index - sum((new_pct - base_pct) * log(new_pct / base_pct)) over aligned bins/categories is a standard for doing so. This is one of the most common "has my model gone stale" checks in production ML monitoring, sitting next to sklearn.metrics conceptually (it's a distance/divergence metric between two empirical distributions, similar in spirit to things like scipy.stats.entropy/KL divergence that sklearn already depends on via scipy). ### Describe your proposed solution sklearn.metrics.population_stability_index(base, new, bins=10) for continuous input (auto-binning via quantiles of base) and direct category alignment for categorical/discrete input, returning the scalar PSI (and optionally a per-bin breakdown table). possibly also some rolling_psi method for evaluating the PSI over different time periods. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant Checked scikit-learn's and statsmodels' issue trackers directly for prior discussion of PSI - found none in either (no open request, nothing closed as wontfix). Purpose-built alternatives exist as separate packages, but nothing really maintained, while PSI is old and widely used operationally. ### Additional context Population Stability Index has been standard practice in credit scoring model monitoring since well before modern ML tooling (commonly attributed to the SAS/banking scorecard literature from the 1990s-2000s); today it's also used more broadly for feature/data drift detection outside credit scoring specifically.

title: Add Information Value (IV) / Weight-of-Evidence binning as metric and feature-selection
text: Add Information Value (IV) / Weight-of-Evidence binning as metric and feature-selection. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable Rank a feature's predictive strength against a binary target by binning it (equal-frequency or optimized) and computing Information Value: over bins. This is a standard univariate feature-screening step in binary classification, conceptually adjacent to things sklearn already ships in ( , , chi2) as a way to rank/filter features before modeling. Notably this metric does not depends on imbalance. ### Describe your proposed solution 'sklearn.metric.IV(X,y, bins=10) would be useful for establishing Information value. Then 'sklearn.feature_selection.information_value(X, y, bins=10)' returning per-feature IV, using equal-frequency quantile binning by default (fast, matches the common textbook definition). ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant Checked scikit-learn's issue tracker for "Information Value" and "Weight of Evidence" - found nothing (no open request, no closed-as-declined). The realistic existing option is , a purpose-built, actively maintained package that solves actual bin optimization (via a CP/MIP solver) rather than plain quantile cuts. IV/WOE binning is old and widely used, but specifically within credit-scoring-style binary classification rather than general ML - similar concern to the adjacent PSI request I'm also filing. Raising it mainly to get a maintainer judgment on record, since I couldn't find this discussed anywhere in scikit-learn's history. ### Additional context already covers "how predictive is this feature" in a distribution-agnostic way; IV specifically gives interpretable, additive-across-bins output that credit-risk practitioners rely on for regulatory model documentation, which is the main reason it persists as a distinct metric rather than being subsumed by mutual information in that field.

title: [BUG] RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None) returns incorrect best_score_ for binary classification
text: [BUG] RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None) returns incorrect best_score_ for binary classification. ### Introduce yourself hello, I am a professor of computer science and a core developer at [aeon ]( We use RidgeClassifierCV as a classifier head for many of our transformation based pipelines and ensembles, particularly the convolution based ones, and this bug was found by our core dev Matthew ( ) when reviewing [this PR] ( that adapted one of these pipeline classifiers, the Arsenal, which is a component of our HIVE-COTEv2 classifier and is one of my finest moments in algorithm naming :) ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact computes an incorrect best_score_ for binary classification problems: it always returns accuracy of 1.0, even when the problem contains substantial label noise and the fitted classifier is clearly not perfect. We use best_score_ as an estimate of each ensemble member's classification accuracy and use it as an ensemble weight. For multiclass problems this appears to work as expected. For binary problems, however, all ensemble members receive a weight of 1.0, effectively disabling the weighting mechanism. The behaviour appears specific to the default cv=None path. title: balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter
text: balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Introduce yourself I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric. This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not. Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together. This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ## Expected Results A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. A score documented as bounded should not return -inf. ## Actual Results On scikit-learn 1.9.0 (installed from PyPI), case 1 returns nan: Case 2 returns -inf: Both RuntimeWarnings come from the same unguarded statement at line 2946. The texts differ — "invalid value" for case 1, "divide by zero" for case 2 — which maps onto the nan/-inf split: case 1 is 0/0, case 2 is -0.333/0. Also reproduces unchanged on main (1.10.dev0), where the filter is at line 2969 and the division at line 2975. ### Expected Results A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. title: [BUG] coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels
text: [BUG] coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels. ### Introduce yourself hi, I am a core developer for the aeon toolkit and an academic at the university of Southampton. I found this bug when trying to raise our upper bound for scikit For context, we have a range of algorithms that use scikit components, in this case the and . We also maintain a range of data archives including the UCR archive, hosted here Our classification data always loads class values as strings, so for example, "1"/"2" or "Run"/"Jump". The basic problem is that relevant parts of scikit 1.9 now always parse class value strings to integers, leading to dictionary errors. I had a good look and couldnt see this issue, sorry if its been fixed already. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In 1.9, fitting a forest ensemble with raises when the class labels are strings that happen to parse as integers ("1", "2", ...). The same code works in 1.8 and earlier. Labels that are genuine integers, or strings that do not parse as integers ("a", "b"), are unaffected. The problem comes from a coercion added to the user-defined-dictionary branch of compute_class_weight in #32644 (commit 9ca766b, "FEA Add array API support for LogisticRegression with LBFGS"): The intent looks like normalising array scalars to Python scalars so that dict lookup by key works under a non-numpy namespace. But int("1") succeeds, so it never reaches the except clause that would have preserved the string. That branch is reached even though the user asked for "balanced", because does not pass "balanced" straight through. It round-trips (sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py:861): It first expands "balanced" into an explicit dict keyed by the original labels — {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, string keys — and then feeds that dict back in. The second call goes through the dictionary branch, the keys are coerced to int, every lookup fails, and all classes are reported as unweighted. Estimators that pass "balanced" directly to take the dedicated branch, which uses a LabelEncoder and never coerces, so they are not affected. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ` Or against compute_class_weight directly, without the forest: ### Expected Results Expected Results Fits without error, as in 1.8.0 and earlier. The direct compute_class_weight call returns array([1., 1.]). ### Actual Results The message is also misleading: it reports the classes as [1, 2] (post-coercion integers) when the real classes are the strings ["1", "2"], which are the dict keys. A mixed example shows the failure is per-label and driven purely by whether int() succeeds — with classes ["0", "a"] only "0" is reported: This effects both ExtraTreesClassifier and RandomForestClassifier ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug yes I would be happy to, I would not convert strings to ints at all, leave them as string and would not use a try ... except block in this context and avoid the round trip, but would need to look more closely, claude suggests this fix (and has helped me pin this down) A narrower guard such as if not isinstance(c, str) around the existing int() call also fixes it, which is probably what I would do, but I obviously dont have the wider picture.

text: Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case). While looking at [builds comparison results]( from my benchmarks ( I noticed was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels. Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown: 1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): in meson doesn't survive an environment that also sets (which conda-forge's compiler activation does). 2. **Version of ** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's defines the macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal / functions instead of . GCC can't recognize or inline those, so 's calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building ( , ) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is -specific (confirmed: , which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned. This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop / call is plausibly exposed the same way. ~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: ### Proposed fix Replace / in and (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test . Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever. ### Root cause, in detail *(pure LLM write-up)* <details> ( , ) and call on data, via . This runs once per sample per feature scan during ; never during . The feedstock's CI pin file ( at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets , . That sysroot's has: Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier is gone from the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic) gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines as directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions ( / ). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning* at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers. Confirmed end to end: - -profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages ( , ): conda-forge spends 12.6% of samples in alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all. - Disassembled both real files directly: conda-forge's has ; PyPI's has no call at all. - Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own section) reproduced nothing *until* was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte. - Same call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on current (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — compiles to the identical byte size on both). </details> ### Everything else that was tried and ruled out Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge / toolchain: <details> - vs in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above) - vs no override - GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact patch build (pinning / / precisely, since has its own build-number sequence independent of the wrapper) - Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up 3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect) - Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current - Editable install vs literal wheel build (matching exactly) - (the extra flag conda-forge adds under ) - joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs </details> ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

text: BIC-based model selection in plot_gmm_selection.py silently picks the wrong model under anisotropy severe enough to break its own initialization. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ## Describe the issue linked to the documentation demonstrates using + BIC to select and for a . It works well on the example's data because the two components are already well separated relative to their own spread, so 's default k-means-style initialization lands close to the true partition and EM refines it correctly. As in [#34842]( that init dependency is invisible in the example and doesn't generalize. If the true clusters are anisotropic enough that Euclidean-distance-based initialization is already unreliable, BIC does not fail loudly -- it fails silently, by scoring every candidate in the grid on a bad fit and confidently reporting the best of a bad set. A reader walks away with "BIC picked , full covariance, done" with no signal that a different initialization would have picked a different, better-scoring model entirely. Concretely, on two anisotropic "parallel cigars" clusters ( + a linear , same construction as [#34842]( ratio 4x rather than 80x), the grid search over and with default initialization selects a 3-component model, when the true generative model has 2 components. The 2-component model is available in the same search space -- it's just never found, because every restart of k-means++ on this data lands in roughly the same wrong place. ## Suggest a potential alternative/fix Add a new section to , after the existing example, showing: 1. The same "parallel cigars" dataset as [#34842]( where default (raw) k-means-style initialization for gives a partition bad enough that BIC-based model selection lands on the wrong . 2. A whitened-init variant: use + only to get an initial cluster assignment, derive / from that assignment on the raw data, then fit and score every model (whitened-init or not) by BIC on the raw data. This keeps the BIC comparison valid while showing that whitening the initialization -- not the model itself -- restores the correct selection. Draft implementation, for review before opening a PR: (this is a fork-internal PR against my own fork, not yet a real PR against -- opening one once there's agreement this is worth doing, per the guidance on [#34842](

text: GaussianMixture is not a universal fix for anisotropy — plot_kmeans_assumptions.py doesn't show the case where whitening is needed too. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. shows failing on anisotropic blobs and proposes as the fix, since it fits a full covariance per component instead of assuming spherical clusters. That's correct for the anisotropy shown in the example, but not universally: is still initialized from a k-means-style partition of the raw data, and EM only ever *refines* that partition rather than searching from scratch. If the anisotropy is severe enough, the initial partition can already be too wrong for EM to recover from, even with unconstrained covariances. **What a reader might do without knowing this:** someone hits poor results on their own anisotropic data, finds this example, and takes away the rule "if k-means struggles with anisotropy, switch to ." They swap it in, returns *some* clustering with no error or warning, and they ship it — never realizing the result can be arbitrarily wrong, because their anisotropy happened to be severe enough to also break the initialization this fix silently depends on. Nothing in the current example signals that this failure mode exists, so there's no reason for them to suspect it. I'd like to propose adding: a more severely anisotropic dataset (built the same way as the file's existing — + a linear , just more extreme) where fails (ARI ≈ 0), and where whitening first with fixes it (ARI ≈ 0.9+) — no custom clustering code needed, just a change of input to the same call. (Caveat: this degrades in high dimension too — same construction at d=30, ARI drops back to ≈0.) Draft implementation, kept up to date: jovo/scikit-learn#1 (opened against my own fork so it stays open and reviewable rather than getting auto-closed like a direct PR here would while this issue is pending triage — happy to open a PR against this repo once there's agreement this is worth doing).

text: StratifiedGroupKFold returns an empty fold when n_groups == n_splits: least-populated-fold tiebreak is defeated by 1-ULP noise. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Describe the bug can return an empty test fold even when , because the "least populated fold" tiebreak in is defeated by 1-ULP floating-point noise. selects a fold with: The first branch uses an exact . When two candidate folds are *mathematically* tied, still returns values that differ by an ULP or two, so fires and that fold wins outright — the comparison never runs. That comparison is the "heuristic for assigning group to the least populated fold in cases when all other criteria are equal" documented in the changelist comment at the top of , and in practice it is largely unreachable. When there is no slack: a single misdirected group leaves a fold with nothing in it. This is distinct from #33085, which was about and was addressed by #33176 (that PR was titled "Towards #33085" and the issue remains open). **Impact.** silently produces for the empty fold, so the aggregate score becomes : ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ### Expected Results Four non-empty test folds. With 4 groups and 4 splits the assignment is forced to one group per fold. ### Actual Results does not help: all 24 relabellings of the four groups, and all of with , still produce an empty fold. ### Mechanism Instrumenting the assignment loop, the second group is the decisive one: Three folds are empty, fold 3 already holds a group, and all four evaluations are mathematically identical. Fold 3 wins on a 1-ULP artefact, and fold 2 is never filled. Measured over 15898 group-assignment decisions from randomised configurations: - 7.0% of decisions have two or more mathematically tied folds whose winner is decided by floating-point noise (median deciding difference **1 ULP**, max 3). - In 6.9% of all decisions the intended least-populated-fold tiebreak would have selected a *different* fold than the one actually chosen. ### Additional counterexamples Found by random search; all reproduce identically on 1.9.0 and 1.10.dev0. | | | | fold sizes | |---|---|---|---| | 4 | 4 | 22 | | | 6 | 6 | 24 | | | 4 | 4 | 20 | | | 5 | 5 | 13 | | Every failing case I found is at ; with one spare group I found none in ~25k configurations either way. ### Suggested fix Require a strictly-better evaluation to be better by more than noise, so the tiebreak becomes reachable: With that change the reproducer yields , and in a sweep of the sensitive regime ( 2-6, 2-4, ) empty folds go from **4/73401 to 0/73401**. is unchanged at 642 passed / 238 skipped. Two caveats worth discussing: 1. **It changes roughly 21% of splits.** That is the size of the latent defect rather than an over-aggressive tolerance: tightening to or gives the same 21%, because these are true ties; exact equality drops churn to 0.3% but does not fix the bug. 2. **Stratification quality is essentially unchanged** — mean fold-size CV 0.2393 both ways, mean per-fold class-proportion deviation 0.10618 vs 0.10620 over 4000 configurations. This is a correctness fix for the degenerate case, not an improvement to stratification (cf. #24656). ### Versions

text: OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category. ### Introduce yourself I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one encoder with , and . On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to: Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below . Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning: The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block. This matters because drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category ( in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature. I caught this by inspecting , transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with . The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent category that can absorb it. ### Expected Results The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding assigns to the dropped category. Something along the lines of: This is also what the docstring already documents: > If the category does not exist, then and > will handle an unknown category as with > . ### Actual Results No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its entry is , no column exists in , and the transformed row is across the whole column-0 block. Also reproduced on main (1.10.dev0) at a456b324bc, with identical output. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I would be interested in opening a PR if this is triaged as a bug. title: ENH: DataFrame.merge raises bare KeyError without saying which DataFrame is missing the key column
text: ENH: DataFrame.merge raises bare KeyError without saying which DataFrame is missing the key column. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description When a key column passed to (or / ) is missing from one of the DataFrames, raises a bare KeyError containing only the column name. It doesn't say which DataFrame (left or right) is missing the column, or which columns are available. import pandas as pd orders = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "amount": [10, 20, 30]}) customers = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["A", "B", "C"]}) orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id") Actual: KeyError: 'customer_id' The traceback ends in pandas/core/generic.py (_get_label_or_level_values), reached via _get_merge_keys in pandas/core/reshape/merge.py. I saw the same bare KeyError on pandas 2.3.3 and 3.0.2, with on="id" (missing on the left), on="zzz" (missing on both), and with typos in left_on / right_on. With on=, the column must exist in both frames, so the user has to inspect both DataFrames to find the cause. ### Feature Description Raise a more informative error, for example: KeyError: "'customer_id' not found in right DataFrame. Available columns: ['id', 'name']" Other merge errors already name the dtypes on both sides ("You are trying to merge on int64 and str columns for key 'k'"), so this would be consistent. One possible place is where _get_merge_keys calls _get_label_or_level_values: catch the KeyError and re-raise it with the side and available columns. ### Alternative Solutions Users can print left.columns and right.columns before merging, but the error message itself should say where the key is missing. ### Additional Context The existing test in pandas/tests/reshape/merge/test_join.py expects the bare KeyError (match="^'E'$" for join(on="E")), so it would need updating together with the message. Related: #65553 (closed) asked for a more descriptive KeyError for df["Age"] and was closed as fine as-is. This request is specifically about merge, where there are two DataFrames. With df["Age"] it's obvious which object lacks the column, but with merge(on="customer_id") the bare KeyError can't tell the user whether the left or the right frame is missing it. If maintainers feel the same reasoning applies here, I understand and am happy for this to be closed. Installed versions: python : 3.12.12 OS : Linux pandas : 2.3.3 numpy : 2.3.5
