text: BUG: DataFrame.to_string(max_cols=0) exceeds terminal width with uneven columns. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description When using , pandas sometimes prints more columns than can fit in the terminal, especially when some columns are much wider than others. I looked into and noticed that it calculates how many columns to remove by subtracting widths from the middle of the DataFrame. The problem is that the final output keeps columns from both the left and right sides. So the columns used in the width calculation aren't always the same ones that end up being displayed. Because of this, a wide column can stay in the output even though its width was already removed from the calculation. ### Actual result Running the example with the original formatting algorithm gives: ### Expected Behavior When using , pandas sometimes prints more columns than can fit in the terminal, especially when some columns are much wider than others. I looked into and noticed that it calculates how many columns to remove by subtracting widths from the middle of the DataFrame. The problem is that the final output keeps columns from both the left and right sides. So the columns used in the width calculation aren't always the same ones that end up being displayed. Because of this, a wide column can stay in the output even though its width was already removed from the calculation. ### Actual result Running the example with the original formatting algorithm gives: Even though the requested terminal width is 20 characters, the result is 57 characters wide. Possible fix I've been working on a fix for this in my fork: [ Instead of subtracting widths from the middle, the change calculates the width of the columns that will actually be shown. It also accounts for the ... separator and keeps removing pairs of columns until the output fits. The already-formatted columns are reused, so there's no need to format the whole DataFrame again. Testing The change was checked in an isolated compatibility setup using pandas 2.2.3. Results: - 51/51 regression cases passed with the proposed implementation. - The original upstream algorithm passed 43/51 of those cases. - Another 400 deterministic randomized cases showed no mismatches. - Basic performance smoke tests were also exercised. The tests included different column widths, Unicode, MultiIndex, custom formatters, missing values, row truncation, and large DataFrames. Related issues This is related to #32461 and #64972. The earlier fix accounted for the width of the ... separator. The issue here is a little different: the algorithm can calculate widths for columns that aren't the ones kept in the final output. text: BUG: pandas 3.1.0 fails to build on s390x — 'load_unaligned' is not a member of 'xsimd' in the scalar fallback TU. ### Problem description Building the pandas 3.1.0 sdist on **s390x** fails to compile , the non-SIMD fallback TU: 3.0.6 and earlier build fine ( does not exist there). s390x has no pandas wheel on PyPI, so every install there builds the sdist, which makes this a hard packaging break rather than a performance question. ### Mechanism correctly routes s390x to , but still includes and instantiates , so the xsimd-dependent header is compiled on every architecture. xsimd 14.2.0 (the pinned version) *does* have an IBM Z backend, but it is gated on , which needs . is only defined with , which pandas never passes, so: | flags | | | | in the TU | |---|---|---|---|---| | pandas' own | undefined | | **defined** | **0** | | | | | absent | 183 | With defined, takes its stub branch and never includes (line 40), so those three functions are never declared. That missing-declarations gap is xtensor-stack/xsimd#954, open since 2023. ### What I verified All on real s390x hardware (z14, g++ 14.3.1, Python 3.12), compiling the one failing TU with the exact flags above so the compiler flag is the only variable: | variant | rc | xsimd errors | object | |---|---|---|---| | baseline (pandas' own flags) | 1 | **14** | none | | | **0** | **0** | **built** | | | 1 | 14 | none | Full sdist, same machine: baseline fails with the error above and produces no wheel; produces , and the resulting SIMD path is numerically correct ( tail = 99499.5, tail = 83416.66666666667). ### Note on the existing workaround In #64884 the suggestion for this situation was to compile with . That does not help here: it is a GCC 15+ option, and GCC 14.3.1 reports , accepting it silently as a no-op. It would also only suppress *warnings*; these are hard s from undeclared functions, so there is nothing to downgrade. (Reported after hit the same wall on Alpine s390x in #64884 -- this is that case with an architecture that has no wheel at all.) ### Possible fixes 1. Enable the backend where it exists: add on s390x in . Smallest change, and it gives s390x real SIMD. Needs a view on the VX baseline (z13/z14) you are willing to require. 2. Make the scalar TU genuinely xsimd-free, so the dispatch does not depend on an xsimd backend existing. More robust for any future architecture xsimd does not cover, and matches the intent of having a non-SIMD fallback. Happy to test a patch on s390x hardware; I have a ~10 second reproduction for the single TU. ### Still present on main Verified today against : still has and still instantiates , so the scalar fallback still requires an xsimd backend. 3.1.0 was released 2026-10-22, so this is likely the first report from an architecture with no wheel. ### Installed versions pandas 3.1.0 (sdist from PyPI), numpy 2.5.4, xsimd 14.2.0 ( ), g++ 14.3.1 (Red Hat 14.3.1-4), Linux s390x, , Python 3.12.15, meson/ninja from PyPI.

title: BUG: DataFrame.shift() with multiple periods returns incorrect columns for empty DataFrames
text: BUG: DataFrame.shift() with multiple periods returns incorrect columns for empty DataFrames. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description produces an incorrect column structure when multiple shift periods are specified for an empty DataFrame that has defined columns. When calling , pandas returns the original DataFrame without generating the expected shifted columns. This behavior is inconsistent with the documented functionality of , where specifying multiple periods should produce a concatenation of individually shifted DataFrames, with appropriately suffixed column names. ### Actual Behavior For an empty DataFrame containing the columns and , the operation returns: The requested shifts are silently ignored, and no suffixed columns are generated. ### Expected Behavior The same operation should return: Even when the DataFrame contains zero rows, its output schema should reflect all requested shift periods. ### Suspected Root Cause The implementation of in contains the following early return: This condition executes before the handling of list-like . Consequently, an empty DataFrame is returned unchanged, bypassing the logic responsible for generating and concatenating shifted columns. The same early-return logic is present in the pandas 3.1.0 source code. ### Impact This issue can affect data processing and machine learning pipelines that dynamically generate lagged features. For example, when a filtering operation produces an empty DataFrame, the resulting feature matrix has a different column structure from that produced for non-empty inputs. This inconsistency can cause: * Unexpected schema mismatches in downstream processing. * Failures in machine learning feature pipelines. * Missing lagged feature columns when processing empty datasets. * Inconsistent behavior between empty and non-empty DataFrames. Because the operation completes without raising an exception, the unexpected schema may remain undetected until subsequent processing. ### Suggested Resolution The handling of multiple shift periods should occur before the early return for empty DataFrames, or the empty-DataFrame branch should generate the expected suffixed column structure. A regression test covering empty DataFrames with multiple shift periods would help prevent similar issues in future releases. ### Expected Behavior When is called with multiple periods, pandas should generate a separate set of columns for each requested shift, even when the input DataFrame contains zero rows. The resulting DataFrame should preserve the expected column structure and apply the specified suffix consistently, regardless of whether the input contains data. For example: **Expected output:** **Actual output:** The expected behavior should be equivalent to concatenating the results of individual shifts: This assertion should pass for both empty and non-empty DataFrames. An empty DataFrame should still produce the correct number of shifted columns with the appropriate suffixes. The absence of rows should not cause the requested shifts to be silently ignored. ### Installed Versions INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit : 0691c5cf90477d3503834d983f69350f250a6ff7 python : 3.13.5 python-bits : 64 OS : Linux OS-release : 6.18.55 Version : #1 SMP Wed Oct 14 19:45:18 UTC 2026 machine : x86_64 processor : byteorder : little LC_ALL : None LANG : None LOCALE : C.UTF-8 pandas : 2.2.3 numpy : 2.3.5 pytz : 2026.2 dateutil : 2.9.0.post0 pip : 25.1.1 Cython : 3.2.4 sphinx : None IPython : 9.14.0 adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite : None bs4 : 4.14.3 blosc : None bottleneck : None dataframe-api-compat : None fastparquet : None fsspec : 2026.4.0 html5lib : None hypothesis : None gcsfs : None jinja2 : 3.1.6 lxml.etree : 6.1.1 matplotlib : 3.10.8 numba : 0.65.1 numexpr : 2.14.1 odfpy : None openpyxl : 3.1.5 pandas_gbq : None psycopg2 : None pymysql : None pyarrow : None pyreadstat : None pytest : 9.0.2 python-calamine : None pyxlsb : 1.0.10 s3fs : None scipy : 1.17.0 sqlalchemy : 2.0.50 tables : 3.10.2 tabulate : 0.10.0 xarray : 2026.4.0 xlrd : None xlsxwriter : 3.2.9 zstandard : None tzdata : 2026.2 qtpy : None pyqt5 : None

title: BUG: tz-aware Timestamp with a year outside 1-9999 is stored as year 1970 or 1972 in Series/DatetimeIndex
text: BUG: tz-aware Timestamp with a year outside 1-9999 is stored as year 1970 or 1972 in Series/DatetimeIndex. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description A tz-aware that year is outside Python range (1-9999) is valid with a non-nanosecond unit and the scalar behaves correctly. However when it is converted into datetime64 storage ( , , , , , , or from object), the stored year silently becomes **1972** for a leap year or **1970** otherwise. Month, day and time are correct. There is no warning and no error. Years below 1 are affected the same way: year 0 becomes 1972 and year -1 becomes 1970. Tz-naive values are not affected and the scalar operations also ( , ). **Likely cause.** For out-of-range years, ( ) builds the underlying with a placeholder year, 1972 or 1970, and keeps the real year in . Its comment warns that is therefore unreliable. In ( ), naive s use directly. Tz-aware values instead go through , then ( ). That function reads and says in a comment that this avoids . However, is typed , and under Cython 3 compiles to the inline property in , which is . So the placeholder year is stored. This is the same mechanism as #53125, which was fixed in by reading . ### Expected Behavior The stored value should be the same as the scalar: year 10000 and 10001 in the example as it already is for tz-naive values. If those years are not to be supported for tz-aware data the should be raised. Silently changing the year should not happen. I think that the another way to solve that I did not tested: in , handle a tz-aware the way the naive branch does, since its is already UTC. Or have read the year through the Python attribute instead of the C macro. ### Installed Versions <details> Also reproduced on pandas 3.0.5 and on main ( , commit bb4297c4e6fc0fd8afc2d05c4bd4b51596d20264). Kernel version lines removed below. </details>

text: BUG: reindex/get_indexer with method returns wrong positions when object-dtype target contains NaN. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description Labels after a NaN get matched to the wrong row, and pandas returns wrong values that too without any error. It happens with ffill, bfill and nearest. text: BUG: interval_range silently produces empty intervals and incorrect interval counts for large int64 values. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description can silently generate incorrect intervals when numeric endpoints are large integers, particularly around , where floating-point precision becomes insufficient to represent consecutive integers accurately. For example, consider: This operation should produce four consecutive, nonempty intervals, each with a width of one. However, in the reproduced failure, pandas returns only three intervals, all having identical left and right boundaries. **Observed behavior:** **Potential root cause:** The numeric interval-generation logic in contains the following implementation: The expression introduces floating-point arithmetic into range generation. For sufficiently large integer endpoints, this can cause the generated boundaries to lose precision because consecutive integers cannot always be represented exactly using . The resulting boundaries may collapse to identical values. The subsequent conversion back to integer types cannot recover the original precision. **Impact:** This behavior can cause: * Silent generation of incorrect interval boundaries. * Incorrect numbers of intervals. * Zero-width intervals despite a positive frequency. * Potentially incorrect results in downstream interval-based operations. Because no exception is raised, applications may unknowingly continue processing an invalid . The issue is particularly relevant to applications using large integer timestamps, identifiers, or numerical ranges. **Suggested direction for investigation:** Consider preserving integer arithmetic when , , and are all integers, avoiding unnecessary floating-point conversions when constructing interval boundaries. Regression tests should cover integer endpoints near and above , including verification of interval count, boundary accuracy, and nonempty intervals. ### Expected Behavior should preserve integer precision and generate the correct number of intervals when integer endpoints and integer frequencies are provided. For the following input: The expected result is four consecutive intervals: Expected properties: Each interval should have a width of exactly one. The generated boundaries should remain accurate regardless of the magnitude of the input integers, provided the values are representable within the supported integer dtype. The function should not silently lose precision, generate zero-width intervals, or return fewer intervals than expected. ### Installed Versions INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit : 0691c5cf90477d3503834d983f69350f250a6ff7 python : 3.13.5 python-bits : 64 OS : Linux OS-release : 6.18.55 Version : #1 SMP Wed Oct 14 19:45:18 UTC 2026 machine : x86_64 processor : byteorder : little LC_ALL : None LANG : None LOCALE : C.UTF-8 pandas : 2.2.3 numpy : 2.3.5 pytz : 2026.2 dateutil : 2.9.0.post0 pip : 25.1.1 Cython : 3.2.4 sphinx : None IPython : 9.14.0 adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite : None bs4 : 4.14.3 blosc : None bottleneck : None dataframe-api-compat : None fastparquet : None fsspec : 2026.4.0 html5lib : None hypothesis : None gcsfs : None jinja2 : 3.1.6 lxml.etree : 6.1.1 matplotlib : 3.10.8 numba : 0.65.1 numexpr : 2.14.1 odfpy : None openpyxl : 3.1.5 pandas_gbq : None psycopg2 : None pymysql : None pyarrow : None pyreadstat : None pytest : 9.0.2 python-calamine : None pyxlsb : 1.0.10 s3fs : None scipy : 1.17.0 sqlalchemy : 2.0.50 tables : 3.10.2 tabulate : 0.10.0 xarray : 2026.4.0 xlrd : None xlsxwriter : 3.2.9 zstandard : None tzdata : 2026.2 qtpy : None pyqt5 : None

title: BUG: read_sas drops trailing XPORT rows when a short record ends in blanks
text: BUG: read_sas drops trailing XPORT rows when a short record ends in blanks. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description When an XPORT record is 80 bytes or shorter and ends in an 8-byte blank character value (a SAS missing string), silently returns fewer rows than the file holds. A file with a numeric and an all-blank 8-byte character reads back 1 of 3, 2 of 5 and 7 of 10 rows, and a 1-row file raises . The same layout with non-blank reads all rows. Output on 3.0.6 (the repro builds the XPORT bytes in memory): in (441-455 at 03e5d938ad, from 0.17.0) handles by reading the last 80-byte card and counting every all-blank 8-byte word anywhere in it as tail padding, then floor-dividing the remaining length by the record length. Blank words that belong to real records are counted as padding too, so comes out short. A fix would count only the trailing blank bytes of the last card (scan from the end, stop at the first non-blank word, at most 80) and take , the largest record count whose remainder is all blank. Keeping the floor division with only a trailing scan would still lose a row when the data fills the card exactly, for example 5 records of 16 bytes. A record that is entirely blank cannot be told apart from padding, which is inherent in the format. A test with a blank trailing character column at row counts that are and are not a multiple of the card size would cover it. I ran this on pandas 3.0.6. I have not run it on a main build, but the code cited above is unchanged on main at 03e5d938ad. ### Expected Behavior Each file reads back all of its rows: 1, 3, 5 and 10. ### Installed Versions <details> </details> I'm happy to open a PR with the fix and a test.

text: BUG: resample("D", closed="right") on a tz-aware index adds empty leading/trailing bins; the tz-naive fix in #64793 did not cover tz-aware indexes (3.0 regression). ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description With and a frequency, a timezone-aware index gets an extra empty bin at the start (when the first value is not exactly on midnight) and at the end (the #62200 case). The tz-naive index no longer does. No DST transition is involved; it happens with . With a non-sum aggregation the empty bin becomes and casts the column to float. #64793 fixed this for tz-naive indexes (closed #62200 and #44996) by routing a tz-naive through the path, and its description says timezone-aware indexes were intentionally left unchanged and out of scope, because a calendar day is not always 24 hours. That is the right call for the bin *edges* across a DST transition, but it leaves the tz-aware on the anchored-offset branch of in , which for always does and , i.e. it steps back/forward a whole day whether or not the first/last value sits on midnight. Unlike , , etc. the rule code also gets no end-of-day adjustment in , so the extra bin can only ever hold values at exactly midnight and is otherwise empty. When the first value *is* exactly at midnight the two paths agree (the extra bin is then a real right-closed bin holding that value), so the mismatch is only for values strictly inside a day. Related: #62200 / #44996 (fixed for tz-naive by #64793), #65740 and #59495 (extra empty bins with for and ). #71261 touches the same branch for DST edges but does not change this. ### Expected Behavior The tz-aware result should match the tz-naive one, as it did in 2.3.3: three bins (2024-02-05 to 2024-02-07) in the first example, 136 bins ending 2000-05-15 in the second. text: ENH: support pd.col in pd.to_datetime and pd.to_numeric. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description can be used in , , and, in main, in / , but not in the two most common data-cleaning functions, and . This breaks method chains that are otherwise written with : import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame({"d": ["2024-01-05", "bad"], "n": ["1", "x"]}) df.assign(t=pd.to_datetime(pd.col("d"), errors="coerce")) # TypeError: boolean value of an expression is ambiguous df.assign(v=pd.to_numeric(pd.col("n"), errors="coerce")) # TypeError: boolean value of an expression is ambiguous Reproduced on pandas 3.0.6 and 3.1.0rc0. Expected: the same result as pd.to_datetime(df["d"], errors="coerce") and pd.to_numeric(df["n"], errors="coerce"). ### Feature Description Follow the existing pattern used by / (pandas/core/reshape/tile.py): if the first argument is an Expression, return a new Expression that calls the function lazily, using Expression._call_with_func. def to_datetime(arg, errors="raise", ...): if isinstance(arg, Expression): return arg._call_with_func( to_datetime, arg=arg, errors=errors, dayfirst=dayfirst, yearfirst=yearfirst, utc=utc, format=format, exact=exact, unit=unit, origin=origin, cache=cache, ) ... The same for (arg, errors, downcast, dtype_backend). Tests would compare df.assign(...) with pd.col against the plain df["col"] version using tm.assert_frame_equal, and check the repr. ### Alternative Solutions Use a lambda: df.assign(t=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d["d"], errors="coerce")), or compute the column into a temporary variable. This works, but it mixes lambda style and pd.col style in one chain, which pd.col was introduced to avoid. ### Additional Context I have verified that an external wrapper using Expression._call_with_func gives results identical to the plain version for errors="coerce", format, downcast, and when combined with other expressions. I would like to implement this and open a PR. Happy to follow up with pd.isna/pd.notna if maintainers want that.

text: BUG: rejects compatible / replacements. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description **Horizontal filling with a dictionary or Series has been partially broken since it was introduced in pandas 3.0.** Previously, horizontal dictionary/Series filling was explicitly unsupported. ([PR 62393 / commit f4403451]( A dictionary or Series passed to specifies which replacement value to use for each label. With the default axis, the labels identify columns. With , they identify rows instead. For example: should replace every missing cell in the row labelled with , and every missing cell in with . Existing non-missing cells stay unchanged. Passing should mean the same thing: its index supplies the row labels and its entries supply the replacement values. However, the observed behavior is: | Frame dtype | Dictionary | Equivalent Series | | --- | --- | --- | | NumPy float64/float32 | ValueError | Works | | object, nullable numeric/boolean, categorical | Works | Works | | string, datetime, timedelta, period, interval | AttributeError | AttributeError | **Cause:** Before filling any cells, pandas checks whether the fill values are suitable for the column. There are two mistakes in this check: 1. **For numeric dictionaries, it checks the wrong thing.** With , the value to insert is . However, the check receives the whole dictionary and rejects it as unsuitable for a numeric column. Supplying the same values as a numeric Series passes this check. 2. **For the other failing types, it calls a method on the wrong object.** The Series mentioned in the error is a DataFrame column. A Series stores its values in an array, and this check needs that array. Instead, it receives the Series and tries to call the array method on it. The Series has no such method, so pandas raises . Both dictionary and Series replacements encounter this mistake. Object, nullable numeric/boolean and categorical columns work because their checks accept these inputs without calling the missing array method. The filling step can then interpret the dictionary or Series correctly. The existing [ ]( has gaps. Despite its name, it only checks the float64/Series case, but not the float64/dict case, so it misses that failure. title: BUG: required initialization imports are deferred by global lazy imports
text: BUG: required initialization imports are deferred by global lazy imports. With CPython's global lazy imports enabled, importing pandas._libs can leave the datetime/parser C API capsules unpublished and pandas configuration options unregistered. The modules registering them are imported only for their side effects, so those imports can be deferred before a dependent use. Reproducer (save as repro.py and run python -X lazy_imports=all repro.py): Expected: both capsules and the option are initialized. Actual: the all-mode subprocess fails; the normal-mode subprocess passes. Explicit __import__ calls for pandas.core.config_init, pandas._libs.pandas_parser and pandas._libs.pandas_datetime make both modes pass. Verified on CPython main 25883627946 (3.16), Windows x64 and Linux x86_64, with pandas main 3e40a817 plus the local initialization patch and NumPy 2.5.4. title: BUG: read_csv silently misparses Unicode thousands and decimal markers
text:
BUG: read_csv silently misparses Unicode thousands and decimal markers. Summary "read_csv" silently misinterprets Unicode thousands and decimal separators when using the C engine, producing incorrect numeric values without warning. Reproducible example from io import StringIO import pandas as pd for engine in ("c", "python"): a = pd.read_csv( StringIO("value
1/234
"), thousands=" ", engine=engine ) b = pd.read_csv( StringIO("value
1k5
"), decimal="٫", engine=engine ) print(engine, a.iloc[0, 0], b.iloc[0, 0]) Observed: c 1234 1.5 python 1/234 1k5 Root cause In "pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx", the C parser truncates Unicode code points to a single byte: self.parser.decimal = <char>ord(decimal) self.parser.thousands = <char>ord(thousands) Consequently: - U+202F becomes ASCII "/" - U+066B becomes ASCII "k" This can silently corrupt numeric data during CSV ingestion. Expected behavior The default engine should fall back to the Python parser with a warning when a Unicode numeric separator cannot be represented by the C parser. Explicit "engine="c"" should raise a clear error instead of silently returning incorrect data. ASCII separators should remain unaffected. Verification Reproduced on pandas 2.2.3. The relevant conversion code also exists on the current main branch, although the reproducer has not yet been executed against main. No exact duplicate was identified in targeted issue searches. AI assistance: GPT-6 helped investigate the behavior and prepare this report.

text: BUG: gufunc reducing object Series to a non-scalar object raises AttributeError. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description The issue is calling a generalized ufunc on a Series fails when the ufunc reduces object data down to one object. Pandas doesn't treat this object as a scalar, but, however, the same call on the underlying numpy array works. I ran into this through geopandas: shapely.geometrycollections has the signature (d)->(), so it returns a single geometry. The error comes from _reconstruct in pandas/core/arraylike.py. It returns the direct result only when lib.is_scalar(result) is True. A shapely geometry isn't recognized as a scalar, so it goes on to check result.ndim, which, in this case, the geometry doesn't have. Moreover, this same thing happens without shapely, e.g. np.vecdot on a Series of custom Python objects. I used Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) to help track this down. title: Agents window: session row keeps the folder icon after its main chat moves to a worktree
text: Agents window: session row keeps the folder icon after its main chat moves to a worktree. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes - VS Code Version: 1.145.0-insider (3c0ec3a089398503a462029e7cc2a5749df5169a) - OS Version: macOS 27.2 In the Agents window, when the **main chat** of a session that has more than one chat moves to a new worktree, the session row in the Sessions list keeps showing the **folder** icon instead of the **worktree** icon. The session hover for the same row correctly shows the worktree path and branch. Steps to Reproduce: 1. In the Agents window, start a local Copilot (Agent Host) session in a plain Git folder (folder isolation, not a worktree). 2. Add a second chat to the session, such as a nested session. 3. In the main chat, ask the agent to move the chat to a new worktree (for example "Move this chat to a new worktree"). 4. After the chat continues in the worktree, look at the session row in the Sessions list. **Expected:** the row's workspace-type icon is the worktree icon, matching the hover, branch, change counts, and GitHub info, which all follow the main chat. **Actual:** the row still shows the folder icon. The Show Sessions Picker quick pick has the same problem. ### Cause - When a session has more than one user chat, the host moves only the calling chat. The session keeps its original primary folder, adds the new worktree, and keeps its folder-vs-worktree setting. This is the documented "Multi-chat isolation" behavior in . - The session row icon ( ) and the Show Sessions Picker quick pick ( ) classify the session by . That is still the original checkout, so they report a folder. - The session hover ( ), the row's change counts, and the session's GitHub info already use the main chat's workspace when the session spans more than one folder. Observed in a real session: the persisted session folders were , the session's isolation setting was still , and the main chat worked in . Related: #335792. A parent row must not show a worktree icon when only a nested session uses one, so the fix should follow the main chat rather than check whether any folder is a worktree.

title: Agents: changing a draft session folder destroys its browser tab (Dev Tunnels)
text: Agents: changing a draft session folder destroys its browser tab (Dev Tunnels). Testing #345466 ## Environment - Windows x64, Code OSS 1.146.0 (Electron 43.8.3). - Client and remote VS Code agent host built from . - Host type: **Dev Tunnel to a Windows VS Code agent host**, authenticated/private tunnel. - ; . - Isolated Code OSS profile. The dev product override supplies only the public tunnel authentication configuration from Insiders; no product source changes. ## Steps to reproduce 1. In the Agents window, open the new-session composer and select a remote host and folder A. Do **not** send the first message yet. 2. Open the integrated browser from the session activity bar and navigate to a web app running only on that host's loopback interface, for example ` 3. Verify the page loads and the remote indicator says . 4. In the composer, change the workspace to another folder B on the **same remote host**. This also reproduces by choosing a previously used folder directly from the workspace picker's recent list. 5. Send the first message. ## Expected The browser tab remains open, preserving its URL while following the draft's new folder/storage affinity. It is still available when the session starts, as specified by the TPI's new-session-composer scenario. ## Actual Changing the folder immediately removes the browser tab. Only the Files tab remains, and the native browser page is destroyed, not merely hidden behind another editor. Starting the session does not restore it. Reproduced twice in opposite directions between two folders on the same source-built host. Before the switch, the tab loaded the correct remote HTML, scripts, image, API response, and WebSocket echo; after the switch, its URL was absent from the browser targets. Existing browser tabs belonging to already-started local and other remote sessions remained intact.

title: CLI-installed canvas plugin loaded twice by local Copilot Agent Host (Written by Copilot)
text: CLI-installed canvas plugin loaded twice by local Copilot Agent Host (Written by Copilot). Human tl;dr I asked Copilot to install a plugin, it did this with the Copilot CLI. This seems like it should be ok. Then when I run the TPI steps, it fails, because I apparenlty ended up with two copies of the plugin present somehow, one from the CLI, one independently discovered by vscode. --- <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates --> <!-- Please attach logs to help us diagnose your issue --> - Copilot Chat Extension Version: N/A; this is the built-in Copilot Agent Host/runtime integration. - VS Code Version: 1.145.0-insider, commit (build date November 1, 2026). - OS Version: macOS 26.7.1, arm64. - Feature (e.g. agent/edit/ask mode): Local Copilot Agent Host chat; canvas extension enablement. - Selected model (e.g. GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet): Not relevant to the failure; it occurs while an extension worker joins the session, before a model request. - Logs: Sanitized excerpts below. Copilot SDK/platform package: . Plugin: version , from the marketplace. Steps to Reproduce: 1. Install a canvas-providing plugin through Copilot's native plugin installation path. The affected installation is : This creates an record in Copilot's config and installs the plugin under . 2. Open a local Copilot Agent Host chat in VS Code. Let VS Code discover the installed plugin and synchronize its customizations to the host. 3. Ask the agent to show the session timeline, or invoke the plugin's skill, and leave the canvas open. 4. In the Canvases customization UI, disable the canvas extension, then enable it again. 5. Observe the error below. ### Actual behavior The UI reports: The underlying worker failure is not specific to disabling a canvas while it is open. Logs also show the duplicate-loading failure during fresh chat startup. ### Expected behavior The same installed plugin should not be loaded twice into the same local runtime. Disabling and reenabling its canvas extension should stop and restart one provider without a duplicate canvas registration. ### Worker logs: the same plugin starts from two directories in the same chat At approximately 14:35:54 local time on November 2, the runtime launched both the original installed extension and VS Code's synchronized copy. Both workers had the same . The two files were also compared locally and were byte-for-byte identical. Paths and the session ID are normalized in these excerpts; no complete session logs are attached. Original installed copy, worker PID 96647: VS Code's synchronized copy, worker PID 96648: Corresponding Agent Host and runtime messages: An earlier attempt in the same chat had the opposite winner: the original worker PID 96488 reached , and the synchronized worker PID 96489 failed with the same error. This is a collision between two concurrent copies, not just an old registration left behind after disabling the provider. ### Investigation The observed behavior is consistent with the following loop: 1. Copilot's runtime discovers the native installation. 2. VS Code's also discovers that installation so its contributions appear in the customization UI. 3. The shared client-customization pipeline forwards the plugin to the Agent Host. A materialized copy appears under VS Code's directory. 4. The local runtime receives that copy as an additional plugin directory while still discovering the native installation. Both extension workers try to register . Relevant VS Code paths: - [CLI-installed plugin discovery]( - [Forwarding local plugin references]( This deduplicates references by source URI, but does not exclude an installation already owned by the same local Copilot runtime. - [Passing plugin directories to the SDK]( The integration needs to recognize the original installation and synchronized copy as the same plugin, or avoid forwarding an already-discovered installation back into the same local runtime. This should preserve synchronization to remote hosts and other providers that cannot discover the original installation. Suppressing the lifecycle error or changing this plugin's canvas ID would not address the duplicate loading. ### Related - #345479 reports a similar native-discovery/client-forwarding duplication for custom agents. This report is specifically about duplicate canvas extension workers and the resulting startup/re-enable failure. - An earlier, separate missing-plugin-directory error was resolved before capturing the failures above. These logs show an existing plugin failing on duplicate canvas registration, not a missing installation directory. (Written by Copilot)

title: Explicit Force Remove recovery fails with "The worktree registration changed" after a partial removal on Windows
text: Explicit Force Remove recovery fails with "The worktree registration changed" after a partial removal on Windows. Testing #345250 Repro Steps: - Open the Agents window on a disposable Git repository and start a new session with Isolation: New Worktree selected. - Have the session run a terminal command (or open a terminal/process inside the session's <repo>.worktrees/<worktree-name> folder) so a process holds the working directory open on Windows. - Make an uncommitted change in that worktree, and cause normal cleanup to fail (or directly trigger a failed state so the row moves to Needs attention, e.g., via a failing prepare-commit-msg hook or a locked file during normal cleanup). - In Open Worktree Cleanup, expand Needs attention, select the failed session row, click Force Remove Worktrees, and confirm the destructive prompt. - Terminate the terminal/process holding the directory lock, then reopen or refresh Open Worktree Cleanup. - Select the remaining row in Needs attention and click Force Remove Worktrees (or Force Remove Failed Worktrees) to retry. **Actual Result:** Cleanup fails with: `Couldn't schedule cleanup: Error: The worktree registration changed. title: 0.137.0: invisible to type checkers in generate_unique_id_function (regression from #15745)
text:
0.137.0: invisible to type checkers in generate_unique_id_function (regression from #15745). ### Discussed in
Originally posted by **tedserbinski** June 15, 2026 ### First check - I searched existing discussions and issues — no existing report for this. - This is about a **type-checker regression in 0.137.0**, not a runtime bug (runtime is unaffected). ### Summary In **0.137.0**, the documented pattern from [Advanced → Generate Clients]( — which reads — now fails static type checking. Type checkers report that has no attribute , even though the docs still show exactly this code and it works fine at runtime. This appears to be an unintended side-effect of #15745 ("Refactor internals to preserve APIRouter and APIRoute instances"): was changed to delegate state-setting to a helper that receives cast to the Protocol, and itself no longer carries a class-level annotation. So the attribute is still assigned at runtime, but it's invisible to type checkers looking at the type. ### Reproducible example This is the docs' own example ( ): Running a type checker ( ) over it on 0.137.0: At runtime the same code builds the app and generates operation IDs correctly — only the static type surface is affected. resolves fine; only is missing. ### Expected behavior should remain visible to type checkers as a public attribute of (it's part of the documented public callback contract), as it was in 0.136.x where assigned directly. ### Environment - FastAPI: **0.137.0** - Python: 3.14 - Type checker: 0.0.49 (also reproduces with strict Pyright per the same root cause); mypy may differ - OS: macOS ### Possible fix Add the lost class-level annotation back to (e.g. ) so it matches what the Protocol already declares. Happy to open a PR if that direction is welcome. Thanks for FastAPI! 🙏

title: Discriminated Unions Break When Wrapped in Annotated[Union, Body(...)] in FastAPI 0.124.1+
text:
Discriminated Unions Break When Wrapped in Annotated[Union, Body(...)] in FastAPI 0.124.1+. ### Discussed in
Originally posted by **atlasale** December 11, 2025 ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title here. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc]( ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description I'm experiencing a breaking change when upgrading from FastAPI 0.124.0 to 0.124.1/0.124.2. What works: - FastAPI 0.124.0 - Both endpoint patterns work correctly - FastAPI 0.124.1+ - Only pet: Pet = Body(...) works What breaks: - FastAPI 0.124.1+ - The pattern pet: Annotated[Pet, Body(...)] fails with: pydantic.errors.PydanticUserError: not provided for choice { 'type': 'tagged-union', 'choices': { 'cat': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'metadata': {'pydantic_internal_union_tag_key': 'cat'}}, 'dog': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'metadata': {'pydantic_internal_union_tag_key': 'dog'}} }, 'discriminator': } used with For further information visit Root Cause: This appears to be caused by commit 42b250d ( /fastapi/fastapi/commit/42b250d14dd42d3c0c24dd085fa53878172a985f) which fixed arbitrary_types_allowed=True but introduced a regression in how discriminated unions are handled. The change in fastapi/_compat/v2.py now includes *self.field_info.metadata when creating TypeAdapters, which causes discriminator metadata to be duplicated/nested when the union is wrapped in Annotated[..., Body(...)]. Workaround: Use pet: Pet = Body(...) instead of pet: Annotated[Pet, Body(...)] ### Operating System Linux, macOS ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.124.2 ### Pydantic Version 2.12.5 ### Python Version 3.12 ### Additional Context - The error shows tags ARE present ('pydantic_internal_union_tag_key': 'cat'), so Pydantic sees them but validation fails - This only affects callable discriminators with Tag(), not field-based discriminators with Literal - Both patterns (= Body(...) and Annotated[..., Body(...)]) should be functionally equivalent - This is a breaking change in a patch release Is this a known issue? Should I file a bug report?

text: Multiple regressions in the handling of forms & form validation. ### Issue Content We have found at least 2 regression in the way forms are handled while trying to migrate to v0.115.11 from version v0.112.4. After investigation we were able to identify 2 commits that introduce 2 separate bugs that break the handling of default values in both and froms. Partial fixes have been proposed that also address a CVE, but the PR has been hanging since october 24. # Breaking in the handling of default value in forms This bug has been introduced in MRE: with the following request: The expected result is that is printed, but instead is printed. this is the offending bit from the linked PR: This patch solves the x-form-urlencoded case. So we indeed have two different regressions. This _get_multi_dict_value gets called for all fields in the schema: we see here the special case for empty fields: This bit here just blindly re-adds all fields from the body: This would be partially fixed by but also requires that ignored fields are not re-added to the form. # Breaking in the handling of default value in forms The breaking of multipart form originates from where the check for empty field was dropped MRE: The same request as the previous bug yields name printing an empty string. text: GZip Middleware Throws "Response content longer than Content-Length" when given a 304 empty-body response. ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc]( ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description curl -sH "Accept-Encoding: gzip" localhost:8000 This will reliably: a) Give the expected 304 empty response. b) Show a stack trace "Response content longer than Content-Length" The root cause I believe is the base middleware (in this example the noop one) creates a StreamingResponse for what is ultimately an empty response, it consists of two streaming chunks ("", more=True), ("", more=False); which bypasses the minimum length check in the GZip middleware. GZip then compresses the 'nothing' resulting in the GZip minimum boilerplate, but an expected content length of 0 then throws. This is post-response so the client wont see the error but the server will. ### Operating System Linux, macOS ### Operating System Details Don't think this is relevant. ### FastAPI Version 0.63.0 ### Python Version 3.8.10 ### Additional Context This is actually the root cause of issue: In the case of that issue the trigger is the StaticFiles mount has not-modified support, and on getting a non-modified static resource returns a 304. I suspect the original issue reporter stopped running into it either as a by-product of not getting 304 as often, or alternatively changing their middleware so as not to create the StreamingResponse.

text: Documentation uses “subtype” incorrectly. The documentation uses the term “subtype” in the context of generic types. E.g. [here][1]: [1]: > As the list is a type that takes a "subtype", you put the subtype in square brackets: The word *subtype* already has a defined meaning in the type theory; it is very close to *subclass* and Liskov Substitutability Principle, i.e. it declares a relationship between two types such that an instance of the subtype can be used in every scenario involving the supertype. is most definitely *not* a subtype of . ( , however, is.) The correct term for the thing in brackets is “generic type arguments” or “type args” for short.

title: "Error getting request body" should not be logged as an ERROR
text: "Error getting request body" should not be logged as an ERROR. ### Describe the bug Generally, the semantics of the "ERROR" log level seem to mean that there is an error in your code- not a client error. At least this is how I interpret it and how Sentry (popular error logging framework) interprets it by default. I believe that a client passing a bad input is an expected case for any API, that's why we have so much validation! I believe we should either not be logging anything at all in this case (to be consistent with other input validation errors, like Pydantic errors) or downgrade the logging level to still record _that_ it happened, without suggesting it's a problem that needs to be addressed in code. According to [this page]( in the Python docs, an "ERROR" levels should be used when "Due to a more serious problem, the software has not been able to perform some function." I would argue that FastAPI is performing exactly its function by validating the input structure. ### To Reproduce 1. Create a file with: 3. Open the browser and call the endpoint with the payload {heelo: world} (or any malformed JSON). 4. It returns a status 400 (as expected). 5. An "ERROR" is logged, indicating to me and Sentry that there was a problem in our code. ### Expected behavior Either nothing at all would be logged (because this is an expected case that could often happen) or the log level will be lower- indicating that it happened but that it's not necessarily a problem. ### Environment - OS: macOS and Linux - FastAPI Version [e.g. 0.3.0], get it with: 0.52.0 - Python version, get it with: 3.8.2 ### Additional context I'm currently filtering out this log with something like the following so that Sentry will stop alerting me to it:

The "that/then/this" implies two steps, and the reference to "this" grammatically applies to the dict that has *already* been generated, and so actually implies you will be generating *another* dict from the first dict. This was so bizarre that I dropped it for a while but now that I've solved my problem I can see the docs are misleading here. Call me close-minded because I'm so pedantic (hah hah) but I think many devs are like me that basically I was trusting the accuracy so much that when it was slightly wrong my brain didn't let in any alternative interpretations. And anyway, the implication of the text is actually strictly wrong. So I do have a (somewhat more verbose) correction for this, that I have applied to a clone I pulled, and can provide a little pull request to correct it. This will also help me get the hang of tiangolo GitHub PRs, which will potentially help down the track since I may have an authorization scheme for a particular bastard Azure approach that I can submit. In the example code, if I run it with , the first five requests will result in the following output - I investigated uvicorn workers and found out they use asyncio [server]( interface, which accepts new connections on python's event loop, which means that as long we're using not-async endpoints (which run on AnyIo threads), there is no limit on the number of new connections a worker gets, which again takes us back to the GIL problem. text: Generate AWS API Gateway-compatible Swagger Schemae. ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc]( ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description One of the major selling points of FastAPI is its ability to generate OpenAPI specs, which are consumable by AWS API Gateway. However, when attempting to import the generated schema above into AWS API Gateway, we receive the following errors: ![image]( Essentially, API Gateway strictly bans non-alphanumeric characters from schema names--even underscores. However, by default the schema names generated by Pydantic do include both module path names and underscores, meaning that API Gateway rejects them. The rather non-obvious solution was to override the class's method: This ensures that we do not generate any schema names with non-alphanumeric characters. ### Wanted Solution This is partially a Pydantic issue. FastAPI uses names generated by , and the offending model names are generated by the and helpers (See line 422 of ). However, there is nothing stopping FastAPI from renormalizing the model names generated by Pydantic. I would propose the following steps: 1. Add a section to the documentation on integrating with AWS API Gateway with instructions for how to override . 2. Add an optional flag to generate AWS API Gateway compatible schema names. Note that in so doing care will need to be taken to avoid generating collisions. 3. File an issue on Pydantic to expose native support for the above, so that FastAPI does not need to essentially rewrite the schema names. ### Wanted Code ` ### Alternatives Another option could be for FastAPI to provide its own extensions of and with overwritten methods. However, this seems a bit off to me. We shouldn't be renaming our models based on the requirements of a consumer; after all, what if we have multiple consumers with different naming requirements? Instead we should be formatting our Open API output to match the requirements of our consumers. ### Operating System macOS ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.85.0 ### Python Version 3.8.9 ### Additional Context _No response_

title: Variability in response times in a mixed cpu+io-bound application. Any way to improve ?
text: Variability in response times in a mixed cpu+io-bound application. Any way to improve ?. ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc]( ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description We have a data intensive application exposed through FastAPI. Most endpoints do a mix of io-bound and cpu-bound work. The whole app is using async clients to the datastores (asyncpg, aioredis), so it's coded in async all the way up to the endpoints. It's deployed in bunch of containers behind a load-balancer (AWS ECS), so, following [fastapi docs]( we opted for uvicorn with 1 worker per container. We notice a quite high variability in response time, and especially what seems to be "waiting times". When the response time is short, the profile looks like this: ![image]( That is, the overall response time is a few ms more than the query time, so it's all good. For some other calls, the profile looks like this: ![image]( The overall response time is much longer than the longuest query, there are much more waiting time, especially at the beginning of the call, where there's essentially no work at all (any cpu-bound work comes after the sql response). (Note: I'm just picking 2 examples on a fairly simple endpoint, but we have more complex endpoints with many DB calls, and the same pattern emerges, with waiting time popping here and there) My understanding so far is that what looks like waiting time is just work being done on other concurrent requests. And we're just hitting the limits of the GIL-based archi of python and async behavior. Is this understanding correct ? From other issues I read, there may be some things to test, but I'm unsure: - changing to gunicorn with n workers, to reduce the concurrency within the process ? - isolate the cpu-bound work from the main thread. What would be the better ? wrapping the identified bottlenecks in run_in_threadpool ? or outright force the use of another thread at endpoint start ? Anything else ? Are there any recommendation to improve the situation ? ### Operating System Linux ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.78.0 ### Python Version 3.9.13 ### Additional Context _No response_

The implementation there differs from the implementation in , which dereferences the attribute to find the namespace the original function was defined in. This allows forward references to be handled correctly: In the "Example Code" section, my example includes assertions showing that handles this situation correctly. I believe this can be fixed either by using the same implementation as typing uses, or by calling , and only doing special FastAPI-specific logic if that fails. ### Operating System macOS ### Operating System Details I first saw this on Ubuntu Linux with python 3.8, then later reproduced it on my Macbook in python 3.9. The example code was tested on the Mac. I do not believe the bug is related to operating systems. I think it's a bug in how pure python code handles type annotations. ### FastAPI Version 0.78.0 ### Python Version Python 3.9.1 ### Additional Context This bug is unlikely to come up in most ordinary code, but is likely to come up when using metaprogramming or decorators (especially in programmatically adding endpoints). The framework uses some decorators to alter the type signature of methods, and passes them to FastAPI to expose task endpoints. This leads to the above error. I definitely understand that such an odd use case is probably not high priority for the maintainers, but I hope you'll be willing to review a PR from me fixing the bug. title: Wrong HTTP Response codes in official docs
text: Wrong HTTP Response codes in official docs. ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI]( - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc]( ### Commit to Help - [x] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ### Description I was following the docs and noticed that many of the HTTP error response code where wrong (Or so do I think...). ## Locations - [Here]( and in all code "widgets" below I'm pretty sure the 401 should be a 403 like mentioned above. And I'm not sure but I believe the 400 should be a 401. - 400 is probably fine for the inactive user. - The errors are also inconsistent between doc pages as [here]( 401 is used correctly. - [Here]( we are using 400 for unauthenticated users again. - I didn't look over everything but these where the ones I saw. ## Explanation ### 401 -> 403 401 might be called Unauthorized but this is the problem here. It's used for invalid credentials or invalid authentication method where the server doesn't yet recognize the client. But when we are checking for scope permission the server already knows who the client is and actively refuses to authorize it. Thus *403 FORBIDDEN*! It doesn't make sense giving a *WWW-Authenticate* header if it changes nothing about the tokens permissions. ### 400 -> 401 I don't really understand why 400 was used in some places in the first place in case of failed authentication. If you use 400 you have to give a detailed explanation about the error to make it clear how the client messed up. It would be more fitting to use 401 so the whole situation is easier to understand to the client. ## Links to sources - [This]( is the most comprehendable explanation. - For convenience links to MDN docs: [401]( and [403]( ### Operating System Linux ### Operating System Details I use arch btw. ### FastAPI Version xxx ### Python Version xxx ### Additional Context I just learned about the differences about the error codes a few weeks ago but my sources *seem* to be relatively clear and I saw for example the Azure DevOps REST API use the response codes in a similar way as described here. But I'm open for discussion ;) I believe it is important to fix this issue becuase official docs of big libraries tend to be seen as the ultimate example how to do things (At least for me). Also: We definitely need an issue form for doc improvements/bugs.

The real problem here seems to be that a new session is created when the stream starts. We used the following example to stream contents: For now a workaround is to explicitly save the session after modifying, before rendering the template / starting the stream. Expected output is always the same, one time session open and one time session save. title: Bug in Flask docs
text: Bug in Flask docs. Hi, flask seems very well done. The docs are well organized, with quick links to other sections. However there's one bug I have encountered in the docs. Specifically [this page]( has the following content: > Welcome to Flask’s documentation. Get started with [Installation]( and then get an overview with the [Quickstart]( Beautiful, prominent links to install and quick start. > There is also a more detailed [Tutorial]( that shows how to create a small but complete application with Flask. Common patterns are described in the [Patterns for Flask]( section. The rest of the docs describe each component of Flask in detail, with a full reference in the [API]( section. Tutorial, patterns, reference API. Fantastic! > Flask depends on the [Werkzeug]( WSGI toolkit, the [Jinja]( template engine, and the [Click]( CLI toolkit. Be sure to check their documentation as well as Flask’s when looking for information. A bit off the rails with minutia here, we can recover... > ## User’s Guide > Flask provides configuration and conventions, with sensible defaults, to get started. Good to know. > This section of the documentation explains the different parts of the Flask framework and how they can be used, customized, and extended. Great! > Beyond Flask itself, look for community-maintained extensions to add even more functionality. Ok... Here's where the bug is. In all that great intro information, there was not one single sentence telling me what in god's name Flask is. Is it a cocktail app? Is it for powder horn management? Is it a movement tracker for minutemen militia? Who knows? You wouldn't have any earthly idea. Obviously I or anyone can google it. But we shouldn't have to. You did such a great job with the rest of the intro. You already have great explanatory text on the github readme: > Flask is a lightweight [WSGI]( web application framework. It is designed to make getting started quick and easy, with the ability to scale up to complex applications. Just put that at the top of the docs landing page and you're golden!

title: Making the docs for blueprints more explicit about usecases with some examples.
text: Making the docs for blueprints more explicit about usecases with some examples.. A lot of people have confusion about the use case of blueprints in Flask. This is also based on the first-hand experience of introducing flask to a lot of developers. some random examples when you search on : - [example 1]( - [example 2]( - [example 3]( - [example 4]( **NOTE**: _I am happy and willing to do these changes/add examples myself, just wanted to know the views of others on this._ Afaik these confusions are from people who come straight to flask for web app development without having any prior experience. Even for such cases, we should try to be clear about what can/cannot be done by blueprints (including examples where possible) 1. The first point in the official doc tries to make the point of modularity but the wording might be a bit confusing. >Factor an application into a set of blueprints. This is ideal for larger applications; a project could instantiate an application object, initialize several extensions, and register a collection of blueprints. If we change this to (or anything else, the idea is just to make it clear): _Factor an application into a set of related logical components to modularize the code. This is ideal for larger applications; a project could instantiate an application object and instead of stuffing every route/view on the main app object, which makes code hard to maintain/extend, create and register a collection of blueprints on ._ 2. Add an example for this: >Register a blueprint on an application at a URL prefix and/or subdomain. Parameters in the URL prefix/subdomain become common view arguments (with defaults) across all view functions in the blueprint. 3. Make templating behaviour of blueprints(templating is where blueprint really shines) explicit with example. This is mentioned in the official doc but lacks an example so it is not easily understood by many. >Register a blueprint multiple times on an application with different URL rules. we may add some example like the one below to make it clear. An application that is used for the online digital library should also provide access to books, authors, billings. As soon as the library blueprint is registered on the app, the app has access to all the features of the library under different namespaces but with similar behaviours.

title: Discuss terminal copy/paste issues on security page
text: Discuss terminal copy/paste issues on security page. The [security]( page in the docs discusses various security issues that Flask might not prevent. Add a section discussing things that could happen when copying and pasting code into a terminal. The discussion doesn't need to be exhaustive. Mainly focus on "if you're allowing users to enter code, such as comments on a programming blog, and expect other users to copy it, you might want to apply extra filtering, such as ." See pallets/markupsafe#71, which discussed making also escape backspace characters. I concluded that it was better for terminals to handle it than for MarkupSafe to expand its scope beyond HTML syntax. The main issue is the backspace ( , ) character. It is not rendered by browsers, but it does affect text in a terminal. So renders as but becomes when pasted in a terminal. Most modern terminals detect invisible control characters and offer to remove them when pasting, but some terminals may still have this issue. Other issues include newlines causing multi-line blocks to execute automatically, invalid characters being interpreted together as the escape key, commands hidden after other commands with , triggering Vim commands, etc. There are lots of ways to craft commands that look familiar or innocuous and have them cause unexpected behavior. title: eager loading is not documented
text: eager loading is not documented. I have been annoyed for a while by Flask's lazy loading feature, without even knowing about the feature or why it was annoying me. (The specific problem: when I have a bug in my app factory that should cause an immediate crash on startup, Flask swallowed the exception and only showed it to me with the first request.) So this morning, I dug into the code and learned that this is not a bug, but clearly a deliberate feature added back in 2014 ago. I also learned about the workaround for this feature: . Perfect! Nothing to fix here, right? So what's the problem? Documentation! I had to dig into the source code to understand what was going on, and to figure out how make Flask behave the way I want. That should be described in the manual. ### Expected Behavior In my perfect world, a bug in the app factory would cause an immediate crash on startup. But since delaying such crashes was clearly added deliberately to Flask, and has been there for 5 years, I do NOT propose changing this behaviour. What should happen: the next person who is annoyed or confused by this behaviour should find an explanation and a workaround in the docs. ### Actual Behavior I google'ed, I searched the manual, and I could not figure out why Flask was making it hard to see my bugs. title: Logging Documentation, Patterns & Extending
text: Logging Documentation, Patterns & Extending. I've spent the last month digging through flask and building a large application. Figuring out and configuring logging has been one of the most difficult things to get under control. I still don't understand it well enough that I'm comfortable or have things configured the way I'd like. When learning a new python package/framework/utility - the first thing I _typically_ do is setup debug logging, so that I can see exactly what's going on. The more verbose the debugging messages are, the easier things are to figure out. Typically - debugging logs will dump information like: - a configuration file was loaded - a configuration value was set - API providers have been initialized and are ready for use - when API calls are performed, etc. As far as I can tell, Flask doesn't do any of that - 'logs' are reserved for the instantiated flask application object itself - out of the box, running in debug mode - the only information I get out of the logs is that a request was received and answered. The debug logs don't seem to provide any information about flask's internal activities, things like: - a flask object was instantiated - a blueprint was registered - a route was configured - an extension was loaded - an extension was configured - extension specific things These are all things I've had to "jump through hoops" to understand (while designing my application, application structure, application patterns, etc) - things that seem like they would have been _much_ easier to understand, had logs been available. As I dig further into Flask Internals while building out my application further, there's more and more stuff I'd like to be dumping to my logs so I know exactly what's going on, internally. As an initial attempt to set this up - I started by using [logging_tree]( to dump out the logger heirarchy to see what's what. Based on that - I basically hooked the Config object (similar to how [flasky]( is doing this). Then I read through all the logger docs I could find, I started putting logging statements all over my application code, for example: This uses the default log format, which is very verbose (and is tailored to provide robust information about requests - not really great for what I'm trying to do here). Instead of getting 7 lines that that are tabularized and easy to read, this generates 28 lines, that not easy to scan for this use-case. I spent awhile trying to use as a object, until I finally figured out (yes, it's in the docs, but a little counter-intuitive) that it's not actually a object - it's actually a logging.StreamHandler() object. Then I spent a bunch of time learning more about logging and structured logging and reading through Flask's source, trying to understand exactly what's going on here. I've got some basic experience with structured logging in python, but what's going on here was well above my head and not easy to adjust. I ended up finding the [Flask.debug_log_format()]( API, and used that to set my debug message format to the standard log messaging format - but when dealing with requests - now I miss the old format - and there's logs of other information I'd like to start injecting into _those_ debugging messages as well, that I don't want in my standard messages. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. ### Introduce yourself While packaging upgrade of Python 3.14.7 for openSUSE/Factory, we hit this sudden failure of on architecture (see [complete build log]( with all packages used and steps taken to reproduce, basically just running the test suite). ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact The impact is that the test suite doesn’t pass for us, and we have to skip one more test. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce See above, just running the test suite leads to: ### Expected Results just running the test suite ### Actual Results ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug ## Description The following scikit-learn test fails intermittently or consistently on i586 with Python 3.14.7: The failure occurs only for the process-based case with . The thread-based cases and the case pass. ## Environment - scikit-learn: 1.9.0 - Python: 3.14.7 - Architecture: i586 - joblib: 1.5.3 - pytest: 9.0.3 - pytest-xdist: 3.8.0 - OS: openSUSE Tumbleweed ## Reproduction Run: The failing parameter combination is: The relevant test code creates a callback-bearing estimator and sends it to process workers through joblib: ## Actual result The test fails while joblib/cloudpickle serializes the task: This is then reported by joblib as: Full traceback excerpt: ## Expected result The test should complete successfully, as it does for: ## Analysis stores its records in a regular list: When the worker processes execute the estimator, callback messages are sent back to the parent process. The listener thread appends those messages to . At the same time, joblib/cloudpickle serializes the estimator and callback to send work to another process. This means that cloudpickle can be iterating over while the listener thread appends to it. The failure appears to be a timing-dependent race between callback message handling and process-task serialization. It was observed on i586, where the slower execution may make the race easier to trigger. I have not determined whether this is caused by a Python 3.14 behavior change, or whether Python 3.14 merely exposes an existing race in the test or callback implementation. Could this test or callback state be made safe to pickle while callback records are being received? For example, should the live recording state be excluded from the pickled state, synchronized during serialization, or otherwise handled specially?

text: BUG: Callback's _worker_connections cache grows too big. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact Using a in a lot of sub-estimators in sub-processes eventually raises an when trying to create the connection for the callback to communicate across processes. title: 's path compression never touches the queried node — quadratic linkage labelling
text: 's path compression never touches the queried node — quadratic linkage labelling. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact 's path-compression loop never actually shortens the path of the node it was called on, so path compression is effectively disabled. degenerates to a plain, uncompressed find. Callers that build a dendrogram (e.g. ) allocate a new parent node per merge, so single-linkage/chaining inputs produce O(n)-deep union-find trees; with compression disabled, the repeated uncompressed finds sum to **O(n²)**. This is invisible on small inputs but dominates end-to-end runtime at scale (tens of seconds at n≈200k in a comparable reproduction — see the linked hdbscan report for measured numbers against the same code pattern). **File:** — **Also affects:** , which calls in its inner loop; and, within , / , both of which route through / (the unconstrained and connectivity-constrained paths, respectively) in . Other linkages ( , , ) use a separate heap + implementation and are **not** affected. **Type:** performance (results are correct; time is quadratic) **Related:** the same defect exists independently in the package ( , ), which has its own vendored copy of this . Bug report: [ **LLM usage**: found using Claude, reviewed manually. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ### Expected Results Each doubling increases the runtime by a factor close to 2. ### Actual Results Ratio is close to 4. ### Versions ### Interest in fixing the bug ## The code ## Root cause The "shortcut" line is a chained tuple assignment . Cython (like Python) evaluates the full right-hand side first — as a tuple, using the *current* value of — and only then performs the assignments, **left to right**: 1. Evaluate using the old . 2. Assign target 1: — is rebound *now*, to its old parent. 3. Assign target 2: — but this indexes with the **already-updated** from step 2, not the node the loop meant to compress. The write lands one hop up from where it was intended. The node originally passed to is therefore never repointed at the root; only its ancestors shift by one hop per call. Reproducing the assignment in isolation: Every subsequent re-walks , and this compounds across the whole tree, producing the O(n²) behavior. ## Impact - Any caller that builds a chained union-find structure and repeatedly calls on it is quadratic in the number of points, dominated by re-walked, uncompressed paths. This includes in (used by HDBSCAN) and / in . - **Results are unaffected.** still returns the correct root (the outer loop correctly finds it), so linkage/hierarchy output is unchanged; this is purely a performance bug. ## Suggested fix Walk to the root first, then compress every node on the path in a second pass. This sidesteps the tuple-assignment aliasing trap entirely: Roots are unchanged, so output is bit-identical; only the amortized complexity of repeated calls improves (from effectively uncompressed to near-inverse-Ackermann with compression restored). ## Notes - See the companion package report (linked at the top of this file) for a worked measurement of the same pattern in a near-identical (ndarray-backed, rather than memoryview-backed) .
