title: OOB calculation in Random Forests seems to use incorrect indices
text: OOB calculation in Random Forests seems to use incorrect indices. ### update 9 March 2021 After the discussion below and further testing, I came to the conclusion that this is _**not**_ a bug after all. The indices are computed correctly, because _make_estimator always generates a new random _seed_ that is stored in the random_state variable of each tree -- even if a np.random.RandomState() object was passed to _make_estimator . Apologies for the false alarm. I got confused by the interchangeable use of random_state as a seed or a random generator (but, interestingly, not as the actual state of the random generator). ### original report I have been looking into the OOB score calculation for random forests, and I am concerned that the indices considered to be "out-of-bag" are not actually the same as those held out for training. A few years ago, PR was implemented, which replaced the explicit storage of indices by a regeneration procedure. Specifically, this resulted in the following code fragment in _compute_oob_predictions(self, X, y) in sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py : for estimator in self.estimators_: unsampled_indices = _generate_unsampled_indices( estimator.random_state, n_samples, n_samples_bootstrap, ) y_pred = self._get_oob_predictions( estimator, X[unsampled_indices, :] ) oob_pred[unsampled_indices, ...] += y_pred n_oob_pred[unsampled_indices, :] += 1 If estimator.random_state is a np.RandomState object instead of a constant seed then this appears to generate new random indices instead of the original set of indices. I noticed that this potential shortcoming was also observed by in the discussion about but no follow-up was included there: > Silly question: This fails if a was passed to the forest, right? Because then the would have been altered by building the tree? (or I'm tired) _Originally posted by in I think this is more generally a concern, because even if a constant seed was passed to the RandomForest initializer, then BaseForest.fit(..) implements which makes random_state a RandomState() object, followed by (a few lines below): All trees appear to share the same RandomState() instance, which is then used to generate indices. Calling _generate_sample_indices(...) again as part of _generate_unsampled_indices(..) would seem to _always_ generate different indices. Am I missing something, or can this procedure _never_ work correctly?

title: [RFC] Improve the Ridge solver speed / convergence tradeoff with better solver defaults
text: [RFC] Improve the Ridge solver speed / convergence tradeoff with better solver defaults. I did some follow-up work for the discussions on potential problems for in #19426 and #17444 in the following gist: This gist compares the results between a minimal implementation of ridge with LBFGS by against scikit-learn's , , and other solvers. The main conclusion is that those models seems to converge to the same solution, if we set a low value of and if we are not too strict on the tolerance: see how I defined atol in the gist. I cannot get convergence to machine precision (only around 1e-6/1e-7 in float64), but maybe this is expected. I am not so sure: I tried to tweak on top of but it did not improve. On large-ish problems, L-BFGS can be significantly faster than our the always accurate svd solver (but not always, depends on the regularization) but never faster than the (LAPACK-based) solver. The cholesky solver (our default for dense data) is sometimes faster or slower than lsqr and L-BFGS (depending on regularization) but always faster than SVD (at least with high regularization). The sag/saga solvers are not necessarily as fast as they could be: I noticed that they do no benefit from multi-threading on a multicore machine, so that might be the reason. I have never seen then run faster than lsqr. sag/saga can be significantly faster than L-BFGS despite using fewer cores on problems with / and not too much regularization (alpha=1e-6). There are still problems with as reported in #17444 but maybe we don't care so much because we are going to deprecate this option, see #17772 by that I plan to review soon. Proposed plan of actions: - [x] proceed with the deprecation of in #17772 and <del>therefore put #17444 on hold (or less of a priority)</del> actually no, see: #19616. - [x] improve the ridge tests in scikit-learn by explicitly evaluating the min function for different solvers and maybe using a utility such as the of my gist. Tight tests (but without checking the minimum explicitly) #22910 - [ ] maybe add the ridge_bfgs function as a reference to compare against in our test suite? Since it does not seem to always converge to a very high quality optimum, I am not so sure of the value. - [ ] maybe we could conduct a more systematic evaluation of various datasets with different shapes, conditioning and regularization to select a better default than "cholesky" for dense data? "cholesky" is reputed to not be numerically stable, although I did not observe problems in my gist, maybe because of regularization. seems to be very promising, both in terms of speed and accuracy of the solution (according to my thingy). - [x] I am not sure that our default value of is safe. It's probably very solver dependent, but I doubt that it's a good idea for the fast solver for instance (to be benchmarked if we do the above evaluation). Other ideas: - maybe we should consider adding l-bfgs an option? That would require doing more evaluation on sparse data / ill-conditioned data with various values of alpha. Not sure of the benefit compared to or though: they seem to always be more accurate than l-bfgs and faster (especially ). And l-bfgs can be very slow when alpha is small. - and maybe add a QR-based solver that is supposed to be [more numerically stable]( or is this what LAPACK is doing internally when we use the solver?

title: Memory mapping causes disk space usage bloat in big models with many search parameters
text: Memory mapping causes disk space usage bloat in big models with many search parameters. Hello, We use GridSearchCV in a project where our training data is quite large (approx, 20,000 rows x 100 columns/features). We search a large space of hyperparameters, and with 5-10 cross-validation runs total number of model sometimes up to 1000. When running default parallelization using joblib, the tool generates a lot of memory-mapped disk data and uses a lot of disk space on the scale of hundreds of gigabytes. **Solution:** Once we disable memory mapping, it runs successfully without using the disk. The solution is to call joblib's Parallel(..., max_nbytes=None) within GridSearchCV, see the link to code below. The default for joblib is '1M', which is 1 megabyte. When we pass None, it disables memory mapping. Suggested improvement is to add a kwarg to GridSearchCV that gets passed to Parallel's max_nbytes.

title: [RFC] Should scalers or other estimators warn when fit on constant features?
text: [RFC] Should scalers or other estimators warn when fit on constant features?. As discussed in #19527, fitting models on data with constant feature can be surprising. For instance a fit on a column with constant values set to will let those values passthough unchanged because the variance of the column is null. It can be surprising but is this a problem? Should we warn the user about the presence of such constant features which are typically not predictive for machine learning models? Which estimator should warn about such constant features? The scalers can naturally detect those because they can detect them when computing the attribute. The could also probably warn about this degenerate case. and can also do it efficiently when binning the feature values. If we do so: - what should be the warning message? Should it be the same for all the models? - shall we add a standard constructor param to this estimators with as the default? - should we generalize this to all estimators? (ogrisel: probably not because it could be expensive and redundant input validation check so we could restrict to the estimators above where it's cheap to check) Are there legitimate cases where such a warning would be frequent and annoying? For instance after with dense output with a categorical feature that has a category that is significantly more frequent than the others in cross-validation loop? A similar problem could happen with after . But would would actually make sense to use in those cases? title: Improvement of PDP and ICE plotting
text: Improvement of PDP and ICE plotting. Some discussions from a workshop on interpretation lead us to propose some potential improvements regarding the PDP and ICE plotting utilities. Regarding PDP, it could be nice to get information regarding the distribution of the in-domain samples for a specific feature. Zhao and Hastie illustrate this in-domain values with a scatter plot in the [following paper]( (p. 7). We potentially could provide such visualization or an alternative representation that could encode this information (e.g., histogram or box-plot). We should probably make some proposal and see what is best. Regarding ICE, we currently offer the option that will randomly subsample the available ICE. However, it seems to be more meaningful to build percentile from the available ICE lines instead of plotting the ICE lines. Optionally, we could use to compute the different percentile.

title: t-SNE default parameters and clarifying documentation
text: t-SNE default parameters and clarifying documentation. Following a conversation with on Twitter ( 1) Scikit implementation of t-SNE has a factor of 4 in the gradient that most other implementations (the original Barnes Hut implementation, FIt-SNE, openTSNE) do not have. This factor is there in the formula, but the original implementation absorbed it into the learning rate and other implementations followed this convention. This means that your corresponds to 4 times higher learning rate in any other implementation. Your 200 is equivalent to 800 of other implementations. This should be mentioned in the docs. 2) The scale of random Gaussian initialization is std=1e-4. The scale of PCA initialization is whatever the PCA outputs. But t-SNE works better when initialization is small. I think what makes sense is to scale PCA initialization so that it has std=1e-4, as the random init does. I would do that by default for PCA init. 3) I would suggest to use as default, and not . PCA init performs much better. 4) It has been shown that learning rate needs to grow with the sample size, especially for large datasets. A recently suggested heuristic is learning_rate = n/12 (this would be n/48 using your definition of the learning rate): I would suggest to implement this as and make it default.

title: Allow scoring callable to return a dict {name: score}
text: Allow scoring callable to return a dict {name: score}. Following on from #14593, and an enabler for #12385. A user is currently able to specify multiple metrics for scoring in cross validation or model selection, by setting to a dict, mapping names to scoring functions/callables. We also allow for the shorthand of specifying multiple predefined scorers by a list of names. Following on from #14593, it should be relatively easy to allow the user to instead provide a callable which has the same input parameters as a scorer (estimator, X, y, ...) but which returns a dict mapping names to scores. This would allow the computation of scores to be more efficient (e.g. computing confusion matrices once then aggregating them in various ways), and also enables us (or third parties) to provide prefabricated scorer collections (per #12385), which would amount to a diagnostic suite for your cross validation performance. had expressed interest in implementing this but I thought I'd make an issue so it doesn't get lost and so that we can let Thomas focus on other things if there is a contributor willing to do it. title: Use SVD of covariance matrix instead of X if #features < #data
text: Use SVD of covariance matrix instead of X if #features < #data. Correct me, if I am wrong, but the idea of a PCA is to decorrelate a given data sample X, right? Typically, this is achieved by diagonalizing the covariance matrix C of X, i.e. finding an orthonormal matrix R, such that (R^T C R) becomes diagonal. **If** X is centralized, this is equivalent with the SVD of X though, since C = (X^T X) / (n-1) in this case. Given X = (U S V^T) is the result of the SVD, then V is equivalent with R (hence X -> XR = XV is decorrelated). My point here is, that if X is a (m x n) matrix with (m > n, i.e. more data (rows) than features), the former approach is much cheaper than the latter, since finding the covariance matrix roughly scales like O(mn^2) and the SVD (aka diagonalization) of the square (n x n) covariance matrix is basically for free for small n. This makes it way more efficient than the (bi)diagonalization via SVD of a full-blown (m x n) matrix (i.e. X), which is O(mn^2 + nm^2). (Note the m^2!) My proposal: Replace the SVD of the (m x n) matrix X with a SVD of the (n x n) covariance matrix of X. You can then even relax the centralization requirement of X since the proposed solution works always. (N.B: The ordering of the PCA components is preserved if you use the SVD of the covariance matrix.)

title: Suggestion: Fill with feature mean instead of 0 for VarianceThreshold.inverse_transform
text: Suggestion: Fill with feature mean instead of 0 for VarianceThreshold.inverse_transform. [Today, method fills in zeros to features which were removed for having too-small variance. ]( This is certainly predictable, easy to implement and easy to explain. However, filling in zeros without respect to the data passed to means that the reconstruction error can become arbitrarily large. For example, suppose that one of the features in your data always takes the value . This clearly has zero variance, since it always takes the same value; however, filling in zeros for that feature when the data via and will result in an output which dramatically differs from the input. Instead, I think it would make sense to fill in the mean of the columns when using . The means can be computed and stored from the data passed to . This will make the reconstruction of the transformed data via more closely reflect the data that was passed to because any columns which are removed for having variance less than must, by definition, be tightly grouped about the sample mean. Naturally, in the special cases where the sample means of input features passed to are *already* zero, the proposed method will function the same way it does today, as it will fill in zero values for those features. In terms of code, this just means keeping an array of column means in addition to the indices of the removed columns. Of course, it's possible that I have missed an important subtlety, or there is a competing concern which outweighs the argument that I've outlined here. If that's the case, I'd like to know what I've missed!

Here is a working example: import numpy as np from matplotlib import pyplot as plt from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, ConstantKernel as C def f(x): """The function to predict.""" return 1.5*(1. - np.tanh(100.*(x-0.96))) + 1.5*x*(x-0.95) + 0.4 + 1.5*(1.-x)* np.random.random(x.shape) X = np.array([0.803,0.81,0.82,0.827,0.83,0.84,0.845,0.861,0.875,0.892,0.905, 0.91,0.92,0.925,0.935,0.941,0.947,0.96, 0.974,0.985,0.995,1.0]) X = np.atleast_2d(X).T # Observations and noise y = f(X).ravel() noise = 0.6/y y += noise kernel = C(1.0, (1e-10, 1000)) * RBF(100, (1e-4, 1e4)) gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, alpha=noise ** 2, n_restarts_optimizer=50) gp.fit(X, y) x = np.atleast_2d(np.linspace(0.8, 1.02, 1000)).T y_pred, sigma = gp.predict(x, return_std=True) plt.figure() plt.errorbar(X.ravel(), y, noise, fmt='k.', markersize=10, label=u'Observations') plt.plot(x, y_pred, 'k-', label=u'Prediction') plt.fill(np.concatenate([x, x[::-1]]), np.concatenate([y_pred - 1.9600 * sigma, (y_pred + 1.9600 * sigma)[::-1]]), alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval') plt.xlabel('x') plt.ylabel('y') plt.xlim(0.8, 1.02) plt.ylim(0, 5) plt.legend(loc='lower left') plt.show() provides me with the expected result for (y_*,\sigma_*^2): [![y][1]][1] But now I would like to compute \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} and its associated error. I try this via 2 approaches: **1)** I know that k(x_*,x_*) = \sigma^2_*, so if I simply take the gradient of \sigma^2_* with respect to x_* twice, then I should recover \frac{d^2k(x_*,x_*)}{dx_*^2}, which is exactly equal to the expression in (9.1). When I do this: dkdx = np.gradient(sigma**2.,x[:,0]) d2kdx2 = np.gradient(dkdx,x[:,0]) dydx = np.gradient(y_pred,x[:,0]) d2kdx2_old = d2kdx2*1. d2kdx2[d2kdx2 < 0.] = 0.01 inds_new = np.where(d2kdx2 >= 0.) #I set all negative errors to 0 for plotting purposes cov_grad_used = d2kdx2[inds_new] x_plot = x[inds_new] dydx_err_plot = np.sqrt(cov_grad_used) dydx_plot = dydx[inds_new] plt.figure() plt.plot(x_plot, dydx_plot, 'k-', label=u'Prediction') plt.fill(np.concatenate([x_plot, x_plot[::-1]]), np.concatenate([dydx_plot - 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot, (dydx_plot + 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot)[::-1]]), alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval') plt.xlabel('x') plt.ylabel('dy/dx (using sigma)') plt.legend(loc='lower left') plt.show() [![dy/dx v1][2]][2] the output looks almost right, but when I compute , or, equivalently, , I get a negative quantity! Yet we know that the variance of \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} should be purely positive! **2)** When I try an alternative but supposedly equivalent approach of evaluating the trained covariance kernel directly via and trying to take the second derivative of the values along the diagonal, I get simply zero. This is displayed below: i = 0 just_k = [] while i < len(x): kern_eval = gp.kernel_(np.array([x[i][0]]).reshape(1,-1),np.array([x[i][0]]).reshape(1,-1))[0][0] just_k.append(kern_eval) i = i + 1 just_k = np.array(just_k) K_used = just_k dkdx_kern = np.gradient(K_used,x[:,0]) #derivative of kernel (along diagonal) evaluated for the radial profile d2kdx2_kern = np.gradient(dkdx_kern,x[:,0]) #second derivative, which would correspond to error on dy/dx inds_new_kern = np.where(d2kdx2_kern >= 0.) cov_grad_used_kern = d2kdx2_kern[inds_new_kern] x_plot_kern = x[inds_new_kern] dydx_err_plot_kern = np.sqrt(cov_grad_used_kern) dydx_plot_kern = dydx[inds_new_kern] plt.figure() plt.plot(x_plot_kern, dydx_plot_kern, 'k-', label=u'Prediction') plt.fill(np.concatenate([x_plot_kern, x_plot_kern[::-1]]), np.concatenate([dydx_plot_kern - 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot_kern, (dydx_plot_kern + 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot_kern)[::-1]]), alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval') plt.xlabel('x') plt.ylabel('dy/dx (using kernel)') plt.legend(loc='lower left') plt.show() [![enter image description here][3]][3] where and both equal zero; or equivalently, is zero everywhere! This makes sense mathematically since I am applying a stationary kernel, but given (9.1), I thought this quantity was supposed to represent the variance of my derivative, so something appears off here. Essentially these are two examples of codes trying to compute the variance associated to the derivative of y_*. But why do I get negative values for the derivative's variance using the first approach (i.e. via the second derivative of the conditional variance), and only zero using the second approach (i.e. via the second derivative of )? What step(s) are necessary to compute the variance of \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} properly using scikit-learn's Gaussian process framework? [1]: [2]: [3]:

title: Unclear behavior of max_train_size argument in TimeSeriesSplit
text: Unclear behavior of max_train_size argument in TimeSeriesSplit. #### Description So I am trying to understand the behavior of [ ]( Especially the parameter. I was initially surprised that it is an absolute number and not a ratio like it is in other splitting operations. I traced this parameter to issue #8249 and PR #8282 and I realized that it was added to support window-based splitting, as it is described [here]( This was very surprising for me because this is not really clear from documentation that this is happening. Moreover, I found parameters , , and much easier to understand, especially with that image. I would suggest that: * Documentation is improved here. Such visualization as shown in would really help a lot. * We consider using or sample based parameters, like , , and , or ratio/fold based ones, but not both, because it is very confusing. If we have splitting done by number of folds (which I prefer because it makes things adapt to different dataset sizes automatically), then also window size should be expressed in folds. In a way, parameters could then be: * How many folds to do. * Number of folds used in horizon, i.e., used in test data. It looks like this is currently fixed to 1 in this splitting operation and cannot really be configured. I suggest we allow this to be configured. * Number of folds used in the window, i.e., training data. Default could be None, which would mean a non-fixed window and would mean to use all folds before the test data. Or you could fix it to get a sliding window. #### Versions Relates to how it is in sklearn v0.20.3.

title: tSNE with non-Euclidean metric should be able to square the distances
text: tSNE with non-Euclidean metric should be able to square the distances. Our tSNE implementation uses squared Euclidean distances by default, but does not square the distances when other metrics, or precomputed data, are provided. We had no certainty about whether the theory underlying tSNE was even valid for non-Euclidean metrics (which was raised in the partial rewrite before version 0.19) but if it is valid I would think using a matrix of squared pairwise distances would be more appropriate than raw distance matrices. I think we should at least facilitate squaring the distance matrix, if not deprecate the default behaviour. I propose: * Add a parameter square_distance, setting is default value to 'warn' (or 'legacy') * Current (legacy) behaviour would square only if metric='euclidean' * When True, all distance matrices will be squared explicitly, including precomputed * When False, no distance matrices will be squared * When 'warn', a FutureWarning will be emitted if metric is not Euclidean: from version 0.23 square_distance will default to True

title: Improvements to check_array to handle heterogenous / object data
text: Improvements to check_array to handle heterogenous / object data. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. With the recent improvements to and , we now have estimators in scikit-learn that explicitly accept object-dtyped data or heterogenous data / DataFrames. In several cases, we have noted that we need to update utility functions like to better handle those new use cases. Some cases encountered: * In the , we have some special code to deal with lists of strings / mixed numeric and string: This part is specifically targeting lists, where numpy converts everything to string once there is at least a single string in the lists. * Also in the , there is a second part to check for NaN values in case of object data: which could also be moved to (see * In the , we want to convert lists to arrays, but preserve DataFrames / sparse matrices (active PR: for which we currently are adding this workaround: * In the , we do encoding column by column, so it would not be needed to first convert a DataFrame to an array before accessing columns, we could do the checking of the data only after accessing a single column (to avoid dtype conversion). title: Cannot distinguish missing and zero valued features load_svmlight_file
text: Cannot distinguish missing and zero valued features load_svmlight_file. #### Description The LibSVM format (also SVM-Light) is commonly used to store datasets. It was originally devised for SVMs which cannot handle non-numerical data or missing data. The data format is as follows <target_value> 1:<feature_1_val> 2:<feature_2_val> ... The format can be used to handle sparse data-sets - if a feature is not included, when loaded into a sparse matrix, it will be assumed to be zero. The function sklearn.datasets.load_svmlight_file takes a file in this format and converts it into a sparse matrix ( scipy.sparse.csr_matrix ). This can pose a problem with techniques which can handle missing data or in situations where the absence of data is important i.e. the data is not missing completely at random or there are features for which a zero value is different to the data being missing. For example, if imputation is being used, it is important that the values which are genuinely zero are not being imputed. Whilst this may be a limited use case, I propose modifying the function sklearn.datasets.load_svmlight_file to include an additional option: missing_data_value which will be the value that all missing data takes (e.g. np.NaN ). The default value should remain at zero to avoid breaking existing code. (I apologises if I have not followed the guidlines for reporting an issue properly - this is the first time I've made an issue - thank you for your understanding!).

title: Treat Predict as a Numpy Generalized Ufunc
text: Treat Predict as a Numpy Generalized Ufunc. My understanding is that prediction is always a row-wise broadcastable operation, making it trivially parallelizable across parallel collections like dask.array/dask.dataframe. We implement this in dask-ml with meta-estimators like ParallelPostFit ### Today Alternatively people might just use dask array options directly ### Tomorrow? These workarounds are a little awkward and not a major pain point, but it still might be nice to support this kind of operation directly in scikit-learn ### GUFunc protocols We would want to avoid explicit checks within the Scikit-Learn codebase, so presumably we would want to find some sort of protocol that any sort of array library might be able to implement to inform scikit-learn that it is able to take over. That protocol may already exist in Numpy's [GUFunc]( model. If it was easy to make Scikit-Learn's a Numpy GUFunc then we would get this for free today (Dask array supports gufuncs through the protocol (see [dask gufunc documentation]( for more information). However, there are challenges to implementation. My understanding is that it can be quite difficult to implement the GUFunc protocol today, but I wonder if this might be a nice use case to motivate future development on the Numpy side. (cc )

title: In macro-averaged multiclass precision, and recall, the default set of labels should come only from the target outputs (y_true) not from the predicted outputs (y_pred)
text: In macro-averaged multiclass precision, and recall, the default set of labels should come only from the target outputs (y_true) not from the predicted outputs (y_pred). #### Description In macro-averaged multiclass precision, and recall, the default set of labels should come only from the target outputs (y_true) not from the predicted outputs (y_pred). The target outputs come from the test set. I believe it is a solid assumption is that the classes we are interested in (at all) are the classes present in the the test set. We don't want to average over classes that we are not interested in. In the case where a label occurs only in the predicted argument Trying to calculate recall on classes that only occur in the test set is (as the warning say) ill defined anyway. This would make the behavior consistent with , which only averages over true classes. More consideration at the bottom, though it is a bit long winded even by my standards. #### Steps/Code to Reproduce / Actual Results python In [1]: from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_fscore_support In [2]: precision_recall_fscore_support(list("aabbb"), list("aabbc"), average='macro') Out[2]: (1.0, 0.83333333333333326, 0.90000000000000002, None) python In [1]: import platform; print(platform.platform()) Linux-3.16.0-4-amd64-x86_64-with-debian-8.10 In [2]: import sys; print("Python", sys.version) ('Python', '2.7.9 (default, Jun 29 2016, 13:08:31) \n[GCC 4.9.2]') In [3]: import numpy; print("NumPy", numpy.__version__) ('NumPy', '1.9.3') In [4]: import scipy; print("SciPy", scipy.__version__) ('SciPy', '0.15.1') In [5]: import sklearn; print("Scikit-Learn", sklearn.__version__) ('Scikit-Learn', '0.19.1') ` ### Extended Motivation. Now, in normal supervised multi-class ML circumstances you will not have a label that appears in the *predicted* output but not the *target* output. There are times when you can, (I am working with one in (though the question then becomes is Macro Averaged P/R/F1 a good metric for these? Maybe not) Anyway, we must assert that we *are* in such a circumstance, as otherwise, why have we bothered to search both target and predicted output. Consider: These measures come from information extraction. They are binary measures. The precision is "Of all the times I found LABEL, how many of them were where they should have been " The Recall is precision is "Of all times I should have found LABEL, how often did I actually find it?" When define a test set (i.e. the target set), the classes in it must be the ones that matter. It is the ground truth. We wouldn't make a test set that didn't have a class that matters (or would we?) When we same Macro averaging, we are thinking: For each class rewrite the outputs so that it is binary as to (Found, Not Found) for the class in question. And calculate the information extraction precision/recall for each class. Then average those. In that binary view, you never see the classes from the *predicted output*. Just "Not Found" for every class in the *target* output. Because it is the *target* output classes that you are asking questions about -- that is why they are in the test set. Now consider the math for some class that *is* only in the *predicted* output lets say it occurs times. then and since it has no true positives or false negatives since it never occurs. and since any time it occurs is a false positive. Its (binary) precision will be 0. its (binary) recall will be Undefined: its F1 will thus also be undefined. Sklearn gives a warning and sets the binary recall and F1 to zero. This in turn decreases the (overall) macro average since it adds a class that scores 0 for precision and recall.

title: Handling of missing values in the CategoricalEncoder
text: Handling of missing values in the CategoricalEncoder. Currently the CategoricalEncoder doesn't handle missing values (you get an error about unorderable types or about nan being an unknown category for numerical types). This came up in an issue about imputing missing values for categoricals ( but independently of whether we add such abilities to Imputer, we should also discuss how CategoricalEncoder itself could handle missing values in different ways. Possible ways to deal missing values (np.nan or None): * Raise an error when missing values are present: * This is still a good default I think (we should only make sure to provide a better error message than currently is raised) * Ignore missing values (treat as unknown): * This would give a row of all zeros for dummy encoding, and would no be implemented for ordinal encoding. * In this way, it is similar in behaviour as unknown categories with , apart from the fact it can also occur in the training data. * Regard missing value as a separate category * For ordinal encoding this would give an additional integer, for dummy encoding an additional column. * Something similar is available in if you specify keyword. * Implementation-wise, a problem that would occur is that if your categories consist of a couple of strings values and a missing value (np.nan or None), it becomes unorderable, while in the CategoricalEncoder we normally sort the unique categories (as a possible solution, we could fallback in such a case to sort the non-missing ones first and then add np.nan in the end). * This would be similar to a an indicator feature * Preserve as NaN: * from comment of ( I suppose the idea would be to first see it as a separate category but before returning the result replace that category again with NaN (so it can be imputed after encoding). * This might make sense only for ordinal encoding, unless we want a full row of NaNs for dummy case. This option could actually also be a way to deal with the "imputing categorical features" problem (see also next bullet), as it allows an easier and more flexible combination of encoding / imputing. * Impute missing values (eg with 'most_frequent' option): * Personally I think this one should be left to itself, but adding it here instead could limit the scope of to numerical features. Those options (or a subset of them) could be added as an additional keyword to the CategoricalEncoder. title: Disregard NaNs in preprocessing
text: Disregard NaNs in preprocessing. As per #9854, I think it would be good if our scalers and similar worked despite missing values. title: warm_start for GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV
text: warm_start for GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV. In practice it is useful to search over some parameter space and then continue the search over some related space. We could provide a parameter to make it easy to accumulate results for further candidates into (without reevaluating parameter combinations that have already tested). Issues: * What do we do when the parameter space is reduced rather than expanded; do we delete former results? * I'm not sure that this is identical semantics to other uses of . Do we let things change other than the parameter space? The set of scorers for instance? * Given that calling split multiple times on a cv splitter does not guarantee identical splits, this means we would need to store the first cv split indices and reuse them in subsequent warm started fits. This in turn means that we cannot use warm start in a way that allows us to change the CV splitter (which I think mentioned as a potential use of grid search a while ago). * Does calling 's fit twice mean that it should do 10 iterations for each call, or 10 in total (0 in the second call)? * Is this unnecessary complexity to add to GridSearchCV when users can just concatenate the multiple dataframes?

title: discrete branch: quantile and kmeans strategies
text: discrete branch: quantile and kmeans strategies. We recently merged a discretizing transformer into the [ branch]( (see [diff between that branch and master]( The current discretizer there makes fixed width bins based on each feature's input range. While we could do quantile bins by preceding this in a pipeline with a QuantileTransformer, this is inefficient. Quantile bins is quite a common approach to discretizing. Another approach to discretizing performs KMeans clustering (or perhaps even another clusterer or mixture model) in each feature. We should either have separate classes for these discretization approaches, or provide a parameter to the current proposed discretizer. title: NMF with missing data
text: NMF with missing data. As far as I can tell, there is currently no way to do NMF (or other decomposition methods) with missing data. This could be useful for at least a couple of reasons: 1. Data imputation: Using factorization to fill in missing data can be a more refined technique than other data imputation schemes. It can also serve as the basis for recommender systems. 2. Cross-validation: Even when all data is present, holding out a random subset of elements in the matrix to be factored gives a way to evaluate model fit -- which can in turn be used to set hyperparameters (e.g. rank of decomposition, regularization strengths, etc). Both of these use cases are explained (and implemented) quite nicely in R's package: (See sections "Missing value imputation and application in recommendation system" and "Determine rank k via missing value imputation"). At that API level, this might just look like assuming values are missing data. Conceptually, it seems like it would be simple. In the NMF objection function, when computing , simply skip the missing values in the sum over elements in the Frobenius norm. At the level of implementation in the solvers, I have no idea how hard this would be, as I'm not very well-acquainted with the code base.

title: All kernel regression methods should accept precomputed Gram matrices
text: All kernel regression methods should accept precomputed Gram matrices. SVR has an option If this is chosen, then the X array passed to the fit method is the Gram matrix of the training examples. This option should also be available for GPR and KRR. Here is some motivation. Many machine learning projects begin by defining a feature set, and many algorithms intrinsically require a vector of real numbers for each sample. e.g. linear regression. Kernel methods take a different approach: the modeller supplies a function, the "kernel", which measures the similarity between two samples. This need not be expressed in terms of features. For example, it is easy to say what it means for two DNA sequences to be similar, but hard to reduce a DNA sequence to a vector of features. So SVR correctly is willing to build a model with: (My current project is a cheminformatic one.) It would be great if the other kernel methods supported this. At present, they require a kernel function which they pass the X values to, after checking that X is an array of floats. So some of the value of kernel methods is denied.

title: min_impurity_split in tree is very odd behavior
text: min_impurity_split in tree is very odd behavior. From the implementation and name it looks like that's intended, but the current behavior of min_impurity_split seems odd to me and not what is usually used as stopping criterion in the literature. In the literature, you do not do a split unless it decreases the impurity by a given threshold. In scikit-learn, you do not do a split if the impurity of the current node is not above a given threshold. Check out the example on breast_cancer here: ![image]( The left node has an impurity of 0.08, so it is not split any further - even though there is a very good split possible here that would decrease the gini a lot: ![image]( Basically even if another split could create entirely pure leaves, it's not considered because this leaf is considered "pure enough". You can see that the tree above is very imbalanced and this imbalance is really arbitrary. I don't think this is a good stopping criterion, and I think we should implement the standard stopping criterion from the literature. again ping the tree builders

title: RFC: Cloning estimators in pipeline
text: RFC: Cloning estimators in pipeline. This is an RFC on the lack of cloning of estimators in the pipeline. # Current situation The modifies in the fit method the estimators that are given in it's argument, in violation of the scikit-learn convention (bad bad coder). # Specific issue raised To implement caching of the fit of transformers reliably, cloning of them is crucial ( this way the caching is dependent only on the model parameters of the transformers. In the PR (#7990), the first attempt was to implement a new class, that would behave like the but clone the transformers and cache them. The drawback is the multiplication of classes that are very similar, which makes features harder to discover and give surprises as there is a subttle difference between and . # Proposal The proposal (put forward IRL by , but that has my favor too) is to deprecate the fact that is modified and introduce a attribute (and a attribute). That way we could merge and . # Implementation The difficulty is the deprecation path, as often. Two options: 1. Make and be properties, and add a warning upon access. Make it so that, for two releases, they return the modified estimators, ie what is stored in and . In two releases, dies in favor of , and we remove the properties. 2. Create a new class, for instance , that has the new logic with optional caching. I have no strong opinion on which deprecation path is best. Option 1 is more work but may less intrusive on the users.

title: Multilabel as list of lists or list of arrays should be supported
text: Multilabel as list of lists or list of arrays should be supported. Multilabel is currently represented as a 2d or matrix of binary indicators. We explicitly forbid a list of lists or list of arrays, even if it represents the same binary indicators, in etc. This prohibition is for legacy reasons (lists of lists used to indicate multilabel data with different semantics) and we should be able to safely support non-array array-likes as multilabel representations. Everywhere that multilabel is supported (metrics, estimators), this format should be too. Derived from #5959.

title: Multivariate SVMs: precompute kernel by default
text: Multivariate SVMs: precompute kernel by default. When using SVMs (or other kernel-based estimators) in a multivariate context with MultiOutputRegressor/-Classifier it is faster to precompute the kernel matrix once and distribute it to all estimators with more columns of multivariate output. This is because the kernel computation is happening inside SVM/SVR/..., and is repeated for every output-column, which is expensive (at least when not parallelized). Current: Proposal: --------------------------- Implementation thoughts: There are many options to achieve this, I think the most elegant way would be to have a kernel class (see #7816) and pipeline this into a SVM. If a SVM is then used in a multivariate context with many output columns and not using a precomputed kernel matrix, a warning might be shown, suggesting the pipelined kernel class. If needed I can provide a script showing the speedup achieved. _Thanks for considering this._

title: Batch pairwise_distances in neighbors to reduce memory consumption
text: Batch pairwise_distances in neighbors to reduce memory consumption. The subpackage uses in a number of cases where and cannot be applied. it calculates distances between all pairs but then retains/outputs only information about the nearest neighbours. Rather than requiring intermediate memory for storing the complete O(n^2) pairs' distances, we can limit it to a fixed maximum intermediate storage requirement. 64MiB works well in the similar case in (proposed in #7177), and we use a similar approach in . The general solution would add a parameter or similar to which turns it into a generator of blocks; or a if we'd rather a separate function. This would then be used by , , , collecting sufficient statistics from each block and releasing other intermediate scores. I think specified in MiB or MB is more useful than specifying slice size directly. iterates over square blocks of the pairwise distance matrix. I think it may be more practical to iterate over row slices of the output, although this means there may be a minimum valid block size.

title: Alternative parametrization for GaussianMixture covariance for faster inference
text: Alternative parametrization for GaussianMixture covariance for faster inference. By reading the new code, I think it might be interesting to parameterize the full covariance models in terms of precision matrices instead of covariance matrices. This would allow us to skip the call to in which is called both by the E-step and the / methods. Note that this change will not speed up training as the empirical covariance matrix inversion will just be moved to the M-step in that case. But it would speed-up calls to and which might be very important in some use cases (e.g. estimate the likelihood for new test samples for an outlier / novelty detection system on low dimensional data). Furthermore, instead of storing the square precision matrix, we could store it's lower triangular cholesky factorization which would additionally spare a call to the cholesky solver when calling to compute the determinant. This would move the call to the cholesky solver from the E-step to the M-step too. Or alternatively we could just store the value of the determinant as an additional model parameter. Disclaimer: I have not tried to implement those changes myself so I have missed something. I just want to use this github issue to discuss the relevance of the proposed change.

title: RFC Array API support for and its inititialization
text: RFC Array API support for and its inititialization. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. I prototyped some array API support for with the help of a coding agent. I did that by iteratively running experiments and logging results in an HTML journal maintained in an branch of an external repo that I dedicate to de-novo experiments: - The descriptions of the repo has an up to date detailed summary of what was explored. There are even more details with experimentation results and plots in the [agent's managed journal]( but the journal entries are iterative and therefore harder to interpret than the high level summary in the linked PR's description. ### Main results - on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU, a generic array API implementation of kmeans++ and Lloyd iterations can be competitive with cuML and both can be much faster (up to 7x) than the best CPU implementation on that AWS host; - the same array API code on CPU is not competitive with our existing Cython implementation and even less so when taking optimizations proposed by (in particular into account; - I also explored Torch- and CuPy-specific optimizations on top of the generic array API code path: those can improve performance a bit for some cases (large numbers of clusters) with moderate added complexity. ### My take - I think I would be in favor of expanding our KMeans class to include a array API codepath for non-NumPy inputs, in particular to leverage the capabilities non-CPU devices. - I don't think it's worth bothering with the Torch and CuPy specific codepaths in a first PR. Making a decision about backend specific array API code branches should be discussed in follow-up issues and PRs if people feel the need for them. - I think we should keep the Cython codepath for the CPU case. It means that we will have a bit of code duplication to maintain but I think it's ok. text: Optimize Performance of SGDOptimizer and AdamOptimizer with Vectorized Operations. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable I aim to enable a more efficient training workflow for Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) in scikit-learn by optimizing the performance of the and classes. Currently, these optimizers use list comprehensions in their methods to compute parameter updates, which can be computationally expensive for large neural networks with many parameters (e.g., hidden layers with thousands of neurons). The proposed vectorized operations will allow users to train larger MLPs faster, particularly on datasets requiring extensive iterations, without altering the existing API or user experience. Additionally, the optimization will address redundant computations in when using Nesterov’s momentum, further improving training speed. This enhancement will benefit users working on deep learning tasks within scikit-learn, such as image classification or regression with complex models, by reducing training time and improving scalability. ### Describe your proposed solution To optimize the performance of and , I propose the following changes to : 1. **Vectorized Operations**: - Replace list comprehensions in with in-place NumPy vectorized operations. This will leverage NumPy’s optimized C-based implementation, reducing Python loop overhead. For example, in , the current list comprehension for updating first and second moments can be replaced with a single vectorized operation across all parameters. - Example implementation for : 2. Optimize Nesterov’s Momentum in SGDOptimizer: Streamline SGDOptimizer._get_updates to avoid redundant computations when nesterov=True. Currently, updates are computed twice (once for velocity updates and again for Nesterov correction). The proposal reuses the updated velocities to compute the final update in a single pass. Vectorized NumPy operations are preferred as they leverage existing optimizations without external tools. Parallelization with Multithreading: Implementing parallel updates across parameter arrays using Python’s multiprocessing or threading could improve performance on multi-core systems. However, this approach would add overhead for synchronization and is less practical for the relatively small-scale computations in MLP training, where NumPy’s vectorization already provides efficient single-threaded performance. ### Additional context Maintainability: The proposed changes use existing NumPy functions, ensuring compatibility with the current codebase and ease of maintenance. text: HistGradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor 15x slowdown on small data problems compared to disabled OpenMP threading. > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines]( and in particular the sections for [new contributors]( and the ["Needs triage"]( label. This problem was first described as part of #14306, but I think it might make sense to open a dedicated issue for the particular problem of small data shapes. The fundamental problem seems to be that the OpenMP threadpool overhead is frequently detrimental to performance on. Note that OpenMP threading is enabled by default in general in scikit-learn. Here are the relative durations of running cross-validation on this model on data with various size with and without enabling threads: ![Image]( ![Image]( ![Image]( Speed-up are measured in relative improvement in fit speed compared to a sequential fit (multi-threading disabled). This was collected on an Apple M1 CPU with 4 performance cores and 4 efficiency cores with llvm-opemp installed from conda-forge. <details> </details> Here are my conclusions: - Using threads can cause a huge slowdown on the smallest problems (15x slower than when running with the threads disabled); - OpenMP threading becomes benefitial only with large datasets (more than 100k data points with hundreds of dimensions); - Using the 4 efficiency cores is almost always detrimental. For Intel/AMD x86 CPUs we already disable SMT/HyperThreading for a similar reason (see #26082). But I don't know how to do something similar for efficiency cores in platform-agnostic way; - We should probably disable multi-threading, or at least reduce the number of threads with a heuristic that depends on the data shape such as: - Implementing [sample-wise parallelism]( could probably help a bit on some case ( , but I still think OpenMP threading should be disabled on the smallest problems. - Results will probably also be impacted if we merge #27168. ## Benchmark result data [bench_num_threads.parquet]( ## Benchmark code <details> </details> ## Plotting code <details> </details>

title: Change forcing sequence in newton-cg solver of LogisticRegression
text: Change forcing sequence in newton-cg solver of LogisticRegression. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable I'd like to have faster convergence of the solver of based on scientific publications with empirical studies as done in [A Study on Truncated Newton Methods for Linear Classification (2022)]( (free [pdf]( version). ### Describe your proposed solution It is about the inner stopping criterion in a truncated Newton solver, i.e. when should the inner solver for "hessian @ coefficients = -gradient" stop. $eta = \eta$ is the forcing sequence. #### Current stopping criterion $residual ratio = \frac{\rVert res\lVert_1}{\rVert grad \lVert_1} \leq \eta$ with $res = residual = grad - hess @ coef$ and $\eta = \min([0.5, \sqrt{\rVert grad \lVert_1]})$ (this eta is called adaptive forcing sequence. #### Proposed stopping criterion As recommended by Chapter VII. - Replace residual ratio with the quadratic approximation ratio $j\frac{Q_j - Q_{j-1}}{Q_j}$ and $Q_j = grad @ coef_j + \frac{1}{2} coef_j^T @ hessian @ coef_j$ and $j$ is the inner iteration number. - Optionally replace L1-norm by L2-norm. For the quadratic ratio, this does not matter much. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

title: Configure OpenBLAS to use scikit-learn's OpenMP threadpool
text: Configure OpenBLAS to use scikit-learn's OpenMP threadpool. OpenBLAS v0.3.28 will have a new feature allowing OpenBLAS to use the threadpool chosen by the user, (see This is very interesting because it would solve a performance issue happening when there's a quick succession of BLAS calls and OpenMP (prange) calls. The issue happens when OpenBLAS and OpenMP don't share the same threadpool because both threadpools are in active wait mode when they're idle (see for details), which is a current situation since numpy and scipy wheels are built against OpenBLAS with the pthreads threading layer. This issue is currently impacting some estimators like KMeans ( NMF ( pairwise_distances ( ... Being able to configure OpenBLAS to use our OpenMP threadpool would allow to get rid of this issue even if numpy and scipy keep building their wheels against OpenBLAS pthreads (which is very likely). I'm not sure yet if or how would make this possible so I'm opening this issue to track the progress on this subject.

title: Path for pluggable low-level computational routines
text: Path for pluggable low-level computational routines. The goal of this issue is to discuss the design and prototype a way to register alternative implementations for core low level routines in scikit-learn, in particular to benefit from hardware optimized implementations (e.g. using GPUs efficiently). ## Motivation scikit-learn aims to provide reasonably easy to maintain and portable implementations of standard machine learning algorithms. Those implementations are typically written in Python (with the help of NumPy and SciPy) or in Cython when the overhead of the Python interpreter prevents us to efficiently implement algorithms with (nested) tight loops. This allows us reasonably fast implementations as binary packages (installable with pip/PyPI, conda/conda-forge, conda/anaconda or Linux distros) for a variety of platforms (Linux / macOS / Windows) x (x86_64, i686, arm64, ppc64le) from a single code-base with no external runtime dependencies beyond Python, NumPy and SciPy. Recently, GPU hardware have proven very competitive for many machine learning related workloads, either from a pure latency standpoint, or from the standpoint of a better computation/energy trade-off (irrespective of the raw speed considerations). However, hardware optimized implementation are typically not portable and mandates additional dependencies. We therefore propose to design a way for our users to register alternative implementations of low-level computation routines in scikit-learn provided they has installed the required extension package(s) that matches their specific hardware. ## Relationship to adopting the Array API spec This proposal is related and complementary to another effort, namely: - #22352 The Array API spec is useful to make it possible to have some scikit-learn estimators written using a pure numpy syntax to delegate the computation to alternative Array API compatible libraries such as CuPy. However, some algorithms in scikit-learn cannot be efficiently written using NumPy operation only, for instance the main [K-Means loop is written in Cython]( to process chunks of samples in parallel (using and OpenMP), compute distance with centroids and reduce those distances to find assign each sample to its closest centroid on-the-fly while preventing unnecessary memory transfer between CPU cache and RAM. If we want to run this algorithm efficiently on GPU hardware, one would need to dispatch the computation of this low level function to an alternative implementation that can work on GPU, either written in C/C++ with GPU-specific supporting runtime libraries and compilers (e.g. OpenCL, NVIDIA Cuda, Intel oneAPI DPC++, AMD ROCm...) or using a Python syntax with the help of GPU support provided in numba for instance. ## List of candidate routines - the main k-means loop (pairwise distances between samples and centroids with on-the-fly argmin reduction) - the core k-nearest neighbors computation loop (pairwise distances with on-the-fly arg-k-min reduction) - pairwise distances (without arg-k-min reduction) - pairwise kernels computation (e.g. for use in Nystroem) - ... ## Explicit registration API design ideas I started to draft some API ideas in: - Feel free to comment here, or there. This design is subject to evolve, in particular to make it possible to register both Array API extensions and non-Array API extensions with the same registration API. ## Next steps - start a proof of concept implementation in a branch + external repo using either numba or C++ for k-means. Edit: this is happening here: - #25535 - - once the API design has converged on the PoC, write a formal SLEP.

Specifically changing [this]( and [this]( which leads the mwe to produce: which is in line with expected behavior. Looking at cProfiler results, we see that a lot of the additional time in the slow scenario is spent waiting for locks - presumably when dispatching the jobs (since the random forest is passed to each child process). I assume other than the scenario, differences in performance can be explained by random factors (memory assignment etc.). I don't see any reason to pass the whole forest (presumably it stems from legacy code where multiple properties were used and not evaluating the implementation in this particular setup? no matter). **background:** I was trying to make work with (see #22044 , but for now only locally in [the automl benchmark project]( and ran into some issues with the parallelization backend. It turned out that when using warm-start within cross-validation, the default backend reverts to "loky" which is substantially slower than the "threading" backend to the degree where not warm-starting was faster by 6x (fitting 100 trees twice). While I can now consciously set the backend to threading in our case, I can imagine there are cases were the loky backend is still preferred/required and this contribution is useful. title: Multicore scalability of the Histogram-based GBDT
text: Multicore scalability of the Histogram-based GBDT. I observed that our OpenMP based GBDT does not scale well beyond 4 or 8 threads. who already contributed scalability improvements to xgboost sent me the following analysis by email, reproduced here with his permission: I had initial looking at histogram building functions and observed a few things: Scikit-learn’s code spends too much time in np.zeroes() functions. It is used for creation and filling histograms by zeroes. Theoretically – it is a cheap operation, but this is sequential and uses not native code. I replaced usage of np.zeroes() by np.empty() and scaling was improved, for max number of threads performance improvement – around 30%. For low decision-tree nodes - # of rows can be very small < 1000. In this case creation of parallel loop brings more overhead than value. Similar issue was covered here - to understand background of the issue – you can read readme in the repository. I hope, you will find smth interesting for you there. Link above also says about impact of conversion float <-> double into performance. I have looked at Scikit-learn’s assembler of histogram building and observed conversions too. I haven’t tested, but removing of this conversion can help. If exclude np.zeroes() – building of histograms scales okay if we use only one processor. If we say about multi-socket systems (NUMA) – it scales very poor. ## Here I can recommend you: - Split bin-matrix to <# of numa –nodes> parts by rows and allocate memory on each numa-node separately. - Pin threads to numa-nodes. Each thread should use bin-matrix only from pinned numa-node. /cc

title: calling ComplementNB.predict_proba with sparse X converts feature_log_prob_ to sparse
text: calling ComplementNB.predict_proba with sparse X converts feature_log_prob_ to sparse. <!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: --> #### Description *Surface Level*: is slow when you call predict_proba with a sparse X - far slower than if you call predict_proba with a dense X. *Deeper Problem Description*: converts to a sparse matrix on every call to predict_proba, which is expensive and wasteful. Ideally, when BaseNB calls , it should do so with matrices that are either both sparse, both dense, or if they are not both the same "kind", then the matrix that gets converted should be cheap to do so. The unfortunate reality is the current implementation results in the usually large matrix getting converted to sparse and then thrown away, on every predict_proba call. Some suggested fixes: 1. Call safe_sparse_dot with the mathematically equivalent in , which results in X.T getting converted to a dense matrix rather than self.feature_log_prob_ getting converted to a sparse matrix. This results in a speedup when is much smaller than 2. Represent both densely and sparsely, using one or the other for safe_sparse_dot depending on whether X is sparse or dense, or perhaps other considerations (for example, I noticed that sometimes it is just faster to densify X) 3. Create separate APIs for working with dense vs. sparse X. Note on 2: There are some technicalities with logsumexp that would need to be resolved. Calculating logsumexp isn't supported on a sparse matrix because the "log-sum-exp" trick basically makes all entries non-zero, albeit temporarily. Surely there's a workaround to get logsumexp to work on sparse matrices, I just haven't thought of a solution yet. Details: - When the developer calls , this calls , which calls , which in turn calls on the sparse X and the dense - In , if the first argument is sparse and the second is dense, the second argument is converted to a sparse matrix. - can be expected to be very wide (vocab) and tall (classes) for CBOW-type problems. - Thus, the conversion to CSR is very time consuming and costly - Thus, predict_proba is far slower than it needs to be. My work-around is to densify X before calling predict_proba. This works for when len(X) is reasonably small. However, isn't supporting sparse matrices a major selling point of the sklearn Naive Baye's implementation, and kind of essential for being a good solution? I've spent some time looking into changing the representation of to sparse in my own implementation. What it comes down to is that a dense/dense multiplication is going to be faster for smaller X but doesn't scale well,, whereas a sparse/sparse multiplication is going to be slower than it needs to be for smaller problems but scales well in both speed and memory. Moreover, there are technical problems with scipy.special.logsumexp (particularly, getting the "log-sum-exp" trick to work in a sparse context) that I just don't have the time to solve completely. I do wonder if the log-sum-exp trick is truly necessary in this use case. Perhaps feature_log_prob_ should be represented both ways and _joint_log_likelihood should choose the multiplication thought to be best give some heuristic? Or, better yet, perhaps we should fork the naive bayes implementations into ones that support sparse and dense? #### Steps/Code to Reproduce Train a ComplementNB model with a large (100's of thousands vocab, ~500+ classes) vocabulary. Call predict_proba using a sparse X with a single row. Note the execution time. Call predict_proba with a dense X with a single row. Note the vastly reduced execution time. #### Expected Results <!-- Example: No error is thrown. Please paste or describe the expected results.--> Acceptable performance when X is sparse. #### Actual Results <!-- Please paste or specifically describe the actual output or traceback. --> - With an of 1 x 250K, and a of 503 x 250K , the combined cost of sparsifying and performing on the result is in the neighborhood of 4 seconds. With dense X, 0.088 seconds. - The sparsification of is repeated on every call to , rather than once or never. #### Versions <!-- Please run the following snippet and paste the output below. For scikit-learn >= 0.20: import sklearn; sklearn.show_versions() For scikit-learn < 0.20: import platform; print(platform.platform()) import sys; print("Python", sys.version) import numpy; print("NumPy", numpy.__version__) import scipy; print("SciPy", scipy.__version__) import sklearn; print("Scikit-Learn", sklearn.__version__) --> System: python: 3.7.1 (v3.7.1:260ec2c36a, Oct 20 2018, 14:57:15) [MSC v.1915 64 bit (AMD64)] executable: C:\git\brightfield-jobtitle-classification\.venv\Scripts\python.exe machine: Windows-10-10.0.16299-SP0 BLAS: macros: lib_dirs: cblas_libs: cblas Python deps: pip: 19.1 setuptools: 41.0.1 sklearn: 0.20.1 numpy: 1.15.4 scipy: 1.2.1 Cython: None pandas: 0.23.4 <!-- Thanks for contributing! -->

title: Smarter BaseSearchCV memory management
text: Smarter BaseSearchCV memory management. In a search made to optimize a the pipeline is copied with a **deep** copy. The deep copy has the problem that can copy multiple times things that should be shared between two objects. This problem happens during a scikit-learn search if you want to share information contained in one transformer to another. E.g. In this case, during the , is copied two times in two different address. This result in an unfitted into the Solving this problem would add much more possibilities to scikit-learn e.g. - destandardized metrics - possibility of pre-train and fine-tune approaches in a grid search and much more I suppose that this can be solved by implementing in the right way the in the BaseSearchCV as mentioned in the python's copy documentation: > The difference between shallow and deep copying is only relevant for compound objects (objects that contain other objects, like lists or class instances): A shallow copy constructs a new compound object and then (to the extent possible) inserts references into it to the objects found in the original. A deep copy constructs a new compound object and then, recursively, inserts copies into it of the objects found in the original. Two problems often exist with deep copy operations that don’t exist with shallow copy operations: Recursive objects (compound objects that, directly or indirectly, contain a reference to themselves) may cause a recursive loop. Because deep copy copies everything it may copy too much, such as data which is intended to be shared between copies.

title: NMF is extremely slow.
text: NMF is extremely slow.. Hi, I haven't had a chance to look at the sklearn code to figure out where the bottleneck is, but the currently implementation of NMF is vastly slower than it needs to be. I wanted to factor a very sparse 10,000 x 50,000 matrix and left it running last night to find that it still hadn't converged this morning. I implemented my own version using the Fast Hierarchical Least Squares algorithm from the Cichocki et. al. paper referenced on the NMF page with one iteration of regular Alternating Least Squares as initialization, and it converged within a tolerance of 1e-4 in 20 iterations of Fast HALS in less than 5 minutes. If I had to guess, I think the computation of the error is probably *much* slower than it needs to be, and that may be substantially slowing the algorithm down. When I first implemented my version, I used: which is extremely slow when X is sparse. is orders of magnitude faster since scipy fixed sparse*dense to return sparse. I would appreciate it if someone is willing to look into this. Thanks, Shawn

title: SelectFromModel.transform is very slow: > 0.25 seconds to run on a single row
text: SelectFromModel.transform is very slow: > 0.25 seconds to run on a single row. ### Description When profiling unexpectedly slow production code, I was shocked to find out that took over a quarter of a second to run on a single row, while everything else in the Pipeline took very roughly a microsecond to run on a single row. We're using this in production with private data, so I can't copy exactly the example we're using. But the dataset that we feed into has many hundreds of data points, while the pruned version of the dataset after feature selection has only dozens of data points. The compute time required for over tens of thousands of rows is only a fraction of a second longer than the compute time required for a single row. We can probably pre-calculate a lot of what is calculating on the fly each time. At some point, I'll dive into the code a little more and submit a PR to speed this up. This slowness would have prevented us from using a pipeline built using scikit-learn in production. Everything else runs very quickly (that's one of the reasons I like scikit-learn so much: a very active community of developers optimizing the performance all the time), but this one bottleneck took orders of magnitude longer than all the other calculations combined when getting a prediction on a single row. #### Versions Thanks, as always, for running such an awesome project! Hopefully this will help speed up other peoples' production code as well, and encourage even wider adoption of scikit-learn. It seems a shame to have such a highly optimized library bottlenecked by such a primitive piece of functionality.

However, I'm running into an error in the symmetric decorrelation step: The problem seems to be due to the fact that the eigenvalue decomposition here: sometimes returns negative eigenvalues, which yield NaNs in the square root. I tried using a more numerically stable method for orthonormalizing using the SVD: This is incurs a slightly greater computational cost, but this can be largely mitigated by overwriting in place and disabling checks for NaNs and Infs ( will simply raise a if it encounters these anyway). In any case, evaluating the contrast function seems to be more of a bottleneck than the decorrelation step. With this more stable decorrelation function, converges successfully and I get sensible-looking ICs. title: sparse-sparse and sparse-dense dot product with dense output
text: sparse-sparse and sparse-dense dot product with dense output. has an option which allows to specify that the dot product between two sparse matrices or between a sparse matrix and a numpy array should be output to a numpy array. However, scipy currently always return a sparse matrix, therefore converts it afterwards with . It would be better if we had Cython utilities that can directly output to a numpy array, thus avoiding needless memory allocation and copying. Those utilities are fairly low level and should probably be contributed to scipy too but I feel we should have them in scikit-learn, until the version of scipy that implements them becomes mainstream. Used in: - euclidean_distances - linear_kernel - ridge regression (n_features > n_samples case) - NMF Necessary functions for sparse-dense: - dot(X_csr, Y_c, out) - dot(X_csr, Y_fortran, out) Necessary functions for sparse-sparse: - dot(X_csr, Y_csc, out) Other situations can be handled by using: - dot(a, b) = dot(b.T, a.T).T

title: Spectral Clustering: normalize the spectral embedding?
text: Spectral Clustering: normalize the spectral embedding?. scikit-learn version 0.24.1 Let c = n_components. sklearn's spectral embedding ( ) computes the *c* eigenvectors (*v_1*, ..., *v_c*) corresponding to the smallest eigenvalues of the symmetric normalized graph Laplacian. Then, each node *i* in the graph is given an embedding Currently, directly performs k-means on this spectral embedding. However, this is not what the canonical spectral clustering algorithms do, according to the references cited on the page. The differences among the spectral clustering algorithms in the literature are: 1) unnormalized spectral clustering (Luxburg): use eigenvectors of *unnormalized* graph Laplacian for spectral embedding 2) Shi and Malik (2000): use eigenvectors of the *non-symmetric* normalized graph Laplacian for spectral embedding 3) Ng et al. (2001): use eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized graph Laplacian for spectral embedding, *then scale each embedding to have unit Euclidean length* 4) [Peng et al. (2015)]( use eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized graph Laplacian for spectral embedding, *then scale the embedding of each node by , where is the degree of node * 5) current scikit-learn implementation: use eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized graph Laplacian for spectral embedding, *no scaling is applied* The main reference given on the scikit-learn website ("A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering", 2007 by Ulrike von Luxburg, describes the first three algorithms listed above. So far, I haven't seen any literature that actually suggests the scikit-learn approach. Is there any reason why scikit-learn's spectral clustering algorithm doesn't apply any normalization to the spectral embedding to match either Ng et al. (2001) or Peng et al. (2015)?

title: OrthogonalMatchingPursuit reproducibility with OpenBLAS and different number of cores
text: OrthogonalMatchingPursuit reproducibility with OpenBLAS and different number of cores. We've been experiencing reproducibility issues with _OrthogonalMatchingPursuit_ in different computing environments. The output has been very stable for us when running on hosts with two cores, but we noticed we were getting different results on hosts with eight cores. The two result sets are stable, but different. Searching the project's issues it looks like there was some OMP reproducibility issues in the CI environment around 2014, which led to the OMP tests being disabled. Looking at the code, there isn't a lot of potential culprits explaining such a behavior. [Parallel/delayed]( is used in _OrthogonalMatchingPursuitCV_, but can be controlled with n_jobs and this doesn't change the outcome. Diving deeper brings us to scipy's use of OpenBLAS. We noticed the sklearn test suite is running with [in CI]( Setting this environment variable in the 8 cores environment solved our reproducibility issue. So now to the questions: - is this a known OpenBLAS issue? - are the results with more correct than without with more than two cores or are the results different but equally valid? - what are the performance implications of running sklearn with ?

title: r2_score metric incorrect?
text: r2_score metric incorrect?. Hello, The r2_score metric is something that many functions in sklearn use but right now I think it generally is set as 1 - RSS/SYY, which would the right formula to use if you run a regression with an intercept. If you did not use this, however, and ran a regression with no intercept then the r2_score should be equal to (y_pred^2).sum()/(y_true^2).sum() and notice that we do not demean. Moreover, for other models, 1 - RSS/SYY might be negative or not between 1 and 0, which again is bad. For a standard regression with an intercept term, 1 - RSS/SYY = corr(y_pred,y_true)^2 and this number, no matter what the model is, is between 0 and 1 with 1 as the goal. I think the definition should then be changed on a per model basis or it should be changed to corr(y_pred,y_true)**2. The book "Applied Linear Regression" by S Weisberg mentions the issue I address above on page 84 of the third edition. It suggest to use corr(y_pred,y_true)^2 for nonlinear models and to alternate the definition as above for regression through the origin. Finally, with regards to regression, statsmodels does use a different formula for the r2_score depending on if you use or do not use the intercept in a regression. Maybe this is known already, but the codebase does not seem to differentiate at all so that's why I am putting the issue here. Thanks!

title: BUG: Index comparison with itself skips nullable dtype semantics (numpy bool instead of boolean with NA)
text: BUG: Index comparison with itself skips nullable dtype semantics (numpy bool instead of boolean with NA). ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description Index._cmp_method has a fastpath for self.is_(other) that builds a plain np.ones/np.zeros bool array and sets the NA positions to False (for ==, <=, >=) or True (for !=), regardless of the index dtype. For nullable dtypes this gives a different dtype and different values from every other comparison path: | | idx != idx (identity fastpath) | idx != idx.copy() | | --- | --- | --- | | Int64 | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | BooleanArray [False, <NA>] | | Float64 | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | BooleanArray [False, <NA>] | | boolean | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | BooleanArray [False, <NA>] | | string | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | ArrowExtensionArray bool[pyarrow] [False, <NA>] | | float64 | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | ndarray[bool] [False, True] | Series, IntegerArray and the non-identity Index path all return boolean dtype with <NA> where a value is missing. Only the identity fastpath differs. Same for ==, <= and >=. Came up in #70869, where a test pinning the current fastpath output was dropped per review ("this looks buggy. dont we expect the Int64 case to return with boolean dtype?"). ### Expected Behavior idx != idx returns the same result as idx != idx.copy(): for extension dtypes, the array's own comparison result (boolean / bool[pyarrow] with <NA> at missing positions). The fastpath can stay for numpy dtypes, where its output already matches the slow path. ### Installed Versions <details> </details>
