title: BUG: str.replace/contains/match/count with \w, \d, \s, \b only match ASCII for default str dtype
text: BUG: str.replace/contains/match/count with \w, \d, \s, \b only match ASCII for default str dtype. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description What goes wrong: With the default string dtype, regex character classes like \w, \d, \s, and \b behave as ASCII-only. As a result, accented and other non-English characters can be incorrectly treated as non-word characters. Which methods are affected: The issue affects str.replace, str.contains, str.match, str.fullmatch, and str.count. Object dtype and pandas 2 behavior are Unicode-aware. Why it matters: This can cause silent data changes or corruption in common text-cleaning workflows when users upgrade, especially for datasets containing international or accented text. Cause: These string operations are routed through PyArrow/RE2, where these regex character classes are ASCII-only. The issue is related to #63683, but that issue does not explicitly cover this case. Fix ready: I already have a proposed fix with tests and can open a PR once the issue is triaged and confirmed. AI disclosure: I used Claude Code with claude-opus-5-5 at medium effort to help identify the bug, investigate the behavior, and prepare the fix and tests. ### Expected Behavior Regex character classes such as \w, \d, \s, and \b should handle Unicode characters consistently with object dtype, including accented and non-English letters. title: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError
text: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description On a 1-row DataFrame, df.loc[:, col] = <NumPy ndarray/Series> into an existing PyArrow-backed column raises TypeError, even when every value is a valid float (e.g. 5000.0). The same assignment succeeds when the frame has 2 or more rows. 5000.0 is not invalid. The error text is misleading. What happens: The RHS is a length-1 float64 array, array([5000.]). SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace unwraps any 1-d length-1 ndarray to a 0-d array to avoid the NumPy 1.25 deprecation (value[0, ...], added in [#52906]( if isinstance(value, np.ndarray) and value.ndim == 1 and len(value) == 1: value = value[0, ...] # array([5000.]) -> array(5000.) is_list_like(array(5000.)) is False, so ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa takes the scalar path. pa.scalar(np.ndarray(...), type=pa.float64()) fails: ArrowInvalid: Could not convert array(5000.) with type numpy.ndarray: tried to convert to double pandas 3 rewraps that as TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]' and, unlike 2.x, does not fall back to recasting the column. This is the same unwrap that #59249 / #57923 / #65452 discuss for object-dtype cells. Here the symptom is different and is a hard error on valid numeric data, not an API question about whether a cell should store array([1.]) vs 1.0. Related, but not the same report: ### Expected Behavior A valid float should be written into the double[pyarrow] column. 1-row and N-row frames should behave the same. A narrow fix would be enough and does not require settling the whole single-element listlike-RHS matrix in #65452, for example: in _box_pa_scalar, if value is a 0-d ndarray, use value.item() before pa.scalar, or in setitem_inplace, skip the length-1 unwrap when the target is an ExtensionArray. ### Installed Versions <details> python : 3.13.5 pandas : 3.0.5 (also reproduced the failure mode on 3.0.6 source; main still has the unwrap) pyarrow : 25.0.0 numpy : 2.5.2 OS : Windows On pandas 2.2.3 / 2.3.3 the same assignment does not raise. It emits FutureWarning: Setting an item of incompatible dtype is deprecated... and recasts the column to NumPy float64. pandas 3 turned that warning into this TypeError, so the 1-row unwrap now surfaces as a hard failure on Arrow columns. Confirmed on all released pandas 3.0.x; 3.0.6 fixed a different loc[:, col] Arrow issue (GH 67990, CoW aliasing), not this one. </details>

text: BUG: DataFrame.plot.bar raises "Must supply freq for datetime value" with datetime x column. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description DataFrame.plot(kind='bar') raises: ValueError: Must supply freq for datetime value when a datetime64[us] column is supplied through x=. The exception occurs inside pandas plotting code while BarPlot initializes PeriodConverter with data.index.freq. The DatetimeIndex has freq=None, although its frequency can be inferred as QS-OCT. Relevant end of traceback: File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/core.py", line 1877, in __init__ PeriodConverter.convert_from_freq( self._get_xticks(), data.index.freq, ) File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/converter.py", line 245, in convert_from_freq values = PeriodConverter._convert_1d(values, freq) File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/converter.py", line 281, in _get_datevalue return Period(date, freq).ordinal ValueError: Must supply freq for datetime value The same plotting operation works in another tested environment using: - Python 3.12.11 - pandas 2.2.3 - Matplotlib 3.8.4 - date dtype datetime64[ns] - DatetimeIndex.freq is also None - DatetimeIndex.inferred_freq is QS-OCT The failing environment uses: - Python 3.13 - pandas 3.0.5 - Matplotlib 3.11.1 - date dtype datetime64[us] The data itself can be plotted successfully by either: 1. converting the datetime values to strings before calling DataFrame.plot.bar; or 2. calling matplotlib.pyplot.bar directly with the original datetime values. I confirmed that the issue reproduces in a fresh **Jupyter notebook** using the minimal standalone example, without reading external files or performing a merge. This suggests a regression or compatibility issue in the pandas bar-plot datetime conversion path. I have not established whether the trigger is pandas 3.0, datetime64[us] resolution, Matplotlib 3.11, or their interaction. ### Expected Behavior The bar chart should be created with the values from date on the x-axis and gdp as the bar heights, as it is under pandas 2.2.3. title: BUG: zoneinfo transition times causes incorrect localization of some Timestamps on 32 bit platforms
text: BUG: zoneinfo transition times causes incorrect localization of some Timestamps on 32 bit platforms. Agent (Claude Opus 5 High)-investigated bug This is due to how we populate the transition times cache for ZoneInfo objects which is a result of this line leads to this failure progression in > Every TZif file opens with a "big bang" transition at -2**59 seconds, which does not fit in int64 nanoseconds. > That multiplication wraps it to exactly 0, because 2**59 * 10**9 is congruent to 0 mod 2**64. > trans[1] therefore becomes 0 (1970) sitting between the NPY_NAT + 1 sentinel and the first real transition, so the array is unsorted — on every platform and for all 597 bundled zones. > Localizer searches that array with bisect_right_i8, which assumes sorted input, so its answer depends on the array length since every pivot is derived from n. > Separately, the POSIX-rule validation calls datetime.fromtimestamp(future_ts + 1, timezone.utc), which routes through the platform time_t and raises OverflowError on 32-bit for every future_ts >= 2**31. > The except handler discards all 124 post-2038 transitions, so len(trans) is 238 on 32-bit versus 362 on 64-bit. > With 362 the descent probes index 2 (the 1883 EST transition) and returns -18000s; with 238 it lands exactly on the poisoned 0 and returns deltas[0] = -17762s (LMT), off by 3m58s.

The DataFrame has a column MultiIndex. 2. The second level has dtype due to mixed element types. In the example above, (string) is on level 1 alongside integers , which forces to . 3. The top-level label being assigned to contains exactly **one** sub-column (here ). Top-level labels with multiple sub-columns (here with and ) are assigned correctly. I isolated the trigger by varying level 1: | level 1 | multi sub-col ( ) | single sub-col ( ) | |----------------------------------|----------------------------|---------------------------| | all int | ✅ divided | ✅ divided | | all string | ✅ divided | ✅ divided | | **mixed ** | ✅ divided | ❌ silent no-op | So the bug is specifically the combination of an object-dtype level and a single-element top-level group going through the frame-assignment path. text: BUG: round on object columns no longer raises a TypeError. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description pd.Series.round() appears to have changed behaviour in 2.2.3 compared to 2.1.4. This is a regression from 2.2.3. According to the documentation (stable and dev): > Interpolation technique to use. One of: > > - ‘linear’: Ignore the index and treat the values as equally spaced. This is the only method supported on MultiIndexes. > [...] > - ‘index’: The interpolation uses the numerical values of the DataFrame’s index to linearly calculate missing values. title: REGR/DOC: pd.concat(axis=1) should special case DatetimeIndex to sort even when sort=False
text: REGR/DOC: pd.concat(axis=1) should special case DatetimeIndex to sort even when sort=False. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description For a very long time now it used to be the default behaviour that calling on DataFrames with DateTimeIndex would result in a DataFrame with sorted index. This is very reasonable default behaviour and pretty much what one wants in this case the vast majority of times. With this was considered a bug simply because it wasn't documented correctly, and now the default behaviour, without any warning, was suddenly changed. This means likely code breakages across many users' libraries that were written based on the (up until now true) assumption that concatenating timeseries-like DataFrames/Series would give another timeseries-like object, i.e. something with a clearly sorted DateTimeIndex. Making work in the DateTimeIndex case is of course something that should be ensured, as it is something that might come in handy in some rare cases, but having that the default I don't think is a good idea at all, given the opposite has been the default for a long time and frankly makes more sense. ### Feature Description Change the default back to in the case of DataFrames/Series with DateTimeIndex and update the documentation to more accurately reflect this original default behaviour. ### Alternative Solutions Many users suddenly (and without clear warning) need to put in **all** the places they call on timeseries-like Pandas objects. ### Additional Context _No response_

title: REGR: DataFrame.stack was sometimes sorting resulting index
text: REGR: DataFrame.stack was sometimes sorting resulting index. #53825 removed the argument for DataFrame.stack that was added in #53282 due to #15105, the default being . Prior to #53825, I spent a while trying the implementation in #53921 (where I had implemented sort=True), and test after test was failing. Implementing instead made almost every test pass, and looking at a bunch of examples I concluded that sort wasn't actually sorting. It turns out this is not exactly the case. Note both #53282 and #53825 were added as part of 2.1 development, so below I'm comparing to / running on 2.0.x. On 2.0.x, DataFrame.stack will not sort any part of the resulting index when the input's columns are not a MultiIndex. When the input columns are a MultiIndex, the result will sort the levels of the resulting index that come from the columns. In this case, the result will be sorted not necessarily in lexicographic order, but rather the order of that are in the input's columns. This is opposed to e.g. which always sorts lexicographically rather than relying on the order in I think we're okay with the behavior in main as is: it replaces the sometimes sorting behavior with a consistent never-sort behavior. From #15105, it seems like sort=False is the more desirable of the two; users can always sort the index after stacking if they so choose. However, I wanted to raise this issue now that I have a better understanding of the behavior on 2.0.x to make sure others agree. If we are okay with the behavior, I'm going to make this change more prominent in the whatsnew. <details> <summary>Examples on 2.0.x</summary> </details> cc

text: BUG: call to _constructor of Series before __init__ is finished if initialized from dict. ### Pandas version checks - [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description The constructor of a Series is expected to return a callable that in turn returns a Series or subclass of a Series. When a Series is initialized from a dictionary specifically (and only then), internally a call to is made before has finished. This results in the following unexpected behaviour: is undefined because instantiation of the object hasn't finished. Similarly, many other attributes and methods of self are unavailable because hasn't finished. In my opinion, should not be used from within to prevent this. This problem does only concern Series, not DataFrames. It was introduced by 60013a26 in series.py/_init_dict and is new in 2.0.0. ### Expected Behavior In my opinion, is an instance method (or rather a property) that is intended to be overridden by subclasses of Series. It should therefore behave like an instance method at all times. text: BUG: Plotly scatter plots no longer produce color correctly, color alias for c in 1.5. ### Pandas version checks - [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description Plotly (and perhaps other backends) take a color argument that is a _column name_ to use to make distinct colors for each variable (or even continuous color.) This is very convenient compared to the variable in the pandas backend that takes a list of colors. text: DOC: version added notes missing for the new DataFrame.filter / Series.filter parameters. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on [here]( ### Location of the documentation Source: NDFrame.filter in pandas/core/generic.py, around line 5635. ### Documentation problem Documentation problem Filtering with a boolean mask is listed as a new feature in doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst (section "Filtering with a boolean mask in and "), and that page says these methods "now accept a boolean mask through the new" parameter. The signature in pandas/core/generic.py is: filter(arg=None, /, like=None, regex=None, axis=None, *, items=None, cond=None, na=False) The docstring describes all of these parameters, but it contains no version directive at all: no , no . So on the rendered API pages a user cannot tell that , and only exist in 3.1.0, while , , and are older. Someone reading the docs of a 3.0 install sees arguments they cannot pass. Pandas already documents new parameters this way in the same file, for example the entry of ends with . ### Suggested fix for documentation Add at the end of the description of , and in the docstring in pandas/core/generic.py, each preceded by a blank line so the directive renders as a note instead of literal text.

title: DOC: pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray methods missing from the API reference
text: DOC: pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray methods missing from the API reference. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on [here]( ### Location of the documentation ### Documentation problem Documentation problem — content the box must carry doc/source/reference/extensions.rst lines 31-80 list which ExtensionArray members get generated pages. Ten public methods of ExtensionArray in pandas/core/arrays/base.py are absent from that list: to_numpy, size, T, transpose, argmin, argmax, value_counts, delete, round, map. Consequence: pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.map and the other nine have no doc page, while sibling methods such as astype, take, unique do. The page's own comment (extensions.rst:29-30) says the autosummary block exists so that methods and attributes are generated, so an omitted method is simply undocumented. doc/source/reference/extensions.rst opens by saying these pages are for library authors extending pandas, which is the audience that needs map and to_numpy. ### Suggested fix for documentation Suggested fix for documentation Add the ten missing entries to the existing .. autosummary:: block in doc/source/reference/extensions.rst, keeping the current api.extensions.ExtensionArray.<name> prefix style, and confirm the new pages build with python doc/make.py --single pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.map. Why it is better: the reference then matches the class, so authors discover the override points instead of reading pandas/core/arrays/base.py. Effort: one file, ten added lines. Only risk: newly page-generating members are run through the numpydoc pre-commit checks, so a thin docstring may need its Parameters/Returns finished.

text: DOC: clarify and document ODS support in read_excel(), write_excel() and user guide. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on [here]( ### Location of the documentation This concerns three parts of the docs: * The [ docs]( * The [ docs]( * The [IO section of the User Guide]( ### Documentation problem Even though pandas is able to read and write ODS files using and respectively (thanks to fixes to and it is still difficult to find out about it. Exposing the feature further with aliases like and would be great in my opinion, but seeing that there is overlap between the various engines' capabilities (e.g. between calamine and odfpy) and that ODS is not the only Open Document format supported, it's not as straightforward as a plain alias with a default value for the argument. And I assume renaming the function itself to not use "Excel" would be too controversial, so this ticket is only about documentation. Docs have been improved when fixing and however there are still issues: ### Suggested fix for documentation * The [ docs]( start with "Read an Excel file into a DataFrame.", which is not a full picture: "Excel file" makes it sound like it only supports file formats designed specifically to be used with Excel, so mainly and , at the exclusion of others (that are supported by Excel, or that are not tied to a specific tool). Because the actual file formats supported are already listed in the next sentence, I suggest changing the first sentence to something like: "Read Excel and Open Document formats into a DataFrame." Alternatively, it could be made more product-agnostic by using words like "spreadsheets" or "workbooks", but I think it might not be specific enough and could confuse the distinction with the functions. * The [ docs]( don't mention the availability of the engine. In fact, they don't mention "ODS" or "Open Document" at all. And the first sentence could be modified similarly to above. * The [IO section of the User Guide does explain]( how to import and export to ODS, but [its summary table]( hasn't been updated accordingly, making it look like writing to ODS is not possible. I'm happy to submit a PR.

title: DOC: user guide SQL section lacks PostgreSQL (psycopg 3) recipes
text: DOC: user guide SQL section lacks PostgreSQL (psycopg 3) recipes. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on [here]( ### Location of the documentation ( , section ; the driver notes in are also psycopg2-only) ### Documentation problem The SQL documentation and cookbook examples only reference psycopg2: - The driver list and the note in the user guide SQL section mention psycopg2 only. - The dialect string shown for PostgreSQL engines is the generic form; (psycopg 3) appears nowhere in the docs. - The cookbook SQL section has no recipes at all — just a link to the docs and a Stack Overflow answer. Meanwhile psycopg 3 has been the current major version since 2021 and the recommended driver for new deployments, and the warning for non-SQLAlchemy DBAPI connections ("Other DBAPI2 objects are not tested. Please consider using SQLAlchemy.") sends users to SQLAlchemy without showing the modern dialect string — leading to the common pitfall. Questions about fast bulk loads to PostgreSQL ( being slow at scale) also recur on Stack Overflow without a documented cookbook pattern. ### Suggested fix for documentation Add a subsection at the end of the cookbook SQL section with three small recipes: 1. The recommended connection path: a SQLAlchemy engine on the dialect. 2. A raw-connection pattern (cursor → , columns from ), noting the pandas emits for raw DBAPI connections. 3. A -based bulk-load recipe (staging table + upsert) for writes beyond 's performance envelope. Compared to the current pointer-plus-link, this gives tested, concrete patterns for the most common PostgreSQL integration questions. The recipes come from production usage (an ingestion pipeline loading ~46M daily price rows into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB) and have been executed as written against PostgreSQL 17 with psycopg 3.3.4 / SQLAlchemy 2.0.52.

text: BUG: DataFrame.eq() incorrectly rejects scalar strings in type annotations. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version]( of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch]( of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ### Issue Description DataFrame.eq() incorrectly rejects scalar string values in the type annotations. According to the pandas API, DataFrame.eq() accepts scalar values, including strings. title: ENH: default behavior should default to tagging all duplicates as
text: ENH: default behavior should default to tagging all duplicates as. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description Hi, folks. I don't complain much about excellent open-source freeware, and I'm reasonably proficient at Pandas. I have about three years of solid use under my belt; before that, I had about six using Stata and am (was) a Stata maven. Pandas is generally much better...BUT... has what seems to me to be very confusing default behavior. In Stata, for example, one might use the equivalent duplicate-tagger function (in Stata, a "command") to locate people who are duplicates on a particular column to then hand inspect some of the rows to see if these are data entry errors or if, by contrast, one has perhaps missed a nuance and should expect a small number of duplicates on some col. This might sound sloppy, but when the codebook/docs for the DF sucks, this is a good way to figure out precisely what it might mean for a row to be a duplicate on some subset. For that reason, I propose that should be the default behavior. I just spent around 30 minutes trying to figure out the problem with my code or possibly with the df, etc. because I was trying to locate people who are duplicates on a col that should in theory have a few duplicates but not many, and I could not actually see any duplicates after the following. Of course, I realized that this is because the default behavior is to *not* tag the first duplicate as a duplicate; in my case, since the multiplicity of a duplicate is almost always two, that meant that subsetting the data to only include duplicates was actually omitting those duplicates from view. I did even skim the Docs, obviously inefficiently at first, but the wording *itself* seems extremely confusing. I did not realize that would solve my problems because this is not really about keep/drop behavior but tagging behavior. Changing the option's actual name to or something similar would probably lead to less confusion/make it more obvious that the default behavior is odd. On that note, another reason to change this, I think, is that there is no particular reason to expect the first duplicate to be the one to keep (at least without more context on the df; certainly, this is not true in general). This might make sense if it is a duplicate on all cols, but if the subset is anything but the full set of cols, this seems like behavior that might lead to very unexpected results. If someone does simply have outright duplicate records, it doesn't really cost significant time or memory (AFAICT) to then go back and set once it's been confirmed that one might as well keep any record. ### Feature Description I'm not a backend dev., merely a fairly tech-savvy sociologist. I think the technical side of this would be very easy. ### Alternative Solutions People could read the docs very carefully before seeking other solutions. ### Additional Context _No response_

text: DOC: Clarify rolling window behavior with negative offset strings and froward rolling windows. ### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on [here]( ### Location of the documentation ### Documentation problem There is no documentation on a forward-looking rolling windows with offset strings. I often need to make a forward-looking rolling window on datetime data. To do so, I've tried different ways and the only one I found was using two (reverse the series order) with the rolling occurring in the middle. nb: Because the data has irregular DateTimeIndex (not every 2 hours for example), I can not use the This is what this shows : - The behavior of negative offset strings (e.g., "-5h") in Series.rolling() and DataFrame.rolling() is not documented and produces counterintuitive results. They don't inverse the rolling window, the window just collaps into 1 element windows. The negative int values are actually prohibited by the function ( ) so I would expect the same to be for offset stings. > Maybe a bug ? - Using .iloc[::-1] to invert the series before performing the rolling window (suggested by works. But, you still have to use a positive offset even if your dataset is anticrhonological order when the rolling occurs. ### Suggested fix for documentation For me, adding something like the following text on the examples ( would do the tricks: Rolling sum with forward-looking windows with 3 seconds >>> df_time.iloc[::-1].rolling("3s").sum().iloc[::-1] B 2013-01-01 09:00:00 1.0 2013-01-01 09:00:02 3.0 2013-01-01 09:00:03 2.0 2013-01-01 09:00:05 4.0 2013-01-01 09:00:06 4.0 Note: Negative offset strings (e.g., "-5h" ) do not create forward-looking windows and should be avoided. They collapse to single-element windows.

title: Hosting of the pandas website and documentation
text: Hosting of the pandas website and documentation. Until recently, the website and docs were hosted on an OVH server (xref The access has temporarily been restored, but in the meantime I changed pandas.pydata.org to point to the github pages set up at as a quick solution. Those github pages should have most content (e.g. I didn't add all versions, but only the ones accessible from the dropdown down to 1.5) to ensure a working website, but we should discuss how to host the website and docs long term. Some possible options: - GitHub pages - Improve the current temporary solution. Since it is "just" a github repo, this is quite transparent and easy to manage. - We might run into issues with max repo size (officially 1 GB? although they don't seem to enforce that) and bandwidth limits, but on the other hand, other projects like numpy (split over and and scikit-learn (all in one are also using github pages, and don't seem to run into those problems. Cloudfare being in front of github pages might also help. - Readthedocs - Would also be nice to use, and would eg give an automatic option for previews for PRs - I _think_ historically we didn't use RTD in the past (speaking about many years ago) because our pandas build + doc build took too long / too many resources. But I assume nowadays that should be OK. - The main hurdle for using RTD is that their setup doesn't really match with our current URL structure for stable/dev/versioned docs. That is maybe something be could be solved with symlinks/redirects, but so that is something someone will have to investigate. - Cheap hosting for a static website - The actual server we were using on OVH would also have only cost around 10$/month for just the website (it were the compute servers that consumed the credits), and we would probably find even cheaper hosting for a simple static website somewhere - Another option would be using an Object Storage bucket for putting the content, as a cheap way to host a static website. For example a [Cloudfare R2 bucket]( or [OVH object storage]( would both be very cheap in storage (around one dollar for our website size). This might not support symlinks? But if storage is cheap, we can also duplicate things instead of heavily using symlinks cc -dev/pandas-core preferences? other options, or other aspects we should consider in a decision? ### Size of the website/docs sources Checking the content we have currently hosted (after a bit of cleanup, we had some versions of the docs duplicated in a nested directory), this is 24 GB right now. However, we currently keep the docs of _all_ versions, including bug-fix releases (eg for 2.3.0, 2.3.1, 2.3.2 etc). If we would just keep one latest version (i.e. just have 2.3 for the example), and removing versions we don't have to keep (like RCs), this goes down to 5.2 GB) Currently, the size of a single doc build (i.e. single version) is 266MB (for the latest 3.0.1 release) ### TODOs Short term for the github pages: - [ ] Add the remaining versions that are now missing from the dropdown, and add symlinks for all bug-fix versions we previously hosted (eg link 2.3.0/2.3.1/2.3.2 to 2.3, just to make sure those URLs keep working, in case someone is actually using them) - [ ] After deciding the hosting solution, further todo items: - [x] The CI workflow to push the latest website and docs needs to be updated (at the moment the dev docs are not getting updated), and the same for the released versions: - [ ] Find a solution for the redirect for the dev docs. On the current OVH server, I don't find how this was actually set up (since itself is also a symlink to , which is a symlink to the latest versioned docs). Maybe there was some redirect on the Cloudfare side? (I temporarily fixed this by adding a linking to `/pandas-docs/dev/, but that would then need to be updated every time when doing a release) - [ ] Depending on the choice, find a new solution for doc previews of PRs (those are currently also hosted on OVH)

title: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations
text: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination. Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed. It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution. For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows. This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations. The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards. ### Feature Description result = df[“column”].apply( expensive_function, checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”, checkpoint_every=10, ) ### Alternative Solutions for i, value in df["column"].items(): df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value) if i % 10 == 0: df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl") ### Additional Context _No response_

title: ENH: move the postgresql extra from psycopg2 to psycopg 3
text: ENH: move the postgresql extra from psycopg2 to psycopg 3. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description still installs psycopg2. Current pin on main, in : postgresql = ['SQLAlchemy>=2.0.42', 'psycopg2>=2.9.10', 'adbc-driver-postgresql>=1.7.0'] After #67968 the SQL user guide names psycopg 3 as the example SQLAlchemy driver for PostgreSQL, so the packaging and the docs now point at different generations of the driver. This came up in the review of that PR: I wish installed the driver the docs recommend. ### Feature Description Swap for a (3.x) pin with an appropriate floor, moving the coupled spots together: - the extra in - the extra in (same psycopg2 pin today) - - the optional-dependencies table in (lists psycopg2 as the PostgreSQL engine for SQLAlchemy) The psycopg project describes psycopg2 as fully supported for legacy applications and recommends psycopg 3 for new projects. One compatibility question decides the floor and the shape of the change: in SQLAlchemy, psycopg2 remains the default dialect for bare URLs, so replacing the pin changes what a fresh install can connect with unless the engine string is explicit. ### Alternative Solutions - Ship both drivers in the extra ( and ): no breakage for users relying on psycopg2 being pulled in, at the cost of a heavier install. The two packages coexist and SQLAlchemy picks the dialect from the URL scheme. - Keep psycopg2 and treat the docs recommendation and the extra as separate concerns; the user guide already shows both dialect strings explicitly. - Replace psycopg2 with psycopg and accept that bare users must add psycopg2 themselves or move to the explicit scheme shown in the user guide. ### Additional Context - Raised by in the review of #67968 (link above). - psycopg project statement: "Psycopg 2 remains fully supported for legacy applications. New projects should use Psycopg 3." (psycopg.org) - SQLAlchemy 2.0 dialect docs: psycopg2 "remains the default dialect for the dialect series"; psycopg 3 requires the explicit scheme. - I run the explicit path in production (pipeline loading ~46M rows per day into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, psycopg 3.3.4 with SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 against PostgreSQL 17).

text: ENH: Add limit_distance parameter to Series/DataFrame.interpolate. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description I wish I could use pandas' interpolate method such that I could pass a parameter 'limit_distance' which will make it so that when two values differ by more than limit_distance, pandas will not interpolate. I think this is similar to how the existing limit parameter works to prevent interpolation when there are too many NaNs in between, but instead of counting missing values, it prevents interpolation if the actual coordinate or time gap between two valid points is too big. I encountered this issue while trying to work on ECG data and was instructed not to interpolate over long gaps, I realized that the most efficient way is not to interpolate conditionally, but rather to interpolate and then filter (remove unwanted interpolations); I think this is due to CPu and cache optimization but I am deviating from the main topic, I had to write code to do it and I thought that this could be cleaner to have this feature built in pandas. Also, I think this may be related to issue #64588, which discusses limiting by consecutive NaN count, but this feature request specifically targets limiting by the actual numerical distance or time gap between anchor points rather than the number of missing cells.) ### Feature Description I already implemented and tested this functionality locally. Here is the core helper method handling the vectorized gap logic: python # 1. Reindex and interpolate across the whole grid hr_interpolated = ser.reindex(combined_index).interpolate(method='index') hr_1hz = hr_interpolated.loc[t_grid].to_numpy(copy=True) # 2. Manually find the surrounding intervals and mask gaps > 5.0 seconds next_beat_idx = np.searchsorted(df_ecg_clean['t_beat_sec'], t_grid) next_beat_idx = np.clip(next_beat_idx, 0, len(df_ecg_clean) - 1) interval_sizes = df_ecg_clean['rr_interval'].to_numpy()[next_beat_idx] hr_1hz[interval_sizes > 5.0] = np.nan ### Additional Context I have the implementation ready to submit in a Pull Request, including the update feature and a few tests

title: ENH: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings
text: ENH: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction. When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix. Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2): with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f: f.write(b'name,note\n') f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n') # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8 import pandas as pd pd.read_csv('test.csv') Result: UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem. ### Feature Description Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding. Rough approach, in the CSV reading error handling path: try: ...read with utf-8... except UnicodeDecodeError as e: if encoding_was_default: raise UnicodeDecodeError( e.encoding, e.object, e.start, e.end, e.reason + ". Tip: this file may not be UTF-8 encoded. " "Try encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252', common with Windows Excel exports." ) from e raise This only changes the message text, not behavior, and only fires when encoding wasn't explicitly passed by the user, so it doesn't affect anyone who already specifies an encoding. ### Alternative Solutions Currently the only options are: 1. Manually try common encodings one by one (utf-8, latin-1, cp1252) until one works, usually after searching Stack Overflow to learn this is the fix 2. Use a third-party library like chardet or charset-normalizer to detect the encoding beforehand, which is a heavier dependency for a one-line hint 3. Open the file in a text editor that reports encoding, then pass it explicitly None of these are discoverable from the error message itself, which is the actual gap this request addresses. ### Additional Context This is intentionally scoped narrower than a full encoding='detect' feature, since I understand that's a bigger design discussion. This is just improving the existing error message text for the common case.

In the code above indexes a and b are both present in s1 and s2 and s1>s2 can be done as both indexes are present in both s1 and s2 but currently it is not allowed as there is a strict requirement that for relational operators the order of the indexes must also match. It would be intutive if the requirement of index order is relaxed for relational operators and only matching index is checked. ### Additional Context _No response_

title: ENH: Add accessor to inject random faults and typos for Data Science education
text: ENH: Add accessor to inject random faults and typos for Data Science education. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description In Data Science and AI education, teaching students how to clean and preprocess "dirty data" (handling missing values, detecting outliers, removing duplicates, and fixing text typos) is a critical skill. Currently, professors and students struggle to find realistic, messy datasets for practice. When using clean benchmark datasets (like Iris or Titanic), users have to write long, repetitive custom scripts from scratch just to artificially mess up the data for testing and educational purposes. There is no built-in, one-stop tool in Pandas to inject controlled chaos into a DataFrame. ### Feature Description import pandas as pd import numpy as np import random import string .api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("corrupt") class CorruptAccessor: """ A vectorized Pandas DataFrame accessor to inject synthetic anomalies, missing values, outliers, duplicates, and smart human-like typos for educational and pipeline testing purposes. """ def __init__(self, pandas_obj): self._obj = pandas_obj def _resolve_count(self, param, total_elements): """Helper to support both exact integer counts and float percentages.""" if isinstance(param, float) and 0.0 <= param <= 1.0: return int(param * total_elements) elif isinstance(param, (int, np.integer)): return int(param) else: raise TypeError("Parameters must be either an int (count) or a float between 0.0 and 1.0 (ratio).") def __call__(self, num_nan=0, num_outliers=0, num_duplicates=0, num_typos=0, random_state=None): if random_state is not None: np.random.seed(random_state) random.seed(random_state) # Work on a deep copy to guarantee immutability of the source dataset df = self._obj.copy() num_rows, num_cols = df.shape total_cells = num_rows * num_cols if num_rows == 0 or num_cols == 0: return df # --- 1. Resolve and Validate Injection Targets --- n_nan = self._resolve_count(num_nan, total_cells) if n_nan > total_cells: raise ValueError(f"Resolved NaNs ({n_nan}) cannot exceed total cells ({total_cells}).") numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns total_numeric_cells = num_rows * len(numeric_cols) n_outliers = self._resolve_count(num_outliers, total_numeric_cells) if n_outliers > total_numeric_cells: raise ValueError(f"Resolved outliers ({n_outliers}) cannot exceed total numeric cells ({total_numeric_cells}).") n_duplicates = self._resolve_count(num_duplicates, num_rows) text_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns total_text_cells = num_rows * len(text_cols) n_typos = self._resolve_count(num_typos, total_text_cells) if n_typos > total_text_cells: raise ValueError(f"Resolved typos ({n_typos}) cannot exceed total text cells ({total_text_cells}).") # --- 2. Vectorized Fault Injection Pipelines --- # Pipeline A: Global Vectorized NaN Injection if n_nan > 0: flat_indices = np.random.choice(total_cells, size=n_nan, replace=False) nan_mask = np.zeros(total_cells, dtype=bool) nan_mask[flat_indices] = True nan_mask = nan_mask.reshape(num_rows, num_cols) for i, col in enumerate(df.columns): col_mask = nan_mask[:, i] if col_mask.any(): df.iloc[col_mask, i] = np.nan # Pipeline B: Statistically Robust Outlier Injection (Vectorized per Column) if n_outliers > 0 and len(numeric_cols) > 0: flat_num_indices = np.random.choice(total_numeric_cells, size=n_outliers, replace=False) outlier_mask = np.zeros(total_numeric_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(numeric_cols)) outlier_mask.ravel()[flat_num_indices] = True for i, col in enumerate(numeric_cols): col_mask = outlier_mask[:, i] if col_mask.any(): std_dev = df[col].std() if pd.isna(std_dev) or std_dev == 0: std_dev = 1.0 df.loc[col_mask, col] = (df.loc[col_mask, col] * 3) + (5 * std_dev) # Pipeline C: Vectorized Duplicate Injection if n_duplicates > 0: duplicated_rows = df.sample(n=n_duplicates, replace=True, random_state=random_state) df = pd.concat([df, duplicated_rows], ignore_index=True) # Pipeline D: Smart Realistic Text Typo Injection if n_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0: flat_text_indices = np.random.choice(total_text_cells, size=n_typos, replace=False) typo_mask = np.zeros(total_text_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(text_cols)) typo_mask.ravel()[flat_text_indices] = True def _mutate_string(val): """Helper to simulate realistic human typing errors dynamically.""" s = str(val) if not s or s == "nan": return s # Randomly pick an error type: deletion, substitution, or insertion operation = random.choice(['delete', 'substitute', 'insert']) random_char = random.choice(string.ascii_lowercase) if len(s) <= 1: return s + random_char if operation == 'delete': return s[:-1] elif operation == 'substitute': return s[:-1] + random_char else: # insert return s + random_char for i, col in enumerate(text_cols): col_mask = typo_mask[:, i] if col_mask.any(): # Apply the dynamic typo mutation function strictly to the masked cells df.loc[col_mask, col] = df.loc[col_mask, col].apply(_mutate_string) return df ### Alternative Solutions ### Current Workaround / Alternative Code: Currently, users and educators have to write verbose, loop-heavy, or non-vectorized custom functions to perturb their data cell-by-cell. A typical suboptimal workaround looks like this: `python import pandas as pd import numpy as np import random def manual_corrupt(df, num_nan=0, num_typos=0): df_dirty = df.copy() # 1. Non-vectorized manual loop for NaNs if num_nan > 0: for _ in range(num_nan): r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1) c = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[1] - 1) df_dirty.iat[r, c] = np.nan # 2. Slow cell-by-cell scalar string manipulation for typos text_cols = df_dirty.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns if num_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0: for _ in range(num_typos): r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1) col = random.choice(text_cols) current_val = str(df_dirty.at[r, col]) # Naive typo injection (just drops the last character) if len(current_val) > 1: df_dirty.at[r, col] = current_val[:-1] return df_dirty ### Additional Context This feature would significantly benefit the Data Science, Machine Learning, and AI educational ecosystem (such as university courses, bootcamps, and online interactive notebooks). Teaching "Data Cleaning" is notoriously hard without messy data, and creating realistic "dirty data" natively with one simple, reproducible function call ( ) would seamlessly close the gap between pristine benchmark datasets and real-world preprocessing challenges. I am willing to contribute or iterate on this implementation based on core-dev feedback regarding where this best fits into the Pandas codebase.

text: ENH: pd.crosstab with normalize='index' and margins=True drops the marginal 'Total' column.. ### Feature Type - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description When creating a contingency table using pd.crosstab, if a user specifies normalize='index' while also requesting margins=True, the resulting DataFrame includes the marginal row (at the bottom) but excludes the marginal column (on the right). While the marginal column would mathematically consist of constants (1.0), its omission prevents the generation of a complete "framed" table for reporting and visualization purposes. It is normal in data science to display both row and column totals in a crosstab. If you select row or column as the sum, it's expect to show 100% on the non-selected column, this is supported by the grand total selection where only the total in the bottom right is 100%. This helps users quick understand what you are trying to convey and reinforces the choice of display The default should be to hide the result which is 1.0 ### Feature Description def _add_margins(self, table, margins_name): # CURRENT BEHAVIOR: # Pandas calculates the sum of columns and rows. # If normalize='index', the row sum is always 1.0. # PROPOSED FIX: # Explicitly check if normalize is 'index' or 'columns' # to prevent the 'Total' column/row from being optimized away. if self.normalize == 'index': # Force add the marginal column of 1.0s table[margins_name] = 1.0 # Calculate the marginal row (the distribution of the columns) # This is the mean of the normalized rows or a separate total calculation column_totals = table.iloc[:, :-1].mean(axis=0) table.loc[margins_name] = column_totals table.at[margins_name, margins_name] = 1.0 return table ### Alternative Solutions none ### Additional Context _No response_

title: ENH: Simplify reading vertically stacked CSV tables
text: ENH: Simplify reading vertically stacked CSV tables. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description The overall goal is reading vertically stacked CSV files, with multiple tables. There is no difficulty in writing such a file with pandas (just append) or reading and splitting horizontally stacked CSV files (but they can be inefficient and more complicated to write). This is not technically a CSV format (according to RFC 4180, since column sizes differ) but a very slight generalisation of it. It doesn't really have a name, but has been re-invented several times, with different ways of determining where to split the table. I think the only form that really needs supporting are known specified lines, e.g. [[''], ['Col1', 'Col2']] would split on blank rows but also on Col1,Col2 rows. I had considered "when the number of columns changes", but I think that's a strictly less useful format (you can't have multiple tables with the same number of columns consecutively), and it could be extended in later if wanted. ### Feature Description Possible solutions I can think of (any one of the following): #### A) Part of TextFileReader chunking This would require the ability to reset the columns state of the reader (either by the user or as part of the implementation). If that is easy to do, then this might be the most straightforward way of implementing this feature. The simplest way of doing this is adding an option chunk_on = None, which can be set to a list of row values (permitted to include the blank row). Importantly the presence of this does not just cause the chunks to be broken off but also the number, header, names and types of columns to be reset (if not specified as a parameter) as if reading a new file. (But it does not reset if chunking because of chunksize, so the two are compatible.) If skip_blank_lines is True, then blank lines can end (if [''] is in chunk_on) but not begin or contribute to a chunk. I.e. consecutive skipped blank lines do not lead to 1x1 NA chunks, do not lead to 1x1 NAs before EOF or before other chunk_on rows, and do not lead to 1xN NA rows in previous or following chunks. If skip_blank_lines is False, then a blank line is interpreted as a row [''] and behaves the same as any other row (perhaps aside from NA conversion). If skip_blank_lines is True and [''] is not in chunk_on, then it is as if reading the file without blank lines in. (This should be the same as currently, aside from the new parameter cases.) Usage would look something like this #### B) Implement a function to directly read vertically stacked CSV (or an parameter read_csv is overloaded with). This is the simplest and fastest from the user's perspective but possibly the least convenient to implement, and raises many questions about the interface. This could return an iterable (forward compatible if changed to some object type) of the distinct tables. One option that might not cost much in terms of implementation is to convert the existing read_csv implementation to work on a stack (via growing array) of the states it currently uses one of. Everything works mostly the same (with the new additions e.g. new header rows) but on the state at the top of the stack. If splitting is not permitted (read_csv) then nothing new is ever pushed to the stack (beyond the first element). When a split is identified, it simply pushes a new state to the stack and works on that. #### C) Based on the skiprows/nrows approach: implement a way of reading this data from the file somehow, so that the file can then be read again several times for each table. This is bad for performance because it multiplies IO operations. Also the interface is a bit questionable and specific (e.g. if split by known headers - does it take a list of them and generate a new column indexing it?). Basically a much worse version of A. #### D) Improve the post-processing of the merged file This might be easier to implement than A and could be more generically useful, but is going off the path a bit and has some corner cases. This would probably involve: A splitting operation (which would involve the processing steps 1, 2 & optionally 5 since you might want to keep the index in some cases) One or more operations for re-interpreting the table with the first row as headers, newly inferred dtypes, removal of columns (covering processing steps 3, 4, 6) ### Alternative Solutions There are several possible approaches for reading the file today (but then splitting and processing is where it gets complex): A) read_csv with header=None and names=range(N) where N >= the number of columns in each table. An upper bound on N has to be known in advance. B) Multiple read_csv calls with skiprows and nrows. This requires knowing the split indices in advance. C) Use the standard library csv module and put the results into one or more dataframes (either splitting there or later). This doesn't have many of the niceties of pandas' read_csv including performance, but If splitting with pandas (there is probably room for improvement here as I am only a beginner with pandas): 1. Use df.groupby(<df condition>.cumsum()) to split on splitting rows 2. Optionally (depending on the type of splitter), remove splitting rows and empty group items (or replace multiple empty groups with one) 3. If there are header rows a) Set each df's columns to the first row b) Drop the header row c) Unset the column name on the df 4. Remove columns that should not be present. If splitting by known column counts or names then keep only those e.g. df[['col1', 'col2']]. If splitting by blank rows or knxown lines the best approach is probably to remove all-NA columns (technically though it could still be a valid column that just happens to be all NA) 5. Reset all indexes with drop=True 6. If you know the types of the data, convert them all. If you don't, then you are out of luck, and must leave them as strings or use a series of try-catches on each element with conversion operations to guess a type. Possibly you would have to set the NA parameters so that a present column is never treated as NaN (might not work for float NaN) As you can see this is quite involved and somewhat error prone. Arguably the reason for all this complexity is because it was not a very well defined data frame to begin with. It would be nice if some or all of this process could be simplified. ### Additional Context Related: As mentioned in the related issue, this is not a good format for long-term or professional storage. I think it is worth supporting to some degree because people have mentioned needing to read this format several times - not just the related issue, but there are some examples on stackoverflow, and the documentation link "read_csv in action" FAQ for multiple tables says: "If the file structure is complex, you might need to pre-process the file or use additional libraries to extract the specific table. Pandas alone may not directly handle complex multi-table CSV files." It would be good if pandas just supported this use case directly or more easily. I do believe it has its own niche for short-term, informal and internal data where the schema is implicit (whatever data I happen to be dumping). The use case I have is testing information from a language that isn't Python. Reaching for HDF or SQL here is extremely heavy handed (dependencies, file/dataset setup) and unnecessary while CSV is a very natural and convenient human readable format, requiring no dependencies. (Because I can just write out the format myself, without having to think about the binary layout.) I have a couple of very big tables (proper CSV files), and then several small tables (often metadata). I don't really want to have a single CSV file for each very small table (which probably isn't very efficient in terms of IO operations, and is more files to manage).

text: ENH: Add DataFrame.memory_report() for actionable dtype optimization suggestions. = 50% savings potential """ ### Alternative Solutions df.info(memory_usage='deep'). This is the closest native.But no guidance on how to fix it. ### Additional Context Design Decisions Zero side effects. memory_report() never modifies the DataFrame. Applying suggestions is always an explicit opt-in via report.apply(df). Safe-only suggestions. Every suggestion is lossless by default: Integer downcasts are validated against actual min/max values Float32 suggestions are validated: values are cast to float32 and checked for overflow before recommending apply() wraps each conversion in a try/except and warns on failure — it never raises Null awareness. The report flags columns with nulls so users know before applying dtype changes that may affect null representation. Overflow guard for floats. The implementation detects when a finite float64 value would become ±inf after float32 cast, and keeps float64. Composable return type. Returning a MemoryReport rather than just printing means the output is usable in notebooks, CI pipelines, and data quality checks.

title: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs
text: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs. Hi pandas team, thank you for maintaining such a foundational library. pandas is often the first stop for people who are building data workflows that later feed into LLM or RAG systems (corpus cleaning, chunking, metadata enrichment, offline evaluation, and so on). I maintain an MIT-licensed project called **WFGY Problem Map**, which is a 16-question diagnostic checklist for RAG / LLM pipelines in production. It focuses on data and retrieval failure modes (ingestion gaps, chunking pathologies, vector store issues, evaluation leaks, etc), not on model weights. Why I think this might be relevant for pandas users: - Many real-world RAG systems start from pandas DataFrames (documents, logs, event streams) before anything is embedded or indexed. - Several of the 16 failure modes are about how tabular and semi-structured data are transformed and filtered before they reach a retriever. - The checklist is tooling-agnostic and can be applied no matter whether people use pandas alone or in combination with other frameworks. For credibility: the same checklist has already been included in a few curated / academic ecosystems such as - ToolUniverse by Harvard MIMS Lab - Multimodal RAG Survey by QCRI LLM Lab - Rankify (University of Innsbruck) Suggestion: If you think it could be useful for your users, would you consider adding a small link in your docs or resource section such as > “RAG / LLM debugging checklist: WFGY Problem Map (16 failure modes)” > Project home: Thanks again for all your work on pandas and for considering this small suggestion. Best, PSBigBig

title: ENH: Nearest_in_time fill for time series data
text: ENH: Nearest_in_time fill for time series data. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description While working with time series data, I ran into a case where missing values needed to be filled using observations that were closest in time, rather than only forward or backward. pandas currently offers ffill / bfill and numeric interpolation, but neither fits this use case well. The data was irregularly sampled and contained a mix of numeric measurements and categorical state columns. Forward or backward fill was too directional, and interpolation was not applicable to categorical data and also introduced new values. What I needed was a way to fill missing values by looking at the nearest observations in time, regardless of direction, and to optionally consider more than one nearby point, with closer observations having more influence. There does not seem to be a built-in, time-aware way in pandas to express this kind of nearest-neighbor imputation during preprocessing. ### Feature Description Assume we have a numeric time series indexed by timestamps. Some values are missing, and the data is not assumed to be evenly spaced. Timestamp -> Value 2024-01-01 00:00 -> 10 2024-01-01 01:00 -> 12 2024-01-01 02:00 -> nan 2024-01-01 03:00 -> 16 2024-01-01 04:00 -> nan 2024-01-01 05:00 -> 20 2024-01-01 06:00 -> 22 2024-01-01 07:00 -> nan 2024-01-01 08:00 -> 27 2024-01-01 09:00 -> 30 for the missing values, i ended up reasoning in terms of how old the nearby observations were. at 2024-01-01 02:00, the closest known values are at 01:00 and 03:00. both are one hour away, so neither feels clearly more relevent than the other. in that case it makes sense to take something in between, which gives a value around 14. at 2024-01-01 04:00, the situation is similar. the surrounding values at 03:00 and 05:00 are equally close in time, so the missing value naturally falls between 16 and 20, giving roughly 18. for 2024-01-01 07:00, the nearest values are 22 at 06:00 and 27 at 08:00. again, both are one hour away, so neither should dominate. a value around 24.5 reflects that both nearby points are equally informative. what matters here is not whether the value comes from the past or the future, but how close it is in time. closer observations feel more reliable than older ones, and when two observations are equally close, they should influence the result equally. if this direction seems reasonable, i can put together a small prototype or share some exploratory code to illustrate the behavior and edge cases. ### Alternative Solutions - ### Additional Context _No response_

title: ENH: Data Entropy & Information Loss Tracking for DataFrame Transformations
text: ENH: Data Entropy & Information Loss Tracking for DataFrame Transformations. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description Pandas does not provide any method to measure the information loss which occurs when DataFrame transformations are applied. Data resolution decreases permanently through common operations because users cannot observe this reduction which results from rounding and binning and aggregation and encoding and filtering and deduplication. Users create data compression that exceeds proper limits which leads to the loss of valuable information without their awareness. I want pandas to provide users with information loss measurements which show how transformations affect data processing because this will help them choose preprocessing methods and identify excessive operations which will improve their data pipeline trust. ### Feature Description The system will start tracking operational data transformations through its mandatory tracking system which will record every DataFrame transformation that occurs. The feature would: - The system will calculate entropy values at the column level using Shannon entropy for discrete data and histogram-based entropy for continuous data. - The system will measure information loss through its normalized entropy difference calculation which compares two different states. - The system will track information loss from operations that occur within a monitoring environment. Example API: with df.track_information() as info: df["price"] = df["price"].round(0) df["age_group"] = pd.cut(df["age"], bins=5) info.report() Conceptual implementation def entropy(series): if is_discrete(series): p = value_counts(series) / len(series) return -sum(p * log2(p)) else: bins = adaptive_bins(series) p = histogram(series, bins) / len(series) return -sum(p * log2(p)) The system performs lazy entropy calculations which apply to specific columns that undergo changes. The system applies adaptive binning to continuous data in order to produce consistent estimation results. The system calculates dataset-level information loss by summing all column-specific information losses. The feature requires user activation because it creates no performance impact until the user decides to use it. The system enables users to monitor DataFrame transformation impacts on information content while maintaining the original pandas functional behavior. ### Alternative Solutions Multiple different methods exist as potential alternatives for evaluation. Relying on documentation or user discipline Users would need to decide how much information they lost through their transformation work. The current system proves unmanageable because it creates errors while users cannot track the total impact which develops throughout their different workflows. Heuristic warnings for specific operations Pandas should develop a system which generates alerts about dangerous functions which include binning and rounding as destructive actions. The system would operate at a broad level but its results would not show the actual information loss degree which occurs through a specific dataset. Downstream model metrics (e.g., feature importance, performance) The model behavior permits users to infer information loss yet this method only works during the machine learning stage and it does not serve general data analysis or reporting purposes. External profiling or data quality tools Existing tools examine missing data and data distribution patterns and schema validation processes, but they lack the ability to monitor how data transformations create information loss which they can trace back to particular processes. The available alternatives failed to meet requirements because they lacked the ability to show information loss which occurs during pandas operations at both direct and transformation-level contexts. ### Additional Context _No response_

text: ENH: Add .center() method to DataFrame/Series for inspecting middle rows.. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description I wish I could use pandas to inspect the middle rows of a DataFrame or Series using a simple method like .center(), analogous to .head() and .tail(). ### Feature Description def center(self, n: int = 5): """ Return the middle n rows. Parameters ---------- n : int, default 5 Number of rows to select. Returns ------- type of caller The subset of the DataFrame or Series. """ total_len = len(self) # Edge case: If the requested window is larger than the data, return the whole object # (consistent with .head() and .tail() behavior) if n >= total_len: return self # Calculate the middle index mid_idx = total_len // 2 # Determine start index (integer division handles odd/even n automatically) start = max(0, mid_idx - (n // 2)) # Determine end index end = start + n return self.iloc[start:end] ### Alternative Solutions # Manual slicing with iloc mid = len(df) // 2 df.iloc[mid - 2 : mid + 3] ### Additional Context This feature addresses a gap in the API symmetry. head() allows inspection of the start, and tail() allows inspection of the end. center() would complete the inspection triad, making it intuitive to check the interior of the dataframe without leaving the method-chaining syntax.

title: ENH: Decay-weighted rolling aggregations with defined behavior for duplicate timestamps
text: ENH: Decay-weighted rolling aggregations with defined behavior for duplicate timestamps. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description Pandas provides rolling and time-based window aggregations for time-indexed data, but there is currently no built-in way to compute decay-weighted aggregations (e.g. exponential time decay) with well-defined behavior under irregular sampling and duplicate timestamps. In practical datasets such as event logs, financial transactions, or sensor bursts, multiple observations may share the same timestamp, and users often want recent observations to contribute more heavily via a decay function rather than a fixed window cutoff. Today, users typically work around this by: manually computing weights and applying + resampling or reindexing to a regular grid (which can distort the data) using ad-hoc NumPy logic outside pandas These approaches are error-prone, slow, and lack consistent semantics for ties and normalization. ### Feature Description This issue proposes discussing support for decay-weighted rolling aggregations over time-indexed data, where weights are a function of time distance rather than observation order. Key aspects to clarify include: How decay functions (e.g. exponential) should be parameterized in time units How duplicate timestamps ("ties") should be aggregated before or during weighting How normalization should behave when windows contain sparse or coincident observations Whether this should extend existing APIs or be introduced as a new aggregation mechanism At a high level, the goal would be to define consistent, well-documented semantics rather than immediately finalize an API. If this direction aligns with pandas’ design principles, I would be happy to prototype or iterate on an implementation based on maintainer feedback. ### Alternative Solutions Current workarounds include manually computing decay weights and using + , resampling irregular data to a fixed frequency, or exporting data to NumPy/SciPy and re-importing the results. These approaches work in some cases but tend to be verbose, error-prone, and inconsistent, especially when dealing with irregular sampling or duplicate timestamps. Pandas’ existing methods cover exponential weighting based on observation order, but they don’t directly address time-based decay on irregular time indexes or define behavior for coincident timestamps in rolling/windowed contexts. ### Additional Context _No response_

title: ENH: Add an opt in operation report for time memory and copy behavior
text: ENH: Add an opt in operation report for time memory and copy behavior. ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description I want a reliable way to understand why a single pandas operation is slow or uses far more memory than I expect. When a merge, groupby, sort, or rolling call suddenly takes minutes or crashes with out of memory, pandas completes the work or fails without telling me what path it took, how many temporary arrays were created, or where the time went. That leaves me guessing, rewriting code, and trying different dtypes and arguments until something improves. External profilers can show Python level hotspots, but they do not answer the pandas specific questions I need in the moment. I need something that can tell me whether a join built a large hash table, whether groupby spent most of its time building the grouper, whether a sort triggered large copies, and whether Copy on Write forced unexpected materialization. With that information I could make simple changes like adjusting key dtypes, choosing observed or sort settings, reducing columns earlier, or validating join cardinality. Without it, debugging performance and memory spikes is slow, fragile, and hard to reproduce. ### Feature Description A practical way to build this is to introduce an opt in collector that wraps a single pandas operation and produces a compact report. When diagnostics are turned off, nothing happens apart from one cheap check, so there is no meaningful overhead in normal use. The public entry point can be pd.diagnostics.report(func, *args, **kwargs) with an optional context manager for the same behavior. Internally, the wrapper sets a thread local reference to the active collector, starts wall time measurement and optional memory tracking, executes the operation, then stops tracking and clears the thread local. After the call completes, the collector freezes the captured metrics into a DiagnosticsReport object, which is attached to the returned result via a private attribute. A public DataFrame.explain() method can then format that report as text or json. On the pandas internals side, the only required plumbing is a small helper such as pd.diagnostics._collector() that returns None when diagnostics are disabled. Hot paths can call this helper and, when it is present, record a few coarse phases using begin and end markers, plus counts for allocations and copies at places where pandas already allocates new arrays or forces a copy. Instrumentation can start with merge, groupby, sort, and rolling. Memory reporting can rely on tracemalloc as a best effort estimate and remain optional because it adds overhead. ### Alternative Solutions Today the closest options are general purpose profilers and memory tools. We can time operations with timeit or perf_counter, profile CPU with cProfile or py spy, and track allocations with tracemalloc or external packages like memory profiler or scalene. These tools are useful, but they are not pandas aware, so they do not explain which internal path was taken, how many intermediate arrays were created, or what simple argument and dtype changes would help. Pandas itself offers pieces like DataFrame.info() and memory_usage() plus performance guidance in the docs, and merge validation can catch some join blowups early, but none of these provide an on demand structured report for a single operation. ### Additional Context The idea was basically from other existing frameworks. For e.g. Apache Spark has a built in DataFrame.explain(), polars has LazyFrame.explain(), duckdb has EXPLAIN, etc. Please let me know if the idea sounds good, i can dedicate some time and start working on the PR.
