title: Sandboxed Copilot sessions hang during MCP startup when using a localhost proxy
text: Sandboxed Copilot sessions hang during MCP startup when using a localhost proxy. <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates --> <!-- Please attach logs to help us diagnose your issue --> - Copilot Chat Extension Version: Not recorded; affected session uses the native Copilot Agent Host. - VS Code Version: 1.141.0-insider, commit - OS Version: macOS 26.7.1, Apple Silicon - Feature: New Copilot session in the Agents window, sandbox enabled - Selected model: Not recorded; the failure occurs during MCP initialization, before model dispatch. - Runtime: Copilot SDK , runtime - Logs: Sanitized diagnostic evidence below; full logs are not attached. ## Steps to Reproduce Using Environment Variables 1. Run an HTTP proxy on (tested with Proxyman). 2. Add Playwright to , preserving existing entries: 3. Fully quit VS Code Insiders. Set both proxy environment variables and launch VS Code from the same terminal: No VS Code proxy setting is needed. Use both variables: alone does not reproduce because npm uses for its HTTPS registry requests. 4. Create a new Copilot session in the Agents window. Enable sandbox and Playwright MCP; leave local-network access disabled (the default). 5. Send "Say hello." **Alternative using a VS Code setting:** This also reproduces if, instead of setting the environment variables, you set `"http.proxy": " in VS Code and fully restart it. The setting forwards both proxy variables to the runtime; repeat steps 4-5. ## Actual The new session stalls during MCP initialization. Confirmed comparisons: | Configuration | Result | |---|---| | Only , sandbox on | Does not reproduce | | Both proxy variables, sandbox on | Reproduces | | Same proxy variables, new session with sandbox off | Works | OTel is working and is not part of this issue. ## Expected Sandboxed MCP startup should use the configured proxy without requiring the entire sandbox or general localhost isolation to be disabled. ## Diagnostic Evidence An isolated test with the same SDK/runtime, real , and a non-forwarding localhost proxy reproduced: - npm registry fetches fail with . - No requests reach the proxy. - With normal npm retries, startup takes approximately 65 seconds and fails with . VS Code supplies proxy environment variables but does not populate the runtime's sandbox route. The sandbox denies localhost access by default. A controlled MCP test succeeds when that explicit sandbox proxy route is supplied, while direct loopback access remains denied. This points to missing proxy/sandbox integration rather than proxy authentication or TLS. The separate upstream deferred-MCP-startup fix addresses premature startup/repeated waits, not this missing proxy route. The newer runtime has not been end-to-end retested for this report. *🤖 Authored with GitHub Copilot on behalf of .*

title: HydraFusion: hydrafusion_turn total_nano_aiu misses background subagent spend after a phase ends
text: HydraFusion: hydrafusion_turn total_nano_aiu misses background subagent spend after a phase ends. Related: microsoft/vscode#339921, microsoft/vscode-internalbacklog#8904 ## Problem The (and ) under-reports the cost of a HydraFusion turn. The complete cost is . In a live Critique turn in Code OSS (gpt-5.6-luna draft, gpt-5.6-terra critic): | Source | nano-AIU | |---|---:| | (matches the per-call sum exactly) | 1,917,421,000 | | | 1,314,302,000 | | **Missing** | **603,119,000** | The gap splits into two causes: | Missing | Cause | Runtime bug? | |---:|---|---| | 183,154,000 | 3 calls by the rubber-duck subagent that the draft phase started. They billed after the phase ended. | **Yes** | | 419,965,000 | The follow-up turn the runtime runs after a background agent finishes ( , then ). It bypasses the HydraFusion orchestrator. | By design | ## Root cause (the runtime part) A root phase's usage is the session-wide usage measured just before and just after the phase runs: / around in (github/copilot-agent-runtime). Because the window is time-based: - Background subagents started by a phase that bill after the phase returns are left out. - Unrelated work running during the phase (for example, a background agent from an earlier turn) can be charged to the phase. Review phases don't have this problem: totals the events tagged with the phase. Also, is sent when the chosen phase is applied, before background work finishes, so it can't be a complete per-turn total. ## Proposed fix - **Runtime:** attribute root-phase usage by ownership rather than by time window. Tag subagent and background usage with the phase that started it ( already carries the parent identity), and total phase usage from tagged events, as does. Usage that arrives after the phase ends needs a home too, for example a supplementary or late aggregate. - **Analysis:** until then, use for cost per turn, and treat as a lower bound covering only the workflow. ## Repro ### Setup 1. Launch Code OSS with the Copilot harness and select the HydraFusion model. 2. Set permissions to **Allow all** so the draft phase can start a background subagent without pausing. 3. Run **Developer: Set Log Level...** and select **Trace**. 4. Run **Developer: Open Logs Folder**, open the newest window's , and note the current end of the file so the next turn is easy to isolate. ### Prompt Use a repository where read-only investigation is meaningful, then send: The important ingredients are , , and : they let the phase that owns the subagent finish while the child is still making billed calls. Routing is model-driven, so repeat if the turn does not select Critique or does not start a background agent. ### Verify the event order In the new portion of , isolate one host turn and confirm: 1. has . 2. A root (normally the draft) completes. 3. One or more later events have a subagent / . These are calls made by the rubber-duck child after its owning phase completed. 4. is emitted before that background work is fully accounted for. 5. An notification triggers the follow-up that calls ; its model calls are outside the HydraFusion orchestrator by design. 6. closes the host turn. ### Compare the totals For that host turn, record: - **A** = the sum of across all events. - **T** = on . - **L** = the sum of the rubber-duck calls that occur after the owning root phase completed. - **F** = the sum of from the post- follow-up. Expected: is the runtime attribution bug. is the separate, by-design follow-up cost. In the observed turn: ### Control Repeat with the same prompt but require the subagent to run synchronously (or require the parent to wait for it before finishing the phase). The late-subagent component should disappear because the child bills inside the current phase's before/after window. This distinguishes the timing/ownership bug from a general token-accounting mismatch.

title: Agents window: worktree size scanning, high renderer CPU/memory, and hours-old AHP log backlog
text: Agents window: worktree size scanning, high renderer CPU/memory, and hours-old AHP log backlog. ## Summary The running Agents window becomes very sluggish while client-side worktree disk-usage traversal and AHP transport logging appear in renderer CPU profiles. The renderer has ~10.34 GiB private committed memory on a 16 GB machine, and an actively written AHP log is approximately 137 minutes behind its event timestamps. The evidence implicates worktree measurement and its logging overhead, but this is **not yet a controlled reproduction proving that automatic cleanup suggestions initiated the scans or that this explains all the slowdown**. The storage-management UI is another possible entry point. ## Environment - Windows ARM64, 12 logical processors, 15.61 GiB usable physical RAM. - VS Code 1.141.0-insider, commit ae1080a9ed1098a8b532c6cfd50977d784b29e6d; build timestamp 2026-10-05T04:48:02Z. - Long-lived Agents window with multiple session worktrees, including a large dependency tree. - Investigated live using global ; no restart, setting changes, or mitigation applied. - The supplied user-settings snapshot contains no explicit override of . Effective configuration/experiment treatment was not queried. ## Measurements ### Live process sample (8.02 seconds, around 23:39 CEST) | Metric | Agents renderer | Local agent-host server | | --- | ---: | ---: | | CPU seconds consumed | 8.83 | 3.03 | | Equivalent logical cores busy | 1.10 | 0.38 | | Resident RAM | 3.60 GiB | 0.15 GiB | | Private committed memory | 10.34 GiB | 0.35 GiB | Only 1.23 GiB physical memory was free. Private commit is not resident RAM; paging was not measured. The renderer had earlier shown ~4.9 GiB resident RAM. ### Renderer CPU profiles Two captures were taken with , using 1 ms and 2 ms sampling intervals, and exported as files (retained locally; not attached here). First capture: 24.91 s elapsed / 24.50 s sampled: - Garbage collection: 3.81 s (15.6%). - String encoding: 2.71 s (11.0%). - Buffer concat: 2.03 s self (8.3%). - MessagePort callback in : 2.47 s self. - Idle: 0.106 s (0.43%). - , , and per-file calls appear in mapped stacks. Second capture: 13.53 s, with 3.13 s GC (23.1%) and sustained IPC/logging activity. **44-51% of sampled time was unattributed time; this portion is not assigned to the scan.** These are sampling observations, not a complete causal breakdown. ### Request volume and delayed logging A bounded 4 MiB tail of the active local AHP log contained: - 4,749 requests. - 376 requests. - 3,796 responses. - All sampled requests were under one local worktree. - 5,035 / 5,125 requests (98.2%) targeted paths inside . - The 8,921 messages spanned 1.324 seconds of **historical event timestamps** (~6,738 messages/s). This is not the current request-generation rate. In a fresh 8.36-second observation, that log grew by 18,870,356 bytes (~2.15 MiB/s). Events being written around 23:39 local time were timestamped around 21:22:47: **~137 minutes behind**. This establishes a delayed log drain, not SSD saturation. The renderer log contains **111 worktree-measurement timeout warnings across 23 distinct sessions**, from 13:34 through 23:24. This does not establish 111 concurrent scans. ## Relevant client-side code 1. [worktreeDiskUsage.ts:35]( batches eight directories, then uses nested to issue a for every child. The limit does not bound per-file RPC concurrency; the traversal accepts no cancellation token. 2. [sessionWorktreeCleanupService.ts:200]( places a two-session limiter around a 10-second . [raceTimeout, async.ts:156]( stops waiting but does not cancel the operation. Timed-out traversals can therefore continue after limiter slots are released. 3. [ahpJsonlLogger.ts:119]( buffers serialized messages for a queued asynchronous drain. Logging/encoding/concatenation appear in the profiles. No heap-retention analysis was performed, so the 10.34 GiB commit is not conclusively attributed to this queue. The expensive traversal orchestration is in the **client renderer**. The agent host serves the metadata requests; a separate server defect has not been established. ## Status in newer builds I checked the same traversal and measurement code in both the latest published Windows ARM64 Insiders ( ) and current main ( ) on October 5. Both retain the per-file fan-out and non-cancelling timeout. Related: #338502 introduced the feature; #339348 / 06a1c70075c89ce81acd39767b024e904c6d3066 added the timeout and progress reporting, not cancellation of the underlying traversal. ## Reproduction status / expected behavior Observed in an existing long-lived window, not yet reproduced from a clean window. A useful targeted repro would trigger worktree storage measurement with multiple large dependency-heavy worktrees, let measurements exceed 10 seconds, and verify that in-flight scans/RPCs stop rather than accumulate. The initiating action/configuration in the observed session remains unknown. Expected: background worktree-size measurement should have bounded concurrency, effective cancellation, and bounded logging overhead, without starving the UI. Potential fixes to investigate: bound actual file RPC concurrency, propagate cancellation through the traversal, consider host-side aggregate size measurement, and bound the transport-log backlog. Disabling automatic suggestions plus reloading was suggested but **not tested**. Assigning to as author of the feature and measurement-timeout change for initial triage.

text: Extension host crashes repeatedly — EXC_BREAKPOINT at constant offset 0x547a240 in Electron Framework (macOS arm64). # Extension host crashes repeatedly — EXC_BREAKPOINT at constant offset 0x547a240 in Electron Framework (macOS arm64) ## Versions and environment - VS Code version: 1.143.1 (installed Oct 22, 2026) — commit hash: e646868227c3e3a9e3f24277c8c7220be42c0be7 [vscode-exthost-crash-report-20261027.zip]( [exthost.log]( - OS version: macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple Silicon (Mac15,9), 64 GB RAM - Extensions running at crash time: mistralai.mistral-vibe-code, druideinformatique.antidote, ms-python.python, ms-python.vscode-pylance, ms-python.debugpy, ms-python.vscode-python-envs, mhutchie.git-graph, stkb.rewrap, mechatroner.rainbow-csv, mathematic.vscode-pdf ## Summary Since the evening of Oct 24, 2026, the extension host process crashes repeatedly (10+ times over three days), each time killing all running extensions and the AI-agent child process they manage. The interval between crashes varies from a few minutes to half a day. There is no reliable reproduction: crashes happen during normal work (edits, extension interaction), including while the machine was otherwise idle overnight. ## Steps to reproduce Not reliably reproducible. Crashes occurred during ordinary editing sessions, most frequently while the Mistral Vibe extension was actively running agent sessions (its child process emits a high volume of stderr log lines streamed through the extension host logger). ## Observed behavior - renderer.log records each event as: - exthost.log ends cleanly before each crash — no exception, no shutdown trace. - VS Code auto-restarts the extension host; extensions reload. - Not memory-related: 64 GB RAM, 93 % free, zero swap; no jetsam kills, no OOM evidence. - No third-party antivirus or cleaning tools involved. ## Crash dump analysis Crashpad minidumps are written to . I parsed them with a custom minidump parser (exception stream + module list). Every dump from Oct 24 onward shows the same signature: - Mach exception type 6 (EXC_BREAKPOINT — an intentional abort/trap in native code) - Faulting address inside **Electron Framework**, at a **constant offset ** in every single dump (ASLR base differs across launches; the offset does not) Crash times (all matching an exthost restart): Timeline context: VS Code 1.143.1 installed Oct 22; the mistralai.mistral-vibe-code extension was updated to 1.27.0 on the morning of Oct 24; the first crash at this exact offset occurred Oct 24 at 19:50. ## Attachments - — 11 Crashpad minidumps (Oct 24–27), all with the identical signature above - , — logs of window session 20261026T123124 containing four of the crashes Local file paths in the logs/dumps ( ) are machine-local; happy to provide symbolized stacks if given instructions for the Electron dSYM symbols.

title: Large Codex chat restore stalls in JSON-RPC buffering and accessibility Markdown block counting
text: Large Codex chat restore stalls in JSON-RPC buffering and accessibility Markdown block counting. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> Opening large existing Codex chats in the native Agents window takes tens of seconds to minutes, affecting the Agents view across workspaces. Local profiling identified two expensive paths during restoration. - VS Code: stable 1.142.0, commit - OS: macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon, 64 GB RAM - Harness: Codex in the native Agents window - Nonstandard configuration: a local Codex SDK 0.161.0 override was already in use. This has not been independently reproduced with the bundled SDK. - All extensions disabled: not tested. Insiders: not tested. - No system memory pressure or swap exhaustion was observed during diagnosis. Steps that exposed the issue: 1. Use the native Agents window with a large existing Codex conversation containing Markdown and tool responses. 2. Select the pinned conversation, or restart VS Code and restore it. 3. Observe a long stall before the conversation becomes usable. Expected: selecting an existing conversation should remain responsive, with history loading and accessibility-label generation avoiding repeated work over large payloads. The affected conversations are private, so this report does not include an exact end-to-end transcript reproducer. The observations below and proposed synthetic tests are intended to help isolate the relevant code paths. **Observed hotspot 1: JSON-RPC stdout buffering** The Codex client's callback repeatedly concatenates and scans a growing partial JSON-RPC response. When a large response arrives across many stdout chunks, bytes already seen are processed repeatedly. Approximately 90.7% of one hung Agent Host CPU sample was in this callback. A local experimental parser retained fragments and joined only complete messages. It passed 95 boundary, Unicode, ordering, and error checks. An isolated synthetic 32 MiB fragmented-response benchmark improved from approximately 2,023 ms to 35 ms. This is a microbenchmark, not an application-wide speedup claim. **Observed hotspot 2: accessibility Markdown block counting** The session renderer accessibility provider's uses the full Markdown lexer to count table and code blocks. A local trace attributed 47.6 seconds to , although this operation only needed top-level block counts. A local experimental replacement used with equivalent CR/CRLF normalization for this count operation. It passed 6,637 count comparisons, including CommonMark and generated edge cases. An isolated synthetic 490,041-character case improved from approximately 2,863 ms to 4 ms with identical counts. The change was limited to accessibility block counting; the general visible Markdown-rendering path was unchanged. **Diagnostic workaround and limits** Both changes were applied locally in memory as version-checked temporary diagnostic workarounds, with the original signed application preserved. They are not upstream fixes. Afterward, three large pinned conversations loaded in approximately 1-5.5 seconds when selected in a running app. Full startup plus restoration of the largest conversation still took approximately 19 seconds. These are local observations, not controlled results across machines or a guarantee for other conversations. Suggested maintainer validation: 1. Feed the JSON-RPC receiver one large valid message split across many small chunks. Also cover multiple lines per chunk, CRLF, Unicode boundaries, and malformed lines followed by valid lines. Verify ordering and error behavior. 2. Exercise accessibility labels on large synthetic Markdown payloads with expensive inline emphasis/link patterns. Compare table/code block counts and resulting label contents. 3. Validate normal and screen-reader modes, active streaming, switching conversations, and cold startup. The local comparison checks do not replace upstream regression testing. Potentially related: #342794 describes Codex output-related heap growth, and #337688 describes large Claude history restoration causing OOM. This report concerns measured CPU stalls in stdout buffering and accessibility block counting; it does not establish the same cause as either OOM report. Only sanitized aggregate measurements and software/hardware version information are included. No chat history, private project details, user paths, session identifiers, credentials, raw traces, or attachments are included.

title: [Windows] Critical memory usage and OOM in Chat/Agents, concurrent sessions, and Agent plugin handling
text: [Windows] Critical memory usage and OOM in Chat/Agents, concurrent sessions, and Agent plugin handling. Bug summary VS Code Stable has become extremely difficult to use because of excessive memory consumption and repeated Out of Memory (OOM) errors in my normal profile, particularly when using Chat and Agent features. This appears to be more than a single plugin problem. Agent plugin handling and synchronization are unreliable, and running several Chat/Agent sessions can result in a very large overall memory footprint. These issues seriously affect the stability and usability of VS Code and need urgent attention. Environment - OS: Windows 11, version 25H2 - VS Code: Stable - AI configuration: Custom OpenAI-compatible provider through 9Router - Feature area: Chat, Agent mode, concurrent agent sessions, and Agent plugins - Exact VS Code version: To be added from Help → About Observed behavior I performed a clean-profile test on the same PC to determine whether the problem was caused by my hardware or by my existing VS Code environment. 1. I launched VS Code using a fresh, isolated user-data directory and extension directory, with extensions disabled. 2. The clean instance opened successfully and remained stable without crashing. 3. Task Manager showed approximately 600 MB of memory usage for this clean instance. 4. My normal VS Code profile, which contains my existing configuration, Chat/Agent environment, and extensions/plugins, has reached approximately 6 GB of memory usage and has repeatedly experienced OOM errors. 5. When running approximately four agents concurrently, total VS Code memory usage can reach around 8 GB in my setup. The clean-profile test is important: the same computer can run a fresh VS Code instance normally, while the full environment has a dramatically larger memory footprint. These observations do not prove that a single extension is responsible, but they strongly justify investigating the existing Chat/Agent state, extension host, Agent host, plugin synchronization, and renderer memory usage. Agent plugin support and synchronization problems I also disabled "episodic-memory -marketplace" after discovering the existing report about Agent plugin synchronization causing renderer OOM. However, the broader memory problem needs to be investigated separately rather than treated as solved by disabling one plugin. The current Agent plugin experience appears insufficiently robust. Plugin synchronization can involve large directories and binaries, while plugin enablement and synchronization behavior can be confusing. The VS Code renderer should not need to construct enormous intermediate Base64 strings to transfer large plugin resources, and a user disabling a plugin should be able to rely on that disablement being respected. Please investigate plugin discovery, installation, synchronization, enablement/disablement, and memory management as part of this stability problem. Steps to reproduce 1. Launch VS Code Stable on Windows using a normal profile containing Chat/Agent configuration and extensions/plugins. 2. Use Chat and Agent features, including multiple concurrent agent sessions. 3. Monitor the VS Code process group in Windows Task Manager. 4. Observe the memory footprint grow substantially compared with an isolated clean profile. 5. In my environment, normal usage has reached approximately 6 GB, while running around four agents can bring usage to approximately 8 GB. The normal profile has also experienced repeated Out of Memory errors. Clean-profile comparison: Launching VS Code with "--disable-extensions" and fresh "--user-data-dir" and "--extensions-dir" paths results in a stable instance using approximately 600 MB in Task Manager. I have disabled the episodic-memory plugin as a workaround, but I have not yet established through a controlled before/after measurement whether this alone resolves the plugin-specific synchronization crash. Expected behavior - Chat and Agent sessions should have predictable, bounded memory consumption. - Memory should be released when sessions, rendered code blocks, editor references, and agent processes are no longer needed. - Running multiple agents should not cause uncontrolled memory growth or repeated renderer/extension-host OOM crashes. - Large plugin resources should be streamed or transferred in bounded chunks rather than materialized as massive intermediate strings in the UI renderer. - Disabling a plugin must reliably prevent its activation and any unnecessary synchronization, with a clear and consistent source of truth for plugin enablement. - VS Code should remain responsive and stable during ordinary development workflows involving Chat and several agents. Why this is urgent This is a critical productivity and stability issue. The combination of excessive Chat/Agent memory usage, concurrent-session scaling, and fragile Agent plugin handling has made VS Code extremely frustrating and, at times, practically unusable for my daily development work. The ability to use multiple agents is a major part of the intended workflow. If opening and using these features can consume several gigabytes of memory and lead to OOM crashes, that workflow becomes unreliable and risks interrupting ongoing work. Please prioritize this as a high-impact stability and performance problem and investigate the combined behavior of Chat, Agent sessions, plugin synchronization, renderer memory, and extension/agent hosts. Related issues - "#334892 — Agents window renderer OOM during plugin sync: resourceRead Base64 encoding reaches 4 GB heap" ( - "#332725 — Renderer and extension host OOM when running multiple concurrent Copilot chat/agent sessions (Windows)" ( - "#336200 — Renderer OOM in JSON.stringify / serializeRequestArguments when invoking agent with large chat history" ( These reports describe closely related failure modes involving Agent plugin synchronization, concurrent Chat/Agent sessions, and memory exhaustion while processing large chat histories. I am reporting the additional evidence from my own environment: a clean VS Code profile runs at approximately 600 MB without crashing, while my normal profile reaches approximately 6 GB and concurrent agents can bring usage to around 8 GB. If this report overlaps with an existing investigation, please link these reproduction details to the appropriate tracking issue rather than losing the broader memory-usage and plugin-management concerns. Additional diagnostic information I can provide the exact VS Code version, Process Explorer readings, relevant logs, and a more controlled comparison with the plugin disabled if needed. No API keys, credentials, personal chat transcripts, or private project files are included in this report.

title: Agent host crash-loops with V8 OOM when a large Claude session (GB-sized subagent transcripts) is restored, taking down all sessions
text: Agent host crash-loops with V8 OOM when a large Claude session (GB-sized subagent transcripts) is restored, taking down all sessions. - VS Code Version: 1.139.0 (also 1.138.0) - OS Version: macOS 27.0 (arm64, 24 GB RAM) - Harness: Claude agent host, native Anthropic auth, Agents window ## Summary Restoring or opening one large Claude Code session makes the agent host process run out of V8 heap. It restarts 5 times, gives up, and every other session in the Agents window then fails with "Couldn't open session / Agent Host process stopped after 5 restarts." The heap is at about 3.2 GB when it dies, roughly 7 seconds after the agent host starts. ## The session A Claude Code CLI session discovered by the agent host from : - main transcript: 268 MB - : 1,365 subagent transcripts, 9.4 GB total (a long batch job whose subagents read images) ## Evidence | Launch | OOM crashes | Log lines mentioning the large session | |---|---|---| | 1 | 10 | 16 | | 2 | 21 | 57 | | 3 | 6 | 25 | | 4 | 18 | 44 | | launches that did not touch it (4 of them) | 0 | 0 | Renaming the session's folder stopped the crashes; the main transcript still restores ("Restored session claude:/<id> with 24 turns"). ## Expected The agent host should not need the full transcript and every subagent transcript in memory to list or restore a session. Stream or page history, cap what is loaded for subagents, and if a session is too large, fail that one session instead of taking down the agent host and every other session. A second session with a 1 GB main transcript is at risk too. Related: #336200 (renderer OOM with large chat history), #335232 (large Agent Host conversation over a tunnel).

title: Agents window hangs with thousands of binary text models and a stale origin/HEAD base branch
text: Agents window hangs with thousands of binary text models and a stale origin/HEAD base branch. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested. - VS Code Version: 1.139.0-insider ( , 2026-09-21) - OS Version: macOS, Darwin arm64 25.6.0 - Hardware: Apple M1 Max, 64 GB RAM - Observed: 2026-09-23, approximately 08:28-08:34 CEST ## Summary The **Agents** window became unresponsive while a trivial image-transcription session in was idle with **zero session changes**. Its reported branch comparison was , even though the repository's actual default branch is . The local still pointed to obsolete , at a 2021 commit. That comparison covers **9,883 files**. During the hang, logs show thousands of diagnostic updates for agent-host resources and sustained creation/disposal of text models for PNG/GIF/MP4 files. The Agents renderer reached roughly **200% CPU and 8-9 GB memory**, and its extension host roughly **100-110% CPU**. The stale base branch is a strong candidate trigger for the excessive work. The exact hot JavaScript function and causal link have **not** been confirmed by a JS CPU profile or a controlled before/after test. ## Observed reproduction conditions This was investigated in an existing live session, not yet reduced to a clean-profile reproduction: 1. Open a checkout of on whose local still points to rather than . 2. Create/use a session in the Agents window. In the observed case, the task only transcribed image text and made no file changes. 3. The session metadata reports base branch and offers . 4. The Agents window becomes unresponsive while processing many resources, including binaries. The precise UI action that initiated the resource loading has not been isolated; it is not yet established whether explicitly opening Branch Changes is required. ## Base-branch evidence Commands run in the affected checkout: points at the 2021 commit ( ). The agent-host content-reference URIs in the affected renderer log also reference this SHA. The intended comparison against the locally available is much smaller; this does not imply it has zero branch changes. ## Runtime evidence identified: Separate observations showed the renderer at 12.5-13.9% of the machine's memory. The extension host remained near 100% CPU when the renderer's utilization later dropped. Five-second native samples of both hot processes showed activity in V8/JavaScript execution. They did not provide symbolized JavaScript stacks sufficient to identify the responsible function. ### Incident-specific log counts Across the rotated window-1 extension-host logs, filtering to **2026-09-23 08:xx**, diagnostic updates for resources yielded: - **2,759 diagnostic batches**, from 08:28:41.977 through 08:33:47.117. - **1,491 distinct resource paths**, all associated with the same session. - These included **1,431 PNGs, 21 GIFs, 29 MP4s, and 8 JPGs**. These are counts of logged diagnostic updates, not necessarily nonempty diagnostics, and do not establish that the extension-editing extension caused the hang. The renderer log showed sustained text-model lifecycle activity for binary paths. Sanitized examples: The observed log rate was around 100 model/resource events per second for much of the 08:31-08:32 interval. The log snapshot at 08:32:03 contained 638 , 638 , and 637 entries for agent-host resources that morning. These counts alone do not distinguish a finite backlog from a repeating loop. ## Expected behavior / investigation areas - Handle large branch comparisons without freezing the Agents window or eagerly materializing thousands of binary resources as text models. - Investigate how the session base branch is selected when local is stale and the hosted repository's default branch has changed. - Determine what initiates this resource loading for an idle session and whether it can be bounded, lazy, or cancelled. ## Potential workaround (not yet verified) Repair the local remote-HEAD reference using , then reload/reopen the Agents window. A previously persisted session base branch may need separate correction. Neither the reference nor the session was changed during this investigation, so recovery is not claimed as verified. Related: reports irrelevant Agents branch changes/base selection; this report adds the observed UI hang and large-scale binary text-model processing.

title: Testing: automatic result eviction leaves extension-host run trackers retained
text: Testing: automatic result eviction leaves extension-host run trackers retained. ### Problem Automatic eviction at the test-result history limit disposes the renderer-side result but does not notify the extension host to release the corresponding test-run tracker. This is a remaining ownership path after #333244: that change disposes the result-specific store, while the ordinary eviction branch still does not emit the existing result event. ### Reproduction In the existing test fixture: 1. Push a and mark it complete. 2. Subscribe to , collecting events with a field. 3. Push and complete another 128 distinct results. 4. Check that the original result is disposed and absent from , and that the retained list has 128 entries. 5. Check that exactly one removal notification contains the original result. On the inspected source, step 4 succeeds but step 5 fails: the ordinary eviction path never emits the removal notification. A proposed PR adds this regression to the existing suite, together with immediately-evicted and active-result cases. ### Source path - : calls without firing with . - : the event is the path that forwards to the extension host. - : the coordinator consequently retains the tracker in its request and run-ID maps after ordinary history eviction. Explicit result clearing already emits a removal notification; the reproduction concerns automatic history eviction. ### Expected behavior Notify consumers when history eviction removes a result, and eventually release its extension-host tracker. If the evicted tracker still has genuine running tasks, cleanup should wait for those tasks to end rather than synthesize completion or cancel them. Repeated removal requests and later grouped tasks should remain safe. ### Evidence and limits Observed with VS Code 1.137.0 on macOS arm64. A 129-run probe found 129 corresponding extension-host trackers while renderer history retained 128 results. Those captures were taken at different times, so they are supporting observations, not a settled heap measurement or an exact leaked-byte claim. The deterministic notification regression and source ownership path establish the missing cleanup signal. Source inspected: ; the proposed patch has passed the two complete relevant browser suites (50 tests), lint, client transpilation, and client typechecking on that revision. This report does not claim complete-application memory bounds. Controller-unregistration cleanup is a separate concern.

title: Renderer OOM in JSON.stringify / serializeRequestArguments when invoking agent with large chat history
text: Renderer OOM in JSON.stringify / serializeRequestArguments when invoking agent with large chat history. I'm sorry, I can't do the extension bisect, it's not something I have bandwidth for, nor repro is stable. Dump is available, feel free to ping. Copilot generated based on dump # Renderer OOM in JSON.stringify / serializeRequestArguments when invoking agent with large chat history Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested. The observed workflow uses Copilot Chat with tools; extension bisect has not been performed. ## Environment - VS Code: 1.137.0, Windows x64. - Electron: 42.10.0. - OS build reported by the dump: 10.0.26200.9448. - Affected process: workbench window renderer, not the extension host. - Renderer uptime: approximately 47 hours. - Separate Copilot extension version at crash time: not captured in this analysis. - Latest Insiders reproduction: not tested. ## Summary A renderer terminated with an out-of-memory exception while serializing a chat-agent invocation. The Crashpad V8 annotation records reached through , , and the chat agent invocation path. This is not a session-save stack. The JavaScript heap was using approximately 1,571 MiB of its 4,096 MiB limit. V8's main memory cage reported , despite approximately 2,405 MiB free in aggregate; the largest contiguous free region was only 477 MiB. ## Observed Workflow 1. Use a long-running local Copilot Chat conversation with many tool calls, including multi-megabyte text results. 2. Restore the accumulated conversation and continue interacting with chat. 3. A chat-agent invocation reaches RPC argument serialization, and the renderer terminates with OOM. This describes one investigated crash and its surrounding workflow, not a deterministic minimal reproduction. The exact allocation size and the smallest triggering history have not been established. Expected: Large retained chat data is bounded, externalized, streamed, or rejected with a recoverable error before a renderer-fatal allocation. Actual: The entire workbench window renderer terminates. The parent log reports: ## Crash Evidence Native exception: , raised through . Captured V8 annotation, with installation URLs removed and bundle locations retained: | Crash annotation | Value | | --- | --- | | Heap used | 1,571.1 MiB | | Heap limit | 4,096 MiB | | Heap utilization | 38.3% | | Main cage last allocation status | ran out of reservation | | Main cage largest free region | 477 MiB | | Main cage total free | 2,405 MiB | | Main cage size | 4,096 MiB | | Last OS error | 0 | Two last-resort Mark-Compact collections left live heap usage essentially unchanged at approximately 1,570.6 MiB. These annotations support a contiguous-reservation failure inside the V8 cage, not merely reaching the configured heap limit. They do not measure total machine memory pressure or identify the exact failed allocation size. ## Supporting History Evidence The conversation restored shortly before the crash had an approximately 509 MB JSONL session file when inspected afterward. Its initial snapshot was approximately 476 MB and contained 141 requests. These are decimal file sizes; the file was modified after the crash and is not an exact crash-time payload capture. Inspection of that snapshot, reporting aggregate sizes only, found: - Approximately 256 million string characters under request response content. - Approximately 127 million string characters under request result metadata. - One tool result of approximately 15.8 million characters was identical in a serialized tool-display entry and in . The installed bundle's forwards each included prior response's into invocation history. The chat bridge calls , and the captured serializer branch calls on the argument array. Important distinction: the response-history filter excludes and display entries. The duplicated text is confirmed in persisted storage, not proven to be transmitted twice over RPC. Result metadata is still forwarded. Persisted size is not equivalent to RPC payload size. The large retained history is a strong candidate for the serialization failure, but the minidump does not establish the exact triggering field, complete object graph, or failed allocation size. A fix may involve both core chat/RPC handling and the producer of retained tool-result metadata. ## Related Issues - #305122: Workbench OOM during session storage; closed with a fix, milestone 1.122.0. Its documented stack is / mutation-log extraction, unlike this invocation/RPC stack. - #311225: Open report of Copilot Chat memory growth and crashes. A maintainer notes chat-terminal memory improvements; this report adds a specific RPC serialization failure path. - #332725: Open report of renderer and extension-host OOM during concurrent Copilot sessions; similar symptom, but the same serialization cause is not established. No exact match was identified in the issue searches performed. Please merge or redirect this report if the invocation-serialization failure is already tracked.

title: Agents window renderer OOM during plugin sync: resourceRead Base64 encoding reaches 4 GB heap
text: Agents window renderer OOM during plugin sync: resourceRead Base64 encoding reaches 4 GB heap. Opening Agents window crashes renderer near 4 GB heap limit during plugin resourceRead/base64 transfer VS Code stable 1.136.1, commit a44adf7f53e00964ab890f9f8758a334f1fc15bc, Windows x64, Electron 42.10.0. Workspace is a WSL UNC folder. No prompt or coding operation is required: simply opening the Agents window triggers the failure. Observed twice on 2026-09-07: - 03:31:33: AgentPluginManager starts syncing episodic-memory from the Copilot installed-plugins directory; 03:32:31: renderer exits with reason oom, code -536870904. - 03:35:07: the same plugin sync starts; 03:36:06: the same renderer OOM. Both local Crashpad dumps contain: The installed bundle maps the caller to _handleReverseRequest, resourceRead: The callee builds the output using four per-character string concatenations for each three input bytes. The agent host plugin sync calls fileService.copy on the plugin directory. The plugin directory is approximately 751 MiB including node_modules. Its largest file is node_modules/ -ai/claude-agent-sdk-win32-x64/claude.exe (228410016 bytes). It also includes 20-36 MB ONNX/runtime binaries. The precise file being encoded is not available in the dumps; the largest executable is a strong candidate, not independently proven. The dumps do prove OOM inside this resourceRead encoding path during plugin sync. Related disablement surprise: user settings already contained The settings file predates both crashes. However agentPlugins.enablement in global state does not contain a disabled entry for this plugin URI. The installed bundle uses inspect("chat.plugins.enabledPlugins").policyValue for plugin enforcement and a separate URI-based enablement model. Consequently this user-level setting did not prevent synchronization. Please clarify/migrate the user-facing disablement behavior if this setting is now policy-only. Expected: opening Agents must not exhaust the renderer heap while copying an installed plugin. Large binary transfers should be bounded/chunked or avoid per-character Base64 string accumulation; plugin synchronization should not require materializing huge strings in the UI process. A user-level disablement setting should either work or clearly indicate that it is ineffective. Validation limits: two real crashes and matching local dump/bundle analysis; no clean-profile repro or patched-build validation yet. No crash dumps, personal file contents, credentials, or session transcripts attached.

title: Extension host unresponsive ~40s at startup: synchronous macOS system CA load evaluates every keychain cert via trustd XPC
text: Extension host unresponsive ~40s at startup: synchronous macOS system CA load evaluates every keychain cert via trustd XPC. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: No The freeze needs at least one extension that makes an HTTPS request at startup, so Extension Bisect blames whichever extension fetches first (GitLens in my case). The blocking code is not extension code: it is the extension host's synchronous macOS system certificate load, per the stack sample below. Any network-using extension triggers it. - VS Code Version: 1.135.0 (arm64) - OS Version: macOS 26.6.2 (Darwin 25.6.0) Steps to Reproduce: 1. On macOS, have a login keychain containing many certificates. Mine has 272, mostly expired S/MIME certificates that Apple Mail auto-collects from digitally signed email over years of use. This is a common state for DoD/CAC users and other S/MIME-heavy environments. 2. Open any workspace with at least one extension that performs an HTTPS request during activation (e.g. GitLens). 3. The extension host goes unresponsive for 40-48 seconds. All extensions are frozen for the duration. It recurs on every new extension host (each window open or reload), because the certificate result is only cached per process. Evidence: renderer.log: 10:42:24.172 [info] Started local extension host with pid 79010. 10:42:28.507 [info] Extension host (LocalProcess pid: 79010) is unresponsive. 10:43:10.665 [info] Extension host (LocalProcess pid: 79010) is responsive. Sampling the extension host process ( ) during the freeze shows the main thread pinned for 100% of samples in one stack: node::crypto::GetSystemCACertificates node::crypto::GetOpenSSLSystemCertificates node::crypto::ReadMacOSKeychainCertificates node::crypto::IsCertificateTrustedForPolicy SecTrustSettingsCopyTrustSettings / SecTrustSettingsXPCRead This is the synchronous system CA read ( ) running on the extension host main thread. It performs one XPC round-trip to trustd per keychain certificate. Standalone reproduction of the underlying cost, no VS Code involved: $ node -e "console.time('ca'); require('tls').getCACertificates('system'); console.timeEnd('ca')" ca: 40.132s (Node v26.6.0, 272 keychain certs, 29 returned) Suggestions: load system CAs off the extension host main thread, and/or cache the result across extension host restarts. Workarounds confirmed: , or pruning the keychain.

title: Navigating to Automations can recursively rerender a long chat and freeze the renderer
text: Navigating to Automations can recursively rerender a long chat and freeze the renderer. ## Type of issue Performance / renderer hang ## Description Navigating from a long Agents chat to the Automations custom view can freeze the entire renderer for roughly 20–30 seconds. The Automations navigation appears to expose an unbounded synchronous re-entrancy in the dynamically-sized list scroll-anchor correction. During the transition, the chat list is hidden/resized and its rows can be measured in a collapsed layout. The resulting height changes cause scroll-anchor correction to synchronously fire , which enters again before the previous rerender completes. Observed recursive stack shape: ## Steps to reproduce 1. Open an Agents window chat with a long transcript (approximately 140+ request/response items; heavy Markdown/tool content makes the issue easier to trigger). 2. Keep the chat scrolled near the bottom. 3. Run **Manage Automations** to navigate to the Automations custom view. 4. Observe that the renderer can become completely unresponsive before eventually recovering. ## Observed results Two occurrences from the same Insiders session: - Navigation at ; renderer reported unresponsive at and recovered at . - Navigation at ; renderer reported unresponsive at and recovered at . During those intervals: - Approximately 9,300–9,900 calls per occurrence. - Approximately the same number of calls. - Only 140–148 actual transcript items were involved. - Individual transcript indices were rendered as many as 136–139 times. - The mounted range repeatedly unmounted and remounted while its start index ratcheted through the transcript. - Listener-leak warnings captured the recursive stack. A short 12-item transcript produced only 43 renders and 42 disposals during the same navigation and did not freeze. ## Suspected mechanism Relevant paths: - : hides/replaces the current workbench parts and performs a final layout. - : chat list layout and scroll-to-end behavior continue through the transition. - : performs dynamic-height probing and scroll-anchor correction. may synchronously flush scroll dimensions, fire , and re-enter without a guard. Collapsed rows were observed behaving as if their measured heights were roughly 15px, far below normal chat-row heights. Because the height never converges, each nested pass mutates the render range and performs another full mounted-range render/dispose cycle. ## Expected behavior Navigating to Automations should complete promptly regardless of the current chat transcript size or scroll position. Hidden or degenerate list layouts should not publish invalid dynamic heights or recursively re-enter rerendering. ## Potential fix directions - Add a re-entrancy guard or bounded follow-up pass around . - Avoid synchronously re-entering while applying scroll-anchor correction. - Skip dynamic-height probing/caching for hidden or zero-sized viewports and re-probe after a valid layout. - As defense in depth, avoid laying out or scrolling the chat list while it is hidden or has no renderable viewport.

title: VS Code renderer causes severe memory/commit leak while idle, eventually freezing Windows
text: VS Code renderer causes severe memory/commit leak while idle, eventually freezing Windows. # VS Code renderer causes severe memory/commit leak while idle, eventually freezing Windows Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested yet * VS Code Version: 1.135.0 * Commit: 08d4889f9ec4a1685d257b9b95de036c8e1ce1e5 * Architecture: x64 * OS Version: Windows 10.0.26200.9168 * Physical RAM: approximately 32 GB ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Start VS Code with my normal development environment. 2. The environment includes WSL, Docker Desktop, Node.js/Next.js server and worker processes. 3. Leave the development environment running while the machine is mostly idle. 4. After some time, system committed memory starts increasing rapidly. 5. Commit usage eventually reaches approximately 98–100%. 6. Windows becomes almost completely unresponsive. At that point I cannot reliably open Task Manager or execute diagnostic commands. 7. A hardware reset/reboot is required. ## Actual Behavior VS Code appears to cause a severe memory/resource leak while the machine is mostly idle. During one captured occurrence, system committed memory increased from approximately: to approximately: in about 11 minutes. The commit limit at the time was approximately: so commit usage reached approximately: Once this happened, Windows became effectively unusable. ## Suspicious VS Code Process The primary suspect is a VS Code renderer process. Immediately before the system became unusable, this renderer process showed approximately: * PID: * Working Set: * Private / committed memory: * Handle count: The handle count appears extremely abnormal. For comparison, another main VS Code process had only approximately: Total committed memory for all VS Code processes at the time of the snapshot was approximately: The unusually high handle count in this renderer process is the most suspicious observation from the captured diagnostics. ## Node.js Processes Node.js processes were also using a significant amount of committed memory. One Next.js process running showed approximately: * Working Set: * Committed memory: Total committed memory for all Node.js processes at that time was approximately: It is possible that the issue involves an interaction between VS Code, the renderer, file watchers, extensions, Node.js/Next.js, or the development worker. ## WSL / Docker Observations WSL and Docker do not appear to be the primary source of the memory growth. At approximately the same time: * : * Actual used memory inside WSL: * Redis Docker container: The system-wide increase in committed memory therefore does not appear to correspond to memory usage inside WSL or Docker containers. ## Important Reproduction Detail There is one unusual behavior that may be relevant. I initially used a diagnostic PowerShell script that periodically queried: * WSL memory * Docker statistics * Windows performance information When this diagnostic script was running continuously, the memory leak often did not reproduce. When the machine was left genuinely idle without those periodic WSL/Docker queries, the memory growth occurred again. This suggests that the issue may depend on an idle state, timing, renderer behavior, file watching, background cleanup, or another process state that is changed when WSL/Docker are periodically queried. In other words, periodically waking/querying the development environment appears to influence whether the problem reproduces. ## Impact This is not only increased memory usage. The end result is a complete system-level failure: 1. VS Code and the development environment are left running. 2. The machine becomes mostly idle. 3. Committed memory starts increasing rapidly. 4. Commit usage approaches 100%. 5. Windows becomes too unresponsive to terminate VS Code or collect further diagnostics. 6. The computer has to be physically reset/rebooted. ## Additional Testing I am currently testing: * VS Code with GPU hardware acceleration disabled * VS Code with extensions disabled * different combinations of the Node.js/Next.js server and worker processes * a larger Windows page file so that the system remains responsive long enough to collect more diagnostics I have a larger diagnostic archive from the affected system, but I am not attaching it publicly because it contains machine/user metadata. If useful, I can provide specific sanitized logs, process information, handle data, performance traces, renderer dumps, or other targeted diagnostics requested by the VS Code team.

title: Gesture handler never releases touches cancelled by touchcancel
text: Gesture handler never releases touches cancelled by touchcancel. ### Bug description The singleton ( ) listens for , and but never for . When the browser takes over a touch (system gesture, palm rejection, navigation), it delivers instead of , so never runs and the entry in stays forever. Consequences per leaked entry: - the DOM node reference in is pinned (no garbage collection while the page lives), - bookkeeping on that node is never undone, - with exactly one remaining active touch, the inertia dispatch branch treats the session as multi-touch, so single-finger inertia scrolling stops working after a few cancelled swipes. finds no match: nothing under handles cancellation today. ### Steps to reproduce 1. On a touch device, start a scroll gesture and trigger a UA takeover mid-gesture (e.g. invoke the system edge swipe) a few times. 2. Single-finger inertia scrolling stops responding afterwards; DevTools shows stale entries in 's internal touch map. ### Expected behavior releases the cancelled touch identifiers silently: no tap, context menu or inertia dispatch for an interrupted gesture, and the internal state is cleaned up like a normal end. ### Version tested Commit on ; verified by executing the compiled Gesture handler with synthesized cancel events. A fix is ready.

title: Agent Host session load causes child-chat subscription storm and memory spike
text: Agent Host session load causes child-chat subscription storm and memory spike. ## Summary Loading and reopening a large Agent Host session can generate thousands of duplicate child-chat subscriptions, causing a sharp renderer/transport memory spike and hundreds of MB of AHP traffic. ## Reproduction Using the session **Agent Host session migration** (39 subagent chats): 1. Open the session and wait for history/Changes to settle. 2. Open another session. 3. Reopen the original session. Controlled runs with isolated copies of the same profile: | Build | AHP bytes | Child-chat snapshots | |---|---:|---:| | (good Insiders) | 42.3 MB | 78 | | (bad Insiders) | 343.2+ MB | 1,005 retained after rotation | ## Bisect and root cause A source-level bisect identified commit (#331079): | Source revision | AHP bytes | Child-chat snapshots | |---|---:|---:| | Parent | 42.9 MB | 85 | | | 367.7 MB | 864 | The triggering change is the new synchronous external-changes scope check in : is subscription-backed. Calling while it is unobserved recomputes its dependencies for each visible changed-file editor, transiently acquiring and releasing all child-chat subscriptions. The target session has 39 child chats, so repeated file scope checks create a large overlapping subscribe/unsubscribe storm. Line-level verification on : - Removing only the new check: **43.0 MB / 87 child snapshots** (baseline restored). - Removing the separate new subagent annotation-restore await instead: **375.1 MB / 866 child snapshots** (still reproduces). Confidence in this causal attribution is very high; the immediate-parent, child, and single-expression A/B tests were all run against the same profile and automated scenario.

title: automatically embeds image paths from stdout without an aggregate limit, causing renderer OOM
text: automatically embeds image paths from stdout without an aggregate limit, causing renderer OOM. - Copilot Chat Extension Version: 0.62.0 - VS Code Version: 1.134.0 Stable ( ) - OS Version: Windows 11 Pro 25H2, build 26200.9168, x64 - Feature: Agent mode - Selected model: GPT 5.6 - Logs: Not attached. The cause is directly reproducible and the relevant implementation is identified below. Steps to Reproduce: 1. Open a workspace containing many image files smaller than 5 MiB. 2. Start an Agent chat with the built-in terminal tool enabled. 3. Have the agent run a command that prints path-like image filenames, such as . 4. Continue using the task or reopen it and observe rapidly increasing renderer memory. The built-in tool scans the full terminal output for paths ending in PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, or BMP. It resolves every matching path relative to the terminal working directory, reads the file, and appends its bytes to the tool result. The relevant result path is effectively: enforces a 5 MiB per-file limit but has no image-count or aggregate-byte limit. It also receives the full raw output, so terminal output truncation and do not prevent the issue. This means commands such as , , recursive directory listings, asset inventories, and build reports can unintentionally attach every image path they print. The image bytes are subsequently serialized as base64 into the task state and duplicated between tool-result metadata and response details. In my reproduction: - Approximately 120 KiB of terminal text produced 72 embedded image parts. - One serialized terminal result grew to approximately 33.5 MiB. - The active task exceeded 500 MiB on disk. - Reopening or rendering the task expanded memory usage until the renderer reached its heap limit and crashed with OOM. Expected behavior: Terminal stdout should be returned as text. Paths printed by arbitrary commands should not be dereferenced and attached automatically. Images should only be loaded following an explicit image-view request. At minimum, please add an option such as: Image extraction should preferably default to disabled. If retained, it should have conservative image-count and aggregate-byte limits and should only inspect output retained after compaction.

title: Renderer and NodeService memory growth causes repeated Linux OOM kills and V8 OOM crash (code 132) during long Copilot Agent sessions
text: Renderer and NodeService memory growth causes repeated Linux OOM kills and V8 OOM crash (code 132) during long Copilot Agent sessions. ### Additional data point This appears closely related to #315630 and #311225. The problem is still reproducible on VS Code 1.134.0. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: **Unknown**. The failure is intermittent and generally takes several hours. GitHub Copilot is bundled with this VS Code build. ### Environment - VS Code: 1.134.0 - Commit: 110a328ea54b42367b803ec53ee0bf52ef26b419 - Package: 1.134.0-1787078834, amd64 - Electron: 42.8.1 - Chromium: 148.0.7778.280 - Node.js: 24.18.1 - V8: 14.8.178.38-electron.0 - Bundled GitHub Copilot: 0.62.0 - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, x86_64 - Kernel: 6.17.0-1022-azure - Desktop/session: XFCE, X11 via xrdp - CPU: 4 vCPU, Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C - Memory: 15 GiB, no swap - Installed extensions: 99 ### Usage pattern 1. Open multiple local VS Code windows containing large Python/TypeScript workspaces. 2. Use Copilot Agent for tool-heavy, long-running sessions. 3. Keep the windows open for several hours. 4. Renderer memory grows until the kernel kills the process or V8 terminates it. The exact action that triggers the final allocation failure is not yet known. ### Crash evidence shows four renderer losses in one session: ~~~text 2026-08-20 16:59:47.877 [error] CodeWindow: renderer process gone (reason: killed, code: 9) 2026-08-20 17:03:11.206 [error] CodeWindow: renderer process gone (reason: killed, code: 9) 2026-08-20 21:57:21.059 [error] CodeWindow: renderer process gone (reason: killed, code: 9) 2026-08-21 04:22:24.800 [error] CodeWindow: renderer process gone (reason: crashed, code: 132) ~~~ The first three events match Linux kernel OOM-killer records: ~~~text Out of memory: Killed process 640503 (code), anon-rss: 4365680 kB Out of memory: Killed process 655846 (code), anon-rss: 3995044 kB Out of memory: Killed process 639699 (code), anon-rss: 4081976 kB ~~~ The code-132 crash matches a kernel native trap: ~~~text 2026-08-21 04:22:23 kernel: traps: code[676025] trap invalid opcode ... in code ~~~ Crashpad completed report identifies the crashed process as and contains V8 OOM data: ~~~text heap.used: 1617648408 Heap: used=1542.7MB limit=4096.0MB Mark-Compact (reduce) 1542.7 -> 1542.7 MB current mu = 0.000 allocation failure; GC in old space requested ~~~ A second completed report, , was generated on 2026-08-19. It identifies as the failed utility process: ~~~text heap.used: 3501854508 electron.v8-oom.location: CALL_AND_RETRY_LAST Mark-Compact (reduce) 3339.6 -> 3339.6 MB current mu = 0.000 ~~~ After the renderer crash, the extension host reports that the renderer closed its MessagePort and then exits normally with code 0. This suggests the extension-host shutdown is a consequence rather than the initial crash. A current post-crash snapshot shows 44 VS Code processes using approximately 12.91 GiB aggregate RSS on a 15 GiB machine. ### Expected behavior Renderer, Copilot Agent, and utility-process memory should remain bounded. Long-running sessions should not exhaust system memory or terminate workspace windows. ### Crash dumps Both minidumps are retained locally and can be provided privately to maintainers. I am not attaching them publicly because they contain recoverable Copilot session content and local filesystem paths.

title: Agents sessions context menus leak transient Action instances
text: Agents sessions context menus leak transient Action instances. ## Description Opening a context menu in the Agents Window sessions list can produce warnings for transient instances. The first observed warning points to , but the same context-menu code path creates several other instances with no owner. ## Reproduction steps 1. Run a Code OSS development build with disposable leak tracking enabled. 2. Open the Agents Window. 3. Open a sessions-list context menu, such as by right-clicking a session row, group header, or empty list area. 4. Dismiss the menu and allow or force garbage collection. ## Expected behavior All context-menu actions are either non-disposable values or are disposed when the menu closes. ## Actual behavior The disposable tracker reports an that was garbage-collected without being disposed: ## Root cause **Confirmed:** extends , while creates short-lived actions inside context-menu delegates without registering or disposing them. Affected code is in , including: - - Add/Move to Group submenu actions - Remove from Group - Rename Group - Delete Group - Extension-command wrapper actions created in The issue is present at commit . ## Possible implementation direction These actions do not need mutable state or change events. Replace the transient instances with the lighter-weight, non-disposable helper. Alternatively, explicitly own all created actions in a menu-scoped and dispose it from . Add coverage that opens and closes each sessions-list context-menu variant under disposable leak tracking.

title: macOS: update restart hangs indefinitely in uv__threadpool_cleanup
text: macOS: update restart hangs indefinitely in uv__threadpool_cleanup. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested. The hang begins after every extension host has exited normally. - VS Code Version: 1.133.0-insider, commit 780ea331b2861816fe6bb8215d812933c81df83b - OS Version: macOS 26.5.2, arm64 - Electron Version: 42.8.0 - Chrome Version: 148.0.7778.280 Steps to Reproduce: 1. Leave VS Code Insiders running until an update has downloaded and is ready. 2. Trigger the update restart. 3. Observe that all windows close and extension hosts exit, but the main Code - Insiders process remains alive indefinitely and the updater cannot install the staged build. This reproduced on two consecutive daily updates using the same installed build. A force quit allows the updater to continue. The staged build in the second occurrence also contains Electron 42.8.0. ### Native stack findings A macOS spindump and a separate live 10-second sample show the same stable main-thread stack for every sample: The main thread is waiting for the only remaining libuv worker, which remains blocked for every sample: All extension hosts exited with code 0 before the main process entered this state. No child processes remain attached to the main process. CPU usage is effectively zero. The observed behavior is consistent with the libuv thread-pool exit-message relay failing to wake its final worker: other workers exit, while waits indefinitely to join the last worker. This looks like an Electron/libuv process-teardown issue rather than an extension-host shutdown veto. No diagnostic files are attached, but additional sanitized stack details can be provided if needed.

title: Code Helper (Renderer) sustains >200% CPU and grows to 12 GB with thousands of IOSurface regions on macOS
text: Code Helper (Renderer) sustains >200% CPU and grows to 12 GB with thousands of IOSurface regions on macOS. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested yet - VS Code Version: 1.131.0 (Universal/arm64), commit e4c7e7b1d6d060162f4aa7f8225271b67ce1df75 - Electron: 42.7.0 - OS Version: macOS 27.0 (26A5388g), Apple Silicon (M5), 16 GB RAM - Remote OS: Linux x64 over Remote - SSH ## Summary A single VS Code window renderer ( ) intermittently enters a sustained high-CPU state and rapidly accumulates memory and graphical resources. The affected window is a Remote - SSH workspace. Other VS Code windows remain idle and small, and the extension host remains near idle. During one observation period, the affected renderer used 109–222% CPU and its physical footprint grew from approximately 9.4 GB to 11.6 GB, later reaching a 12.3 GB peak. The VS Code GPU process concurrently used approximately 15–25% CPU, but its stack was dominated by Metal command submission and appears to be downstream of the renderer workload. ## Steps to Reproduce The exact trigger is not known yet, but the problem has reproduced in the same workspace/window: 1. Open a Linux workspace using Remote - SSH. 2. Keep the window open with two small untitled editors (one Markdown document, about 54 KB) and normal workbench UI. 3. Continue using VS Code or leave the window open. 4. After some time, observe the window process in or Process Explorer. ## Actual Behavior The affected renderer enters a sustained high-CPU state and its footprint/resource counts grow continuously. Representative measurements from the same renderer: A second newly opened VS Code renderer, measured at the same time, stayed at approximately 45 MB physical footprint and 0% CPU. mapped the affected process to the Remote - SSH window. The related processes were approximately: The untitled Markdown backup was only 54,419 bytes, 965 lines, with a longest line of 787 bytes, so this does not appear to be a large-file case. A 10-second macOS of the renderer showed the main thread continuously executing V8 microtasks, object/property enumeration, serialization/deserialization, allocation, and GC-related paths. A simultaneous GPU-process sample showed repeated Metal command-buffer, texture copy, and render command submission. The system experienced severe memory pressure while this happened (16 GB system RAM, about 8 GB of this renderer's writable regions swapped). Closing/reloading the affected window releases the resources. ## Expected Behavior An idle or normally used Remote - SSH window should not continuously consume multiple CPU cores or grow to 10+ GB physical footprint and thousands of IOSurface regions. ## Additional Context - The VS Code binaries and processes are native arm64, not running through Rosetta. - GPU acceleration was enabled with ANGLE Metal and Skia Graphite. - The affected window had restored workbench state for the built-in Chat panel and extension-contributed sidebars, but no specific extension has been proven to trigger the leak. - The local extension host was mostly idle, suggesting the CPU time is in the window renderer rather than extension-host computation. - The current process had only about 265 Mach ports, so this does not look like port-space exhaustion. - I can provide the macOS reports for both the renderer and GPU process if useful. ## Diagnostics Available - 10-second report of captured during the high-CPU state - 8-second report of the VS Code GPU process captured at the same time - snapshots showing footprint, swap, App-Specific Tag regions, and IOSurface growth - process-to-window mapping

title: Agents window: background session terminals keep their renderer-side xterm alive, growing unbounded
text: Agents window: background session terminals keep their renderer-side xterm alive, growing unbounded. Found while analyzing a renderer heap snapshot from the Agents window (484 MB self-size). ## Summary **80 MB (~16% of the renderer heap)** was xterm buffer data: 10,791 allocations traced to . There were **38 live instances** (76 roots = 38 terminals × normal + alternate buffer), which matches exactly: ~33 entries in plus ~7 in . ## This is by design, but it doesn't scale ( ) distinguishes two paths: - **Session removed** → → (pty torn down). - **Session archived / "Mark as Done"** → → — deliberately keeps both the pty *and* the frontend xterm alive so unarchiving is instant. Since archiving is the common flow and removal is rare, the live xterm count grows monotonically with the number of sessions ever opened, at roughly **1 MB each** (default 1000-line scrollback × cols × 4 bytes per cell). At 38 sessions this is 80 MB. Someone with a few hundred archived sessions would be well into the hundreds of MB, purely in renderer-side scrollback for terminals that aren't visible. ## Options 1. **Release the renderer-side xterm for backgrounded terminals, keep the pty.** The pty host already replays scrollback on re-attach, so the content is recoverable. This is the correct fix but requires teaching to drop when moved to background and lazily recreate it, which touches shared terminal code. 2. **LRU cap on background session terminals.** Keep the N most recently used xterms hydrated, dispose the rest. Cheaper, bounded, and mostly invisible in practice. 3. **Lower scrollback for backgrounded terminals.** Cheapest stopgap, proportional rather than bounded savings. ## Effort estimate Medium. Option 2 is contained within ; option 1 is the real fix but spans . Lowest priority of the three memory issues from this snapshot — it's a design tradeoff rather than a leak, and 80 MB is the smallest of the three. (Written by Copilot)

title: Copilot Chat leaks the window renderer to OOM (-536870904) on idle Remote-SSH; disabling Copilot Chat is a confirmed fix (1.127.0)
text: Copilot Chat leaks the window renderer to OOM (-536870904) on idle Remote-SSH; disabling Copilot Chat is a confirmed fix (1.127.0). Type: **Bug** ## Summary On **VS Code 1.127.0** with **Remote-SSH** (Windows client → Linux host), the **local window renderer crashes with ** on a metronomic ~4-minute cycle, with little or no user interaction (it happens even when only image files are "open"). I traced the driver to the **GitHub Copilot Chat machinery / bundled SDK**: the corresponding **remote extension host leaks 0.6–1.2 GB/min autonomously — with zero clients attached and no files open** — and **disabling GitHub Copilot Chat stops the crashes completely** (before/after monitor below). Same crash signature and cure as the closed #11997 and open #313762 / #303387 / #312318, now with the leak quantified and the culprit isolated. ## Environment - **VS Code:** 1.127.0, commit , 2026-06-30 (same build client + remote server) - **Client:** Windows x64 (the exception form is Windows-specific) - **Remote:** Linux x64, shared multi-core host over NFS home, accessed via Remote-SSH - **Workspace:** multi-root (several folders on the remote) - **Relevant extensions:** GitHub Copilot Chat, Claude Code ( ), Pylance/Python, rainbow-csv - **Crash code:** = (Chromium , per-process allocation failure — not system-wide OOM; the remote node has ~3 TB RAM, ~2.9 TB free throughout) ## Steps to Reproduce 1. From a Windows laptop, connect to a remote Linux host via Remote-SSH and open a (multi-root) workspace. 2. Leave GitHub Copilot Chat enabled (a chat-session view is restored on each window — here the Claude Code chat session, activation event ). 3. Leave the window largely idle (no heavy files needed — reproduced with only small images open, and even with **no** editors open). 4. The window renderer memory climbs and the window dies with after ~3–6 minutes; VS Code offers to reopen, restoring the same chat view → the loop repeats. ## Observed Behavior — the leak, measured The **remote extension host** for each window grows monotonically and keeps growing **after its window has already died and with zero clients attached**: | Extension host | Age / state | RSS | |---|---|---| | PID A (window already dead, 0 clients, no files) | 13:24 | 9,870 MB | | — | 13:25 | 11,467 MB | | — | 13:26:59 | 12,932 MB (~92% CPU, 396 threads) | | — | disposed at 5-min grace expiry (exit 0, **not** OOM) | ~12.2 GB | | PID B (replacement, fresh window) | age 266 s | 2,838 MB — same trajectory | Rate ≈ **0.6–1.2 GB/min**. Window lifetimes were metronomic: 8 non-graceful client losses at 3.3–6.4 min each. The remote node never runs low on RAM; the identical machinery mirrored in the **local ~4 GB renderer** reaches its ceiling in ~4 min, matching every observed window lifetime. (Consistent with #303387's maintainer note that "the leak is in the window process, not the extension host.") ### Leak fingerprint - The **only non-core native module mapped** in the leaking host is the bundled Copilot SDK runtime: - **384 threads** (= host ) spawned by that runtime, at ~92% CPU. - A recurring **timer-driven error** fires ~2× per session in : — a retry loop consistent with the fixed cadence. - : +200 MB/25 s (cached/socket churn), only +100 KB/25 s → in-memory growth, not disk I/O. ## The fix / decisive test **Disabling GitHub Copilot Chat eliminates the crash.** An 18-minute monitor (45 s sampling) after disabling it: | | Before disable | After disable | |---|---|---| | New window's extension host | climbing 7.2 → 9.2 GB (~0.7 GB/min) until grace-disposed | **FLAT: ~340 / ~530 MB, Δ ≈ +1 MB over 17 min** | | Window crashes in the window | every ~4 min | **0 in 18 min (~4.5 would-be cycles)** | This matches the independently-reported cure in the closed #11997 ("When I disable the Copilot extension on the Windows desktop, I no longer have any issue"). ## Expected Behavior An idle Remote-SSH window with Copilot Chat enabled (and a restored chat-session view) should not leak the window renderer to its per-process ceiling. Extension-host memory should not grow unbounded with no client attached and no files open. ## Key Observations - **Content-independent:** crashes recur at the same cadence regardless of open files (reproduced with only small images, and with no editors); image decode is ruled out (open images decoded to ~49 MB total, ~1.2% of the ceiling; one crash preceded the first image's creation). - **Webviews run locally under Remote-SSH** (per the Remote Extensions docs: "the Webview API is always run on the user's local machine"), so a leaking chat-session webview lands in the local renderer even though the workspace is remote. - ** SDK is now bundled in VS Code core** ( ), so this affects stock 1.127.0, not just the marketplace Copilot Chat extension. - Known-ineffective mitigations from the related reports: adding RAM (#313762 crashed with 48 GB free), (#175792, cannot raise past 4096), (#226484, null result). ## Related issues - #313762 — near-identical: idle Remote-SSH (Windows → Linux) renderer OOM , onset ~1.116/1.117, still open on 1.127; that reporter also runs + . - #303387 — Copilot Chat inflates the **window process** 366 MB → 20+ GB to the identical ; maintainer: "the leak is in the window process, not the extension host". - #312318 — same signature, . - Closed corroboration: microsoft/vscode-copilot-release#11997 and #4219 ( ) — same code, same "disable Copilot fixes it". ## Logs
