title: Extension host crash loop: EXC_BREAKPOINT on V8Worker thread during Maglev concurrent compilation (macOS arm64, VS Code 1.126+/Electron 42.2.0)
text: Extension host crash loop: EXC_BREAKPOINT on V8Worker thread during Maglev concurrent compilation (macOS arm64, VS Code 1.126+/Electron 42.2.0). [vscode-maglev-crash-minidumps.zip]( this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: No — the trigger requires a sustained extension-host JS workload (see Steps to Reproduce). However, the crash site is entirely inside V8's background compiler; there are no extension frames on the crashing stack. - VS Code Version: 1.126.0, 1.127.0, and 1.128.0-insider commit 86df0e5dc86a78298b5ffce1c6f6793ad79c3e93 (all reproduce; stock downloads, untouched) - OS Version: macOS 15.x, Apple Silicon (arm64) - Electron: 42.2.0, Node 22.x ## Summary Under a sustained agent-style chat workload, the extension host process ( ) deterministically crashes with **exit code 5** after 2–8 minutes. The crash is an (V8 CHECK/trap, ) on a background **V8Worker** thread, at a byte-identical PC in every crash: We collected **9 Crashpad minidumps** across three VS Code versions (including 1.128.0-insider), two storage backends, an automated test harness *and* an interactive developer session. All 8 stable-build dumps have a frame-for-frame identical crash-thread stack (heatmap below), the Insiders dump shows the same EXC_BREAKPOINT-in-Electron-Framework-background-thread signature (different raw offsets, as Insiders ships a different Electron Framework build), and disabling V8's Maglev compiler ( ) makes the crash disappear entirely in an otherwise unchanged A/B. **Conclusion: a V8 Maglev concurrent (background) compilation bug in Electron 42.2.0 tripping an internal CHECK while compiling extension-host JS.** ## Dump heatmap (8/8 dumps, single failure path) Symbolicated against stock Electron 42.2.0 breakpad symbols. VS Code ships a patched Electron build, so some neighboring symbol names are approximate (*), but the Maglev frames form the exact real nesting order of a concurrent Maglev compile — not producible by symbol skew. | Heat | Frame | Symbol | |---|---|---| | 8/8 | pc, lr | / — CHECK/trap site (*) | | 8/8 | frame[0] | (*) | | 8/8 | frame[1] | | | 8/8 | frame[2] | (*) | | 8/8 | frame[3] | | | 8/8 | frame[4,5] | | | 8/8 | frame[6,7] | | | 8/8 | frame[8,9] | worker-pool thread bootstrap (*) | | 8/8 | frame[10,11] | ( ) | Zero variance across all 8 dumps: same PC, same LR, same 12-frame stack. ## The discriminating A/B: Same machine, same day, same stock 1.127.0 binary, same test, same config: | Run | | Outcome | |---|---|---| | A | **yes** | **passed** — 1031 s sustained session, 45 chat turns, clean exit 0, peak ext-host RSS 405 MB | | B (30 min later) | no | **crashed** — 334 s, exit code 5, minidump with the identical stack | Two flagged runs survived a combined ~33 minutes of the workload that reliably kills unflagged instances in 2–8 minutes. ## Ruled out - **Native modules** — reproduced with the extension's only native module ( / LevelDB) fully replaced by an in-memory Map. - **Window reloads** — reproduced with reload cycles disabled. - **Version-specific regression** — reproduces on 1.126.0, 1.127.0, and 1.128.0-insider (commit 86df0e5d, 2026-07-06 build): extension host crashed with code 5 at t=344s (16 turns), t=99s (4 turns) on retry, and t=454s (13 turns) in a third run that captured a minidump (included in the attachment): EXC_BREAKPOINT, PC in , background (pthread) thread — same signature class; raw offsets differ because Insiders ships a different Electron Framework build. - **Memory pressure / OOM** — ext-host RSS stays < ~500 MB throughout; crash is a CHECK trap, not . - **Extension/JS code** — crash thread is a V8 background compiler thread; no extension frames on the crashing stack. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Install our extension (Augment) in stock VS Code 1.126.0, 1.127.0, or 1.128.0-insider on macOS arm64. 2. Run a long-lived AI-agent chat session in the extension host: repeated multi-turn streaming requests, large JSON message payloads, and periodic state persistence, sustained for up to 30 minutes. 3. The extension host ( ) crashes with exit code 5 after 2–8 minutes (149–480 s across runs in our automated Playwright harness). 4. Repeat with on the extension host (e.g. via ): the identical workload runs to completion. The workload requires our extension + backend, so it is not trivially portable; we are happy to run the reproducer on request, capture additional dumps, or test candidate fixes/flag combinations. The crashing stack itself contains no extension frames. ## Crash log excerpt (renderer/main log) Crashed thread name: ; exception: . ## Workaround on the extension-host process fully mitigates. title: Main process crashes with SQLITE_BUSY on new APPLICATION_SHARED storage (.vscode-shared\sharedStorage\state.vscdb) when two instances run concurrently
text: Main process crashes with SQLITE_BUSY on new APPLICATION_SHARED storage (.vscode-shared\sharedStorage\state.vscdb) when two instances run concurrently. ## Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled? Yes (root-caused in core, not extension-related — see analysis below) ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open VS Code (stable, v1.127.0) normally. 2. While it's running, open a second, independent VS Code window/instance shortly after (e.g. a second process launching close in time to the first). 3. Within a few minutes, one or both windows crash with an uncaught main-process exception. ## Observed behavior shows the application starts up fine and successfully creates/initializes the new application-shared storage database: The failure happens ~4 minutes after successful startup, during an ordinary write **transaction** (not the initial DB open/creation), which strongly suggests a second, independent OS process was concurrently writing to the same file at that moment. ## Root cause analysis (from source, commit , v1.127.0) - is the new storage scope added in #311317 ("Add storage scope for cross-app state sharing"), implemented by in [ ]( It is explicitly designed to be shared **across separate processes** (VS Code and a companion "Agents" app). - The underlying in [ ]( only retries once on when **opening** the DB connection ( , 2s ), with this comment: > "SQLITE_BUSY should only arise if another process is locking the same DB we want to open at that time. This typically never happens because a DB connection is limited per window." That assumption no longer holds for , since it is intentionally opened by multiple independent processes. - Crucially, the ongoing method (used for every subsequent read/write after the DB is open) has **no busy-retry/backoff logic at all** — a there just calls and rejects the promise. That rejection appears to end up as an unhandled rejection reaching in [ ]( logged as , and the process/window subsequently crashes. - Additionally, constructs without a option, so is never set for this shared DB — SQLite has no chance to wait/retry internally before surfacing on lock contention between the two processes. ## Suggested fix - Set a ( ) when opening 's , since it is the one scope explicitly meant for multi-process access. - Add retry-on- handling to (not just the initial ), at least for the scope. - Ensure a in this path can't escalate to an uncaught/unhandled exception that crashes the process. ## Environment - VS Code version: 1.127.0 (stable), commit - OS: Windows - : (from ) I searched existing issues for , , and and didn't find an existing report of this specific crash — apologies in advance if this duplicates something I missed.

title: Renderer crashes with V8 heap OOM (~4 GB cap) — regression introduced in 1.125 (runtime unchanged from 1.124)
text: Renderer crashes with V8 heap OOM (~4 GB cap) — regression introduced in 1.125 (runtime unchanged from 1.124). # Renderer crashes with V8 heap OOM (~4 GB cap) — regression introduced in 1.125 (runtime unchanged from 1.124) <!-- Paste into → "Bug report" --> ## Type: Performance Issue / Crash **Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled? — Not yet fully confirmed.** The OOM is in the **renderer** process; my heaviest extension (Sapling SCM) runs in the separate **extension host**, so disabling extensions may not be conclusive. However, the regression is reproducible on the *same machine and same workspace* purely by changing the VS Code version (see A/B below), which points at workbench renderer code, not an extension. ## VS Code Version - Version: **1.126.0** (also reproduced on 1.125.x) - Commit: - Date: 2026-06-23 - Electron: 42.3.0 / Chromium: 148.0.7778.180 / Node: 24.15.0 - OS: macOS 26.5.1 (25F80), Apple M4 Pro, **48 GB RAM** **Last known good: 1.124.2** (identical Electron/Chromium/Node — see "Runtime is unchanged"). ## Summary The workbench **renderer process's V8 JavaScript heap grows until it hits V8's ~4 GB per-isolate ceiling, then aborts**. The window dies with: is how Electron surfaces a V8 fatal OOM abort at the window level — the Crashpad minidump confirms it is an out-of-memory (annotations below). Physical RAM is irrelevant (48 GB free headroom); V8 caps each renderer heap at 4 GB. GPU acceleration is **disabled**, so this is not a GPU/WebGL issue. Large integrated-terminal output (e.g. on a big directory) reliably triggers the final crash, but the heap is already sitting near 4 GB — the terminal output is the last allocation, not the root cause. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open a large multi-root / multi-window workspace (I run ~8 windows; heavy SCM activity). 2. Work normally for a while so the main renderer heap climbs (watch it in **Developer: Open Process Explorer** — the window renderer approaches ~4000 MB). 3. Produce a burst of integrated-terminal output (e.g. ). 4. The renderer crashes; the extension host then exits cleanly ("renderer closed the MessagePort"). Repeats reliably: **20 of 20** recent Crashpad dumps carry annotations. ## Runtime is unchanged — so this is a VS Code JS regression Per the community version tracker (ewanharris/vscode-versions), **1.124, 1.125 and 1.126 all ship the identical runtime**: Electron 42.3.0, Chromium 148.0.7778.180, Node 24.15.0. Combined with the controlled A/B below, the increase in renderer heap consumption is in **VS Code's own workbench JavaScript shipped in 1.125**, not in Chromium/V8. ## Controlled A/B (same machine, same workspace, same synced settings) | VS Code | Result | |---------|--------| | 1.124.2 | Stable, no crashes | | 1.125.x / 1.126.0 | Renderer OOM-crashes; recurs within a session | A second laptop with the **same synced settings/extensions** does not crash — consistent with Settings Sync not replicating open windows/folders/panels or on-disk workload, i.e. the second machine's renderer simply never accumulates to 4 GB. ## Evidence — Crashpad minidump heap annotations (renderer, main isolate) Extracted from : Embedded V8 GC log at the moment of death (GC freeing nothing, efficiency → 0): ## Interpretation (what to look at) - ** , ** → not a leaked-webview / detached-DOM leak. - ** , ** → not ArrayBuffers / external buffers. - Therefore ~3.88 GB is **ordinary JS objects on the managed V8 heap in the main workbench renderer** — a growing in-heap data structure in workbench JS. Given the terminal trigger, the integrated-terminal buffer/scrollback or an accumulating workbench cache are prime suspects. A live heap snapshot (retainer graph) is needed to name the exact structure; the minidump doesn't carry the object graph. ## What I ruled out - GPU / WebGL — already off; crash is JS-heap. - Physical memory — 48 GB, crash is at V8's 4 GB per-renderer cap, not OS OOM. - Settings / extensions config — identical (synced) on an unaffected machine. - Chromium/Electron/Node — byte-identical across 1.124–1.126. ## Ask Please investigate what in the 1.125 workbench renderer increased steady-state / peak JS heap usage enough to reach the 4 GB V8 ceiling. Happy to attach a and full Crashpad dumps on request.

title: Renderer process crashes ( ) — built-in agent sessions cache ( ) imported from grows unbounded (~140 MB) and cannot be disabled
text: Renderer process crashes ( ) — built-in agent sessions cache ( ) imported from grows unbounded (~140 MB) and cannot be disabled. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes (see note — the data source is built-in, not an extension) - VS Code Version: 1.126.0 - OS Version: macOS 13.3.1, Apple Silicon (arm64) ### Description VS Code's built-in agent/chat **sessions** feature automatically discovers external CLI agent history on disk — in my case the Claude Code CLI directory . It serializes **every** discovered session (including a full per-session file-change/diff list) into the **workspace** key inside . There is **no size cap / eviction** on this cache. After ~150 CLI sessions in one project it reached **~140 MB in a single key**. On window load this blob is read into the renderer, and the renderer process crashes: shows **no JS exception and no OOM message** at crash time — the renderer is killed at the native level. The dialog shown is "The window terminated unexpectedly (reason: 'crashed', code: '5')". ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Accumulate a large Claude Code CLI history for one folder ( ~150 sessions / ~120 MB). 2. Open that folder in VS Code 1.126.0. 3. Inspect the workspace storage: → 4. The renderer crashes (most reliably under an Extension Development Host / second window, where memory headroom is smaller). ### What does NOT stop it (the core complaint) - Uninstalling the extension — **no effect**; the discovery/caching is built into the workbench ( hardcodes , , , …). - - None of these prevent the background scan of or the cache from being rebuilt to 140 MB. The only effective workaround was to **delete the key** and **archive most of the CLI history** so the cache rebuilds small. ### Design problems 1. VS Code scans a **third-party CLI's private data directory** ( ) by default, without an opt-in. 2. The per-workspace cache ( ) has **no size limit and no eviction**. 3. The blob is loaded **synchronously into the renderer**, so an oversized cache can crash the entire window — there is no guard against an oversized state entry. 4. The user-facing settings that look like they should disable the feature do **not** stop the scan/caching. ### Suggested fixes - Cap / paginate / lazily load ; never block-load multi-hundred-MB values into the renderer. - Provide a setting that actually disables external CLI session discovery (and honor it for the disk scan, not just the view). - Make external-agent (Claude Code / Copilot CLI / Codex) discovery opt-in. ### Workaround for others hitting this Quit VS Code completely, then: and move old sessions out of .

title: [Linux][Wayland] Severe memory leak in VSCode main process on Fedora 44 (GNOME/Wayland) – persists with --disable-gpu, --disable-extensions, and fresh profile
text: [Linux][Wayland] Severe memory leak in VSCode main process on Fedora 44 (GNOME/Wayland) – persists with --disable-gpu, --disable-extensions, and fresh profile. Environment OS: Fedora 44 Workstation (Linux) Kernel: Linux 7.0.13-200.fc44.x86_64 Display Server: Wayland (GNOME 4x, X11 session not available) Graphics Driver: Mesa 26.0.8 (Compatibility Profile) Version: 1.126.0 Electron: 42.2.0 ElectronBuildId: 14159160 Chromium: 148.0.7778.97 Node.js: 24.15.0 V8: 14.8.178.14-electron.0 Steps to Reproduce Start VSCode with a fresh, clean profile and no extensions: bash code --disable-extensions --user-data-dir=/tmp/clean-vscode Open a typical workspace (e.g., a medium-sized project with a few folders). Leave VSCode running for 4–6 hours (or overnight) with minimal interaction. Monitor memory usage via GNOME System Monitor or VSCode's Process Explorer (Developer: Open Process Explorer). Actual Result The main process (code) continuously consumes more memory over time. After ~4 hours, memory usage reaches 6–8 GB and keeps growing. System responsiveness degrades; swapping may occur; eventually the OOM killer may terminate the process. This happens regardless of: --disable-gpu flag --disable-extensions flag --ozone-platform=x11 (though X11 may slow the leak, it does not stop it) Changing GNOME shell extensions (tested with both dash-to-dock and dash-to-panel) Cleaning cache directories (~/.config/Code/GPUCache, etc.) The Process Explorer shows the main process as the primary consumer, not extension-host or GPU process. Expected Result Memory usage should stabilize after initial workspace load and remain within a reasonable range (e.g., ~500 MB – 1.5 GB) during idle periods. Additional Observations Firefox (using native Wayland) does not show this leak under the same workload, indicating the issue is Chromium/Electron-specific. The leak is observed in all Chromium-based applications (Chrome, Edge, VSCode) on this system, suggesting a common root cause in the Chromium engine or its interaction with the Fedora/Wayland/Mesa stack. journalctl shows repeated GNOME Shell warnings about stage view updates (e.g., Can't update stage views actor...), but these persist even with shell extensions disabled – likely a symptom of deeper compositor communication issues. No obvious GPU-related errors appear in dmesg or journalctl; the leak appears to be in user-space memory (heap or shared memory). This issue is distinct from the known kdialog file-picker leak (KDE Bug 494160), as it occurs without opening any file dialog. What I've Tried (with no effect) Disabling GPU acceleration (--disable-gpu) Disabling all extensions (--disable-extensions) Forcing X11 backend (--ozone-platform=x11) Running with a fresh profile (--user-data-dir=/tmp/clean-vscode) Updating to the latest VSCode stable/insiders Switching GNOME shell extensions (dash-to-dock → dash-to-panel) – leak persists Removing cache directories (~/.cache/mesa_shader_cache/, ~/.config/Code/GPUCache, etc.) Setting "files.watcherExclude" to exclude node_modules, dist, etc. Setting MALLOC_CHECK_=3 – no heap corruption output Suggested Investigation Areas Wayland buffer management or shared memory allocation in Electron's Ozone platform backend. Interaction with Mesa's gbm or dri components (Fedora 44 uses Mesa 26.0.8). Potential reference counting leak in the compositor communication layer. Compare with Chrome/Edge behavior to isolate VSCode/Electron-specific vs. common Chromium code paths. Additional Logs If needed, I can provide: VSCode Process Explorer screenshots showing main process memory chrome://tracing-style memory snapshots (if applicable) Full journalctl -b logs strace output

title: Intermittent 20–50 second unresponsive startup on macOS; reproduces with extensions disabled and fresh user-data directory
text: Intermittent 20–50 second unresponsive startup on macOS; reproduces with extensions disabled and fresh user-data directory. ## Description VS Code intermittently opens its window quickly but remains slow or unresponsive for approximately 20–50 seconds before becoming usable. The problem is intermittent. Reopening the same repository is often fast, so a single successful startup does not demonstrate that a configuration has fixed the issue. It occurs across different repositories rather than one specific large workspace. In some slow runs, records a 35–52 second delay in extension registration. In other visibly slow runs, including one captured with , the startup performance marks report only approximately 1–2 seconds and do not contain the full user-visible delay. ## Environment * VS Code: 1.124.2 * Commit: 6928394f91b684055b873eecb8bc281365131f1c * OS reported by VS Code: Darwin 25.5.0 * Hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 36 GB RAM The problem was also seen with VS Code 1.123.0. ## Isolation already performed The problem still occurs after: * Disabling all marketplace extensions * Starting with * Starting with a new temporary user-data directory * Combining both: * Reinstalling VS Code * Testing multiple repositories One clean-user-data and extensions-disabled run recorded: * : approximately 35 seconds * : approximately 36 seconds * : approximately 37 seconds Another run with marketplace extensions disabled recorded: * : 24 ms * : approximately 52 seconds * : approximately 52 seconds In that second run, the extension host appeared to be waiting for initialization data rather than executing a slow marketplace extension. ## Latest profiling run I fully quit VS Code and launched it using: The application was noticeably slow to become responsive, but the startup performance marks reported: * : 1531 ms * : 180 ms * : 1663 ms The generated CPU profiles cover only approximately 4–5 seconds each, so they do not appear to include the complete perceived delay. I have attached: * Main-process CPU profile * Renderer CPU profile * Extension-host CPU profile * Startup Performance reports from multiple slow runs * macOS process samples captured during a slow run ## Expected behaviour The window should become responsive shortly after appearing, and the performance diagnostics should account for the period during which the UI cannot be used normally. ## Actual behaviour The window appears, but interaction can remain delayed or unresponsive for tens of seconds. Sometimes this corresponds to extension-registration timing, while other times the user-visible delay is not represented in Startup Performance or the automatically generated startup CPU profiles. title: Memory Leak in Screenshot Annotation Tool
text: Memory Leak in Screenshot Annotation Tool. Title: Unmanaged Event Listeners Causing Memory Accumulation in Editor Annotations Description: The screenshot annotation feature attaches multiple event listeners (input, keyup, click, select, keydown, blur) to text editor elements without ever removing them. When users interact with the annotation editor multiple times during their session, these listeners stack up in memory. Each edit operation adds new listeners on top of the old ones, creating exponential growth in memory consumption. This is particularly problematic for users who frequently use the screenshot/bug report annotation feature, as listeners accumulate with no disposal mechanism. Over an extended session, this causes noticeable performance degradation and increased memory usage. Kindly Assign this to me . Id love contributing !!

title: Enabling Explore (Code Research) subagent may trigger Electron GPU instability and full macOS reboot on Intel Mac mini 2018
text: Enabling Explore (Code Research) subagent may trigger Electron GPU instability and full macOS reboot on Intel Mac mini 2018. * Copilot Chat Extension Version: * VS Code Version: 1.119 (Release) * OS Version: macOS 13.7.8 (22H730) * Hardware: * Mac mini 2018 (Macmini8,1) * Intel-based Mac * Feature: Explore Agent / Explore (Code Research) subagent * Selected model: Multiple models tested Steps to Reproduce: 1. Enable the experimental "Explore (Code Research) subagent" feature in GitHub Copilot Chat. 2. Use Copilot Agent / Explore functionality during normal development workflows. 3. After some usage, the entire macOS system freezes and automatically reboots. 4. Disable the Explore subagent feature, and the issue no longer occurs. Observed Behavior: * This is not a normal VS Code crash. * The entire macOS system becomes unresponsive and then reboots automatically. * The issue appears consistently reproducible when the Explore subagent is enabled. * Disabling the feature appears to completely prevent the issue. Diagnostic Information: I observed repeated Electron GPU-related resource diagnostics under: /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ Including: * Code Helper (GPU)_*.wakeups_resource.diag * WindowServer_*.wakeups_resource.diag One diagnostic report shows: * "Code Helper (GPU)" * Electron Framework * Excessive wakeups: "45001 wakeups over the last 225 seconds" This appears to indicate abnormal Electron GPU process activity. Additional Notes: * The machine is an Intel Mac mini 2018 using Intel integrated graphics. * I suspect the issue may be related to Electron GPU acceleration or Intel macOS graphics compatibility when using the experimental Explore subagent feature. * I am currently testing whether disabling GPU acceleration mitigates the issue. title: Chat memory leak: OutputMonitor
text: Chat memory leak: OutputMonitor. # Memory leak: disposables leak when foreground terminal is reused after ## Summary PR #311011 ("Do not move fg terminal to the bg when it needs input") introduced a memory leak in the tool. When a foreground terminal detects , the terminal now stays foreground and is reused by subsequent calls. However, the registered via under the old is never cleaned up, causing event subscriptions to accumulate. ## Evidence **CI Run:** The leak check (3 iterations × 16 scenarios, 10 MB threshold) reported: | Phase | Heap (MB) | DOM Nodes | |-------|----------:|----------:| | Baseline | 95.54 | 965 | | Iteration 1 | 105.89 (+10.29) | 1002 (+37) | | Iteration 2 | 107.36 (+1.48) | 1002 (0) | | Iteration 3 | 108.19 (+0.83) | 1002 (0) | | **Final** | **108.19** | **1002** | **Total residual growth:** +12.65 MB heap, +37 DOM nodes — exceeds 10 MB threshold. The GC-based disposable tracker reported **9 leaked disposables** across the run, all with the same stack trace: These correspond to 3 leaked instances per iteration (one per scenario), consistent with the pattern of foreground terminal reuse without cleanup. **Last known good commit:** ## Root Cause In ** ** (PR #311011), the code path was changed to keep the terminal foreground instead of converting it to background: **Before:** Terminal was moved to background → next created a new terminal → no accumulation. **After:** Terminal stays foreground and is reused → each reuse creates a new , but the old one registered in under the previous is orphaned because: 1. Each invocation generates a fresh (UUID). 2. calls with the **new** , so the old notification under the previous is never found. 3. The terminal isn't disposed (it's reused), so never fires to trigger cleanup. 4. The old and its subscription survive indefinitely. ## Affected File - - Leak source: ( ) ## Suggested Fix When a foreground terminal is reused after , the old entry for that terminal instance should be cleaned up before registering a new one. One approach: index background notifications by terminal instance ID (not just ) so reuse of the same terminal disposes the previous .

title: Copilot Chat: ChatSessionWorkspaceFolderService polling loop freezes VS Code when large numbers of chat sessions have accumulated
text: Copilot Chat: ChatSessionWorkspaceFolderService polling loop freezes VS Code when large numbers of chat sessions have accumulated. ## VS Code Version 1.115.0 (commit , arm64) ## Extension 0.43.0 ## OS macOS 26.4.1 (arm64) ## Bug Description VS Code freezes (entire UI becomes unresponsive for several seconds) repeatedly after recent Copilot Chat updates. The freeze is triggered by running in a polling loop that iterates over every loaded chat session. On startup, the extension loads sessions from **all** workspace storage folders — not just the currently open workspace. With a typical long-term user accumulating sessions across many workspaces, this loop becomes heavy enough to block the extension host and freeze the UI. ## Log Evidence The following warning fires in a tight loop on every startup, once per loaded session per poll cycle: In a single ~90-second startup window, this warning was emitted **58 times** across sessions from multiple workspaces (timestamps 15:19:08 → 15:20:41). ## Scale of the Problem After diagnosis, the following data was collected on an affected machine: | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Workspace storage folders with | **85** | | Largest single folder | **841 session files / 667 MB** | | Second largest | 67 files / 114 MB | | Total data across all workspaces | **~1 GB** | | Total size | 3.7 GB | ## Why "Chat: Clear All Workspace Chats" Does Not Help The command only clears chat sessions for the **currently open workspace**. Sessions in all other 84 workspace storage folders are untouched and continue to be loaded and iterated on every startup. ## Workaround Manually deleting all directories resolved the freeze entirely: **macOS/Linux:** **Windows:** After deletion, workspace storage dropped from 3.7 GB and VS Code stopped freezing. ## Suggested Fixes 1. **Lazy loading**: Only load chat sessions for the currently open workspace, not all past workspaces simultaneously. 2. **Polling guard**: Once a session is found to have no repository properties, skip it in subsequent poll cycles rather than retrying it every time. 3. **"Clear All Workspace Chats" scope**: Extend the command to optionally clear sessions across all workspaces (with confirmation), not just the current one. 4. **Session retention limit**: Cap stored sessions per workspace (e.g. keep last N) or enforce a max size/age to prevent unbounded growth.

From user-level logs, the direct crash reason is always the **VS Code main process** hitting the V8 heap limit at around 4 GB: This does **not** look like a kernel OOM kill or GPU/driver reset. I checked kernel logs and did not see , , , , , etc. ### What I observed in the crashing session Latest crash: - Local time: - Main process: User journal shows: - heap near - then V8 OOM in the main process - then all VS Code windows exit together In the corresponding log session ( ), I did **not** see extension host restart loops. Each window's extension host appears to start once and remain running. However, I repeatedly see document/editor lifecycle related errors from Pylance in multiple windows. Typical stack shape: - - - - - I also see repeated warnings like: - - - These continue for hours and are still present close to the final crash. ### Why I am filing this in vscode and not only in Pylance The app-level symptom is a **shared main process OOM that takes down all windows**, not just a single extension host crash. The extension-side logs strongly suggest that Pylance is one trigger or reproducer, but I am not sure whether this is: 1. a bug in Pylance itself, 2. a VS Code lifecycle regression affecting extensions handling document/editor deltas, 3. or an interaction between the two. I am filing here because the final failure is a VS Code main process crash, and there may be a core memory leak / retention issue after repeated document/editor lifecycle churn. ### Approximate repro pattern I do not yet have a minimal repro, but this is the rough pattern that seems to trigger it: 1. Open multiple VS Code windows. 2. At least one window uses Remote-SSH. 3. Open/edit/close Python files in one or more windows so that Python + Pylance activate. 4. Keep VS Code running for a while and continue normal editing/navigation. 5. Eventually the shared VS Code process grows until it reaches ~4 GB heap and all windows crash together. ### Additional observations - In this specific session, Remote-SSH did log , but the remote authority still resolved successfully, so this did not look like the immediate crash trigger. - I had previously removed GitLens from my profile, but in this exact crashing process it had already been loaded before uninstall, so I cannot use this session as a clean “without GitLens” control. - The strongest active errors close to the crash come from Pylance/document lifecycle handling, not from extension host restarts.

title: Host becomes unresponsive during synchronous subprocess wait instead of timing out cleanly
text:
Host becomes unresponsive during synchronous subprocess wait instead of timing out cleanly. Type: Performance Issue ## Description When an external subprocess stalls, the host can become unresponsive if the subprocess is waited on synchronously from a UI-thread or event-loop-owned execution path. I believe this is a separate resilience issue from the child-process bug itself. I created a self-contained reproduction showing the host-side failure mode without depending on the original application code. The reproduction demonstrates that a blocking on the event-loop thread starves the host loop, while offloading the same wait preserves responsiveness. This report is about the host freeze behavior, not the original child-process locking bug. ## VS Code Version Observed in a Windows environment. Exact VS Code build should be filled in from the affected machine when filing. ## OS Version Windows ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Run the self-contained reproduction in [host_freeze_repro.py]( 2. Observe the section. 3. Compare it with the section. 4. Optionally run [test_host_freeze_repro.py]( with pytest. Commands: ## Expected Behavior - A slow or stalled subprocess should not freeze the host. - UI/event-loop work should continue while the child process is pending. - Timeout and cancellation should remain serviceable. - The host should surface an error state rather than becoming unresponsive. ## Actual Behavior - If the host performs a synchronous wait on the same thread that services events, event-loop progress stalls. - In the repro, heartbeat activity pauses for approximately the same duration as the child-process wait. - The offloaded version does not show the same starvation pattern. ## Does This Issue Occur When All Extensions Are Disabled? The original symptom involved extension-driven subprocess execution, so the real-world scenario is extension-related. The attached repro is extension-independent and demonstrates the host-side design risk directly. ## Reproduction Files - [host_freeze_repro.py]( - [test_host_freeze_repro.py]( - [HOST_FREEZE_REPORT.md]( ## Why I Think This Belongs In VS Code Even if an extension or child process misbehaves, the host should avoid blocking the execution path responsible for responsiveness. If VS Code or an extension-host layer exposes or encourages a synchronous subprocess wait pattern in a latency-sensitive path, that is a host resilience problem. ## Likely Fix Area Please inspect the process-launch and process-wait path used by the extension host or related integration layers for any of the following on a responsiveness-critical thread: - synchronous or calls - blocking process output draining - sync-over-async bridges around subprocess completion The likely fix is to move waiting and stream handling off the host thread or use a fully asynchronous subprocess flow. title: High CPU usage caused by file watcher
text:
High CPU usage caused by file watcher. Type: Bug I've seen other issues about this, but they're all closed and locked. All of the ones I found were about projects with a Typescript workspace, and the suggestion was to disable a switch on the TS language server options; However, I'm working with a flutter project (and I don't target web). Just like in those issues, I don't really know how to offer a repro, as this bug happened only a few times, seemingly at random. What I do know is that something triggers it and, when that happens, file-watcher starts using 100% of a single thread whenever VS is in the background. If I bring VS back to the foreground, the CPU usage decreases significantly, albeit still higher than normal. As soon as I alt-tab, it starts again. I don't mind the slightly higher CPU usage tbh, but the fact it's concentrated on a single thread means it creates a hotspot, the CPU gets very hot very fast and fans spin up really loudly. Looking at the Process Explorer inside VS, a process with name "file-watcher [2]" was the culprit. Killing it mitigated the issue, but I don't know if there are any consequences (and it's a bit annoying having to do that). I've recently experienced the same issue with [Bruno]( which also uses Electron. In that case I was able to find out a repro, and it was related to deleting files that were being watched. One detail, not sure if relevant, is that my workspace is on a Windows Dev Drive. title: Copilot Chat OOM crash (20+ GB memory leak) on large structured responses — reproducible across models
text:
Copilot Chat OOM crash (20+ GB memory leak) on large structured responses — reproducible across models. Type: Bug ## Summary Copilot Chat causes a catastrophic memory leak in the VS Code window renderer process when processing chat requests that involve large directory/file analysis. The window process balloons from ~350 MB to 20+ GB, consuming all system RAM until Windows OOM-kills it. Reproducible across multiple models (Gemini 3 Flash Preview and GPT 5.4 both tested). ## Environment - Windows 11, 32 GB RAM - VS Code latest stable - Two windows open on separate repos with separate profiles - GitHub Copilot Chat extension (latest) ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open a workspace containing a photography archive with ~1,716 files across 15 subdirectories (mix of JPEG and RAW folders) 2. In Copilot Chat, attach a naming-conventions document (~280 lines) as context 3. Send a prompt asking Copilot to compare RAW and JPEG folder structures and verify every directory and file is a 1:1 sister match 4. Copilot processes the request and begins generating a large structured response (comparison results, integrity checks, folder-by-folder file counts table) 5. The VS Code window renderer process memory begins climbing uncontrollably ## Observed Behavior The window renderer process allocates memory without bound. Measured via Process Explorer and PowerShell : ### Test 1 — Gemini 3 Flash (Preview) | Snapshot | Window Process | Total VS Code | |---|---|---| | Baseline | 366 MB | 3,055 MB | | Spike | 5,150 MB | 8,530 MB | | Climbing | 9,478 MB | 14,125 MB | | **Peak** | **22,820 MB** | **24,014 MB** | | OOM crash | process killed | 150 MB | ### Test 2 — GPT 5.4 | Snapshot | Window Process | Total VS Code | |---|---|---| | Baseline | 366 MB | 3,055 MB | | Spike | 5,150 MB | 8,530 MB | | Climbing | 9,478 MB | 14,125 MB | | **Peak** | **19,741 MB** | **21,272 MB** | | OOM crash | process killed | 435 MB | Both tests terminated with: > "The window terminated unexpectedly (reason: 'oom', code: '-536870904')" ## Expected Behavior Copilot Chat should render large structured responses without unbounded memory allocation. A response covering 1,716 files across 15 directories should not require 20 GB of RAM to render. ## Key Observations - **Model-independent**: Both Gemini 3 Flash and GPT 5.4 trigger the same leak, confirming this is a renderer/client-side issue, not a model backend issue - **The leak is in the window process**, not the extension host — the extension host stays at ~400 MB while the window process balloons - **Other processes get starved**: As the window process grows, all other VS Code processes shrink (OS reclaiming pages), eventually causing cascading failures across windows - **Not caused by extension stacking**: Reproduced with a minimal profile (only Copilot Chat + Python + PowerShell) - **Smaller chat requests work fine**: Normal coding questions in the same session do not trigger the leak — only large structured responses involving many files/directories ## Workaround Avoid sending prompts that generate large structured tabular responses involving many files. Use CLI-based AI tools for large repo analysis instead. title: Renderer OOM crash: event listener leak in chat tool invocation UI (appendToolInvocation/trackToolState)
text: Renderer OOM crash: event listener leak in chat tool invocation UI (appendToolInvocation/trackToolState). ## Bug Description VS Code's renderer process crashes with OOM ( ) during long-running Copilot Chat agent sessions. The root cause is an event listener leak in the chat tool invocation rendering path -- listeners attached by / in tool invocation widgets are never disposed, causing unbounded memory growth until the renderer hits its V8 heap limit. ## Environment - VS Code: 1.110.1 (61b3d0ab13), x64 - Copilot Chat: 0.38.2 - OS: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26100.7840 (x64) - RAM: 32 GB - System memory at crash: ~54% (crash is per-process V8 heap limit, not system RAM) ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open a workspace with a large Python codebase (~300+ files) 2. Run 2-4 concurrent Copilot Chat agent sessions 3. Have agents perform tool-heavy work (file reads, terminal commands, subagent spawns) 4. Memory climbs steadily over ~55 minutes regardless of conversation compaction 5. Renderer process OOMs ## Evidence from Logs ### Listener leak warnings (renderer.log) The renderer logs show **3,043 listener leak warnings** across the session, with listener counts growing monotonically: | Log file | Time range start | Leak warnings | Max listener count | |---|---|---|---| | renderer.4.log | 20:46 | 670 | 1,177 | | renderer.3.log | 21:11 | 716 | 1,361 | | renderer.2.log | 21:24 | 890 | 1,402 | | renderer.1.log | 21:33 | 680 | 1,461 | | renderer.log | 21:41 | 87 | 1,536 (crash) | ### Leaking stack trace Second leaking emitter: ### Key observations - **Conversation compaction does not reclaim the leaked memory** -- the leak is in renderer-side UI widgets (tool invocation tracking), not in conversation context - **The leak is proportional to tool invocations**, not conversation length - The session had ~884 agent/subagent LLM calls before crashing - Growth is monotonic -- no disposal occurs between compaction events ## Expected Behavior Event listeners created by , , and should be disposed when tool invocations complete or when conversation history is compacted. ## Workaround Starting a fresh chat session periodically is the only effective mitigation. Setting extends the runway but doesn't prevent the eventual crash.

title: Chat panel should virtualize DOM for long conversations (performance degrades over time)
text: Chat panel should virtualize DOM for long conversations (performance degrades over time). <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- Describe the feature you'd like. --> ## Description During extended chat sessions with Copilot (or any chat participant), the VS Code UI becomes progressively slower — clicks, scrolling, resizing, and typing all develop noticeable lag. This correlates directly with conversation length. ## Root Cause Analysis The chat panel webview keeps **all messages in the DOM** regardless of how many there are. After a long session with hundreds of messages (each containing code blocks, tool call outputs, markdown rendering, etc.), the DOM grows to tens of thousands of nodes. This causes: 1. **Layout/reflow bottleneck** — every new message triggers layout recalculation across the entire DOM 2. **Repaint overhead** — scrolling repaints large composited layers 3. **Memory growth** — the renderer process grows to 1.5-2+ GB over a long session The pattern is well-understood in web development. The VS Code **editor** handles this correctly via line virtualization (only visible lines are in the DOM, enabling million-line files). The chat panel does not apply the same pattern. ## Expected Behavior The chat panel should: - **Virtualize the message list** — only render messages visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer above/below for smooth scrolling) - **Lazy-load old messages** — messages scrolled far out of view should be removed from the DOM and reconstructed on-demand - **Cap DOM complexity** — consider collapsing or summarizing very old messages (e.g., tool call outputs beyond a certain age could be collapsed by default) ## Reproduction Steps 1. Open VS Code with Copilot Chat 2. Have a long conversation (100+ messages with code blocks and tool calls) 3. Observe progressive UI degradation: - Click response delay increases - Window resizing becomes stuttery - Typing in the chat input has visible latency - Scrolling within the chat panel is not smooth 4. Open Task Manager: the renderer process ( ) will show 1-2+ GB memory ## System Info - VS Code: 1.99+ - OS: Windows 11 - RAM: 16 GB - Extensions: Minimal (3 extensions, Copilot Chat is the primary one) - Settings: Fully optimized (minimap off, animations off, smooth scroll off, etc.) ## Impact This primarily affects users who rely on long agent-mode sessions where ending the conversation means losing context. The longer the session, the worse the degradation becomes, eventually making VS Code nearly unusable until the conversation is cleared. ## References - Virtual scrolling is a solved pattern: react-window, react-virtuoso, /virtual - VS Code's own editor uses line virtualization for exactly this reason - Similar to how Slack/Discord handle long message histories with windowed rendering

title: Chat Constantly Frozen
text: Chat Constantly Frozen. Summary GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code (Windows workspace) frequently hangs during chat and agent-driven actions (panel/editAgent, tool/runSubagent, searchSubagentTool). The hang manifests as extremely long-running requests (15–17+ minutes), repeated Code Search diff failures, periodic network suspension errors, and at least one hard failure where a Node worker terminates due to JS heap out-of-memory. Environment VS Code: 1.109.4 Copilot Chat extension: 0.37.6 Account: JSunRae (token acquired successfully; SKU plus_yearly_subscriber_quota) Agent: ChatGPT 5.3 Codex Expected Behavior Copilot Chat responds consistently within seconds. Agent actions (editAgent, runSubagent, code search indexing/diff, repo/file search) complete without freezing the UI. No persistent background error loops or memory crashes. Actual Behavior Copilot Chat intermittently becomes unresponsive / appears “stuck.” Agent requests complete only after very long delays (hundreds of thousands of ms), or not at all. Background services (code search indexing/diff) repeatedly error and appear to degrade responsiveness. A Node worker crashes due to memory exhaustion, after which Copilot reliability degrades further. Timeline & Evidence (from logs) 1) Extension activates successfully, token acquired Activation looks normal at first: Got Copilot token for JSunRae Copilot Chat: 0.37.6, VS Code: 1.109.4 ConversationFeature: Activating contributions 2) GitHub API 404 when fetching org custom instructions (early error) Immediately after token acquisition: GET - Status: 404 Failed to fetch custom instructions for org JSunRae This suggests Copilot Chat is attempting an org-level call for a non-org identity (user vs org) or is misclassifying the account context. It may not be fatal alone, but it’s a clear early error in the session. 3) Hangs correlate with extremely long request durations Multiple requests report durations consistent with “hang” (examples): ... | 873165ms | [tool/runSubagent] (~14.6 min) ... | 900178ms | [panel/editAgent] (~15.0 min) ... | 996263ms | [panel/editAgent] (~16.6 min) ... | 1009519ms | [panel/editAgent] (~16.8 min) ... | 1028516ms | [copilotLanguageModelWrapper] (~17.1 min) ... | 955556ms | [panel/editAgent] (~15.9 min) ... | 1016871ms | [searchSubagentTool] (~16.9 min) These are not normal latency spikes; they strongly indicate blocked work (I/O, indexing, diff, network suspension) or a deadlock/queue stall inside extension host / worker pipeline. 4) Hard failure: JS heap out of memory (worker crash) A critical failure occurs: Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory Once this happens, Copilot Chat often behaves like it’s “hung” even when some requests still complete sporadically. 5) Network layer reports suspended I/O Later errors: net::ERR_NETWORK_IO_SUSPENDED GithubCodeSearchService::getRemoteIndexState(...). Failed Failed to fetch indexing status... This points to Windows/Electron network stack temporarily suspending I/O (sleep/hibernate, power saving, VPN/proxy, network driver, firewall/endpoint security, or electron net stack issues). When remote indexing status calls fail, Copilot code search features can get stuck retrying, potentially cascading into hangs. 6) Persistent CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff failures (repeating loop) A repeating pattern every ~2 minutes: CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff: Failed to get new diff for ... Trading-Win/contracts CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff: Failed to get new diff for ... Trading-Win This looks like a background loop that never stabilizes. If Copilot’s agent relies on diffs/indexing for context, repeated diff failures can stall agent steps or keep the extension in a degraded state. 7) Tool timeouts in workspace-wide grep and file search Additional failures during agent operations: Error from tool grep_search ... Timeout in searching text in files ... Error from tool file_search ... Timeout in searching files ... This suggests the workspace search/diff pipeline is overloaded or blocked (large repo, huge generated folders, node_modules, artifacts, binary files, or file watching issues), which can contribute to memory blow-ups and long stalls. 8) One example of a tool trying to read a non-existent file cannot open ... tf1_dispatch.yml ... Unable to resolve nonexistent file Not necessarily the root cause, but it shows the agent is attempting filesystem operations and encountering errors that may not always be handled gracefully in longer chains. Impact Copilot Chat becomes unreliable for coding workflows in this Windows repo (especially agent operations). Blocks productivity: chat stalls, agent actions don’t complete, and repeated background errors consume resources. After the worker OOM, stability appears significantly worse. Likely Contributing Factors (based on log signatures) Memory pressure / runaway context building leading to JS heap OOM (worker crash). Code search diff/index loop failing continuously (CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff errors), causing repeated background work and preventing stable context updates. Network I/O being suspended (ERR_NETWORK_IO_SUSPENDED), breaking remote indexing checks and potentially causing long extension waits/timeouts. Workspace search operations timing out (grep/file search), likely due to repo size or unexcluded directories. Reproduction (what I’m doing when it happens) Open VS Code on Windows in repo: ...Vs Code Projects\Trading-Win Use Copilot Chat normally, then trigger agent-like actions (edit agent / run subagent / search) After some usage, Copilot Chat stops responding or takes 10–17 minutes to complete simple steps Evenually see worker crash (JS heap out of memory) and/or persistent CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff errors Attachments / Key log excerpts Include these lines in the ticket (they’re the most diagnostic): Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory net::ERR_NETWORK_IO_SUSPENDED CodeSearchWorkspaceDiff: Failed to get new diff for ... text: Copilot Chat stuck at "getting chat ready" on Remote SSH with ulimit -v restriction (WASM OOM). <!-- This issue affects many HPC/cluster users with ulimit -v restrictions using Remote SSH --> - Copilot Chat Extension Version: latest (2026-02) - VS Code Version: 1.97+ (Stable, c3a26841a84f20dfe0850d0a5a9bd01da4f003ea) - OS Version: Linux x86_64 (HPC cluster, remote) / Windows or macOS (local) - Feature (e.g. agent/edit/ask mode): All — Chat never initializes - Selected model (e.g. GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet): N/A — model menu unavailable - Logs: Steps to Reproduce: 1. Connect via Remote SSH to a Linux server where is restricted (e.g. 16GB on an HPC login node) 2. Open Copilot Chat 3. Chat shows "Getting chat ready..." → "Chat is almost ready..." → fails 4. Model menu is empty/unavailable 5. Extension Host (Remote) output shows **Key details:** - Remote server = 16777216 (16GB). Extension Host process alone uses ~12GB virtual memory, leaving no room for WASM allocation. - The error is a **misleading secondary symptom** — the extension fails during WASM init, so subsequent network calls never get properly configured. This sends users down a proxy/network debugging rabbit hole. - Old versions of Copilot Chat (≤ v0.22.4 with Helix fetcher) worked fine because they did not depend on WASM. - This is extremely common on HPC clusters where login nodes have strict ulimit settings that users cannot change. **Workaround:** Add to on the remote server: Then fully disconnect and reconnect Remote SSH (Reload Window is not sufficient). **References:** - General WASM OOM issue: microsoft/vscode-remote-release#11027 - CSC supercomputer center documented this: - Related Copilot SSH issues that may share this root cause: #4766, #8406, #3881 **Suggestion:** Detect WASM allocation failure during Copilot init and surface a clear error message suggesting , instead of the opaque "getting chat ready" timeout.

title: VS Code Insiders Renderer Crash (EXC_BREAKPOINT) When Processing Large Image Attachment in Copilot Chat Agent Mode
text:
VS Code Insiders Renderer Crash (EXC_BREAKPOINT) When Processing Large Image Attachment in Copilot Chat Agent Mode. We have written the needed data into your clipboard because it was too large to send. Please paste. Type: Bug ## Bug Report: VS Code Insiders Renderer Crash (EXC_BREAKPOINT) When Processing Large Image Attachment in Copilot Chat Agent Mode ### Environment | Component | Version | |---|---| | VS Code Insiders | 1.110.0-insider (commit ) | | Electron Framework | 39.5.2 | | Node.js (bundled) | 22.22.0 | | Copilot Chat extension | 0.38.2026021305 | | Copilot CLI (related) | 0.0.410 | | Model | | | macOS | 26.2 (Build 25C56) | | Hardware | MacBook Air M2 (Mac14,2), 24 GB RAM, arm64 | Other installed extensions: 0.129.2026021313, 0.5.75, 2026.0.0, 0.444.0, 0.12.17. ### Summary The VS Code Insiders renderer process for a single workspace window crashed with / in the V8 engine during a Copilot Chat agent-mode session. The window went completely black (blank — all UI elements removed). Other VS Code windows for other workspaces continued functioning normally. macOS generated a formal crash report ( ). ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Open VS Code Insiders with a workspace containing an AGENTS.md, 4 skills in skills, a Makefile with a target, and 43+ scripts. 2. In Copilot Chat agent mode (model: ), work across **20 user turns** over ~13 hours (with overnight idle), performing: - File edits ( , ) — 39 tool calls - Terminal commands ( ) — 129 tool calls - Sub-agent invocations ( ) — 2 tool calls - Todo tracking — 28 tool calls - Total: 211 tool calls 3. Over turns 5-14, session state grows to ~2.57 MB. Agent begins stalling mid-generation (4 events at lines 78, 88, 99, 103 of session JSONL). 4. **At turn 15, attach a PNG screenshot** (~1.5 MB file: ) to the chat. 5. VS Code serializes the image into the chat session state as a **byte-by-byte JSON dictionary**: — producing a **3.78 MB JSONL entry** (4,507,072 character value with numeric keys for each byte). 6. The assistant responds, adding another **3.79 MB** entry (line 110) containing the full response + content references. 7. Session state jumps from 2.57 MB → 10.45 MB in two lines. 8. 3-5 more turns are processed (lines 111-138, ~130 KB additional). 9. **Renderer crashes.** Window goes completely black. No error dialog. No recovery option. ### Expected Behavior - Image attachments should be efficiently encoded (e.g., base64 string, or URI reference to the file), not serialized as a JSON dictionary of byte indices. - The renderer should not crash when processing large entries in the chat session state. If session state exceeds a safe threshold, it should gracefully degrade (e.g., truncate, compact, or warn the user). - At minimum, the window should show an error/reload prompt rather than going blank. ### Actual Behavior - The renderer process self-terminates with / . - The window goes completely black — all UI chrome, sidebar, editor, and status bar disappear. - Other VS Code windows remain functional. - The session file ( ) is preserved at 10.59 MB on disk. - The session cannot be resumed after restarting VS Code. ### Crash Report Analysis **macOS IPS crash report:** | Field | Value | |---|---| | Process | (PID 50143) | | Exception | (SIGTRAP) | | Termination | (Trace/BPT trap), self-terminated via | | Process uptime | 12.75 hours (launched 18:07:44, crashed 06:53:16) | | Faulting thread | (thread 0) | **Crashed thread stack (62 frames, key frames):** The crash path shows V8 failing during **array creation** ( ) while processing microtasks, with repeated checks suggesting it was traversing or validating a large array structure — consistent with the 4.5M-entry byte dictionary from the PNG. **VM state at crash:** | Region | Size | |---|---| | Memory Tag 253 | **32.1 GB** (4,539 regions) | | Memory Tag 255 | **1.3 TB** (2,860 regions) | | MALLOC | 88.9 MB | | Stack | 152.8 MB | | Physical RAM | 24 GB | The 32.1 GB virtual allocation in Tag 253 (V8/JavaScript heap region on Chromium arm64) indicates the V8 heap had grown well beyond the typical ~4 GB limit, likely from accumulating the serialized image data and session history in the renderer's JavaScript heap. **Additional macOS diagnostic:** The same VS Code process was also flagged for excessive disk I/O — **8.59 GB written over 31,502 seconds** (272 KB/sec average), exceeding the macOS limit of 99 KB/sec over 86,400s. This is consistent with the extension repeatedly persisting the 10.58 MB session state to the JSONL file on disk. ### Root Cause: Image Serialization Format The **proximate cause** is the image serialization format used by the chat session state. When a user attaches a PNG file to a Copilot Chat message, the image bytes are serialized as: This creates a JSON object with **one key per byte** of the image. A 1.5 MB PNG produces a 3.78 MB JSON entry with 4,507,072 characters. This is ~2.5x inflate over the raw binary, and orders of magnitude worse than base64 (~1.33x) or a URI reference (0x). When the renderer deserializes this back into V8, each byte becomes a separate property on a JavaScript object, creating millions of allocations that overwhelm the V8 heap. ### Contributing Factors 1. **Long-running session (12.75 hours):** The renderer process accumulated memory over the session lifetime. 2. **Heavy tool use (211 tool calls):** The agent-mode session generated 129 terminal commands, many with multi-KB outputs stored in the conversation history. 3. **Session state already at 2.57 MB before the image:** 14 prior turns of dense tool activity had already consumed significant context. 4. **No session compaction:** Unlike Copilot CLI (which has context compaction), VS Code Chat sessions grow unboundedly. ### Note on Copilot CLI Relationship This session involved heavy use of Copilot CLI (v0.0.410) orchestrated through VS Code Chat's tool — 129 terminal invocations running shell commands, many of which invoked commands in external repos. The CLI itself is **not** the crash cause — it runs in separate processes. However, the **terminal output from CLI invocations** was captured and stored in the conversation history, contributing to the 2.57 MB baseline before the image was attached. The CLI's context compaction mechanism (which keeps CLI sessions from growing unboundedly) is not available to VS Code Chat sessions. ### Suggested Fixes 1. **Critical:** Serialize image attachments as base64 strings or URI references, not byte-by-byte JSON dictionaries. 2. **High:** Implement session state size guards — warn or refuse to persist entries >1 MB, or auto-compact older turns. 3. **Medium:** Add V8 heap monitoring to the renderer — detect approaching heap limits and trigger garbage collection or session compaction before a crash. text: [Linux] Orphaned zygote processes spam "Socket operation on non-socket" errors filling system logs after VS Code crash. ### Issue Type: Bug ### VS Code Version 1.108.1 Commit: 585eba7c0c34fd6b30faac7c62a42050bfbc0086 Platform: Linux x64 Ubuntu 24.04, Kernel 6.14.0-37-generic ### Description When VS Code crashes on Linux, orphaned zygote child processes continue attempting to communicate with the dead parent process, resulting in a massive log spam that fills up the systemd journal and consumes disk space. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Run VS Code on Ubuntu 24.04 2. VS Code crashes (trigger unknown, possibly extension-related or memory pressure) 3. Check - observe hundreds of thousands of zygote errors ### Observed Behavior After VS Code crashes, orphaned zygote processes generate ~750,000 error messages in 24 hours: Evidence from kernel: ### Impact - **Storage exhaustion**: 407MB journal consumed in days - **System log pollution**: Makes debugging other issues difficult - **Repeated pattern**: Issue recurs with each VS Code crash ### Expected Behavior When VS Code's main process crashes, child zygote processes should either: 1. Terminate gracefully when parent dies 2. Have rate-limited logging to prevent log spam ### Related Issues - Similar issue in other Electron apps: - This appears to be an upstream Electron/Chromium issue affecting multiple applications ### Workaround Currently mitigating by: 1. title: Agent sessions: creating new background session is lagging
text: Agent sessions: creating new background session is lagging. Originally reported here * Creating worktree and the like can be slow, while all of this is happening we don't have a new session in the sessions list **Slow points** * Creating worktree * Possibly even starting a new session (this depends on how fast the CLI is, if we spawn a process in future this could be slower) * ✅ Getting list of sessions and session details for each session could be slow (we might want to add telemetry for this and cache some of this in memory) E.g. if user starts a new session, then nothing has changed in the list of session, except to include a new item and return previously returned items ( **Solutions** * List current session in list of sessions and trigger session changed event * However this has a drawback, If we use the new untitled session id and return that in the session list, then this needs to be swapped as well. I suppose this is fine as thats how the UI works today **Summary** * We might as well always list a new session in the sessions list using the (except in cases where we have worktree change migration etc, as in those cases we start a new session)

title: Crashes when attempting to Open folder/Save new file/Navigate various menus, and causes VSCode install to become permanently unusable
text: Crashes when attempting to Open folder/Save new file/Navigate various menus, and causes VSCode install to become permanently unusable. Type: **Bug** - VS Code Version: 1.107.x, 1.106.x - OS Version: Oracle Linux 8, Rocky Linux 8 - Extensions: None I am observing three scenarios where trying to open a folder, save a new file, or visit various menus (Help->About, Help->Report Issue) causes VSCode to crash. Unfortunately this is quite a serious issue, because it can cause a fully-functional VSCode to become permanently stuck in a state where it cannot open folders or save new files -- even when and have been cleared, the system restarted, and VScode reinstalled. The only resolution is to downgrade to 1.105 or earlier. ### Scenario 1: Oracle Linux 8 with VSCode 1.106.x or 1.107.x (Intel i7-13700K-based Dell OptiPlexes, native install) This involves pasting a "large" text file (~2.5+ million lines, ~50MB) into a new tab, which causes VSCode to eventually crash. 1. Open VSCode 2. Create a new text file (Ctrl-N) 3. Paste a relatively large file in (several million lines, which can be short; 16-ish characters) 3a. (Variation 1) Save the file, reload, copy the contents to a new tab, and attempt to close it the new tab. 3b. (Variation 2) Attempt to save the file, but it may not succeed (may appear hung). and restart VSCode, and then try to close the unsaved text file. 5. The application crashes when attempting to close the text file. To be clear, this occurs with zero extensions installed. ### Scenario 2: ( -based install on above-described Dell OptiPlexes) - This was identical to Scenario 1, except a install was used instead of . The steps and resulting failures were identical to Scenario 1. In both scenarios, once this failure occurs VSCode is permanently rendered useless on the host, as it can no longer open folders or save new files. Clearing all configuration and rebooting have no effect. The only way to resolve it is to uninstall and revert back to 1.105 or earlier. There must be state stored somewhere else aside from or that causes this to occur, but it's unclear where that would be ( wasn't helpful here). ### Scenario 3: Rocky Linux 8 Workstation guest on a Debian Trixie Linux host (VirtualBox): 1. Install VSCode 1.106.x or 1.107.x 2. Launch VS Code 3. Attempt to Open a Folder, Create a new Text file and save, or visit Help->About or Help->Report Problem 4. The application crashes. This happens every time for me, so hopefully it is easy to reproduce. In this scenario, VSCode was never functional to begin with (unlike in Scenario 1/2), but seems to be crashing in the same way (on Help->About, closing a new text file, etc), so hopefully it is useful for investigating. The VM had 8GB RAM, 8 cores, and a 120GB HDD. This is a pretty scary issue, so I am hopeful that it can be investigated soon. I for one am stuck on 1.105 until I know it's been resolved.

title: Integrated terminal on macOS freezes permanently after running a program that segfaults — Crashpad fatal error kills PTY host
text:
Integrated terminal on macOS freezes permanently after running a program that segfaults — Crashpad fatal error kills PTY host. Type: Bug ## Description On macOS, when running any native binary (e.g., C/C++ program) inside the VSCode integrated terminal that **segfaults**, the terminal becomes permanently frozen. - The program prints its first output - No crash message appears ("Segmentation fault" is not shown) - The prompt never returns - The terminal stops responding to all input - Creating new integrated terminals does not help - Only fully quitting VSCode restores normal behavior Meanwhile, the rest of VSCode remains completely functional. This issue **does NOT occur** when running the same binary in Terminal.app or iTerm2. It is reproducible in a fresh VSCode window with all extensions disabled. it also doesn't always occur on the first run, but becomes consistent after a few attempts or other interactions with other crashing programs. Once VSCode is in that state, all other VSCode windows also exhibit the same terminal freeze behavior if running crashing programs. After launching VSCode with , I found that the freeze is caused by an **internal Crashpad fatal error**, which seems to kill the terminal's PTY host process. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Steps to Reproduce ### 1. Create a minimal crashing C++ program ### 2. Compile ### 3. Run inside VSCode integrated terminal ### 4. Observed output Starting program that will crash... - No crash message - No prompt - Terminal stops responding Running the same binary in Terminal.app or iTerm2 works correctly. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Observed Behavior - Terminal becomes completely frozen after the segfault - No "Segmentation fault" message is printed by the shell - Child process cannot be killed with - Shell does not receive SIGCHLD (or it is never handled) - All other integrated terminals become stuck - VSCode UI continues working normally - Only quitting VSCode restores the terminal ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Expected Behavior - The program should crash normally - Shell should display a crash message - Prompt should return - Other terminals should not be affected - The PTY backend should not crash ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Critical Debug Log (from ) Immediately when the program segfaults, the following is printed: [1210/101619.570871:WARNING:third_party/crashpad/crashpad/snapshot/mac/process_reader_mac.cc:460] all_image_infos.infoArrayCount is zero [1210/101619.627335:FATAL:third_party/crashpad/crashpad/handler/mac/exception_handler_server.cc:76] Check failed: kr == KERN_SUCCESS. mach_port_request_notification: (os/kern) invalid capability (20) VS Code version: Code 1.106.3 (Universal) (bf9252a2fb45be6893dd8870c0bf37e2e1766d61, 2025-11-25T22:28:18.024Z) OS version: Darwin arm64 25.1.0 Modes:

title: getDefaultAccount() promise never resolves on empty profile -> leaks every listener
text: getDefaultAccount() promise never resolves on empty profile -> leaks every listener. In an empty profile (or when debugging code oss), there is no account provider which calls . This means that the promise returned by never resolves (until the user installs some extension). Thus, every code that repeatedly awaits that promise causes a memory leak of the context in which the promise is awaited (which usually contains ). This was reported first [here]( I fixed some leaks [here]( However, there are more leaks. I suggest to not give out promises (unless you have a strong guarantee that it resolves in a reasonable amount of time). Instead, getDefaultAccount() should return Account | undefined | 'loading', and the on change event should fire when that state changes. Alternatively, there could be , to bundle the value and the event.

title: VS Code native crash on Mac with error 5
text:
VS Code native crash on Mac with error 5. Type: Bug Much like [this issue]( I'm frequently receiving a crash with "error 5", preceeded by heavy slowness. Unlike that issue, I've managed to find a pretty reliable repro for it. What appears to trigger the problem is that a process is writing/deleting a ton of files inside the directory that vscode is looking at for its workspace. I'm unsure if editing the files will do it, but create and delete does. My directory structure is several levels deep, so that may also be involved. For this particular crash dump, I ran the process to create the files and then used to delete them while clicking around in Code. The directory with lots of changes showed a spinning circle for a while, the UI was very slow, and then it crashed. I haven't tried yet without extensions, but I'll do that in a bit next time I'm debugging that particular process, since I have quite a few. I'm assuming for now that it's not an extension, since the other person linked above had basically the same symptoms. title: High CPU / “Extension host unresponsive” when GitHub Copilot Chat is enabled; normal when Chat is disabled (VS Code 1.104.0, Windows 11)
text: High CPU / “Extension host unresponsive” when GitHub Copilot Chat is enabled; normal when Chat is disabled (VS Code 1.104.0, Windows 11). **Problem** Enabling **GitHub Copilot Chat** causes sustained high CPU and periodic “Extension host is unresponsive.” Disabling **only** Copilot Chat (keeping Copilot core enabled) immediately restores normal behavior and low idle CPU. Pylance works normally. **Copilot Chat Extension Version** - GitHub Copilot Chat: 0.31.0 - GitHub Copilot (core): 1.372.0 **VS Code / OS** - VS Code: 1.104.1 (user setup) - Commit: 0f0d87fa9e96c856c5212fc86db137ac0d783365 - Architecture: x64 - OS: Windows 11 x64 (build 26100) **Python / Extensions** - Python: 3.13.2 (workspace venv selected) - Python extension: 2025.15.2025091901 - Pylance: 2025.8.2 **Feature Area** - Copilot Chat “Ask” panel during normal editing (no special prompts required). Default model selection. **Steps to Reproduce** 1. Open Python workspace; select a clean venv as interpreter. 2. Verify Pylance completions (e.g., then ). 3. Enable **GitHub Copilot** and **GitHub Copilot Chat**. 4. Type in a small file for ~20–30 s; then leave the editor idle. 5. Observe CPU in Task Manager and VS Code: CPU becomes very high; occasional toast “Extension host is unresponsive.” 6. Disable **only** Copilot Chat (leave Copilot core enabled): 7. Repeat step 4 → CPU returns to ~0–5% idle; no unresponsive host; Pylance remains fully functional. **Expected Behavior** Copilot Chat should not materially increase idle CPU or trigger extension-host unresponsiveness during light editing. **Actual Behavior** With Copilot Chat enabled, CPU becomes **much higher than 30–40%**: - VS Code often sits **well above 50% overall CPU**; system utilization can reach **90%+**. - Periodic “Extension host is unresponsive” toasts. Disabling **only** Copilot Chat immediately returns VS Code to **~0–5%** idle. **Workspace Notes (to rule out other causes)** - limits analysis scope ( / tuned), large folders excluded; file watchers trimmed; Pylance indexing off. - Clean venv is the interpreter. - Pylance/Python extensions behave normally. - The issue toggles reliably by switching **Copilot Chat** ON/OFF. **Logs / Evidence** - CPU profile (**bad state**, Chat enabled): higher activity; correlates with unresponsive host. - CPU profile (**good state**, Chat disabled, Copilot core enabled): extension host ~**99.9% idle**. - Developer Tools Console (**bad state**): warnings/errors captured. *(Files attached or available on request if size exceeds GitHub limits.)* **Workaround** Run with **GitHub Copilot enabled** and **GitHub Copilot Chat disabled** (commands above), or uninstall Copilot Chat for this workspace. I’m happy to provide additional 30–60 s CPU profiles and full console logs if needed. <!-- Failed to upload "CPU-20250920T205124.920Z.cpuprofile.txt" --> [CPU-20250920T173146.396Z.cpuprofile.txt](
