title: MCP Apps: App-provided tools registered via App.registerTool() are not exposed to Copilot agent
text: MCP Apps: App-provided tools registered via App.registerTool() are not exposed to Copilot agent. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- Describe the feature you'd like. --> Description MCP Apps rendered in VS Code Insiders can successfully connect to the host and call MCP server tools via app.callServerTool(), but App-provided tools registered with App.registerTool() do not appear to be discovered or exposed to the Copilot agent. Environment Visual Studio Code - Insiders: 1.140.0-insider MCP Apps protocol version reported by the host: 2026-01-26 SDK: /ext-apps Scenario An MCP server tool (for example, show-datasources) opens an MCP App UI. Before app.connect(), the App registers an ephemeral tool: app.registerTool( "open-datasource-editor", { description: "Open the editor for the specified datasource", inputSchema: z.object({ name: z.string(), }), }, async ({ name }) => { // switch the current View from list mode to edit mode }, ); The App connects successfully. The App can successfully call MCP server tools through app.callServerTool(). The Host initialization response includes capabilities such as: { "hostCapabilities": { "serverTools": { "listChanged": true }, "serverResources": { "listChanged": true } } } I instrumented the App iframe with window.addEventListener("message", ...) to inspect Host -> App messages. No tools/list or tools/call request is ever sent from VS Code to the App. On a follow-up request such as "open the editor for datasource test", Copilot calls the original MCP server tool (show-datasources) again, creating a second App instance, instead of invoking the App-provided open-datasource-editor tool in the existing View. Expected behavior If the App declares the tools capability and registers tools through App.registerTool(), VS Code should discover those App-provided tools, expose them to the active agent while the View is alive, and route tools/call back to the corresponding App instance when selected. Actual behavior App.registerTool() succeeds. The MCP App itself renders correctly. App -> Host -> MCP Server tool calls work. No Host -> App tools/list request is observed. No Host -> App tools/call request is observed. The Copilot agent therefore appears unaware of the App-provided tool and invokes the MCP server tool again. Question Is support for App-provided / ephemeral tools registered through App.registerTool() currently implemented in VS Code's MCP Apps host integration? If not, is this capability planned?

title: Test: Copilot Connectors discovery, consent, and fresh-session tools
text: Test: Copilot Connectors discovery, consent, and fresh-session tools. PR: #337649 - [x] anyOS - [x] anyOS Complexity: 5 Authors: [Create Issue]( --- ## Context Copilot Connectors are an independently gated, authenticated source in the customization Marketplace and MCP management UI. VS Code owns catalog, consent, and status UI; the Copilot runtime owns session-time MCP projection and credentials. Use a disposable profile with a GitHub account eligible for Copilot Connectors. Enable: Leave on initially so source independence can be checked. If the service is unavailable for the account or rollout, record the HTTP/status shown and mark the test blocked rather than changing account security settings. ## Authentication and connector lifecycle 1. Start signed out of GitHub and run **Chat: Open Customizations**. 2. Verify Discover still shows healthy non-connector sources. The Copilot Connectors source should present an explicit sign-in/recovery action rather than hiding other results or starting OAuth automatically. 3. Sign in with ordinary GitHub scopes. Browse the generic connector catalog and verify passive browsing does not unexpectedly request connector-management consent when the backend permits read-only access. 4. Open a connector such as Microsoft Learn Docs and use **Check Connection** or **Connect**. Verify any missing connector permission is requested explicitly for the same account. Cancel once and confirm no connection is created. 5. Repeat and authorize. Verify status updates without reopening Customizations, connector details remain accessible, and connected MCP servers appear under MCP Servers **Installed** while the product appears under **Connectors**. 6. Disable the GitHub Feed and verify Connectors remain available. Re-enable it, then disable only ; verify fresh connector discovery stops without breaking the other Marketplace sources. 7. Re-enable Connectors, disconnect the connector, and verify its status and MCP entries update. Recoverable HTTP 403 or rollout failures should remain actionable and must not trigger passive re-consent loops. ## Fresh Copilot Agent session tool projection 1. Connect a connector that exposes an easily verifiable read-only tool, such as Microsoft Learn Docs. 2. Immediately create a completely fresh **Copilot Agent** session; do not reuse a session that existed before connecting. 3. Ask the agent to use the connector's tool (for Microsoft Learn Docs, request an official documentation lookup) and verify the tool is available in that first fresh session and returns a relevant result. 4. Verify a user/workspace MCP server with the same name keeps its normal precedence and is not overwritten by the managed connector projection. 5. Disconnect the connector, then create another fresh Copilot Agent session. Verify the disconnected connector tool is no longer exposed. 6. Disable and create one more fresh session. Verify connector tools remain absent while ordinary Copilot chat still starts successfully. ## Accessibility and cleanup 1. Navigate source recovery, connector cards, details, status actions, Installed, and Connectors using only the keyboard. 2. Verify sign-in, consent-required, connecting, connected, disconnecting, error, and disconnected states have understandable labels and do not rely on color alone. 3. Disconnect any test connector and restore the experimental settings. **Expected:** Connector catalog access and consent are explicit and isolated from other sources; lifecycle status stays synchronized in Customizations; and a newly connected connector is reconciled before the first fresh Copilot Agent session becomes usable, without VS Code forwarding credentials directly to connector endpoints.

title: [Feature Request] Display token and cost consumption of external Gateways (e.g., Vercel AI Gateway)
text: [Feature Request] Display token and cost consumption of external Gateways (e.g., Vercel AI Gateway). <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- Describe the feature you'd like. --> ### Feature Description Following the implementation of milestone **1.126.0** (Issue #317977), VS Code introduced excellent per-message token usage and cost metrics badges. However, this telemetry metric framework is currently tightly coupled to internal GitHub Copilot billing schemas. As the **VS Code Agents** environment scales to allow developers to bring their own model endpoints and provider-agnostic infrastructure, there is currently no way to bubble up per-session cost tracking from third-party AI gateways like **Vercel AI Gateway**. Alternative tools like OpenCode already process this by default by remaining completely provider-agnostic while still tracking session spend. When routing model traffic through a custom gateway, providers inject metadata headers directly into the stream payload (for instance, Vercel’s or standard token counters). VS Code currently strips or discards these custom header footprints from the UI layer. ### Proposed Solution 1. **Expose an Extensible Metadata Parser Hook:** Allow the core chat and agent UI components to intercept response headers from the active language model provider stream. 2. **Support Dynamic Cost Badge Mapping:** Introduce a configuration setting or API hook where users or extensions can map arbitrary header keys (like or custom token parameters) directly into the native UI session badge footer. 3. **Preserve Session Mapping:** Ensure that contexts pass downstream response parameters accurately so extensions can reliably track session budgets without requiring brittle, backward-scanning hacks. ### Alternative Solutions Considered - Using third-party extensions, but these cannot cleanly hook into the newly implemented native agent/chat session footer badges because the core framework discards custom provider telemetry headers. - Constantly running in a side terminal, which breaks the flow of development inside the agent workspace. ### Additional Context Giving developers real-time feedback on their chosen agnostic gateway's spending directly inside the active editor pane ensures proper budget boundaries and model optimization during long multi-agent loops. Ref: #317977

title: BYOK custom endpoints: support dynamic/refreshable API key (apiKeyHelper) for OAuth-based gateways
text: BYOK custom endpoints: support dynamic/refreshable API key (apiKeyHelper) for OAuth-based gateways. ### Feature request The BYOK "custom endpoint" model configuration ( ) only accepts a **static** credential in (or ), sent as . There is no way to supply a **dynamically generated / short-lived** token. This blocks any enterprise gateway that uses **OAuth** instead of static API keys, because OAuth access tokens are short-lived (e.g. ~1h) and must be refreshed. Today the only options are (a) manually pasting a fresh token every hour, or (b) running a local reverse-proxy that injects the token — both are poor workarounds for what should be first-class. ### Requested behavior Add a way for the custom endpoint to obtain its credential dynamically per request, e.g.: - An -style setting pointing to a local script/command whose stdout is the current token (same model as Claude Code's [ ]( and/or - Support for / secret references resolved at request time in / . ### Concrete use case Authenticating against a **Databricks AI Gateway** ( ) with OAuth (U2M) instead of a personal access token. The Databricks CLI already mints and auto-refreshes OAuth tokens ( ); an hook would let it feed the current token to VS Code transparently. ### Prior issues This was previously requested and closed **not planned** — #318762 (closed only for lack of 20 upvotes, not on technical grounds) and #322499 (dynamic Bearer token, incl. the Databricks AI Gateway scenario). Re-filing since demand persists. ### Environment - VS Code Version: 1.139.0 - OS Version: macOS 26.6.1 (25G76) - Extension: GitHub Copilot Chat (BYOK / Manage Models) Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: N/A (feature request)

title: Agents Window: Add an extensible environment picker
text: Agents Window: Add an extensible environment picker. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> ## Summary Add an explicit environment picker to the Agents Window new-session experience. Initially, the picker could offer **Local** and **Remote**, **Cloud** while being designed to accommodate additional environment types over time. ## Motivation The place where work runs is a distinct choice from the source or workspace being used. Today these concepts can become coupled, making it harder to understand or extend session creation as more execution environments become available. An environment picker would make this choice visible and establish a scalable model for environments such as: - **Local** — run on the current machine. - **Remote** — run through a supported remote connection or host. - Future environments, such as cloud-hosted, containerized, or other provider-backed environments. ## Proposed direction - Add an **Environment** picker to the new-session UI. - Keep environment selection independent from: - Source/workspace selection. - Agent or harness selection. - Session intent. - Start with **Local** and **Remote** where supported. - Allow environment providers to contribute availability, display information, configuration/connection actions, and capability constraints without redesigning the picker for every new environment type. - Remember the user's explicit selection when appropriate. - Clearly communicate unavailable or unsupported source/environment/harness combinations rather than silently switching environments. - Ensure the selected environment remains visible before launch and is represented consistently when restoring or inspecting a session. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Users can explicitly choose between available Local and Remote environments when creating a session. - [ ] Environment selection is modeled separately from the selected source/workspace and agent/harness. - [ ] The picker can accommodate additional environment types without introducing environment-specific top-level UI. - [ ] Unsupported combinations are disabled or explained with actionable guidance. - [ ] The selected environment is preserved across session creation and restoration where applicable. - [ ] The picker has appropriate keyboard and screen-reader support. Related to #334563, which identifies independent environment selection as part of the broader workspace picker direction.

title: Revamp the Agent Bake Off comparison UI
text: Revamp the Agent Bake Off comparison UI. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> ## Feature request Revamp the Agent Bake Off UI across the full comparison workflow: setup, in-progress attempts, Judge results, and custom synthesis. ## Problem The current experience is functional, but the UI has grown organically and feels dense and inconsistent across stages. In particular: - attempt identity, status, and outcome presentation shift between setup, the Sessions list, and the Judge result; - primary actions compete with secondary actions instead of presenting a clear next step; - the custom synthesis decision matrix becomes difficult to scan as attempts and decisions increase; - narrow layouts can force awkward two-dimensional scrolling, wrapping, and clipped controls; - overflow chrome must consistently use themed workbench scrollables rather than browser-native scrollbars; - the visual hierarchy does not yet make the recommended attempt, supporting evidence, and synthesis choices feel like one coherent workflow. ## Proposed direction Design a cohesive Agent Bake Off experience that: 1. Establishes a consistent visual identity for each attempt across setup, progress, results, and synthesis. 2. Gives each stage one clear primary action while keeping alternate actions discoverable but visually secondary. 3. Makes Judge rationale, validation evidence, strengths, timing, and token usage easy to scan and compare. 4. Reworks custom synthesis so decisions remain understandable with multiple attempts and at narrow widths, without clipped content or native scrollbars. 5. Uses standard VS Code controls, themed scrollables, spacing/type roles, focus treatment, and high-contrast behavior. 6. Preserves complete keyboard operation, screen-reader semantics, accessible-view content, and responsive phone behavior. ## Definition of done - An approved UX proposal covers the end-to-end Bake Off workflow. - Desktop, narrow-window, and phone layouts are specified. - Attempt status and action hierarchy are consistent across surfaces. - Custom synthesis scales to additional attempts and decisions without inaccessible or native overflow UI. - Implementation includes focused component/unit coverage and visual fixtures for the key states. Related implementation context: #335498.

title: Markdown editor: let extensions add syntax, like markdown.markdownItPlugins does for the preview
text: Markdown editor: let extensions add syntax, like markdown.markdownItPlugins does for the preview. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> Extensions cannot add Markdown syntax to the new Markdown editor ( ). The preview has , and many extensions use it to add syntax: footnotes, admonitions, wiki links, definition lists, emoji shortcodes, and so on. The editor parses with micromark through and has its own view, so none of those plugins reach it. Checked in 1.137.0. The editor bundle ( ) has no reference to . As far as I can find, the only extension point the editor has is . It replaces the view of fenced code blocks that match a selector. That helps for diagram-style blocks. It does nothing for inline syntax or for block syntax outside a code fence. The result is that a document that renders correctly in the preview, with the user's installed extensions, renders differently in the editor, and extension authors have no way to close that gap. #337447 (footnotes) is one case of this. Each missing construct now needs its own request against the built-in package. Requested: a contribution point that lets an extension add syntax to the editor. Two possible ways: - Accept micromark syntax extensions plus a matching rendering and serialisation hook. This is the closest match to how the editor parses today, and micromark's extension format is already public. - A narrower version: let an extension claim a node type or an inline pattern and render it read-only, while the source text round-trips unchanged. That would cover most preview plugins, whose output is display-only. Whichever is chosen, the source text must round-trip unchanged when a user edits around the extended syntax, so that installing an extension never rewrites a file.

title: Make agent bake-offs available as an agent-invokable tool
text: Make agent bake-offs available as an agent-invokable tool. ## Motivation Agents should be able to run a bounded bake-off when a task would benefit from comparing multiple models, providers, agents, or configurations. Today this requires manual orchestration and the results are difficult to compare consistently. ## Proposal Expose an Agent Host tool that an agent can invoke to run the same task or evaluation prompt against a selected set of candidates and receive a structured comparison. The tool should support: - Selecting candidate models/providers/agents and an explicit task or evaluation prompt. - Running candidates in isolated child sessions so they cannot interfere with the current session or each other. - Configurable concurrency, timeout, and resource limits. - Consistent result capture, including outcome, summary, changed files/diff, validation results, duration, and available usage/cost signals. - A structured response that lets the calling agent compare results, explain tradeoffs, and optionally recommend or adopt a winner. - Cancellation and reliable cleanup of child sessions/worktrees. - Clear handling for unavailable providers, partial failures, and candidates that require different capabilities. ## Questions to explore - What should the stable tool schema and result format be? - Which candidate dimensions should be supported initially: model, provider, custom agent, permission profile, or prompt variation? - How should success criteria be supplied and evaluated without allowing the judge to silently change the task? - Which telemetry and user-visible progress are needed? - What confirmation or policy gates are required before spawning multiple sessions or consuming significant resources? ## Done when - An agent can invoke the tool with a bounded candidate set. - Candidate runs are isolated, cancellable, and cleaned up. - The caller receives comparable structured results and can identify the selected result. - Tests cover success, partial failure, cancellation, limits, and cleanup.

title: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees
text: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees. ## Motivation Fresh worktree-isolated agent sessions currently defer worktree creation until the first send so the prompt can influence branch naming. That prevents the agent runtime and workspace-dependent caches from pre-warming, adding avoidable latency to the first turn. We should investigate whether worktrees can be provisioned or prepared earlier without sacrificing naming quality, correctness, or cleanup guarantees across Windows, macOS, and Linux. ## Investigation Explore a cross-platform design for pre-warming agent worktrees, including: - When pre-warming can start and which inputs are available before the first prompt. - Whether to create a provisional worktree/branch and rename it later, reserve a path, or split filesystem preparation from Git worktree creation. - Coordination with Agent Host/runtime pre-warming so providers do not materialize against a pending or incorrect working directory. - Cancellation, abandoned composers, restart recovery, stale provisional worktrees, and deterministic cleanup. - Repository locking and races when multiple sessions pre-warm concurrently. - Windows path-length, file-locking, antivirus, junction/symlink, and case-sensitivity behavior. - macOS/Linux filesystem and symlink behavior, permissions, and performance differences. - Interaction with trust, remote workspaces, multi-root workspaces, submodules, sparse checkout, LFS, and . - Disk usage and limits for speculative worktrees. ## Measurements Capture baseline and prototype timings for: - Composer open to worktree ready. - First send to provider dispatch. - First meaningful progress. - Cancellation and cleanup latency. Measure representative repositories on Windows, macOS, and Linux, including cold and warm filesystem/cache states. ## Done when - We have a documented recommendation with platform-specific findings and identified risks. - A prototype demonstrates the viable lifecycle or proves why pre-warming should remain deferred. - The proposal defines state transitions, recovery/cleanup behavior, resource limits, and the integration point with provider pre-warming. - Follow-up implementation work is split into scoped issues as needed.

title: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation
text: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation. ## Feature request Allow an automation to start by executing a script, before creating an AI session. The script should be able to complete the automation entirely without AI participation, or request that a new AI session be started. Conceptually, an automation could support an action such as . A script action would perform deterministic work or checks first and decide whether AI is needed. ## Motivation Many automations can do useful work with a script alone, or cheaply determine that there is nothing for an agent to do. Starting an AI session for every trigger adds unnecessary cost and noise. Conversely, a script may discover work or encounter a failure for which AI assistance is useful. ## Independent outcomes Script success/failure and the decision to continue with AI should be independent, supporting all four combinations: | Script result | Start a new AI session? | Intended behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | Success | No | Complete the automation successfully without involving AI. | | Success | Yes | Start a new AI session with the script's output/context for follow-up work. | | Failure | No | Report the failed script/run without involving AI. | | Failure | Yes | Start a new AI session with the failure details for investigation or recovery; retain the script failure in the run history. | ## Expected behavior - Run the script before creating an AI session, not as a tool invocation inside an already-started AI session. - Provide an explicit, documented way to request or suppress AI continuation independently of the script's success/failure status. - When continuation is requested, allow a configured prompt and script output/context to be passed to the new session. - Preserve script output, errors, and exit status in the automation run history, including runs that never create an AI session. - Surface invalid or missing control output and script execution errors explicitly, with documented behavior. ## Design question: signaling contract The exact protocol needs design. A special exit code (for example, ) or a stdout marker such as could express "no AI needed", but a single special status conflates independent concerns, and free-form stdout markers may collide with ordinary output. Consider a structured result or dedicated control channel that expresses the AI-continuation decision separately from the process exit status. The request is for the four combinations above, not a particular exit code or marker. The design should also define how an AI follow-up affects the overall run status after a failed script.

title: Automations: optionally skip a run while a previous session is still running
text: Automations: optionally skip a run while a previous session is still running. ## Feature request Add an opt-in **skip if still running** option for automations. When a trigger fires and a session started by an earlier run of the same automation is still running, skip the new run instead of starting another session. ## Motivation Scheduled or frequently triggered automations can overlap when a previous session takes longer than the trigger interval. Users should be able to prevent duplicate work and competing changes without having to monitor sessions manually. ## Expected behavior - Make this configurable per automation; preserve the existing behavior when the option is disabled. - When enabled, check whether a session from an earlier run of that automation is still running before starting another session. - If so, skip this occurrence rather than queueing it or cancelling the existing session. - Show the occurrence as skipped, with the reason that an earlier session is still running. - Once the previous session has finished, subsequent triggers can start sessions normally. - Apply the overlap guard atomically so simultaneous triggers cannot both start a session. The precise definition of "still running" (including sessions waiting for user input or approval) should be documented as part of the design.

title: Allow model- and agent-specific color indicators in Copilot Chat
text: Allow model- and agent-specific color indicators in Copilot Chat. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> ## Problem In Copilot Chat I regularly switch between multiple agents and language models. The currently selected agent and model are shown only as text, which makes it easy to start a request with the wrong configuration in a compact chat UI. VS Code theme colors can currently customize generic dropdown and menu states, but they cannot assign a distinct visual identity to a specific agent or model. For example, I would like to immediately distinguish "GPT-5.6 Sol" from "GPT-5.6 Luna" by color, both in the selected controls and in the picker list. ## Requested feature Add support for optional, user-configurable color indicators for individual chat agents and language models. The indicator could be a small colored dot, icon accent, border, or subtle background in: - the selected agent control - the selected model control - the agent/model picker list This should use stable agent/model identifiers rather than display names, so renaming a model does not break the configuration. An API or setting could look conceptually like this: `jsonc { "chat.modelColorCustomizations": { "<stable-model-id>": "#f59e0b" }, "chat.agentColorCustomizations": { "<stable-agent-id>": "#14b8a6" } }

title: Terminal: support crisp font rendering on HiDPI displays
text: Terminal: support crisp font rendering on HiDPI displays. Terminal text in VS Code looks noticeably softer than the same font in Ghostty and other native terminals on macOS HiDPI. I've heard this from a few people: the integrated terminal reads "dull" next to a standalone terminal at the same font and size. I dug into it and the difference on macOS is the font antialiasing policy, not resolution. Editor and workbench text get one policy, terminal text on the GPU canvas path gets another, so terminal glyphs read heavier and blurrier. Proposal: an opt-in setting, as the unchanged default and as the opt-in mode, scoped to terminal text only so the editor, workbench, terminal theme, font family, size and weight don't change. On Windows and Linux the GPU renderer could request grayscale antialiasing through xterm's existing alpha-capable canvas path. Comparison on macOS HiDPI, left , right current: It should apply to normal, detached and sticky-scroll terminals, and keep terminal image transparency working. Upstream: xterm.js doesn't expose a font antialiasing option today, so VS Code has to go through the canvas path to get this. A dedicated antialiasing/font-rendering option in xterm.js (WebGL and DOM renderers) would let this be a first-class setting rather than a side effect, and would help every xterm.js embedder, not just VS Code. Until then this stays experimental, since the visible result depends on OS, display scale, font and theme.

title: Markdown editor: Make the comment box repositionable, with a pointer line to its anchored range
text: Markdown editor: Make the comment box repositionable, with a pointer line to its anchored range. ### Problem The comment boxes that carry agent feedback for a session are drawn over the editor reading view, pinned to the right side of the viewport. They cannot be moved. While a comment box is open it covers the source lines underneath it, and when comments on nearby lines are shown at the same time the right half of the reading area is almost completely blocked. When one comment box is tall enough to push the boxes below it further down, there is also no way to tell which line those pushed-down comments are anchored to. ### Proposed solution - Let a comment box be dragged to any position inside the editor viewport, while the box still follows the reading view as it scrolls. - Moving a comment box must not change the range it is anchored to. - Draw a dashed pointer line between a comment box and the range it is anchored to, the way Word comment balloons connect to their text with a leader line, and Google Docs comment cards link visually to the text they refer to. - While the pointer hovers over a comment box, highlight the range that box is anchored to, so the association is easier to read. ### Alternatives considered - Add a collapse button to the comment box so its content can be folded away. This reduces the overlap, but still gives no visible pointer back to the anchored text. ### Additional context - Comparable implementations: Word comment balloons with leader lines, Google Docs comment cards in the right margin. - Why this matters: the feedback loop of an agent session is reading and writing many short comments across one file. If every box covers the code it comments on, that review pass is much slower than it needs to be. ### Environment - VS Code: 1.138.0 (x64), stable - OS: Windows 10 Pro, 10.0.19045, 64-bit - Area: the feature in the Markdown editor inside the Agents window Reported by . Drafted with GitHub Copilot (agent-assisted).

title: Feature Request: expose an context key for when clauses
text: Feature Request: expose an context key for when clauses. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- Describe the feature you'd like. --> ## Summary Expose the focused Explorer item's symlink status as a when-clause context key, so extensions can contribute Explorer context-menu items that appear only when the selected file or folder is a symbolic link. Suggested name: (boolean), consistent with the existing , , and keys. ## Problem There is no way to conditionally show an menu item for symlinks. Extensions that add symlink-specific commands (for example "Go to symlink target", "Copy real path", or "Reveal original") must currently show the menu item for every file and folder, and reject non-symlinks inside the command handler with an error message. Concretely: 1. The Explorer already tracks this state internally. is set when resolving the file stat, and is used by core code (for example, skips delete confirmation for symlinks). 2. That state is never bound to a context key. binds folder, readonly, root, and editor-availability contexts, but not symlink status. The class likewise exposes scheme, filename, path, and language, but nothing about symlinks. 3. The documented workaround does not work for this case. The suggested pattern is to compute the state in an extension and publish it via the command. But an extension receives no event between the user's right-click and menu evaluation, so it cannot know which tree element is about to be menu-scoped. There is no supported way to set a per-item context key in time. The result is that every user of a symlink extension sees a context-menu entry on all files, and gets an "this is not a symbolic link" notification when they misuse it. The feature is common enough that macOS Finder ships a built-in equivalent ("Show Original"). ## Requested behavior - When the focused Explorer item is a symlink: is . - Otherwise, it is (or unset). - The key follows the existing pattern for Explorer resource context keys: it updates when the selection or context-menu target changes, and it is usable from menu contributions and keybinding clauses. Example contribution this would enable: ## Implementation notes The data already exists per Explorer item at the moment context keys are set, so this looks like a small change: - In , bind the new key alongside the existing ones (approximately one added plus one call). - Register the key in next to the other declarations, so it appears in the documentation. - Multi-root/remote caveats apply as they do for the other resource context keys: the value reflects the item under focus, including across multi-workspace trees and remote file system providers. - No new API surface in is required, so no engine-version bump for consumers. ## Related - #167996 — asked for a when-clause check for symlinks (closed as out-of-scope, but the suggested workaround cannot work, as explained in the issue thread itself). - #179307 — asked for a built-in "Reveal Symbolic Link Original" Explorer menu item; same root cause. - #159722 — users expect symlink indication in the Explorer (the arrow decoration); the context key request is the menu/when-clause counterpart.

title: Transition GitHub and Microsoft authentication to host-owned auth
text: Transition GitHub and Microsoft authentication to host-owned auth. ### Summary Transition GitHub and Microsoft authentication used by agents to the host-owned authentication model proposed in [microsoft/agent-host-protocol#404]( ### Current architecture VS Code owns the authentication state and obtains credentials through its authentication providers, then brokers tokens to the agent host. This couples agent authentication to the VS Code client and extension host lifecycle. ### Desired architecture - The agent host/runtime owns its GitHub and Microsoft account state and credentials. - VS Code no longer retains authentication state solely to pass tokens into the agent host. - When an interactive authentication flow is required, the host delegates client-specific UI operations such as opening a browser to VS Code through the Agent Host Protocol. - Authentication state and flows follow the host-owned auth proposal while preserving an appropriate client-brokered path for sandboxed hosts. ### Scope Focus initially on GitHub and Microsoft authentication, including account discovery, sign-in, sign-out, token refresh, and migration from the existing VS Code-owned token flow.

title: Allow extension keybindings to inherit from another command
text: Allow extension keybindings to inherit from another command. ## Feature request Allow an extension-contributed keybinding to inherit the effective keybindings of another command while executing a different command in a different context. For example: ## Motivation Alternative editors can implement the same editing operation as the code editor but need a different command because their implementation and focus context differ. Today they must copy the code editor's physical default keybindings into their own extension manifest. This has two problems: - User customizations of the code editor command do not apply to the alternative editor command. - Platform-specific defaults, secondary bindings, chords, arguments, and future changes must be duplicated and kept synchronized. The experimental Markdown editor is a concrete example. It has host-routable commands and a generated copy of the corresponding keybindings. It should be possible for one customized keybinding to apply to both the code editor and Markdown editor while each retains its own command implementation. Related: microsoft/vscode-packages#292 and #329414. ## Proposed semantics A keybinding rule is currently resolved approximately as: Inheritance would project the effective bindings in the other direction: and then create target rules: identifies the source command's relevant keybinding family. This is necessary because one command can have multiple bindings with different context expressions and arguments. The outer controls where the projected target bindings apply. The projection should include all matching effective source bindings rather than selecting only one preferred binding. This includes primary and secondary bindings, chords, platform-specific variants, and user-added bindings. ### Arguments Inherited bindings should preserve their source by default. This is important for commands where multiple keybindings target one command ID and arguments distinguish the operation. An explicit outer could replace the inherited arguments: Initial semantics should replace arguments rather than deep-merge them. ### User customizations The expected ordering is: Therefore: - Rebinding the source command also rebinds the target command. - Removing a source binding removes its inherited projection. - Users can still add or remove target-only bindings. - Explicit target bindings take precedence over inherited ones. ## Additional considerations - Detect and reject inheritance cycles. - Preserve the source binding's arguments and provenance. - Expose inherited bindings in the Keyboard Shortcuts editor, including the source command. - Recompute projections when user keybindings or extension keybindings change. - Keep command identity and execution separate: invoking the source command programmatically should not invoke the target command. - Consider whether a future context-key mapping form is needed to preserve residual source conditions instead of replacing the source entirely.

title: Allow TreeItem.command to declare an alternative command for modifier-click
text: Allow TreeItem.command to declare an alternative command for modifier-click. ### Problem A can declare a single , executed when the user clicks the item's label. There is no way to declare a different command for a modifier-click (Alt/Ctrl/Cmd), so extensions that expose a "primary action" and a closely-related variant must either pick one as the click behaviour, or ship a setting that flips it globally. The common shape of this is "open" vs "open in a new window" / "open to the side": conventional in tabbed UIs, and something users expect to work by habit. ### Why this is a gap rather than a new concept VS Code already has exactly this concept, one level down. The contribution point accepts an key, documented as the identifier of an alternative command to run, which must itself be declared in the section. So an inline action *button* on a tree item can already have an alt behaviour, while the tree item's own click cannot. The proposal is only to close that asymmetry. ### Proposal Let be paired with an optional alternative, e.g.: Semantics mirroring : when the modifier is held at click time, the alternative runs instead. Extensions that don't set it are unaffected. ### Alternatives considered - **A setting per extension.** Works, but it's a global flip rather than a per-click choice, and every extension reinvents it with a different name. - **Inline action buttons.** Already used, and fine as a discoverable fallback, but they require hitting a small target on the right edge of the row instead of the row itself — which is the ergonomic problem being reported. - ** .** Solves the folder-opening case specifically, but it is global and changes native behaviour ( , Recent, ), so it isn't scoped to the tree the user is actually clicking in. ### Related - #18064 — the same request for QuickPick items (open since 2017) - #130880 — key bindings on tree view items - Downstream example: alefragnani/vscode-project-manager#825 and #817

title: Long-running Agent Host sessions accumulate issue and pull-request references without cleanup
text: Long-running Agent Host sessions accumulate issue and pull-request references without cleanup. ## Description In a long-running Agent Host session in the Agents Window, the resource pills beside the chat input keep accumulating every recorded GitHub issue and pull request. Older entries remain indefinitely, and there is no visible way to remove individual stale references or clear a collection. In the observed session, the input footer had grown to: - 15 Pull Requests - 15 Issues - 2 Artifacts As the session continues, these collections become increasingly noisy and make it difficult to find the resources that are relevant to the current work. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Start an Agent Host session in the Agents Window. 2. Keep using the same session across multiple tasks involving GitHub issues and pull requests. 3. Record or encounter additional issues and pull requests throughout the session. 4. Observe the resource pills beside the chat input. ## Actual behavior - Issue and pull-request entries continually accumulate for the lifetime of the session. - Old or no-longer-relevant references remain mixed with current ones. - The UI offers no apparent way to remove an individual entry or clear stale references. - The summary counts continue growing, making the collections less useful over time. ## Expected behavior Long-running sessions should have a manageable lifecycle for recorded resources. The UI should remain useful as references accumulate, for example by allowing stale entries to be removed or cleared and by avoiding duplicate entries for the same resource. Explicitly recorded durable artifacts can remain persistent if that is intentional, but ordinary issue and pull-request references should not grow without any user control. ## Related work - #335383 addressed preserving issue and pull-request titles in these pills. - #335896 covers rich previews and interaction with the collections. This report is specifically about retention and unbounded collection growth rather than pill rendering or preview content.

title: Agents Window layout should be restored per session
text: Agents Window layout should be restored per session. When switching between sessions in the Agents Window, the editor layout is currently shared globally across the app instead of being restored per session. For example, a session that uses a diff may have a split layout with a secondary pane. Switching from that session to a no-workspace, chat-only session preserves the split and leaves half of the window occupied by an empty pane. That pane cannot be used directly without opening something through the Command Palette. This becomes increasingly disruptive as sessions vary between chat-only work and sessions using terminals, diffs, or browsers. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Open an agent session and arrange the window so a diff or another resource occupies a separate pane. 2. Switch to a chat-only session, such as a no-workspace session. 3. Observe that the previous session's split layout remains, leaving an empty pane. ## Expected behavior Each agent session restores its own layout, so chat-only sessions can use the full window while sessions with terminals, diffs, browsers, or other resources retain their own arrangement. ## Actual behavior The layout is global across sessions, so switching between sessions with different resource needs can leave large empty panes that are not directly useful. Reported with two screen recordings demonstrating the behavior in Slack.

title: Increase the inter-session messaging limit beyond 50
text: Increase the inter-session messaging limit beyond 50. ## Problem The server currently allows only 50 messages between sessions. Complex multi-session workflows can hit this limit quickly, after which coordination messages are not delivered and the user must manually relay them between sessions. The resulting message is similar to: > Coordination limitation: session messaging reached its limit, so neither relay was delivered. ## Scenario 1. Query all CI failures from the last week and ask an agent to classify them. 2. Ask the agent to start sessions to fix the top 6-10 issues. 3. Many fixes have overlapping changes, so the sessions need to coordinate frequently. 4. The 50-message limit is reached before the work is complete, blocking further inter-session coordination. ## Request Increase the number of server-side messages allowed between sessions from 50 to a meaningfully higher value so coordination-heavy workflows can complete without manual message relaying. ## Verification 1. Set to and start a new Agent Host session. 2. Ask the agent to create enough sessions/chats or send enough inter-session messages to reach the legacy limit. 3. Verify the limit is enforced with a clear error and rejected operations leave no partial session or chat. 4. Change the setting to without reloading. 5. Repeat the orchestration workflow and verify the increased process-wide session, chat, and message limits apply live. 6. Verify reaching a limit does not interrupt already-running sessions. 7. Ask the agent to recursively create nested delegated work and verify spawn depth remains capped at three. 8. Toggle the setting back to and verify subsequent operations use the original limits without restarting. Implemented by #337954.

title: Smart window reuse: seamlessly accept files/folders in multi-root workspace windows from external tools
text: Smart window reuse: seamlessly accept files/folders in multi-root workspace windows from external tools. ## Describe the feature you'd like When a VS Code window contains a multi-root workspace, it should seamlessly accept and open files or folders from external tools (CLI, IDE integrations, error handlers, etc.) that are part of that workspace. Currently, external tools cannot reliably target these multi-root windows, breaking integration workflows. **Current behavior:** - Single folder window + open file from that folder → reuses window ✓ - Single folder window + open different folder → new window ✓ - **Multi-root workspace window + open ANY file/folder from CLI → new window ✗ (BREAKS INTEGRATION)** - **Multi-root workspace window + error link from IDE/tool → new window ✗ (BREAKS WORKFLOW)** ## Why this matters **The multi-root workspace problem:** When you open multiple folders in a single window, they become a multi-root workspace. This is powerful — you get a unified editor, shared terminals, consistent settings, and ephemeral state (open tabs, debug sessions, terminal scrollback). However, VS Code then **rejects all external requests** to open files/folders that belong to that workspace, creating new windows instead. This breaks critical integration scenarios: 1. **Error handling & IDE integration** — Build tools, linters, debuggers emit file paths to open at specific lines (e.g., ). When the file is in a multi-root workspace, it opens in a new window instead of the active workspace. Users lose context (terminals, debug state, layout). 2. **CLI/Git integration** — with can't target the right window when you're using multi-root. Different worktrees open in different windows, breaking developer workflow. 3. **Tool automation** — Test runners, deployment scripts, and documentation generators that emit deeplinks ( ) or CLI calls can't reliably send files to the active workspace. 4. **Ephemeral state loss** — Every external tool invocation that opens a file creates a new window, losing: - Open tabs and file history - Terminal sessions and scrollback - Debug breakpoints and watch expressions - Workspace layout and panel sizes - Search context and find history 5. **Window fragmentation** — A single workspace spawns multiple VS Code windows, fragmenting the development environment. ## Proposed solution Implement intelligent window reuse for multi-root workspaces: 1. When or is invoked from external tools 2. Check if any open multi-root workspace window contains that file/folder in one of its workspace roots 3. **If yes → activate that window and open the file/folder there** (preserving context) 4. If no → open in a new window (current behavior) This should also apply to: - URL handler when the file is in an open multi-root workspace - Files opened via IDE integrations or error dialogs - Folders added to existing multi-root workspaces ## Examples **Before (broken workflow):** **After (seamless workflow):** ## Related issues - #323880 — URL handler with window reuse options - #299540 — File reuse misbehaves with git worktrees (opens in wrong window) - #215749 — Original request to reuse windows with multi-root workspaces (closed, not planned)

title: Show rich GitHub issue previews with title and rendered body in hovers
text: Show rich GitHub issue previews with title and rendered body in hovers. <!-- Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template --> GitHub issue references currently use a compact plain-text hover such as . This requires opening the issue to understand what it is about, even when the title and body could provide enough context inline. When hovering a GitHub issue reference or issue pill, show a rich preview containing: - The full canonical issue title - The issue body rendered as Markdown, including links, lists, and code blocks - Basic metadata such as repository, issue number, and open/closed state - An action to open the issue on GitHub For long bodies, the preview can use a constrained, scrollable area rather than expanding without limit. This would make issue references much easier to understand in Markdown documents and agent-generated content without repeatedly switching to the browser. This feature request goes further by proposing a rich hover based on live issue data, including the rendered issue body.

title: Show MCP server startup errors in the MCP details view
text: Show MCP server startup errors in the MCP details view. ## Feature request When an MCP server fails to start, show its error details persistently in the MCP server details view rather than exposing the raw response inline in the server list. title: Agents: use a cloud-first repository selection workflow
text: Agents: use a cloud-first repository selection workflow. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> The Agents window should provide one clear **Work in Repository** entry point instead of separate cloud and clone actions. title: Agents window: Show confirmation after Commit and Sync actions complete
text: Agents window: Show confirmation after Commit and Sync actions complete. ## Feature request In the Agents window, after I click the **Commit** or **Sync** button in the title bar, the button disappears. I assume this means the action completed successfully, but there is no clear confirmation of the resulting state of my changes. ## Current behavior 1. Open an agent session with changes ready to commit or sync. 2. Click **Commit** or **Sync** in the title bar. 3. The button disappears without an explicit success confirmation or an indication of the new repository state. The disappearing button indirectly suggests success, but leaves uncertainty about whether the action completed and what state the changes are now in. ## Suggested behavior After either action completes, show clear confirmation and the resulting state—for example, a brief success message and/or persistent status indicating that changes are committed, synced, or up to date. Failures should remain clearly distinguishable from successful completion. This doesn't need to be in a modal or anything the user needs to interact with or dismiss, but perhaps inline?

title: API proposal: Expose AuthenticationSession access token lifetime
text: API proposal: Expose AuthenticationSession access token lifetime. ## Problem exposes an access token but not its lifetime. Consumers that integrate with SDKs supporting renewable credentials cannot tell whether a token is static or when it should be refreshed. #152517 previously proposed exposing an absolute timestamp. An absolute timestamp is unsafe across VS Code's client/remote extension-host boundary because the two machines may have clock skew. ## Proposed API ## Semantics - The value is a positive integer representing whole milliseconds remaining when the session is returned. - Cached sessions recompute the value on every return. - means the provider does not know the token's expiry. - The relative lifetime avoids comparing clocks across extension-host boundaries. ## Implementation The proposal lives in . #334418 added it as in seconds, and #335610 renamed it to in milliseconds. The GitHub Authentication extension reports it for Entra-brokered sessions, and the Microsoft Authentication extension reports MSAL token expiry. Related to #152517.

title: GitHub Authentication: Support expiring GitHub tokens brokered through Microsoft Entra
text: GitHub Authentication: Support expiring GitHub tokens brokered through Microsoft Entra. ## Problem The GitHub Authentication extension can broker GitHub access tokens through a signed-in Microsoft Entra account. These exchanged GitHub tokens have a finite lifetime, but the extension previously treated them like ordinary persisted GitHub OAuth tokens with no known expiry or renewal path. Once an exchanged token expired, consumers could lose authentication and fall back to an interactive sign-in prompt even though the Microsoft account was still signed in and could silently mint a replacement. ## Desired behavior - Keep the exchanged token's absolute expiry internally. - Return its current relative lifetime through . - Recompute the remaining lifetime whenever a cached session is returned. - Silently renew Microsoft-brokered GitHub sessions before expiry, including the one-hour threshold required by the Copilot SDK. - Coalesce concurrent renewal attempts. - Retain a still-valid token when proactive renewal fails transiently, and only remove the session after the token actually expires. - Leave ordinary persisted GitHub OAuth sessions unchanged when their expiry is unknown. ## Implementation Implemented by #334418, including mocked coverage for initial exchange, restore, cached lifetime recomputation, renewal, and transient renewal failures.

title: Agent Host: Support expiring GitHub tokens with the Copilot SDK
text: Agent Host: Support expiring GitHub tokens with the Copilot SDK. ## Problem Agent Host currently supplies a static GitHub token when creating Copilot SDK sessions. Some GitHub tokens have a known finite lifetime, and the Copilot SDK supports a callback for refreshing those credentials. Without carrying token lifetime to Agent Host and selecting the provider callback, a long-running Copilot session can continue using an expired token or surface an interactive authentication prompt instead of requesting a fresh credential. ## Desired behavior - Carry optional OAuth-style through Agent Host authentication and reconnect/replay. - Deduct elapsed time when credentials are replayed and do not replay expired credentials. - Use a static when expiry is unknown. - Use when expiry is known, never both options at once. - Coalesce concurrent SDK refresh callbacks and map refresh requests to the existing Agent Host authentication-required flow. - Bound refresh waits so the SDK cannot wait indefinitely when no client supplies a replacement. - Restart the Copilot client when switching between static and provider-backed credential modes. ## Implementation Implemented by #334418, with unit coverage for credential selection, refresh coalescing, timeout behavior, replay, and mode transitions. The refresh path was also validated end to end with a real Microsoft-brokered GitHub token renewal.

title: Agents window: Compare multiple implementation attempts
text: Agents window: Compare multiple implementation attempts. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> ## Compare multiple implementation attempts in the Agents window The Agents window supports multi-chat sessions, peer-chat forks, isolated worktrees, and reviewing changes beside a conversation. However, after exploring more than one approach, users must manually inspect each chat and diff to determine which implementation is better. Add a **Compare Attempts** workflow that runs or selects multiple approaches to the same task and presents their outcomes in a code-oriented comparison. ## Proposed experience Add a **Compare Agents** toggle to the new-session input alongside the existing harness and model controls. - When the toggle is off, the current single-harness behavior is unchanged. - When the toggle is on, the harness picker becomes multi-select and the send action indicates how many attempts will run, for example **Run 3 Attempts**. - The model remains a single shared selection. Only harnesses that advertise that model are eligible; incompatible harnesses are disabled with an explanation. - The prompt, workspace, starting branch or commit, permission level, and isolation configuration are shared across all attempts. Submitting the prompt fans it out to one new session per selected harness. The sessions are placed in a comparison group so they can be tracked together, while a failure to start one harness does not discard successful attempts. Each attempt: - receives the same prompt and starts from the same repository state; - runs in a separate session and isolated worktree; - uses one selected harness and the shared model; - remains independently reviewable and editable. Once at least two attempts have results, VS Code offers a comparison view containing: - a concise implementation summary for each attempt; - changed files and diff size; - test, build, lint, and diagnostic results; - unresolved errors or warnings; - elapsed time and usage; - notable architectural or behavioral differences; - overlapping, conflicting, and attempt-specific changes. The user can then: - **Use attempt A** or **Use attempt B**; - open the diffs side by side; - send feedback to one attempt; - ask an agent to **Synthesize the best of both** into a new attempt; - discard the unused worktrees. ## Why this belongs in the Agents window This makes existing multi-session and worktree support useful as a deliberate workflow rather than just additional tabs. The Agents window can provide a stronger experience than a generic best-of-N response because it understands source control state, diagnostics, tests, diffs, and editor navigation. It also gives users a concrete way to use parallel agents without introducing a separate multi-session dashboard. ## Related approaches Cursor 2.2 introduced **multi-agent judging**, which evaluates parallel agent runs after they finish, recommends a solution, and explains the selection. This validates the need for a decision step on top of parallel execution. The VS Code opportunity is to make the underlying code evidence inspectable and support user-controlled synthesis rather than stopping at a winner recommendation. - [Cursor changelog: Multi-agent judging]( OpenAI Codex has a **Best of N** feature that generates multiple responses for one task so users can explore alternatives and choose an approach. The Codex app also supports parallel agents in isolated worktrees and reviewing and commenting on each agent's diff. This proposal is not a request for exact parity. VS Code can provide a more code-native comparison by combining its multi-chat sessions, worktrees, diff editors, diagnostics, test results, and usage data into one decision surface. The distinguishing workflow is comparing validated implementation outcomes, then selecting or synthesizing them without manually reconciling separate chats. - [Codex changelog: Best of N]( - [Introducing the Codex app]( ## Suggested initial scope An initial version could: 1. Add comparison mode to the new-session input. 2. Let the user select two or more compatible harnesses and one shared model. 3. Fan out the same request into a separate worktree-isolated session for each harness. 4. Keep the resulting sessions together as a comparison group. 5. Compare summaries, changed files, diff statistics, diagnostics, validation results, elapsed time, and usage. 6. Open the chosen attempt's diff and worktree. Automatic synthesis, applying the winner, and worktree cleanup could follow later. ## Acceptance criteria - One submission can launch two or more harness-specific sessions for comparison. - VS Code clearly indicates whether their starting repository state differs. - Validation results distinguish passed, failed, not run, and unknown. - Selecting an attempt does not silently overwrite the user's current working tree. - Unselected attempts remain available until the user explicitly discards them. - The workflow is keyboard accessible and supports any selected harness that provides the shared model and isolated worktrees.

title: Allow explicit worktree selection when agents create independent sessions
text: Allow explicit worktree selection when agents create independent sessions. ## Feature request Allow users to explicitly choose whether an agent-created independent session uses a new Git worktree. The tool should honor that choice rather than relying only on inherited isolation. Implemented by #335076. ## Expected behavior - Set only when the user explicitly requests a new worktree. - Set only when the user explicitly requests working without a worktree. - Omit when the user has not made an explicit choice, preserving existing isolation inheritance/defaults. - Never combine with ; either boolean value is rejected before creating a chat or session. - With , resolve a known existing worktree folder to its project root before creating the independent session. ## Verification steps Use the Agents window with a Git project and inspect the tool arguments and the resulting working directory/branch, not just the assistant summary. 1. **Explicit worktree:** Ask “Start implementation in a new independent session with a new worktree.” Verify , , and a newly created worktree. 2. **No worktree from an existing worktree:** Start from a session already using a managed worktree and ask “Start implementation in a new independent session without a worktree.” Verify ; the new session uses the known project root, not the parent worktree, and no additional worktree is created. 3. **No explicit choice:** Ask for an independent session without mentioning worktrees. Verify the agent omits . For the same project, existing isolation is inherited; a different project retains the existing worktree default. 4. **Current-session work:** Ask for a new chat in the current session. Verify , no argument, and the existing workspace is shared. 5. **Folder fallback:** Request an independent session without a worktree for a folder with no known project mapping. Verify that the supplied folder is used directly. 6. If available, repeat step 2 for a remote project and verify that its remote URI/authority is preserved. Unit tests additionally cover invalid boolean values and rejection of combined with either or .

title: Agents Window: Open Agent Host sessions and chats from browser links
text: Agents Window: Open Agent Host sessions and chats from browser links. ## Feature request Provide product-protocol URLs that can be opened from a browser or another application to focus the Agents window and reveal a specific Agent Host session or chat. Proposed URL shapes: - - ## Motivation The existing links are internal workbench links. They are not registered with the operating system and therefore cannot be opened from a browser, issue, terminal output, or another application. Using an Agents-specific product URL ensures the target opens in the Agents window rather than whichever VS Code window or compatible application happens to be active. The provider remains part of the URL because backend session IDs are provider-scoped. text: AI: Group custom agents by discovery source in the Agent picker. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> ## Feature request Group custom agents in the Agent picker by the location or source where VS Code discovered them. ## Problem When many custom agents are available, the picker shows one long, flat list. It is difficult to tell: - whether an agent comes from an organization, a plugin, an extension, the repository, or the user profile; - which organization owns an organization-level agent; - why an agent is available in the current context; - which agent to choose when names are similar. The list becomes difficult to scan and manage as more agents are installed or discovered. ## Proposed UI Use collapsible groups based on the discovery source, with a second level for organization names: Suggested behaviour: - Show only groups that contain agents. - Allow each group to expand and collapse. - Keep the current agent search, filtering, keyboard navigation, and selection behaviour. - Keep the current discovery, de-duplication, precedence, and execution behaviour unchanged. - Show the organization, extension, plugin, or file location as source information where it is available, for example in a group label or tooltip. - Preserve the current ordering within each group unless there is a strong reason to change it. - Use **Other locations** as a catch-all for configured locations that do not match a known source category. - If an agent is discovered from more than one source, retain the existing resolution behaviour and show the relevant source information where possible. ## Benefits This would make the picker easier to scan and would help users understand the scope and ownership of each agent. It would also scale better for users who have agents from several organizations, extensions, plugins, repositories, and user-level locations. This request is related to #332543, but focuses specifically on a source-based hierarchy for custom agents in the Agent picker rather than the general display of all customization types.

title: API for extensions to register display-only keybinding hints
text: API for extensions to register display-only keybinding hints. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- Describe the feature you'd like. --> ### Problem Extensions that implement a modal or chorded input layer (vscode-neovim, VSCodeVim, Emacs emulations) resolve keys inside their own runtime. VS Code has no knowledge that these bindings exist, so the Command Palette, menu items, and hover tooltips always show the default binding, even when it is not what the user would press. Example: with vscode-neovim, is reachable via a user-defined Neovim mapping ( ). The Command Palette shows . The displayed hint is not wrong, but it is not the binding the user actually uses, and the real one is undiscoverable through the UI. These bindings cannot be declared in because they are defined by the user at runtime, in the extension's own configuration format, and can change without a reload. ### Proposed API A display-only registration, with no effect on dispatch: vscode.keybindings.registerHint(commandId, { label: "space f f", when: "neovim.mode == 'normal'" }) VS Code would surface wherever it currently renders a keybinding for that command, when evaluates true. Resolution and dispatch are untouched. ### Why existing mechanisms do not cover this - is static and cannot express user-defined runtime mappings. - Rebinding through is not viable: these are multi-key sequences with modal context, beyond what the two-chord resolver expresses. - #196835 (read access to keybindings) was closed as not planned, and would not help here regardless, since the binding does not exist in VS Code's registry at all. ### Who benefits Any extension with an internal input layer. The concrete case is modal editing extensions, which have a large installed base and currently give users a UI that reports bindings the user does not press. Two things to expect: it may be closed as a duplicate of the broader dynamic-keybinding threads, and "display-only" is the load-bearing part of the pitch. If it reads as "let extensions own keybinding resolution", it gets closed immediately. Sources: - microsoft/vscode #196835 - microsoft/vscode #1422 - microsoft/vscode #111854 - VSpaceCode/vscode-which-key - VSpaceCode which-key docs
