title: Agents window: enable signed-out use by default via experimentation
text: Agents window: enable signed-out use by default via experimentation. Follow-up to #318578 and #328990. ## Goal Roll out the signed-out Agents window behavior through experimentation by enabling for treatment users. #328990 added the platform capability, but the setting remains experimental and off by default. This issue tracks validating the experience and making it the default behavior through the experimentation system rather than requiring users to opt in manually. ## Treatment behavior When the user is signed out of GitHub and at least one registered session type can run using its own credentials: - Open the Agents window without showing the blocking GitHub sign-in flow. - Keep GitHub sign-in available as an optional action for users who want Copilot-backed models or functionality. - Request GitHub authentication on demand when a selected provider, model, or operation requires it. When no registered session type is usable without GitHub, retain the existing sign-in/setup experience. ## Rollout plan - Configure an experiment whose treatment enables . - Keep the current behavior as the control. - Validate the signed-out entry, provider selection, model selection, account, and authentication-on-demand experiences. - Monitor sign-in conversion, successful session creation and first-turn completion, auth failures, provider availability, and error rates. - Confirm the experiment can be rolled back without leaving the Agent Host and workbench in inconsistent states. - After successful validation, graduate the behavior so users no longer need to set the experimental setting manually. ## Readiness / related work - #329007 — avoid flashing the blocking sign-in modal while provider availability is still resolving. - #329667 — allow Copilot Agent Host BYOK sessions to participate while signed out. - #329656 — Claude native/Copilot provider auth behavior. - #329668 — Codex non-Copilot provider auth behavior. ## Acceptance criteria - Treatment users receive the signed-out behavior without manually changing settings. - Control users retain the current behavior. - Users with no usable signed-out provider are not left in an empty or unusable Agents window. - Provider and account changes update the gate reactively. - Experiment metrics and rollback criteria are documented before broad rollout. - The validated behavior is graduated from the experimental opt-in.

title: Agent Host Codex: allow non-Copilot sessions without GitHub Copilot sign-in
text: Agent Host Codex: allow non-Copilot sessions without GitHub Copilot sign-in. Related platform capability: #318578 ## Feature request Allow the Codex Agent Host provider to run sessions using OpenAI, ChatGPT, or another configured Codex model provider without requiring GitHub Copilot sign-in. Codex can expose both Copilot-backed and independently authenticated model providers. The selected model provider should determine the authentication required by that session; the existence of Copilot-backed models must not make GitHub sign-in a prerequisite for every Codex session or for entering the Agents window. ## Expected behavior - Codex advertises the GitHub Copilot protected resource as optional when the agent has a usable non-GitHub model source. - OpenAI-, ChatGPT-, local-, or custom-provider models remain available while signed out of GitHub. - A signed-out user can create, resume, and send messages in a Codex session using one of those models. - Copilot-backed models are advertised only when Copilot authentication is available. - Selecting or restoring a Copilot-backed model while signed out requests GitHub Copilot authentication on demand. - Model inventories from independently authenticated providers are additive; signing in to one provider does not implicitly change the provider used by an existing session. - The selected model provider is persisted per session and controls subsequent request routing. - If no usable models are available, Codex is reported as unusable rather than falsely opening the Agents window. - Provider account and model-catalog changes are reflected reactively. ## Acceptance criteria - Signed out of GitHub + signed in to OpenAI/ChatGPT: Codex is usable. - Signed out of GitHub + configured API-key/custom provider: Codex is usable. - Copilot-backed Codex model without a GitHub token: authentication is requested on demand. - No usable provider credentials: Codex does not count as an auth-free session type. - Existing sessions retain their selected provider as other accounts sign in or out. - Tests cover mixed provider inventories, model switching, session restoration, and each authentication matrix. ## Implementation Addressed by #328461.

title: Agent Host Copilot: allow BYOK sessions without GitHub Copilot sign-in
text: Agent Host Copilot: allow BYOK sessions without GitHub Copilot sign-in. Related platform capability: #318578 ## Feature request Allow the Copilot Agent Host provider to advertise that GitHub Copilot authentication is optional when it has at least one usable BYOK model. #322977 added BYOK model support to the Copilot Agent Host. However, the provider still advertises the GitHub Copilot protected resource as required at the agent level. As a result, the conditional gate introduced by #328990 continues to treat the Copilot session type as requiring GitHub sign-in, even when its selected model is backed entirely by the user's own provider. ## Expected behavior - When at least one usable BYOK model is available, the Copilot provider advertises that its GitHub Copilot protected resource is optional. - A signed-out user can create and run a Copilot Agent Host session using a BYOK model. - Copilot-hosted models are only advertised when an appropriate Copilot credential is available. - Selecting or restoring a Copilot-hosted model while signed out requests GitHub Copilot authentication on demand rather than failing the turn. - Signing in adds Copilot-hosted models without disrupting existing BYOK sessions. - Signing out removes Copilot-hosted models while leaving usable BYOK models and sessions available. - If the user is signed out and no usable BYOK model exists, the provider must not report itself as usable without GitHub. - Repository-scoped GitHub authentication remains optional and can be requested separately when a GitHub operation needs it. - Changes to BYOK models and authentication are republished reactively to the Agents window. ## Acceptance criteria - Signed out + usable BYOK model: Copilot session type is available without GitHub. - Signed out + no usable BYOK model: Copilot session type still requires GitHub sign-in. - BYOK requests complete without a GitHub Copilot token. - Copilot-backed requests trigger the normal authentication flow when needed. - Tests cover BYOK model registration/removal, sign-in/sign-out, restored sessions, and model switching. ## Related - #318578 - #322977 - #328990 - #327078

title: agentHost: per-session provider (transport) selection for Claude sessions
text: agentHost: per-session provider (transport) selection for Claude sessions. ### Feature request Let each **Claude** agent-host session pick a model whose **provider** decides its transport, instead of pinning the whole host to a single transport: - -provider models route to the **native Anthropic SDK**. - (and any unknown) provider routes to the **Copilot-CAPI proxy**. This mirrors how the Codex provider already behaves. ### Motivation Today a Claude host is pinned to one transport, so a user can't mix a native-Anthropic model and a Copilot-routed model across sessions. Per-session provider selection removes that limitation and brings Claude in line with Codex. ### Proposed behavior - **Provider-qualified model ids** ( / ); bare/legacy ids resume on the host default transport (no migration needed). - **Merged catalog** fetched from both native and proxy sources, each self-gated on its own credential/native-setup; the picker groups rows by vendor ("Anthropic" / "Copilot"). - **Per-session transport resolution** at materialize time from the selected model's provider. - **Live switching** — selecting a model on the other transport re-materializes the session's subprocess on the next send; same-transport model changes hot-swap in place. - **Lazy Copilot sign-in** — the Copilot resource is advertised ; sign-in defers to first send of a Copilot-routed model (matches Codex). Addressed by #329331.

title: BYOK Custom Endpoint: add "gemini" apiType for Google Generative Language API wire format
text: BYOK Custom Endpoint: add "gemini" apiType for Google Generative Language API wire format. ## Summary Custom Endpoint ( ) currently supports three wire formats through : , , and (added in #316189). This asks for a fourth: . It's for endpoints that speak Google's REST format. That covers the official API at generativelanguage.googleapis.com, plus any self-hosted gateway or proxy that mirrors it. This is separate from the existing native BYOK provider (#1310), which is the official-API-key flow. on Custom Endpoint would let people point at any endpoint that speaks the Gemini wire format, the same way they already can for OpenAI-compatible, Responses, or Anthropic Messages endpoints. ## Why and not or Google's own docs call this the Gemini API, as distinct from Vertex AI. Vertex AI needs a GCP project and service-account credentials instead of a plain key. Other tools that support both flavors keep the same split for the same reason: mixing them up means someone pastes in an API key and gets asked for GCP credentials instead. also matches this repo's own native BYOK provider, which already uses . ## Scope notes A few things worth calling out before anyone picks this up: - The model id lives in the URL path itself ( , or for streaming) instead of in the request body. - The auth header is , which is already in [ 's list of known auth headers]( so the header sanitizer shouldn't need any changes there. - Request/response conversion could probably reuse and , which were built for the native Gemini provider and already use SDK types that mirror the REST JSON schema pretty closely. ## Background This started as a comment on #325237. That issue bundles a handful of unrelated Custom Endpoint UX requests, so it seemed worth splitting this out on its own. title: Support selecting specific weekdays for Automations (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri)
text: Support selecting specific weekdays for Automations (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri). <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ --> ### Summary Add the ability to schedule an Automation to run on specific weekdays (for example: every Monday, Wednesday and Friday) instead of only the current options to run daily or weekly. ### Motivation Today the Automations schedule only supports "daily" or "weekly" runs with no way to pick particular days of the week. To run something on multiple specific weekdays users must create multiple automations (one per day) which is confusing and noisy. Being able to select multiple weekdays would make schedules more expressive and reduce duplication. ### Proposed solution - Extend the automation schedule UI to allow selecting multiple weekdays when the cadence is weekly. For example a set of checkboxes or a multi-select with: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun. - Keep the existing "daily" and "weekly" options for backward compatibility; when "weekly" is chosen, provide the new weekday picker. Provide a clear label like "Run on" followed by the weekday selection. - Backend/API: accept a daysOfWeek array (e.g. ["monday","wednesday","friday"]) or equivalent field in the automation schedule model and execution logic that triggers runs on those days. Keep current weekly semantics when daysOfWeek is empty to preserve existing behavior. - Consider exposing the same option in any automation templates or export/import formats so users can programmatically create schedules that include multiple weekdays. ### Examples / Use cases - Run a cleanup task every Monday, Wednesday and Friday. - Run a report every weekday (Mon–Fri) without creating five separate automations. ### Acceptance criteria - The schedule UI allows selecting one or more weekdays for weekly schedules. - Automation execution logic runs jobs on the selected weekdays only. - Existing automations without a daysOfWeek field continue to behave as they do today. - Documentation and API/schema docs updated to show the new field and examples. - Unit/integration tests cover the scheduler behavior for multiple-day schedules. ### Additional notes - An advanced option (e.g., cron expression) could be considered separately for power users, but this request focuses on selecting common weekday combinations via a simple UI. <!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> [View original Slack conversation](

title: Voice mode: distinguish direct answers and app actions from coding requests
text: Voice mode: distinguish direct answers and app actions from coding requests. ## Problem Voice mode sometimes submits a new coding request when the user intended a lightweight spoken answer or an application action. It can also answer conversationally when the user intended to create or control a session. This is especially disruptive while another coding request is already running. ## Desired routing ### Answer or act in the voice backend - Application state: current session, session counts/status, current model, attachments. - Application actions: create/focus a session, select a model, attach a file. - Lightweight general questions that do not require workspace context or durable chat history. - Examples: "What does polymorphism mean?" or "While that runs, what is the difference between TCP and UDP?" ### Submit to the coding agent - Requests requiring workspace context, tools, repository inspection, or project changes. - Answers the user is likely to need in the session history. - Examples: debug a test, explain a compiler error, refactor code, search the repository, review a PR, create a migration, or investigate a build. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Direct voice answers do not create a chat request. - [ ] App-action utterances invoke the matching frontend tool and do not become prompt text. - [ ] "Start a new session" consistently invokes session creation. - [ ] A lightweight question can be answered while a coding request continues in another session. - [ ] Tool failures and ambiguities cause a clarification or honest failure response. - [ ] The backend routing prompt/tool definitions document this boundary explicitly. The recalcs come from: - ([chatTerminalToolProgressPart.ts#L1941-L1977]( - ([#L1930]( - Cost: 0.59 s inside the open task, plus ~2.3 s more in the following 10 s ( attributed to these stacks: 1.15 s + 0.42 s + 0.38 s), as each mirror resolved asynchronously and measured itself. ### Suggestions - Batch mirror measurements (read once per frame for all parts, then write). - Skip measurement while the part is collapsed or off-screen. - Avoid reads immediately after DOM writes.

title: Agent host: viewing a non-resident Copilot CLI session resumes the SDK session and replays its whole event journal
text: Agent host: viewing a non-resident Copilot CLI session resumes the SDK session and replays its whole event journal. **Setup:** Agents window (Insiders, macOS) opening a long-running, completed Copilot CLI session on a remote (SSH) agent host. The chat has 2 turns; one ran ~8.7 days and has 3,891 response parts (~1,700 tool calls including 930 shell and 172 subagent calls, 855 reasoning, 622 markdown). The snapshot is 7.3 MB. The open took 13.4 s ( ). Subscribing to a non-resident session's session and chat channels took ~12 s on a remote host before either snapshot was returned. From the host log: | Host time | Event | |---|---| | +0.2 s | | | +0.2 s → +4.5 s | ( ) | | +4.7 s | | | +4.7 s → +11.9 s | history replay until | Both subscribe results arrived together at +12 s. ### Causes - [ ]( reads persisted history without an SDK session only when . Otherwise resumes the full SDK session just to read history. - [ ]( pages the event journal 1,000 events at a time and runs on the host event loop. The memo is in-memory only, so every host restart replays again. - While this runs, other sessions on the same host are delayed. ### Suggestions - Always use the persisted-history path for read-only restore, and resume the SDK session lazily on the first send. - Persist a materialized chat snapshot (or incremental state) so a subscribe does not replay the journal. - Run mapping off the main loop or yield periodically. - Let the summary snapshot return without waiting for chat-history replay. Related: #344521, #339997

title: Restoring a large chat regenerates hundreds of thinking titles via the utility model
text: Restoring a large chat regenerates hundreds of thinking titles via the utility model. **Setup:** Agents window (Insiders, macOS) opening a long-running, completed Copilot CLI session on a remote (SSH) agent host. The chat has 2 turns; one ran ~8.7 days and has 3,891 response parts (~1,700 tool calls including 930 shell and 172 subagent calls, 855 reasoning, 622 markdown). The snapshot is 7.3 MB. The open took 13.4 s ( ). Opening a long, completed Agent Host chat in the Agents window started ~900 requests with over the next ~3 minutes (229 / 400 / 297 / 168 per minute, ~6–7 per second), continuing after navigating to another chat. The same chat had already generated titles when it was opened earlier the same morning. ### Causes 1. **The persisted cache cannot hold large chats.** ([chatThinkingContentPart.ts#L270-L273]( is one profile-scoped JSON blob with a 7-day TTL and a 1,000-entry cap shared by every chat. In the Agents profile it was at exactly 1,000 entries (213 KB): 529 for this chat, 251 for another. Opening one or two other large chats evicts a chat's titles, so the next open regenerates them. Turns older than 7 days always regenerate. 2. **Every lookup and write processes the whole blob.** calls , which JSON-parses the entire blob for each restored thinking group during the synchronous render. parses, evicts, sorts, stringifies, and stores the whole blob for each generated title. 3. **Restored, completed history calls the LLM.** Serialized thinking groups with no reusable title fall through to ([chatThinkingContentPart.ts#L1970-L1977]( Each completion later updates a title, which can change heights and relayout the response long after the open. ### Suggestions - Persist generated titles with the history (for example in turn or part metadata on the agent host) rather than only in profile storage. - Keep the cache in memory and write it back debounced; store titles per chat instead of in one globally capped blob. - For restored, completed groups, show the fallback title and generate only when a group becomes visible or expanded. Related: #344521

title: Agents window: opening a session waits 2-3 s for Copilot Connector MCP servers to reconnect
text: Agents window: opening a session waits 2-3 s for Copilot Connector MCP servers to reconnect. Opening an existing session in the Agents window that is not loaded yet takes ~2.5–5 s. About two thirds of that is spent waiting for Copilot Connector reconciliation, which restarts the session's Connector MCP servers and only returns after their **remote** MCP handshake has completed — none of which is needed to show the session. **Version:** Insiders 1.144.0 ( ), macOS arm64, Copilot Connectors enabled (agent host ), with one Connector configured (Slack). ## Steps to reproduce 1. Have Copilot Connectors enabled with at least one Connector (e.g. Slack). 2. In the Agents window, click a session that has not been opened since the agent host started (or was evicted). 3. Observe the session takes several seconds to appear. ## Evidence ### One click, end to end Agent Host Protocol transport log ( ) and for a single click (local time): | Time | Step | |---|---| | 22:22:45.996 | client → | | 46.035 → 46.212 | SDK (177 ms) | | 46.212 → 46.729 | agent catalog, script safety, sandbox (~0.5 s) | | **46.729 → 48.537** | ** (1.81 s)** | | 48.618 | | | 48.635 | subscribe result returned to the client (2.64 s after the click) | The renderer was idle during this time (no long animation frames); it was waiting on the agent host. ### The wait is the Connector MCP server's remote handshake The Copilot runtime log ( ) shows the reconcile RPC returns right after the session's Connector MCP server ( ) finishes : This holds for **every** launch in that agent host process: across 35 session launches (create and resume), the log follows a by 0–9 ms (two outliers at ~140 ms under 12 concurrent launches). | | min | median | max | |---|---|---|---| | Connector reconcile (sandbox applied → ) | 1.71 s | **2.08 s** | 3.44 s | | Whole launch ( → ) | 1.92 s | 3.13 s | 5.03 s | | Share of launch spent in reconcile | | **67 %** | | ### Why it blocks [ ]( awaits [ ]( before returning the SDK session. That is → → , and the last call resolves only after the runtime has (re)started the Connector-owned MCP servers. The session cannot be restored — and the subscribe cannot answer — until then. Nothing about displaying a session depends on Connector state. What does depend on it: - a turn's tool set (the Connector servers must be bound to the session account before the model can use them), - MCP server start/stop, - Connector refreshes ( ), - deciding whether a pending MCP auth request belongs to a Connector (a Connector-owned server must never receive a client-provided MCP token). ## Proposal Start the launch-time reconcile at the same point but don't await it in the launcher; hand it to the , which publishes its result (Connector ownership, MCP inventory, ) when it settles and makes the four dependents above wait for it. Opening a session then costs ~0.8 s instead of ~2.6 s in the trace above, and the reconcile usually finishes in the background before the user sends anything. If they send immediately, the first turn waits for the remainder, which is exactly what every open pays today.

title: Opening an agent host session eagerly subscribes to every subagent chat (tens of MB of snapshots)
text: Opening an agent host session eagerly subscribes to every subagent chat (tens of MB of snapshots). ## Summary When you open an agent host session that has many subagent calls, the client subscribes to **every** subagent chat. Each subscription returns the full chat snapshot. On large orchestration sessions, opening a single session transfers tens of MB, and loading is very slow. ## Environment - Insiders - Agents window connected to a remote agent host over SSH ## Data These numbers come from the agent host's AHP protocol log ( ) for one client connection. 124 MB of responses arrived over about 5 minutes. | Session | Subagent chats subscribed | Bytes | Largest single snapshot | |---|---|---|---| | A | 29 | 35.6 MB | 12.8 MB | | B | 30 | 37.6 MB | ~2.2 MB | All subscriptions for a session fire in a single burst when it opens. For session B, that was 30 subscriptions in about 1 second. In session A, all 51 subagent tool calls in the parent chat are already , but 29 child chats were still subscribed and fully snapshotted. Caveat: this host was also in the wedged state described in #342774, where subagent completion confirmations kept failing. If the child chats' catalog status was stuck in-progress because of that, it may be why chose to observe them. Even so, eagerly subscribing to dozens of full child snapshots seems worth avoiding. ## Expected Only subscribe to a subagent chat when it is needed: when it is active, expanded, or visible. Alternatively, have the server return a summarized snapshot for completed subagents and fetch the full transcript on demand. ## Pointers - and the gate in , plus

title: agentHost: Avoid rescanning Codex sessions on existing rollout updates
text: agentHost: Avoid rescanning Codex sessions on existing rollout updates. ## Context #337300 added live discovery for external Codex sessions by recursively watching and refreshing the native catalog after file changes. The watcher currently uses , so appends to an existing session rollout invalidate discovery just like creation of a new session. coalesces invalidations to at most one scan every five seconds, which bounds the work but still permits repeated calls during a long streaming turn even though the set of sessions has not changed. ## Research notes - Codex rollout paths currently look like . - preserves , , and change types, so the listener can distinguish new rollout artifacts from appends to existing ones. - Catalog and transcript refreshes currently share : every discovery invalidation also invalidates subscribed instances. Simply ignoring all events would risk breaking live transcript updates. - The non-recursive home watcher also observes and . SQLite WAL churn may be another source of catalog rescans even when only transcript content changed. - The existing 60-second safety refresh should remain as recovery for missed watcher events and alternate native catalog locations. ## Suggested direction Split storage changes into catalog and transcript invalidation paths, then scope catalog invalidation to changes that can add/remove or materially reclassify a session. A possible first pass: - Treat an session rollout as a catalog invalidation. - Treat rollout files as transcript-only invalidations. - Keep changes as catalog invalidations for title/metadata updates. - Determine whether changes can be classified more narrowly; avoid catalog refreshes for ordinary turn persistence while preserving discovery for state-DB-only sessions. - Retain debounce/retry/safety-refresh behavior as a correctness fallback. The exact filter should account for cross-platform watcher behavior, including creation of dated directories, atomic replacement, and batched add/update events. ## Acceptance criteria - Appending repeatedly to an existing external Codex session does not repeatedly call . - Creating a new external Codex session appears promptly in the VS Code session list. - Live history for an already observed external session continues to update. - Metadata changes that affect the session list still propagate. - Tests cover add versus update events, sustained writes, state DB/index changes, and the periodic safety refresh.

title: Perf: prompt timeline gutter/ruler re-renders every row and recomputes diff stats twice when opening a long session
text: Perf: prompt timeline gutter/ruler re-renders every row and recomputes diff stats twice when opening a long session. ## Summary While investigating a renderer CPU spike reported when opening a very long Copilot session ("Session database redesing"), the prompt timeline (gutter/ruler rail) was identified as a **secondary** contributor: it re-renders every timeline row and recomputes every request's diff stats **twice** while a long session is opened, even though nothing about most rows actually changed between the two passes. The primary cause (an O(N²) observable-notification cascade in the response/approval model during history restore) has already been fixed separately. This issue is scoped to the timeline-specific cost so it can be reviewed/fixed by the timeline's owner. ## Environment (from the original report) - macOS - VS Code Insiders 1.139.0-insider - distro/build: - Two DevTools performance traces captured opening the long session, both showing the same pattern (repro is stable across captures) ## Perf evidence Aggregate renderer-main-thread timings from the trace (secondary, non-approval-related tasks): - Two long tasks per session open: **268.0 ms** and **255.6 ms** - Call stack: - Feeding into that: , including URI/string conversion work per request - These two tasks fire back-to-back for the *same* set of requests — i.e. the timeline hydrates/renders more than once while the session is opening - totaled 435.5 ms (max 4.3 ms) and totaled 86.5 ms (max 1.6 ms) across the whole trace, so this is DOM/JS work in the row-rendering path, not layout or paint ## Analysis derives / (see [promptTimelineModel.ts]( from the chat view model plus each request's diff stat ( → → ). During history restore: 1. The underlying view model fires multiple change notifications while requests/responses are being populated (this is also being reduced by the separate approval-model fix, but the timeline observable recomputes on every one of them regardless). 2. Each recompute previously produced a **new array of tick objects** even when the tick contents were structurally identical to the previous pass, because the derived observables had no custom equality function — a plain reference/array identity check always says "changed". 3. / then re-render **every** row/mark unconditionally for a "same structure" tick list (see the loops calling / for every index), which re-touches every row's DOM ( , , ) and recomputes every request's diff stat again via , even for rows whose stat/text/timestamp didn't change. Net effect: for a session with many prompts, opening it can pay for a full row+stat rebuild of the entire timeline more than once, which is O(N) work repeated multiple times for no visible change. ## Suggested direction (for consideration, not prescriptive) - Give the / derived observables a structural equality function so a recompute that produces the same tick values is a no-op for downstream consumers. - In , skip re-rendering (and re-computing the stat DOM for) a row/mark whose tick is unchanged from the previous render, rather than unconditionally re-rendering every row when the *set* of ticks is unchanged. - Verify this doesn't regress the existing streaming-update behavior (a tick's stat needs to *keep* updating live while a turn is still streaming) or the accessibility/focus-preservation behavior in (roving tabindex / must still update). ## Scope note This issue intentionally excludes the primary cause (approval-model observable batching during history restore), which is already fixed elsewhere. Please treat this as the timeline-specific follow-up. /cc — you're the primary author/owner of , looping you in to review and drive the fix here.

title: Agents window becomes sluggish from responsive toolbar layout storm
text: Agents window becomes sluggish from responsive toolbar layout storm. ## Description The Agents window becomes extremely sluggish, particularly while scrolling, when three agent sessions are running concurrently. A 24-second DevTools trace shows a renderer layout storm strongly correlated with responsive toolbar resize handling: - 3,907 events totaling **18.17 seconds** - 194 renderer tasks longer than 50 ms - Worst renderer task: 192 ms - 1,169 calls at the responsive callback site, enclosing **14.7 seconds** - 1,506,181 elements processed across style recalculations GC, paint, and input event handlers were comparatively small and do not explain the sluggishness. ## Reproduction 1. Open the Agents window. 2. Start three agent sessions and leave them running concurrently. 3. Scroll the sessions/transcript UI while the sessions stream updates. 4. Record a DevTools performance trace. Observed result: scrolling and general interaction become very slow. Expected result: running multiple sessions should not cause sustained renderer layout work or long tasks that block scrolling. ## Technical findings The dominant callback maps to the responsive toolbar observer in: The observer synchronously invokes responsive overflow calculation. That path: - measures the toolbar with ; - measures action items through ; - may push/pull action DOM nodes; - updates action minimum widths and overflow state. These reads occur amid frequent streaming DOM updates and can force style recalculation. Chat creates responsive primary and secondary toolbars for each session, multiplying the cost when several sessions are active. The exact delivery source still needs instrumentation: callbacks may represent genuine parent-driven width changes, a toolbar/consumer observer feedback cycle, or both. normally does not redeliver an unchanged size, so a same-width cache alone is not expected to solve the issue. ## Proposed direction 1. Replace the raw toolbar observer with a named , constructed in the toolbar element's window. - Reuses existing disposal, loop-attribution, and test-constructor support. - Avoids observing auxiliary-window elements with the wrong realm. 2. Coalesce observer-triggered responsive updates to at most one scheduled pass per animation frame. 3. Preserve immediate explicit and behavior, because action content can change at a stable outer width. 4. Preserve custom and behavior used by the integrated browser. 5. Use compatible border-box/effective-width semantics across observer and explicit layout paths. 6. Separate measurement from mutation where practical: read available/action widths first, compute the target overflow state, then apply DOM changes once. 7. Add a decision-level no-op/hysteresis guard only if profiling still shows width oscillation or fractional jitter after coalescing. 8. If the base toolbar change is insufficient, investigate the compact chat toolbar observer/layout cycle as a separate contributor. Changing the default observed element to the toolbar's constructor container is not safe: chat containers share width with sibling controls, and SCM containers can be content-sized. ## Regression coverage - Exercise responsive and . - Multiple resize deliveries in one frame cause one responsive update. - Real width changes update overflow and re-expand actions. - updates overflow when item content changes at a stable outer width. - Custom plus continues to use the derived width. - Border-box width semantics remain consistent. - Auxiliary-window elements use their own observer realm. - Same-state updates cause no toolbar subtree mutations. - Action order, focusability, keyboard navigation, and overflow-menu accessibility remain unchanged. ## Performance acceptance criteria Re-run the same scripted 24-second scenario with three running sessions: - Responsive toolbar work is bounded by frame-level width changes and does not continue while idle. - ToolBar-attributed time drops by at least 80%. - Renderer tasks over 50 ms drop from 194 to fewer than 20. - Trace-wide time drops from 18.17 seconds to below 4 seconds. - Scripted scrolling maintains p95 frame time below 32 ms. - Toolbar overflow/re-expansion behavior remains correct in chat, SCM, and integrated browser consumers. ## Review The proposed direction was independently reviewed by two subagents and challenged by a rubber-duck review. Those reviews rejected an initial same-width-cache-only solution and led to the scheduling, observer-realm, box-model, and oscillation-focused plan above.

title: Agents window scrolling is sluggish while an active subagent has large tool history
text: Agents window scrolling is sluggish while an active subagent has large tool history. ### Type of issue Performance ### Description Scrolling in the Agents window becomes severely sluggish while a session is running an active subagent with a large tool history. This affects both: - scrolling the sessions list - scrolling the active chat transcript The UI may otherwise appear idle except for the running progress indicator. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Open the Agents window. 2. Start or restore a session containing an active subagent. 3. Allow the subagent to accumulate a large number of child tool invocations. The captured reproduction had approximately 112 tools. 4. Keep the subagent section collapsed. 5. Scroll the chat transcript so the response leaves and re-enters the virtualized viewport. 6. Scroll the sessions list or chat transcript. ### Actual behavior Scrolling becomes noticeably delayed and unresponsive. Individual wheel events can block the renderer main thread for hundreds of milliseconds. ### Expected behavior Collapsed or off-screen subagent content should not perform expensive presentation work during list virtualization. Scrolling should remain responsive regardless of the number of historical child tools. ### Performance trace findings A DevTools performance trace was captured while only scrolling: The slowest wheel event blocked the renderer for approximately 280 ms. The dominant stack was: → chat list render → → → → → → Markdown sanitization → For a collapsed subagent with approximately 112 historical tools, reconstruction repeatedly performed work that was not visible: - approximately 147 ms sanitizing and parsing the title Markdown - approximately 107 ms cancelling and recreating open-chat duration timers - transient state observers and microtasks for already-completed tools - repeated toolbar, ARIA, and active-tool presentation updates Layout, painting, and garbage collection were comparatively minor. The regression was caused primarily by JavaScript presentation work on the renderer main thread. ### Root cause When a virtualized chat row was reconstructed, every historical child tool immediately updated the collapsed subagent presentation. Although the detailed tool content was lazily rendered, title rendering, toolbar context, elapsed-duration state, ARIA state, and tool-state tracking were still repeated once per hidden tool. The reconstruction cost was therefore linear in the number of historical tools. ### Related pull request

title: High idle CPU: PR-icon model thrash in Chat Sessions list (create/dispose churn)
text: High idle CPU: PR-icon model thrash in Chat Sessions list (create/dispose churn). ## Summary While VS Code (Insiders) was effectively idle, the renderer consumed high CPU for several minutes. Log analysis points to a create/dispose thrash loop in the **GitHub Pull Requests** PR-icon decoration, driven by frequent re-resolution of the Chat Sessions list. A secondary, earlier spike comes from a session-refresh storm in the Agent Host (git subprocess + SQLite fan-out over all sessions). Logs analyzed: , (window/renderer), ~25 min span (16:24–16:49), with the user-reported high-CPU window being the last ~4 min (16:45–16:49). ## Root cause #1 — PR-icon model thrash (renderer, the "idle" CPU) In the last 4 minutes, is dominated by: - **476 PR-model create + ~476 dispose** cycles in 4 minutes — for only **7 unique PRs** ( + ). - Trigger: fires **12–26×/min**. Each refresh re-decorates every session's PR icon by **acquiring then immediately releasing** a reference to its PR model. Refcount hits 0 → model disposed → recreated on the next pass. Each burst = exactly 14 create+dispose (7 PRs × 2). - The meant to prevent this logs and never holds a warm reference, so nothing keeps the models alive between passes. Net: thousands of full PR-model lifecycles (event wiring, Octokit setup) with **zero state change** — pure wasted CPU. This is the dominant cost during the idle window. **Suspected fix area:** / should hold a stable reference for tracked sessions instead of acquire-and-release per refresh, and/or resolution should be throttled/deduped so it doesn't re-resolve 162 sessions every few seconds. ## Root cause #2 — session-refresh storm (Agent Host, earlier spike 16:27–16:32) A burst (not steady state) in : - **1182×** across **118 distinct ** files — repeatedly re-opening every session's SQLite DB. - ran **~1,100 git commands/minute** (~18 subprocess spawns/sec): , , , , — multiple per session × 118 sessions. - **fails 122×** ( ) and keeps being retried — wasted spawns. - **181×** in one minute — actions dispatched against sessions not in state (churn/desync). title: Default files.watcherExclude patterns cause CPU stall on large repos due to pathological regex
text: Default files.watcherExclude patterns cause CPU stall on large repos due to pathological regex. The default patterns use prefix: These get passed to via , where converts them to regex using . For a pattern like , picomatch produces: The nested negative lookaheads are pathological for (libstdc++ backtracking NFA), which uses in its C++ . On a large monorepo (~650K files), these 3 default patterns alone cause to take **120s** — with 111s of CPU time spent purely in regex matching. The actual filesystem traversal + takes ~5s. Without the leading , the same patterns ( , , ) complete in **16s** — and since , , and only ever exist at the repo root, the prefix provides no additional coverage. | Config | time | User CPU | |---|---|---| | etc. (current defaults) | **120s** | 111s | | etc. (without ) | **16s** | 7.5s | | No excludes at all | **15s** | 6.2s | The current defaults are actually **worse than having no excludes** — they add 105s of CPU overhead while saving zero memory ( and are tiny relative to the total watched tree). I've also filed parcel-bundler/watcher#244 about the underlying + performance issue. **Suggestion:** Remove the leading from the default patterns (since these dirs only exist at the root), or alternatively use simpler regex-safe patterns. For example, generates a much simpler regex than and has simiar behavior for real repositories (apart from the fact that a few nested dirs would be missed).

title: Problems pane constantly re-evaluates frontmatter diagnostics for custom agent/instruction/skill/prompt files — excessive CPU and memory
text: Problems pane constantly re-evaluates frontmatter diagnostics for custom agent/instruction/skill/prompt files — excessive CPU and memory. ## Environment | Property | Value | |---|---| | VS Code | Insiders 1.114.0-insider ( ) | | OS | Linux x86_64 — WSL2 (kernel ), 20 CPUs, 31 GiB RAM | | GitHub Copilot Chat | v0.42.2026032501 | Other extensions v3.3.10 (declarative extension pack, no JS/TS), v2026.38.0, v0.31.2, v2026.4.0, v2026.1.1, v1.24.0, v4.5.6, v2.1.2 ## Bug In a workspace with **472 custom Copilot files** (49 , 349 , 11 , 63 ), the diagnostic collection constantly clears and re-populates frontmatter diagnostics in the Problems pane. The cycle never settles, keeping CPU and memory elevated indefinitely with no user interaction. There is no setting to throttle or disable this behavior. **Of the 349 files, 246 are symlinks** in a directory that resolve back to the same 103 source files in . The scanner appears to follow symlinks and parse both the source and the link, effectively processing each of those 103 files twice. Only 103 unique files exist on disk. **Expected**: diagnostics evaluate once on load/change, then remain stable. Symlinked duplicates should ideally be detected and skipped. ## Root Cause (from extension source inspection) Three issues combine to create a refresh loop: 1. **No debounce on refresh** — fires on every event with no coalescing: 2. **Full re-parse every time** — calls for *every* custom file via , not just changed files. With 472 files (including 246 symlink duplicates) this is expensive. 3. **Cascading events** — after parsing, fires , which multiple downstream providers (ask-agent, explore-agent, plan-agent, org-agents) listen to. Org agents also **poll** periodically, adding more trigger sources. ## Suggested Mitigations 1. **Debounce** (e.g., 500ms–2s). 2. **Incremental parsing** — only re-parse changed files. 3. **Break the cascade** — prevent the post-refresh event from triggering another parse round. 4. **Deduplicate symlinks** — resolve symlinks to their canonical path and skip files that have already been parsed. 5. **Add a setting** to control refresh rate or disable frontmatter validation. ## Additional Context The workspace is [microsoft/hve-core]( which packages agents, instructions, skills, and prompts for VS Code extension distribution. The directory contains symlinks used during extension packaging — all 246 files there are symlinks back to the 103 source files in . An additional 17 transient plan files in the gitignored directory increase the scanning surface further during active development sessions.

title: High CPU usage when multiple extensions register many chatAgent/chatSkill prompt files simultaneously
text: High CPU usage when multiple extensions register many chatAgent/chatSkill prompt files simultaneously. ## Bug Description When two or more extensions each register a large number of and prompt files (e.g. 49 agents + 17 skills total), VS Code enters a sustained CPU active state (does not idle) that never recovers. The **Problems** panel also flickers continuously with validation warnings appearing and disappearing. ## Root Cause An infinite feedback loop forms between (VS Code core) and the extension host: 1. fires 2. serializes agent DTOs and calls to the extension host 3. The extension (e.g. GitHub Copilot Chat) receives the agents, re-parses all prompt files, and fires its provider's event 4. The extension host forwards this back to the main thread via 5. invalidates its cache and fires again 6. **GOTO 1** — infinite ping-pong loop The same cycle applies to and . Each iteration involves full IPC serialization of all agent/skill/instruction DTOs, causing sustained CPU usage that never subsides. ## Reproduction Steps 1. Install two VS Code extensions that each contribute many files via the package.json contribution point (e.g. one extension with ~39 agents + 11 skills, another with ~10 agents + 6 skills) 2. Open a workspace with both extensions enabled: ![Image]( 3. Observe: CPU usage is high when vscode loads, never seems to be able to idle after startup. 4. The Problems panel flickers continuously as prompt validation runs repeatedly ## Notes: - Either extension in the gif above can be disabled and vs code will act as normal. - If the disabled extension is re-enabled then vs code also works as normal until reload. Seems that the issue is only if window startup contains many agents/skills being loaded at once. Once its out of the loop it is fine. ## Expected Behavior CPU should return to idle after extensions finish registering their prompt files. The push cycle should terminate once the extension host already has the current set of agents/skills/instructions. ## Environment - **VS Code**: Insiders (latest) - **OS**: Windows 11 - **Extensions**: Any two+ extensions contributing many chatAgent/chatSkill prompt files ## Proposed Fix Add URI-set deduplication to , , and in . Before pushing to the extension host, compute a sorted string key from the current URIs and compare to the last-pushed key. If unchanged, suppress the push. This breaks the loop after at most 2 iterations (initial push + one bounce-back that matches).

title: Performance: UriIdentityService uses non-optimal caching strategy
text: Performance: UriIdentityService uses non-optimal caching strategy. <!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! bug_report_template ⚠️⚠️ --> <!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: --> <!-- 🕮 Read our guide about submitting issues: --> <!-- 🔎 Search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. --> <!-- 🧪 Test using the latest Insiders build to see if your issue has already been fixed: --> <!-- 💡 Instead of creating your report here, use 'Report Issue' from the 'Help' menu in VS Code to pre-fill useful information. --> <!-- 🔧 Launch with to check. --> Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes <!-- 🪓 If you answered No above, use 'Help: Start Extension Bisect' from Command Palette to try to identify the cause. --> <!-- 📣 Issues caused by an extension need to be reported directly to the extension publisher. The 'Help > Report Issue' dialog can assist with this. --> - VS Code Version: 1.105.1 - OS Version: MacOS 15.7.1 [UriIdentityService]( is heavily used to normalize URIs. While this code is not very heavy it sits on a critical path in many situation and already caused significant performance problems before. See [this issue]( as an example when a user had more then 1 million items in cache. Currently [UriIdentityService] has some room for improvement: 1. For caching it uses with as a comparator. Compare method currently [creates comparison key]( for each URI before comparison. It leads to creation of [2 new URIs]( and stringifying them which is also [non-trivial]( While each individual operation is not very heavy they can build up due to huge amount of them. With (almost) full cache get/set operation will require around 35 comparisons (see SkipList [source]( and [paper]( Which means around 70 URI creations and toString calls in . All together this leads to high costs of reading/writing many items from the list. 2. It is important to mention that huge amount of is needed not only for insertion but also for reads, making reading from the cache almost as expensive operation as insertion. 3. While one can notice problems (1) and (2) only when reading/writing huge amounts of items in cache (thousands of items) which should not happen very often, such a situation actually happens when cache overflows. The current implementation sorts all existing items in cache in chronological order, clears the cache and [reinsert items back to cache]( one by one. With the current limit it is 32768 insertions. It can take up to 200-300 ms 4. Last tiny problem is that current implementation of reverses cache age on cleanup. First it sorts items in descending order (max time === newest first), then resets cache timer, and then reinserts first half of the resulting array into new cache starting from the head of the list. So the most recent item in the old cache gets 0 time in a new cache, so it becomes the oldest. But in fact this is not important because we are not specifically interested in relative timing for items left in cache. Since this is exactly half of the cache, and after cleanup this is by definition the oldest half all of them. If none of them are touched they all together will be removed anyway. And if some of them are touched they will get updated time.

title: Significant VSCodeVim performance slowdowns tied to visible size of another extension's static TreeView
text: Significant VSCodeVim performance slowdowns tied to visible size of another extension's static TreeView. Type: Bug ## Summary When using VSCodeVim and holding down a remapped key (e.g. mapped to ), cursor performance can degrade significantly, with keystrokes lagging and bottling up, depending on how much of another extension's TreeView is visible. The visibility-dependent lag occurs even if the TreeView's contents are static (unchanging as the cursor moves) and its extension doesn't appear to be actively running any code, suggesting the root issue may lie in VSCode's handling of visible TreeViews rather than in either VSCodeVim or the TreeView-providing extension. ## Steps to Reproduce (Screen recordings provided below for extra clarity) 1. Install the [Vim]( extension and some other extension that provides a TreeView, e.g. [Region Helper]( or [JSON Tree View]( 2. Configure Vim to map to and to , via your VSCode settings: 3. If on a Mac, repro'ing may also require enabling key-repeating in VSCode [as described in VSCodeVim's README]( 4. Open a file that has enough contents for the chosen TreeView to fill its containing sidebar 5. Ensure the chosen TreeView is open and small in size, e.g. taking up only the bottom 1/8th of the primary sidebar 6. Hold or for a few seconds each and observe reasonable cursor-moving performance 7. Resize the TreeView to fill up most of the primary sidebar (collapsing other views as needed, e.g. the built-in Outline view) 8. Hold or for a few seconds each, and observe significant lag and bottling-up of keystrokes; the cursor continues moving many lines even after releasing the key 9. Move the TreeView to the secondary sidebar where it can populate the entire sidebar 10. Hold or for a few seconds each and observe even more lag and bottling up of keystrokes ## Screen recordings In this screen recording, Region Helper provides a TreeView ("Full Outline"). I release and start holding each time the cursor visually reaches . When the TreeView takes up most of the sidebar, you can see the cursor travels far past the goal point due to the lagged / bottled-up keystrokes. After expanding the built-in Outline view so that much less of the "Full Outline" TreeView is visible, the lag mostly disappears: In this next screen recording, JSON Tree View has been installed (and Region Helper has been uninstalled). Similarly here, I release and start holding each time the cursor visually reaches around the second mark. The lag is reduced when the built-in Outline is expanded and makes the JSON TreeView smaller. The lag then becomes most extreme when the TreeView is moved to completely fill the secondary sidebar: Note: this issue doesn't occur when holding down keys that haven't been remapped, e.g. and show no lag even with the TreeView at full-size: The fact that the lag only occurs with remapped keys is likely related to VSCodeVim's internals. But regardless of what VSCodeVim is doing under the hood, it seems unexpected for its performance to be affected simply by resizing another extension's TreeView, especially when the TreeView's contents are static and its extension isn't actively running any code (e.g. selection change event handlers). To corroborate this: I've confirmed that the issue persists even after I've removed all listeners from Region Helper's source code and repackaged/reinstalled the extension (with logs confirming no event handlers are running as the cursor moves). Likewise, examining the code for JSON Tree View, which seems to mainly consist of [ ]( and [ ]( I don't see any event handlers that could be the cause of the lagging here as the cursor moves. ## Concluding thoughts Apologies if this is a weird one to debug, or if it seems somewhat out of scope for VSCode itself, given that the repro I'm providing involves these extensions (Vim and a TreeView extension of your choice) and a specific config (the => Vim mapping and possibly Mac key repeat enabling). But, based on the nature of the bug itself, this seems much more like the root cause might lie in VSCode's infrastructure for extensions and/or [ s]( rather than in VSCodeVim or either of the example TreeView extensions. In the meantime, as a workaround I'll keep Region Helper's "Full Outline" view at a smaller size in the primary sidebar, although it'd be more useful at full size. I don't use JSON Tree View (I only installed it for debugging and demo purposes) so there's no issue there. Ideally though, any TreeView could be kept fully expanded without degrading the performance of other extensions like VSCodeVim. I'm not sure what else might be affected by this behavior, but I thought it might be particularly useful to flag it in case it does impact other extensions or VSCode features beyond this specific repro. Thanks so much for the awesome work on VSCode!

title: VSCode uses 10GB of RAM through git
text:
VSCode uses 10GB of RAM through git. Type: Bug I work on an extremely large monorepo repository that has about 1M refs, hundreds of thousands of files + directories, 1M+ commits, and takes about 20-40GB on disk depending on the size of compression used. Our users were reporting that was consuming up to 10-11GB of RAM multiple times per system. I was able to track this down to the invocation of which is invoked by VSCode every time you open a file. This is being invoked by the Timeline view in this function It turns out that git log -- is extremely performance sensitive on larger repos as it has to read in a ton of pack files into memory. We should find an alternative command to get this information, or disable the timeline automatically. We've had to disable the timeline sitewide for our company. title: VS Code event emitter performance improvements
text: VS Code event emitter performance improvements. In working on the remote tunnels SDK, now being used in part for the 'exec server', Martin suggested we publish an official event npm module. I already had a [small VS Code compatible]( module for use in my own code. I updated it to support the full set of EmitterOptions that we do in core, and out of curiosity compared it against the implementation in core. I suspect our usage of linked lists is responsible for the bulk of the performance delta: it's very nice a computer sciencey, but I think that we get dramatically punished by cache locality in practice. There is of course memory overhead for nodes as well. ![image]( I then gathered some [initial data]( on how we use events in vscode. I initially hypothesized we'd have a bimodal distribution between listeners with a small number of events, and ones with large number of events. In reality, it's much closer to a power-law distribution. The plurality of event emitters have no listeners at all, and second most common is a single listener. This data was collected after VS Code started up with an editor open: ![image]( We can also estimate how long was spent in the delivery mechanics during boot. This is the time to create the delivery queue, not call each individual function, so it slightly underestimates the actual time. From a heap snapshot, I manually tallied memory usage per for emitters, which comes to a total usage of about 335KB. Again, this is an underestimation. I believe the biggest benefit is an expected ~15ms improvement in startup time.

title: Experiment: PGO for desktop application
text: Experiment: PGO for desktop application. > From [Profile Guided Optimization]( > > Profile information enables better optimization. For example, knowing that a branch is taken very frequently helps the compiler make better decisions when ordering basic blocks. Knowing that a function foo is called more frequently than another function bar helps the inliner. Optimization levels -O2 and above are recommended for use of profile guided optimization. > > Clang supports profile guided optimization with two different kinds of profiling. A sampling profiler can generate a profile with very low runtime overhead, or you can build an instrumented version of the code that collects more detailed profile information. Both kinds of profiles can provide execution counts for instructions in the code and information on branches taken and function invocation. > > Regardless of which kind of profiling you use, be careful to collect profiles by running your code with inputs that are representative of the typical behavior. Code that is not exercised in the profile will be optimized as if it is unimportant, and the compiler may make poor optimization choices for code that is disproportionately used while profiling. Chromium build configuration has opt-in support for PGO The issue is to track the effort of optimizing the Electron runtime with PGO for VSCode. This will be a multi-step process and initially some manual steps are also involved, we will investigate automating the whole flow if the results are satisfying. For this experiment, we are using the instrumented version to collect the profile. Steps involved are as follows, ### Instrumentation Phase #### Building - [x] :runner: Create MS Electron builds with following additional build flags - [x] Create nightly exploration builds based on the above custom runtime build #### Running - [x] Get builds from corresponding to the branch **robo/explore_pgo** > **NB:** Builds from branch **robo/explore_pgo** will always reflect latest changes from , only difference is the instrumented runtime build, so it will not affect your everyday use. - [x] Selfhost on the build and perform your everyday tasks, at the end of every run files with extension will be generated in the user data directory under folder. - [x] :runner: At EOD, upload the generated files to channel > **NB:** There is no limit on the number of days to selfhost on this build during the experiment. Scheduled nightly updates will be available. ### Optimization Phase #### Building - [ ] Combine the files into using llvm-profdata script - [ ] Build MS Electron builds with generated using the following build flags - [ ] Test startup numbers and feed this build into the instrumentation phase until a stable range is obtained. - [ ] Ship optimized build to Insiders - [ ] Ship optimized build to Stable

title: Investigate why we are disposing of so many things on startup
text: Investigate why we are disposing of so many things on startup. When debugging, I noticed that ends up being called a lot while VS Code is starting up. This is suspicious because it suggests that we may be doing work that is either not needed or doing work that later needs to be re-done. There are valid reasons this can happen to, but I see around 2500 calls to our global function on startup with a single editor open (which does not track places where is called directly on an object) Here's some example code where this happens: This function is called twice on startup (even though the debug toolbar is not visible in the editor). This means that the work that the first call does is likely pointless, as the second call disposes of it and then does the work over again --- With some very basic profiling, I see 2500 calls to the global function on startup, which cumulatively take around 40ms. Of these, 1200 actually seem to dispose of something (this filters out the cases where is called on an empty array or empty iterable) Even though this is a small direct performance cost, this is still something interesting to investigate because: - The profiling above only measures the time spent in the implementations. It does not include the cost of computing the values that are then disposed off. I suspect this is more significant - Looking at these calls can be a good way to track down work that should be deferred. In the debug toolbar example above, it helped reveal that we're updating the debug toolbar on startup even though the debug toolbar is not visible

title: Optimize editor for input latency
text: Optimize editor for input latency. I recently did an exploration into input latency and found it can get pretty bad on slower machines. A lot of the problem is related to how we use synchronous event emitters/listeners work, performing their work after keypress but before the animation frame. ![image]( My proposal to improve is: 1. Review the most time consuming event listeners. If they are clearly safe to be performed at a later time without worrying about race conditions being introduced., move them to use an asynchronous event listener to be performed after the animation frame. For example UI updates like activity bar badge and tab indicator when an editor becomes dirty 2. Review all events and their listeners, defer as much as possible to after the animation frame. One way of doing this is for each important event to have both a sync and an async event. It's unclear how much we can move exactly, but when we do this we need to be extremely careful to not introduce text buffer-related race conditions as there are some assumptions made that we may be breaking by doing this 3. Setup development tools and/or telemetry to easily track measuring latency, I created to demonstrate a technique to approximate input latency 4. Come up with a plan for how we can prevent regressions for this critical path code Tentatively assigning to October

title: Monaco editor performance in virtualized list
text: Monaco editor performance in virtualized list. While looking into 's experiment with webgl in editor, we discussed how we can improve the scrolling performance of notebook as currently the monaco editor creation is not buttery smooth due to the fact that we are rendering multiple in a virtualized list view. For example, if we open and scroll up and down 1. Notebook cell list create M cell templates, each of which contains a monaco editor 2. Scroll down 3. The first visible cell gets disposed, the DOM and monaco editor for the first cell is not removed from the DOM tree, instead it will be reused 4. We reuse the first cell's template, set a new text model from the cell scrolled into view to the monaco editor 5. Step 2-4 repeats Even though we already try to reuse the monaco editor, since we are calling each time, the editor actually will create a view from scratch again. It includes checking bounding rects, validation positions etc, and trigger browser's recalculate styles and layout

title: Unusable due to slow startup. Fresh install win 32, no extensions, startup > 10 Minutes!
text: Unusable due to slow startup. Fresh install win 32, no extensions, startup > 10 Minutes!. - VSCode Version: 1.13 - OS Version: Windows 7 32 bit NOTE: I also have Visual studio 2012 installed on this computer and it's running in a virtual machine. Visual studio 2012 opens within seconds, there is almost no noticeable delay running in this fast virtual machine. Steps to Reproduce: 1. Download and install VS code on Windows 7 32 bit 2. Runs fast first time after installation and opens up to the welcome screen 3. Close, go to command prompt and run again Code --disable-extensions 4. Nothing happens, open task manager and it's showing Code.exe and cpu is pegged at 99% 5. Start a stopwatch, wait 10 minutes cpu varies between 99% and rarely dips to 97%. 6. Give up. No visible Code editor onscreen anywhere, just the task manager process is the only evidence it's doing anything; stop the process. I left it to start one time as I had to go out, came back about half an hour later and it was opened so at some point it *does* actually complete the startup but I have no idea how long it took. Same thing happens when I run it without disabling extensions by the way and I've tried it through several reboots uninstalls etc. Reproduces without extensions: Yes I've used Code on Linux previously (64bit Debian in virtual machine on same host computer) and it runs very fast and is very useful, however I wanted to consolidate all my work to my windows dev machine and ran into this issue. This is a clean install, I'm guessing my difference from others may be that I have vs 2012 installed already? Only thing I can think of that might have some possibility of interfering with it.

title: [Discussion] Enforce workbench contributions before their lifecycle phase
text: [Discussion] Enforce workbench contributions before their lifecycle phase. During verification I saw and it raises an interesting challenge. Workbench contributions are registered for a [lifecycle phase]( at which they are instantiated. For the sake of performance we are interested in having very few contributions during early phases (so that they don't compete with editor opening). The recommendation is to use or and we are very good at sticking to this rule. However, workbench contributions are rarely self-contained. For instance, we often have commands to the side ( ). Those are typically registered statically but depend on what the contribution contributes. This means an action can be invoked _before_ its "partner-contribution" is ready. To tackle this you can * only register actions when the contribution is registered (which can lead to UI flashes and non-working commands) * register contribution for a very early phase (which is correct but not great for perf) Another alternative is to let actions wait for the lifecycle phase of their "partner-contribution" (via ). Tho, that can be frustrating for users (extra waiting) and seems like code smell (spread the phase knowledge). A better alternative might be to ask the workbench to ensure the contribution is now ready. That would force-instantiate it and remove it from lifecycle-phase based instantiation. The code editor does something similar (it took inspiration from lifecycle phases but took this much further, see [EditorContributionInstantiation]( and it might be time to bring those learnings into the workbench. One difference tho is that workbench contributions often only cause side effects, e.g the presence of an editor type which isn't the contribution itself. It might be enough to begin with ). That function would simply ensure a contribution is loaded (instantiate it unless already done). With that we can add an equivalent to [EditorContributionInstantiation#Lazy]( - meaning some workbench contributions are _never_ initialised unless used. Many contributions from the -phase are likely candidates for this

title: Make welcome editors open instantly
text: Make welcome editors open instantly. This is not 100% a startup perf issue but I like to see this as a perceived UX perf issue: ![Recording 2023-06-09 at 06 32 08]( It is also not a regression but something that has always been there: the setting is configured by default to be . However you notice that VS Code first shows the empty editor area with out watermark only then to switch to the welcome page. This is because initially the code to open the welcome page is not loaded and only kicks in a bit later. I think we should show the welcome page right from the beginning. This would require us to return a resolvable untyped editor input (those just have a ) here: For example here we do it when is configured to be untitled file: knows all about editor resolvers so he could probably assist how to make the welcome editor a untyped editor input that can be resolved. Arguably such a dependency of to the welcome page is a bit of a layer break because the welcome page comes from the folder, but I would make an exception here since this is the default experience for all new users.

title: Provide an API from to schedule work when window is busy starting up
text: Provide an API from to schedule work when window is busy starting up. Today we schedule a large amount of work right after the call for a assuming that we can schedule work parallel to the window opening. But as I learned today, there is no guarantee that the can do its business independent from the main process. It is actually very likely that we do work and block the main process while the window wants something from the main process. Ideally electron could provide an API or event that can signal us in the main process that now is a good time to work on something without impacting the loading of the window. ![Screenshot 2022-08-31 at 09 49 15]( Refs: //cc

title: Make eager service registration explicit and revisit existing one
text: Make eager service registration explicit and revisit existing one. The [ ]( supports a -argument. With [ ]( only proxies of services are injected and the actual instantiation happens in "slack/idle" time or at time of first actual use (whatever comes first). This is often overlooked and the default ( , eager) is used. This issue is about: * revisit existing eager usages and check if they can support delayed instantiation. This is the _preferred_ way, helps startup performance 🐎 , and is usually possible * make the eager variant explicit, use , and feel a little bad about it 😳 _Note_ that should only be needed if your service is doing something "by its own", like reading files or so, which is vital to other parts of the system. This should be the exception because most services offer something (a service) to others which means can be delayed until needed

title: Revisit introduction of
text: Revisit introduction of. It looks like recently a was added to signal whether a user data dir is in use or not ( I see numerous issues with that: * writing a file on startup slows down startup, especially if the process has to wait for that to happen. We typically only tolerate this when there is very strong need for it and try to avoid this at all costs (cc ). It seems here we only add the log file for the debug case for debugging VSCode, but every user now will pay the price of slower startup even when not debugging VSCode. * dealing with files as a means to lock a folder is complicated. you cannot assume that [ ]( is ever called, the application might crash leaving a stale lock file around (cc who just implemented a locking solution that avoids these kind of issues for the extension host state process via I don't really understand why the existing IPC socket cannot be used to figure out if an instance is running? The IPC handle is statically computed based on some properties that can all be determined by reading and or : I hope we can find a different solution for this.

title: Do not wait for shell environment resolution before opening window
text: Do not wait for shell environment resolution before opening window. Details: **Today:** The workbench depends on user env to be resolved. Resolving user env envolves spawning a shell and executing the user's init scripts. This can take long. **Ideally:** The user env is only required for specific features: opening terminals, spawning tasks, spawning extension host. Until it's resolved, many other features should actually work, ie explorer, editor, etc. Related: - - - - ### Adoption I made a pass over usages of process environment by looking at: * direct use of * usages of * clients of that spawn child processes Assigning people based on areas and usages. title: Startup performance regression during June
text: Startup performance regression during June. The windows perf bot shows a slight regression during the June iteration. For instance version is fastest 1862ms whereas version is faster with 1666ms. There is surely some 10% fluctuation but there might be more to it. I have measured both versions by hand and code loading shows a slight slowdown (~50ms) tho code size our increased a little (~50kb). One theory is that we now load all "init scripts" via script tags and not via nodejs anymore and the network-tag shows some request stalling. We should investigate and understand that while we also drill into other potential causes.

title: Avoid sync fs-calls in backupMainService
text: Avoid sync fs-calls in backupMainService. The runs synchronous fs-operations on start up. Worst the amount of sync-operations doesn't seem to have an upper bound but perf depends on the number and size of dirty files. All other startup-operations, like establishing IPC channels or setting up telemetry etc, have to wait for this which is bad. Instead, the backup-service should perform async fs operations, and waiting should happen as late as possible, e.g. *before* showing the window but *after* running other startup-tasks.

title: ## [Performance] Prevent OOM crashes by implementing LRU garbage collection in AsyncDataTree
text: ## [Performance] Prevent OOM crashes by implementing LRU garbage collection in AsyncDataTree. ### The Problem When opening massive workspaces (e.g., mono-repos with 500k+ files) or returning massive search results, expanding the Explorer tree causes the to materialize hundreds of thousands of nodes in memory. Even though the DOM is virtualized via , the in-memory metadata for these nodes scales linearly. Eventually, the browser engine exhausts its memory limit and the renderer crashes (**OOM**). ### The Solution Implement an **LRU (Least Recently Used) cache** and aggressive garbage collection mechanism within . When the total number of materialized nodes exceeds a safe threshold (e.g., 50,000), nodes that are not currently visible in the viewport and haven't been accessed recently should be: - Automatically collapsed - Garbage collected from memory This ensures scalability and prevents renderer crashes.

Create a virtual with horizontal scrolling enabled and enough rows to fill the viewport. 2. Insert rows or scroll to render a new range. Each row is currently measured as a separate write, width/computed-style read, and width reset. Because the next row repeats the write/read sequence, rendering N rows can force up to N layouts. Width measurements should instead batch all writes, then all reads, then all resets while retaining each row's own padding and style.
